en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Jagadambā. Now begins the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* within the *Āvantya-khaṇḍa*. Vyāsa said: May that Blessed One named Śrī Mahākāla be victorious—the primordial god of the worlds, whom even the creators of beings bow down to out of intense fear of worldly existence; he who has entered the unmanifest, for those whose minds are disciplined and whose souls are absorbed in meditation, and who bears a manifest *liṅga*, a skull, the crescent moon, and the circle of the earth.
Umā said: "Let those holy places on earth and the sacred rivers that are celebrated be described with effort, so that faith may arise toward them. (2)
Īśvara said: There is in the worlds the river Gaṅgā, renowned as the one who flows through the three paths; she is served by gods and gandharvas and frequented by sages.
The goddess Yamunā, daughter of Tapaṇa, is the purifier of the world; she is the beloved of the ancestors and the destroyer of great sins.
The Candrabhāgā, the Vitastā, and the Narmadā at Amarakaṇṭaka; Kurukṣetra, Gayā, O Goddess, as well as Prabhāsa and Naimiṣa.
Kedāra and Puṣkara, as well as Kāyāvarohaṇa, and likewise the most meritorious and auspicious Mahākālavana, O Goddess. (6)
There dwells the illustrious Mahākāla, the fire that consumes the fuel of sin; his sacred field extends for a yojana and destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

O Goddess, this sacred field bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it destroys the impurities of the Kali age and remains imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution, though it is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Umā said: "O Lord Maheśvara, let the power of this sacred field be told; indeed, let it be known what holy fords (tīrthas) exist there and what lingas are present."
I desire to hear them, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Mahādeva said: Listen with diligence, O Goddess, to the power that destroys sin; it is the primordial sacred field, O Great Goddess, which annihilates all evils.
And in the vicinity of Śrīmeru, there was a peak marked by jewels, an abode of many wonders, crowded with numerous trees.
Variegated with diverse elements, it possessed a pedestal of clear crystal; it was enriched with the splendor of various colors and resounded with the voices of throngs of sages.
It was filled with lordly deer and elephants, crowded with herds of wild tuskers, and thick with the spray arising from the falling waters of mountain torrents.
The groves of trees, struck by the wind, were strewn with blossoms that adorned the ground, while the entire forest was perfumed with the exquisite fragrance of musk.
It was a place of delight within a bower of creepers, a refuge for perfected beings and vidyādharas, resounding with the sweet melodies of flocks of skilled kinnaras.
In that most delightful forest, there is the abode named Vairāja belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, which adorns the entire ground.
There, it resounded with the sweet melodies sung by celestial women, and was adorned with garlands of blossoms from the branches of the Pārijāta trees.
It resounded with the great, swelling noise of many instruments, accompanied by rhythmic timing and tempo, and filled with the sounds of numerous songs and musical performances. || 19 ||
It was laid out with millions of pillars, adorned with spotless mirrors, endowed with various rhythms and tempos, and filled with many great wonders.
Adorned by the playful splendor of the dance-arrangements of the Apsarases, that assembly hall, named Kāntimatī, brings joy to the gods.
It was crowded with throngs of sages, frequented by multitudes of ascetics, resounded with the Vedic chants of the twice-born, and bestowing bliss.
Seated there was the Lord of Speech, Sanatkumāra, a celestial sage born from the mind of Brahmā, who was devoted to the worship of Śaṅkara.
Rising from among the sages, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, prostrated himself according to the prescribed rite.
With palms joined in reverence, moved by devotion to Bhava, and with his body and face bristling with joy, he questioned him with supreme satisfaction.
The majesty of Mahākāla destroys the delusion of living beings. Vyāsa said: Why is the forest of Mahākāla called the best of all?
"O Blessed One, let the majesty of the field of Mahākāla be told; how is it that Guhyavana is proclaimed, as well as Ūṣara, to be a sacred seat (pīṭha)? (27)
The fruit for those dwelling here, as well as the destiny of those who have died, the merit that arises from bathing, and also the fruit of giving—[all this shall be told]. (28)

"How is it that this cremation ground is said to be a sacred field (kṣetra) in such a manner? I have asked this with devotion to Śaṅkara; please explain it, O you who are skilled in the scriptures. (29)
Sanatkumāra said: Because sin is destroyed there, it is called a *kṣetra*; and because it is the station of the Mothers, it is likewise called a *pīṭha*.
Those who have died there are not born again; therefore, this is known as Ūṣara. This is the secret, eternally beloved field of the great-souled Śambhu. (31)
For the cremation ground is indeed highly desired by living beings, as are Mahākālavana and likewise Avimuktika.
Ekāmraka, Bhadrakāla, and Karavīravana, as well as Kolāgiri, Kāśī, Prayāga, and Amareśvara. (33)
Bharatha, Kedāra, and the divine Rudramahālaya—these are the divine cremation grounds that are eternally dear to Rudra.
The Blessed One always delights in these fields of perfection; on earth, Naimiṣa is the supreme sacred ford, as is Puṣkara among sacred fords. (35)
Kurukṣetra is praised as the most excellent among all three worlds; Vārāṇasī is considered ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra.
O Vyāsa, Mahākālavana is ten times superior to that; indeed, whatever holy places (tīrthas) exist here on earth, beginning with Prabhāsa, [are all surpassed by it].
Prabhāsa is the supreme sacred ford, the primordial field of the wielder of the Pināka bow; likewise, Śrīśaila is an excellent sacred ford, as is the Devadāru forest.
Therefore, O Vyāsa, Vārāṇasī is considered even more excellent; for it is declared to be ten times superior to that, as it is the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas). (39)
The Mahākālavana is a secret siddha-field, as is Ūṣara; there are also other somewhat secret cremation grounds and saline wastes.
O Sage, Mahākālavana is proclaimed to be everything: it is a cremation ground, a saline wasteland, a sacred field, a pīṭha, and indeed a forest. (41)
These five are not found together in any place except for the city of Mahākāla.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of Mahākālavana," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth section (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sanatkumāra said: Formerly, when the single ocean had come into being and all things mobile and immobile had perished, there was neither fire, nor wind, nor sun, nor earth, nor the quarters, nor the sky.
There were no stars, no luminaries, no sky, no moon, nor likewise any planets; there were no gods, asuras, or gandharvas, nor piśācas, uragas, or rākṣasas.
Neither lakes, nor mountains, nor rivers, nor oceans existed; everything was enveloped in darkness, and nothing at all could be discerned.
Then the Lord Mahākāla alone, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds, remained surveying all places without exception in every direction.
For the sake of creation, that Mahākāla took Kāma, who was established in his hand, and churned him with the index finger of his right hand until he was dried up.
The *kalala* having become a bubble, and that having been increased by its own momentum, there then arose an exceedingly firm, perfectly round, golden egg.
Struck by his hand, that great [egg] indeed split into two halves; the lower portion became remembered as the earth, and the upper portion, along with the stars, became the sky.
Then, in the midst [of the waters], Brahmā appeared with five faces and four arms; Maheśvara, having honored him, immediately joined him [to his own body].
"O mighty-armed one, perform a diverse creation through my grace. Having spoken thus, the god Brahmā vanished somewhere and did not return.
Though being impelled to create, Brahmā meditated upon the God; and as he was being meditated upon by Brahmā for the sake of knowledge, the Blessed Lord Bhava appeared.

Having been perceived through the austerity of Brahmā, he bestowed the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Even though the Veda was obtained, he was not able to perform the creation for long.
He remained engaged in asceticism even more intensely in order to propitiate Bhava; when he did not see the god, he then offered praise with a purified heart.

Brahmā said: Salutations to Śiva, whose consciousness is of pure sattva, whose expansive splendor transcends the three qualities (guṇas), who is the creator even of me, the author of the six-limbed Veda, and whose eye is the experience of the supreme nature.

Salutations to you who delight in *rajas* during the act of creation; to you who preside over *sattva* for the maintenance of the world; to you who are exalted by *tamas* as the cause of dissolution; to Śiva, the bestower of the bliss of liberation.

Salutations indeed to Śiva, who is beyond the primordial nature of all beings without exception, whose form is the supreme Self; salutations to Him who ordains the intellect, ego, and mind of men, and who is the sustainer in the form of the twenty-sixth principle.
Salutations to Him who pervades this world with these bodies—earth, water, fire, ether, wind, moon, sun, and the self—and who is the past, the future, and the present. 16.
I bow to Him in whose Self all the splendors that exist here, all beings past and future, and all causes, come into being at creation and undergo dissolution at destruction.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, as Brahmā was thus offering praise, the Supreme Lord vanished and spoke these words: "O Brahmā, let a boon be requested."
Out of respect for Bhava, he mentally chose him as his son; perceiving what was in his heart, the Supreme Lord spoke to him.
"O Four-faced One, since you desire me as your son in your mind for some reason or other, therefore I shall cut off your head. (20)
"Since you have asked for that which should not be asked for, my portion shall be Nīlalohita; he will become your son, Rudra, and he will indeed destroy your splendor."
Because you have remembered me with devotion as your father, and because you have undertaken the inquiry into my nature as the Supreme Brahman. (22)
Therefore, the name "Brahmā" shall become renowned here in this world; because you are the grandfather [of all], you are thus indeed the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
Having thus obtained the two excellent boons, he undertook the procreation of sons; as he offered oblations into the fire produced from his own vital energy, sweat broke out upon him.
As he wiped his forehead with a hand holding the sacrificial fuel, a single drop of blood, perspiring and fallen, then fell into the fire. || 25 ||
By the command of Bhava, he indeed became Nīlalohita and Rudra; immediately thereafter, having approached, the son emerged from his presence.
He has five faces and ten arms, wielding a trident, a bow, a sword, and a spear; he has fifteen eyes, is fierce, and wears a serpent as his sacred thread.
Wearing matted hair and clad in a lion’s skin, Brahmā, seeing him thus born, then gave him a name.
"O Bhava, O Rudra, wielder of the Pināka bow, you shall be named Nīlalohita. Thereafter, creation proceeded from the Creator, the Grandfather of the worlds.
First, he begot from his mind the seven [sages] beginning with Sanaka, and thereafter others—Marīci, Dakṣa, and the rest, as well as Manu and the other progenitors of beings.
Having divided the gods into eight classes and the animal kingdom into five, he likewise created humans with their many varieties; thus indeed did he bring forth creation.
Having brought about the creation beginning with the gods and even placing Brahmā beneath them, they then bowed and served Nīlalohita alone.
Then Brahmā said to Rudra: "Indeed, you have been rendered unworthy of worship by yourself; since you are worthy of worship through your own splendor, go therefore to Himālaya."
Nīlalohita said to him, "Indeed, I have not been worshipped by you. Thereupon, that Rudra went to where the Blessed Lord Bhava was.
Then Brahmā became deluded, augmented by the quality of passion (rajas); he scorched the creation with his splendor, thinking it had been created by me.
Indeed, there is no god equal to me, by whom this creation—filled with gods, asuras, and gandharvas, and teeming with beasts, birds, and wild animals—was brought forth and expanded. (36)
Thus that deluded five-faced one became arrogant and was born as Virañci; his eastern face possessed a beautiful voice and was the originator of the Sāmaveda.
His second face was the originator of the Ṛgveda; another bore the Yajurveda, and the fourth was named Atharvaveda.
He studies with his mouth—the fifth eye—the Vedas along with their limbs, sub-limbs, histories, secret doctrines, and compendiums.
All those Asuras and Suras could not shine by the splendor of that mouth of wondrous luster, just as a lamp does not shine at the rising of the sun.
Even with their sons, they became agitated and lost their composure; they were unable to approach, nor could they look upon that splendor for long, as it receded from them.
Considering themselves as if already conquered, yet free from hatred, all those gods consulted together for their own welfare.
"Let us go for refuge to the god who has been deprived of his splendor by the power of Brahman; however, we do not know his location, where he resides. (43)

"We shall behold that Bhīma here through devotion alone, and by no other means. Having thus deliberated, those gods then, with palms joined in reverence, offered a hymn of praise to Maheśa with supreme excellence of voice.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; O Maheśvara, salutations, salutations! (45)
O deluded ones, we do not know your supreme and incomparable greatness, through whose yoga you are the eternal Supreme Brahman of all beings. 46.
You are the foundation of all beings and the cause for the creation of everything; you indeed sustain the Moon, the Sun, and Fire situated within your eyes.
Merely by the chanting of his name, living beings—characterized as earth, water, fire, moon, sun, ether, wind, and stone—are liberated from inauspiciousness.
O Mahādeva, these forms of yours pervade everything without exception; by you the world is set in motion through the states of rajas, sattva, and tamas.

Since you, the Lord of All, who assume every form, do not perceive [this], you bring about the enchantment and dis-enchantment of Brahmā and the other lords of the gods at the time of the turning of the Yugas, which is difficult to endure at that time. (50)
Sanatkumāra said: Having granted a direct vision out of compassion for the gods, he became gracious of countenance and was saluted by the gods as well.
Maheśvara, together with the gods, dwelt there under the name Moha.
Being thus praised by the celestial sages, ancestors, and humans, he vanished and said this: "O gods, speak what you desire."
The gods said: "O Sthāṇu, we always pray for the direct vision of you; and by your compassion, let a boon also be granted to us. (54)
Whatever great vigor, splendor, and prowess we possessed, all of that has been swallowed up by the splendor of the five-faced one’s [Brahmā]. || 55 ||
"O Lord, by your grace all splendors have returned; O Maheśvara, act so that everything may become as it was before. (56)

Sanatkumāra said: Having indeed appeared before his very eyes, Śarva then departed; he went to that place where he [the other] was, embodied as passion and egoism. The gods, praising the Lord of Gods, sat down surrounding him.
Enveloped by darkness, Brahmā did not recognize that god who had arrived, illuminating the world with the splendor of thousands of millions of suns.
Then the Soul of the Universe, the Creator of the Universe, the Source of the Universe, was seen by us seated amidst the entire circle of gods as the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 59 ||
Overpowering him with his splendor, Rudra stood before me; and the face of Brahmā, overwhelmed by Rudra’s splendor, did not shine.
Just as the moon, which emits illuminating rays at night, [fades] at the rising of the sun, so too, upon seeing his son Rudradeva, the eternal one, he became filled with pride.
He saluted him with his very hand and spoke these words with a smile; Virūpākṣa replied to that Brahmā as if laughing.
Since he did not know the Supreme God, being enveloped by His splendor, the Blessed One, whose crest is the moon, then let out a loud laugh.
While all the gods were looking on and listening, he spoke these words; by that sound of loud laughter, he deluded the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Resembling a mass of splendor and the moon, with eyes like the moon, the sun, and fire, he [severed] the fifth head of Brahmā with the tip of his left big toe.
He cut it like a man cutting the core of a plantain tree with his fingernails; and as that mouth was being severed, the Grandfather did not perceive it.
Because he had not bowed down, he was spared from Rudra’s fiery splendor; subsequently, his severed head remained in the hand of Rudra at that time.
Together with the gods, he beheld the fierce [Rudra] blazing with extreme dread; his face shone with the nails situated upon the hand of Maheśvara.
Standing in the midst of the circle of planets like a second moon, the Moon-crested Lord, lifting up that skull, danced.
When his face was severed, like Mount Kailāsa by the sun situated upon its peak, the gods, joyful and refreshed, praised the bull-bannered Lord of Gods, the skull-bearer, with various hymns. (70)
The gods said: "Salutations eternally to the skull-bearer, to Mahākāla, who holds the conch. (71)
Salutations to the one endowed with sovereignty and knowledge, the bestower of all enjoyments, the destroyer of pride, and the embodiment of all the gods. 72.
You are the agent of the dissolution of time; therefore, you are indeed Mahākāla. You are the pacifier of the suffering of devotees and the end of suffering; for that reason, you are pleasing.

Śaṅkara also quickly became a benefactor (śaṃkara) to his devotees by that act; therefore you are remembered as Śaṃkara. Furthermore, because you severed the head of Brahmā and carry his skull-cup (kapāla), [you are so called].
"Therefore, O Lord, you have been praised as Kapālī; be gracious to us. Thus praised, Śaṅkara, with a pleased soul, raised the gods up.

That Blessed One, the ocean of compassion, vanished right there. Victorious is he who stands at the side of Rudra—holding a skull, adorned with a garland, possessing abundant splendor, and having conquered the Creator—wherein his matted locks are illuminated by the rays of the crescent moon, and where the waves of the celestial Gaṅgā flowing through the sky seem to dissolve.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, his face having been cut off, Brahmā, enveloped by the darkness of anger, took the sweat that had arisen on his forehead and struck it against the ground.
From his sweat was born Kuṇḍalī, a hero equipped with a bow and a great quiver, clad in a thousand pieces of armor; he said, "What shall I do? || 2 ||
Virañci, displaying Rudra through his own power, said to him: "Let this evil-minded one be slain, so that he may not be born again."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, he raised his bow and set out behind Maheśa, arrow in hand and filled with intense rage.
Having seen that fierce man, with a divine arrow and bow in hand, moving with swift and powerful strides, Bhava was struck with wonder and approached him.
"This exceedingly powerful one must not be slain by me; he shall become a friend of Viṣṇu. Indeed, I am to be favored by him for the sake of our friendship, as I remain established in penance. (6)
Reflecting thus, O Brahmin, even the Lord went to the hermitage of Viṣṇu; then, having deluded Nara with the sound of a "hum" cry, he [proceeded].
Having cast him down, he was then delighted, performing his sport for the maintenance of the world, at the place where the glorious and powerful Nārāyaṇa performed penance.
Invisible to all beings, the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, and the omnipresent Lord—Virūpākṣa, having arrived there, beheld Madhusūdana.
Standing on the ground on a single big toe, his asceticism was utterly unwavering; he was surrounded by a wondrous radiance like that of a thousand suns at the end of an eon.
Having beheld the ancient Puruṣottama, the god Nārāyaṇa, who was endowed with a stream of merit, he said, "Give me alms."
Having displayed before him a skull blazing with fierce fire, Viṣṇu, beholding Rudra with a skull in his hand, reflected: || 12 ||
"Who else would be a suitable recipient for this gift of alms at this time? Thinking, 'He is worthy,' he offered his right arm. (13)
The moon-crested Lord, who knows what lies within, pierced him with his trident; thereupon, a stream of blood issued from the arm of the powerful one.
Resembling the color of Jāmbūnada gold and pure like a flame of fire, it issued forth from the edge of the skull-cup and was received by Śambhu.
Straight, swift, and shimmering like the rays of the sun in the sky, it is fifty yojanas long and ten yojanas in width.
She bore the arm of Hari for a thousand divine years; for how long a time did the Lord, being thus inspired, accept alms?
Then, having been given by Nārāyaṇa to that excellent and worthy recipient, Nārāyaṇa spoke these supreme words to Hara: || 18 ||
"Indeed, your vessel is full. Then, hearing these words of Hari, which resounded like a water-laden cloud, Hara, the Supreme Lord, [spoke].
With the moon, sun, and fire as his eyes, adorned by the moon upon his crest, he fixed his gaze upon Janārdana within the skull with his three eyes.
Tapping with his finger, he said that the skull was overflowing; hearing these words, Hari drew back the stream of blood.
Then, from the side of Hari, Īśa indeed churned his own blood with his finger for a thousand divine years while maintaining his gaze upon me.
Then, as it was being churned, blood arose; from that, in due course, there appeared the *kalala* and the *budbuda*. Thereafter, he emerged, wearing a crown and holding a bow.
With a thousand arms and red eyes, repeatedly touching the bowstring, he had a quiver around his neck, shoulders like a bull's, and wore finger-guards.
A man resembling Arjuna appeared, illuminating the skull; seeing him, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these words to Rudra: || 25 ||
"O Blessed One, who is this man who has appeared in the skull? Having heard these words of Hari, the Lord said to him: "O Hari, listen."
"He shall be named Nara, a man who is the best among those skilled in supreme weapons; because you called him 'Nara,' he shall therefore become Nara. (27)
And both Nara and Nārāyaṇa will become renowned in this age for their deeds in battle, for the service of the gods, and for the protection of the worlds. (28)
This Nara, the friend of Nārāyaṇa, shall be your companion in battle against you who are alone, O great sage of asceticism. (29)
For the sake of examining consciousness, there shall be light in the world; this divine fifth head of Brahmā is preeminent in its radiance. (30)
Blazing with the splendor of Brahmā, from the blood of your arm, and from the fall of my gaze—these are the three splendors from which [the fire] arises. (31)
Born from that union, he will terrify your enemies—those who would otherwise be unslayable, as well as others who are difficult for you to conquer.
He was terrifying even to Śakra and the enemies of the immortals; thus spoke Śambhu, while [the listener] was struck with wonder by his splendor.
Hari also, right there, offered praise to Hara and Keśava: "Obeisance to you, O Hara and Hari; obeisance to Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu."
Salutations to you who hold a trident in your hand; salutations to you who carry a sword in your hand. Salutations again and again to you, the pure one; O Hṛṣīkeśa, let there be salutations to you.
"Salutation be to the Lord of Speech; salutations again and again to Śrīdhara. To that man who was thus praising him with devotion and with palms joined in reverence, [he spoke]. (36)
Having likewise quickly grasped his two hands joined in añjali and raised him up from the skull, he then spoke these words again: || 37 ||
That very person who was fierce and born from the sweat of Brahmā has fallen into a stupor of sleep by the sound of my *huṃ* syllable.
"Understand that [instruction] quickly," saying this, Hara vanished after having swiftly enlightened Nārāyaṇa in his very presence.
Striking with his left foot, the man rose up in fury; a great battle then ensued between those two who were dripping with sweat and blood.
The entire surface of the earth resounded with the sounds of his drawn bow; he [wore] the single armor of that born of sweat, as well as the two arms of that born of blood.
Thus, O twice-born one, that divine battle was fought on the surface of the earth with perfect fairness for nine hundred years.
O Sage, as the two born of sweat and the one born of blood were fighting, the one born of blood, seeing the one born of sweat clad in a single armor, became two-armed.
With the force of his arrow, Madhusūdana pierced that supreme man of Brahmā; then, with agitation, he spoke these words to Brahmā.
"O Brahman, your man-made dust-heap has been struck down. Hearing this, Brahmā became distressed and spoke to Madhusūdana: || 45 ||
"If my man is lost in another birth, Hari himself, being pleased, will speak thus: 'It shall be so. (46)
Having caused their battle to cease, he spoke to them both: "In another birth, this man shall become mine during the Kali age."
Then, when that great battle had arisen, I summoned Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Sureśvara there and joined them together.

"These two men, Rudra and Pālana, have been described; they are to be protected by you according to your power. However, those born from sweat and those born from blood are portions of yourself upon the surface of the earth; having become your own portions at the end of the Dvāpara age, they are to be appointed by you to the world. (49)
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke these sorrowful words to Viṣṇu.
O Lord, in this Manvantara, during that Tretā Yuga, the mighty-armed one named Vālin was struck down here in your great form for the sake of Sugrīva, seeking his welfare. (51)
"Tormented by that suffering, I will not accept your man. Since the Lord of Gods does not accept him, he must be speaking for some other reason. (52)
Viṣṇu said: "O Maghavan, O Lord, for the sake of relieving the burden of the earth, I too shall take an incarnation in the world of mortals. (53)
Then Śakra indeed became delighted by those words of Viṣṇu; having accepted Nara with joy, he said, "May your word come true."
Having spoken thus, and having sent back both the Sun and the Moon, the lotus-eyed one went to Brahmā in the abode of Brahmā.
O Brahman, a loathsome deed has been committed by you, who desired to kill the Lord, in that you addressed the Supreme Person with anger, O Lord of the God of Gods. (56)
For the sake of purifying this sin, O Brahmin, perform the supreme expiation; taking up the three fires, attend to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
"Let there be one Gārhapatya fire, the second the Āhavanīya, and the third the Dakṣiṇāgni; thus arrange them within the three sacrificial pits. (58)
One should satisfy oneself in a circle, me in the shape of a bow, and the god Hara in a quadrangle by means of the names of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having offered oblations into the fire and worshipped Hara alone through austerity, you shall attain perfection after offering oblations into the fire for a thousand divine years.
Having approached Maheśvara with a soul purified by expiation, you will then become free from stain, and your grief will depart.
Having spoken thus, the high-souled Hari of fierce splendor departed for his own abode; Brahmā, too, fixing his mind on asceticism, then undertook everything as instructed by Acyuta.
Vyāsa said: That archer named Nara who was born from the skull—was he likewise born now at the creation of Viśvakarman?
How was he produced intentionally by the Lord Rudra, or by the Blessed Viṣṇu, or by Brahmā, according to the distinction of their respective dispositions? || 2 ||
By whom and from what was he produced—Śaṅkara, Acyuta, and Brahmā? Who is this Hiraṇyagarbha Brahmā who was born with four faces? (3)
How did his fifth, wondrous face also manifest? How did the Lord Brahmā remain there and fix his mind upon Rudra?
By that deluded soul, this man was dispatched to slay Hara.
Sanatkumāra said: O Satī, Maheśvara and Hari—these two alone remain; there is nothing unknown to those two high-souled ones, whether it be accomplished or unaccomplished.
That fire which was the fifth mouth of the high-souled Brahmā was indeed borne upon his head by that very mind-born son.
The man who is declared to be Brahmā—that Agni was his mental son; Mahādeva held him within the space between his fingers.
Having previously observed its origin in this manner, that great man then produced a skull by rubbing it against his finger. (9)

By means of divine qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, known by names like the supernatural powers of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*), which arise from her disheveled hair, girdle, fangs, and the clashing of her teeth.
With the fierce faces of tigers and serpents, as well as those of crows, herons, and cranes.
With formless bodies, with equal forms, with beautiful forms, and with many forms; with one, two, or three heads, with many heads, or even headless. || 34 ||
They were adorned with one, two, or three crests, shining in various forms; some had many eyes while others were eyeless, and some had one, two, or three eyes.
With one ear, two ears, many ears, or no ears at all; with one, two, three, or many nostrils, or being entirely noseless. (36)
With those having one leg, two legs, many legs, and no legs at all; with those having one foot, two feet, many feet, and no feet.
Some were fair and dark, some dark and fair, some black, and others variegated; they wore serpent necklaces and bracelets, and had fashioned their sacred threads from serpents.
[They were] bearing spears, swords, and battle-axes, with *bhuśuṇḍī* and *pragha* weapons; their hands held discuses, saws, bows, arrows, staffs, and missiles. (39)
With maces, clubs, stones, and pestles as their weapons in hand, they bore thunderbolts, spears, lightning-bolts, darts, lances, and daggers.
They sounded bhaṃbhas and bherīs, as well as vīṇās, paṇavas, and flutes; mṛdaṅgas, vimalas, āḍhakkas, kāhalās, naka-dundubhis, and drums.
Various musical instruments such as the huḍaṅka and śṛṅgika were played by musicians; thus, there were many kinds of fierce, terrifying, and formidable-spirited beings. || 42 ||

Surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, who are exceedingly difficult to overcome—like the sun surrounded by the planets—the Great God appeared, encircled by his own attendants. Behold him then, O Vyāsa, as well as those dwellers of heaven, Brahmā and the others.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, seeing the Lord of the Gaṇas before them, became bewildered in mind, overwhelmed by his splendor.
Then, summoning their fortitude and beholding the God according to the prescribed rite, they—possessing bodies with uplifted hearts—performed the yoga of the six-limbed Veda. || 45 ||
With their hands joined in *añjali* at their heads and their feet touching the earth, they praised the Lord, the creator of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the world.
The gods said: Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, together with his attendants and Nandin; salutations to you, who are seated upon a bull, who are gentle, and who bear the trident and the spear.
Homage to the one whose garment is the quarters of space, to the pure one, to the one of intense splendor; to Brahman, whose body is Brahman, and who is united with Brahman.
Salutations to the destroyer of Andhaka, salutations again and again to the Supreme Lord; salutations to Rudra, the five-faced one, who removes all diseases.
Salutations again and again to Giriśa, the Lord of the gods, the Sovereign; salutations again and again to Vijaya, whose nature is both terrible and fierce. || 50 ||
Salutation to the lord of the Suras and Asuras, the lord of ascetics; salutation to Caṇḍa, who wields a fierce staff and holds the excellent staff of a khaṭvāṅga.
Salutations indeed to the one called Virūpākṣa and Śubha, to the one of universal form; salutations again and again to the peaceful, the charming, and the three-eyed one.
Salutations to the creator of all forms, the destroyer of the Daityas, who is exceedingly compassionate toward his devotees and devoted to the knowledge of Rudra.
Salutations again and again to the one who is multiform and beautiful, who bears a hundred forms, who has five faces, auspicious faces, and a face like the moon. || 54 ||
Salutations again and again to the giver of boons, to the Boar, and to the excellent Tortoise. || 55 ||
O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Tripura, may protection be granted to us; O Maheśvara, we have taken refuge in you with our speech, mind, body, and inner being.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised then by the gods, beginning with Viriñci, Lord Hara beheld the emaciated bodies of the celestial dwellers.
With an inner self possessing divine majesty and the triple Veda.
Having observed their propitiation, the Lord of the Gods said to Brahmā and the others: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate ones! This vow has been constantly observed."
For I have been thoroughly propitiated by you through this divine rite, with great faith and a profound longing for a vision of me.
For mortals and even deities behold me while I am established in my vow; whatever auspicious boons I bestow upon any of you, they shall indeed be granted.
Whether individually, in groups of two or three, or all together, I shall grant this boon to you with impartiality for the sake of accomplishing all your desires.
For your benefit, I have come toward Ujjayinī; the skull has been cast away by me—what more need be said? May it be well with you! (63)
The gods said: "What benefit has been done for us by you casting away the skull? (64)
"For what reason has the earth trembled and the three worlds been thrown into agitation? O Lord, this is not without cause; please tell us the reason for it. (65)
Mahādeva said: "Indeed, this fear has been created and established for the sake of your welfare; listen now to the reason for its existence, which is for the protection of the gods."
An Asura named Drohaṇa, powerful and possessed of yogic illusion, remained stationed there, having taken hold of the foundation of the netherworld (rasātala).
Knowing that you were engaged in penance, many of those powerful Daityas, conquerors of enemy cities, approached that Daitya.

Desiring to slay the gods along with Indra, they moved about disguised by their illusory powers; intent on killing the deities, they marched toward this city of Kuśasthalī, which is enriched with golden peaks, with their weapons raised.
By the falling of their skulls, by their casting themselves upon the ground, and by that most terrible sound, the vital breaths departed from their bodies. (70)
Their endeavor was for the destruction of the world's stability; being excessively arrogant due to their royal power and sovereignty, they were therefore slain by me.

The gods said: "In this very same way, favor has been bestowed once again upon us who were full of trust; you are the bestower of grace upon the gods, served by those who remember and contemplate your virtues. (72)
"O Bhīma, you who have been greatly delighted by those with divine vision for the sake of fame"—having spoken thus, Bhava raised up the gods who were prostrate and spoke again.
Śiva said: It is joined with ritual service, constantly practiced by the fierce ones, perfected through the means of meditation, and is not found among others.
Through the state of mind, speech, and body, austerity is difficult to perform and hard to practice; endowed with this austerity, they endure hardship that is difficult to bear. (75)
May your splendor and your ascetic merit increase on all sides through this great bodily exertion, achieved by you over a long period of time. (76)
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, the deities, led by Brahmā, raised their faces and stood with knees bent before the Lord, saying: [77]
The gods said: "O God, you are the giver of life and the cause of all austerities; you are seen by us. Therefore, O bestower of boons, [act for] us humans who have come forth. (78)
O Lord of Gods, O bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees, grant us protection! 79.
Īśvara said: "Since you have clearly granted me a vision through diligent ritual practice, I shall indeed grant you many boons, even those that are very difficult to obtain."
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Brahmā, standing before the gods, addressed these words to Bhava, who had arisen from the sound he had heard.
O Blessed One, we have obtained a most excellent and great boon; may we possess eternal sovereignty and an imperishable place of residence.
Śiva said: "In this world, those who are my devotees and even those who have been slain by me do not go to an evil state; they attain supreme wisdom."
Together with their matted locks, these terrible hosts, bearing tridents in their hands, shine as they stand at my left side. (84)
For the sake of restraining them and for your awakening, I cast this skull, along with its internal contents, upon the surface of the earth.
I have bestowed my grace upon those devotees who desire devotion; and I have granted my eternal residence in this forest to you, as you have entreated me through the trees.
O sinless ones, since I have come to Mahākālavana and you are performing penance there, therefore [it is called] Mahākālavana.
Endowed with these two names, it shall become renowned in the world as the "Secret" (Guhya). It is the secret forest, the cremation ground, and the great, preeminent field among all fields. || 88 ||
Indeed, this practice of the skull-vow has been proclaimed by me; eating from a skull-bowl, one is adorned with the skull-vow. (89)
Holding a skull in his hand, contented, endowed with the vows of a mendicant, dwelling in cremation grounds, fierce, intoxicated by his observances, and bewildered in intellect—(90).
He rejoices among all beings, remaining always equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant; his entire body is adorned with ashes, and he is especially a man of wisdom.

One who has conquered the senses, who is unattached to all things, who collects earth, ashes, and water, who is ever-disciplined, always pervasive, a reciter of mantras, and one who has mastered the supreme postures.
Endowed with sacred fords and hermitages, and concentrated on his own deity, he attained the supreme knowledge that transcends the worlds—the Great Pāśupata vow.
In former times, I myself undertook the Kapāla-vow; it is the supreme secret, pure, and the destroyer of sins. (94)
This is indeed the vow of the skull-bowl (kapāla-vrata), difficult to maintain and most wonderful; it is exceedingly fierce, terrible, yet non-terrible, and hair-raising. || 95 ||
A man who, out of delusion, hates the Great Vow remains bound by sin alone; he is not released from that sin even in hundreds of millions of births. (96)
Therefore, one should neither kill nor defile a Mahāpāśupata; for if he is killed, ten million [others] are thereby slain.
Thus, for one who, endowed with faith, feeds [a guest] during the Mahāvrata, it is as if ten million Brahmins learned in the Vedas have been fed by him. (98)
He who bestows alms sufficient to fill a skull-bowl upon ascetics is liberated from all sins and shall not fall into an evil rebirth. || 99 ||
"Eating from a skull is the best; this path originates from Brahmā. They say it is honored in the world and in the Vedas by gods and demons alike. (100)
O Brahmin, those learned men who carry the skull that deludes living beings shall be equal to me as they wander upon the surface of the earth.
Devoted solely to the recitation of mantras, steadfast, adorned with skull-ornaments—these Mahāpāśupatas are Rudras in this world, who deliver beings from the cycle of transmigration. || 2 ||
Freed from both merit and demerit, and devoid of the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, they deliver living beings through initiation and the yoga of knowledge.
Whatever holy places exist in this world and hundreds of millions of sacrifices, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of pure discernment.
Just as I am indeed honored by all the gods as the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), so too is this observer of the great vow (Mahāvratī) to be honored above all yogas.
This secret vow of Śiva is for the sake of liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra; through this, which consists of all dharmas, it is the cause of non-rebirth.
He who, having undertaken the skull-vow, abandons it with his senses unsubdued, quickly goes to the Raurava hell, led by the servants of Yama.
He who converses with affectionate intent but does not perform the action—his mind being full of passion and seeking sensual pleasure—he is not one who acts out of love for the Dharma. (8)
Eating alone, a consumer of sweets, fond of deceit, a resident of a wretched village or town, and one who subsists by agriculture, trade, or service; || 9 ||
By even conversing with such a person who possesses these and other wicked faults, a man shall go to hell, for he is a defiler of my vow.
And having seen a person who has broken his vows, a man observing the great vow (mahāvratadhara) should not touch him limb-to-limb; but if he has touched him, he should bathe with water.
Thus has everything been told regarding the liberation of the skull, and how it was cast down here by me through ignorance, thereby destroyed by my own hand.

Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that Blessed One, together with Brahmā and the other immortals, established his residence in the sacred field; I shall describe this to you exactly as it happened.
O Vyāsa, this is recited by the best of sages as the primordial cremation ground, Mahākālavana, where Hara is ever present.
The region of Anugraha is undoubtedly a portion of the earth, intended for the sake of favoring those beings subject to death within this field.
And the ground was made into a terrace with a cross-legged posture of gold and vajra; it was rendered entirely beautiful, adorned with various flowers and jewels. 16.
The ground, marked with golden vajras and covered with excellent green grass, has thirty or forty full jars placed at its corners.
There, four excellent gates shine brightly, and the jars situated there gleam like risen suns.
The Blessed One, together with Nandin and the hosts of gods, accompanied by Kāladaṇḍa and others, delights there in that most excellent forest of forests.
In the Kṛta age, all this was seen directly in the forest; in the Tretā age, there were ascetics devoted to dharma and practicing celibacy.
In the Dvāpara age, those who are virtuous in conduct and endowed with sacred learning and wisdom worship Śaṅkara Hara; but in the Kali age, those endowed with pure realization worship him.
Those preeminent in austerity constantly behold Maheśvara, the God of gods, the wielder of the trident and the battle-axe in the Mahākālavana forest.
This truth has been declared to you, which brings benefit to the world, together with its sequential order, the mantras, and the preceding ritual injunctions. (23)
Those Brahmins who worship Śambhu, the great refuge, with devotion, dwell here in his presence, empowered by the majesty of Mahākāla.

He who recites this here in this world—this arrangement honored by floods of celebrated multitudes of virtues and destructive of faults—he, being of auspicious mind and consecrated, goes to the city of Hara while being worshipped by the immortals; so too does he who listens with one-pointed mind. 125.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, by what rule should men dwelling in the sacred field of Mahākālavana reside, if they desire to attain the world of Rudra?
Whether by men or by women who have entered the stages of life (āśrama) for the sake of attaining perfection, what must be practiced while dwelling [there]? Tell us all of this.

It should be inhabited by men and women, by those belonging to the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas), who are devoted to the practice of their own duties and are free from hypocrisy and delusion.

Tell us what action must be performed by men who are devotees of Rudra—those who have restrained their senses through deed, mind, and speech; who follow the sacred tradition; who are not base; who are devoted to the welfare of all beings; and what kind of ritual acts they should perform. || 4 ||

Sanatkumāra said: Indeed, it is said here that [speech] is threefold, arising from mind, speech, and body; furthermore, it may be worldly (laukikī), Vedic (vaidikī), or likewise spiritual (ādhyātmikī). || 5 ||
Indeed, that recollection of the Rudras through the intellect consisting of meditative concentration and retention is what produces devotion to Rudra; this is called mental devotion.
For those characterized by knowledge and meditation, bodily devotion to Rudra consists of vows, fasts, and observances that restrain the senses.
It was prepared with cow-ghee, milk, and curds, with fragrant water containing red kuśa grass, and with various perfumes, garlands, and minerals.
With incense of ghee and guggulu, fragrant with black aguru, and with ornaments of gold and gems, as well as with variegated garlands; || 9 ||
With showers of garments, hymns of praise, raised banners and fans, and with dances, instrumental music, songs, and every kind of offering; || 10 ||
That devotion which is directed toward Maheśvara by men through offerings of food, edibles, drinks, and even flowers used for worship, is considered worldly (laukikī). || 11 ||
That ritual action which is considered Vedic is performed with Vedic mantras, oblations, and sacrifices. || 12 ||

The Agnihotra sacrifice should be performed on either the new moon day or the full moon day; likewise, the ritual consumption of the offering, the giving of the sacrificial fee, the cake-offering (puroḍāśa), and the hospitable treatment [of the priests] must be carried out.
The performance of desired rites, the drinking of soma, all sacrificial acts, the recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the study of the Saṃhitās. (14)
That which is performed with Rudra as the intended object is known as Vedic devotion (vaidikī bhakti). [One should worship] fire, earth, wind, ether, the moon, and the sun. (15)
Any action performed with that as its objective becomes entirely divine. But, O Sage, devotion to Rudra is established as being twofold in its spiritual (ādhyātmikī) form. || 16 ||
There is another [system] called Sāṃkhya, which is etymological; hear from me its division therein: by number, there are twenty-four principles (tattvas) beginning with Pradhāna.
The insentient [principles] are to be joined together; the twenty-fifth principle is the Puruṣa. The Puruṣa is sentient and the enjoyer; he has no connection with the fruit of action.
Rudra is the twenty-sixth principle; he is the creator, omniscient, conscious, and the Lord. He is unborn, eternal, unmanifest, the presiding authority, and the instigator.

The Puruṣa is eternally unmanifest, and Maheśvara is the cause; [he creates] the creation of the principles (tattvasarga), the creation of the world (bhavasarga), and the creation of the elements (bhūtasarga) according to reality.

By enumeration, for the sake of thorough investigation, there is the Pradhāna consisting of the Guṇas; there is the similarity between the Self and the Lordship, and indeed the Pradhāna is of a different nature.
And that cause is said to be the state of being subject to desire (kāmyatva) on the part of Rudra; agency resides everywhere in Rudra, while the Puruṣa possesses non-agency.
And that lack of consciousness resides in Pradhāna; this is remembered as the fundamental principle (tattva). Through another principle, both the effect and the cause are liberated.

Having understood that there is a diversity of purposes within the principle of the unmanifest (tattva), which is in fact innumerable, the wise who contemplate the meaning of the Rudra-principle state that "there is a number. || 24 ||

Thus, the wise know his true nature and the enumeration of the principles (tattvas) according to reality; they also know that the principle of knowledge (jñānatattva) is superior even to the principle of Rudra.
This devotion established in Sāṃkhya is considered by the virtuous to be spiritual; now hear, O great Asura, of the devotion even for yogins through my grace. (26)
Constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), with his senses restrained, he who meditates upon Maheśvara, having fixed his concentration (dhāraṇā) within the heart, performs meditation. || 27 ||
Seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, he has five faces and three eyes; his belly possesses the luster of the moon, and the region of his waist is encircled by serpents.
White, with ten arms, auspicious, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—O Vyāsa, this mental yoga-born devotion to Rudra is remembered as supreme. (29)
He alone who possesses devotion to Rudra is called a devotee of Rudra. Now hear from me, O Vyāsa, the rule that is prescribed for those dwelling in the sacred field.
It was ordained by Rudra himself in the assembly of Brahmā and the others; previously, it was recounted in detail there in the presence of them all.
Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, unattached, and without acquisitions; devoid of affection for their circle of kinsmen, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
They constantly grant fearlessness to all beings through the three kinds of actions; they are knowers of the rules of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, knowers of Dharma, and have severed all doubts.
Listen to the fruit obtained by those Brahmins residing in the sacred field who, performing various sacrifices, die in the Mahākālavana forest. || 34 ||
They indeed attain the imperishable union with Brahman, which is so difficult to reach; having attained it, they do not undergo birth again, but obtain eternal liberation.
Having abandoned rebirth and remaining steadfast in the Māheśvara rite, others who dwell in the stages of life within phenomenal existence (prapañca) are subject to return again. 36.
Having entered the stage of the householder, they were always devoted to the six duties; restrained by mantras and hymns, they offered oblations according to the proper ritual.
They attain superior fruits, freed from all suffering; and in all other worlds, their progress is never obstructed. (38)
Endowed with divine sovereignty, mounted upon his own vehicle and accompanied by his retinue, he traveled in a resplendent celestial chariot that possessed the brilliance of many suns.
Surrounded by thousands of women and moving about his abode at will, he wanders through all the worlds of the gods without any reflection.
Most desirable among men, the best of all castes and wealthy, he who has fallen from heaven is born handsome in a great family. (41)
He was a knower of dharma, a devotee of Rudra, and one who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge; likewise, he was perfected through celibacy and service to his guru.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas, subsisting on alms, with senses conquered, he is constantly engaged in the vow of truth and finds delight in his own duty.
Having died at the proper time, he traveled in a magnificent celestial chariot that provided all enjoyments, as if accompanied by a second sun.
The host of Rudra known as the Guhyakas is highly esteemed; possessing immeasurable strength and sovereignty, it is worshipped by gods and dānavas. || 45 ||
And he attains equality with them, endowed with equal sovereignty; among gods, dānavas, and mortals, he shall become most worthy of worship. (46)
For thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of years, endowed with such sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
When that man, having indeed dwelt there in great splendor, passes away and falls from the world of Rudra, he dwells upon the earth; of this there is no doubt. || 48 ||
Established in the Brahmacharya hermitage within the sacred field of Mahakalavana, he should dwell there constantly devoted to Maheśvara, whether he lives or dies. || 49 ||
Upon death, he indeed goes to a divine celestial chariot possessing the brilliance of the sun; radiant like the full moon, he is truly pleasant to behold, like the moon itself.
Having reached the world of Rudra, he rejoices together with the Guhyakas; as the lord of the entire universe, he enjoys great sovereignty.
Having enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] for thousands of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra; then, having eventually descended from that world of Rudra, he proceeds by gradual stages.
Having always rejoiced there and enjoyed a world free from affliction, he is born perpetually into a great family among those who perform the rites for the twice-born.
Among human beings, he shall abide in the state of dharma, become exceedingly handsome, possess a body desirable to women, and become a lord of great enjoyments.

Following the conduct of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he avoided the medicinal herbs of the forest; his gathering consisted of withered leaves, and he subsisted on fruits, flowers, and water. || 55 ||
Subsisting on grains, or using a stone for a mortar, or else using his teeth as a mortar; by whatever means possible, he wears worn-out bark garments. (56)

Wearing matted hair, bathing three times a day, with his hair loose, and carrying a fine staff; sleeping in water, practicing the "five-fire" penance, and staying in the open air during the rainy season.
He likewise sleeps on ground covered with insects, thorns, and stones; he is devoted to standing and the heroic posture (vīrāsana), sharing [his possessions] with others, and firm in his vows.
He was a consumer of forest herbs, a bestower of fearlessness upon all beings, eternally devoted to dharma, observant of silence, and one who had conquered anger and subdued his senses.
A devotee of Rudra dwelling in the sacred field of Mahākālavana, the sage had renounced all attachments, delighted in his own self, and was free from longing.
O Vyāsa, listen now to the destiny of him who dwells here, [residing] in that which is radiant as the rising sun and beautified by altars and pillars.
A devotee of Rudra travels by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will, shining in the sky like a second moon.
Surrounded by hosts of apsarases and the sound of singing and instrumental music, he is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred crores of years.
Having fallen even from the world of Rudra, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; falling from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Having passed away from that place as well, he is indeed born on the continents; likewise, in other heavenly realms, he enjoys pleasures according to his desire.

Having enjoyed sovereign power among those mortals and immortals, that man is born as a king or one equal to a king, wealthy and happy; endowed with a beautiful form, fortunate, lovely, and possessed of fame, he is one who has been meditated upon by Rudra.
O Vyāsa, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras dwelling in that land were devoted to their own duties, remaining content with their own means and living by honest service.
Those seekers of liberation who dwell in the sacred field of Mahākālavana are devotees of Rudra with their whole being and act for the benefit of all living beings.
Upon death, they go to the abode of Rudra in beautiful celestial chariots that move at will, assume any form at will, and are accompanied by throngs of Apsarases. (69)
Alternatively, he who offers his body as an oblation into the fire of consciousness, meditating on Rudra, that being of great courage shall dwell in the abode of Rudra.
For them, there is the imperishable and eternal world of Rudra, together with the Guhyakas; it is the most excellent of all worlds, delightful, and the accomplisher of their desired aims. (71)
O Vyāsa, for those high-souled men who abandon their lives through fasting at Mahākāla, their world of Rudra is likewise imperishable.

Those Sāṃkhyas, freed from all suffering, praise that god Rudra, who is joined by all the immortals and accompanied by the hosts of Nandi and the gods; these men, though Śūdras, die through fasting in the Mahākālavana forest.
They travel in celestial chariots yoked with lions, which are as radiant as the sun.

[The chariots] were enriched with gold of various colors, perfumed with delightful fragrances, beautiful with incomparable qualities, and accompanied by the songs and instrumental music of apsarases. || 75 ||
Adorned with banners and flags, resounding with the tinkling of various bells, they were radiant, endowed with excellent qualities, and moved like noble peacocks.

In the world of Rudra, all wise men who have died by fasting dwell for a long time; having enjoyed their desired pleasures there, they are born as wealthy and pleasure-seeking brahmins upon returning to the mortal realm.
The man who prepares cow-dung fuel in Mahākālavana goes to the world of Rudra, liberated from all worldly enjoyments. || 78 ||
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the end of the kalpa occurs.
Having enjoyed great luxuries there, he is born here as a lord of the earth; he shall be handsome and fortunate throughout the entire world. (80)
Vyāsa said: Right conduct is the supreme dharma, the ultimate refuge of all dharmas; those devoted to their own duty, having conquered anger and subdued the senses, [attain this]. (1)
Those who go here to the world of Rudra—of this I have no doubt; they undoubtedly proceed to other worlds that shine with the luster of the moon. || 2 ||
Even without residing in a sacred field and likewise without formal observances, women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, beasts, birds, and wild animals [attain liberation]. (3)
What is the fate of those who are mute, dull-witted, blind, or deaf, and who are devoid of austerity and religious observances, if they die in the Mahākālavana? || 4 ||
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, women, barbarians, the foolish, beasts, birds, and wild animals—when they die in due time, they go to the world of Rudra.
Possessing bodies of divine form and endowed with all enjoyments, they sport together with Śambhu in the cremation ground crowded with spirits.
Formerly, the goddess was rebuked as "Kālī" and "Pārvatī"; then that goddess became enraged toward Śaṅkara at Kaṭaka.
For it was in this very place that the quarrel between Śiva and Gaurī arose; there the deity known by the name Kalakaleśvara manifested.
Then, O Vyāsa, that pool named Kalahanāśana was created there; when one bathes therein, one's beloved wife becomes free from quarrelsomeness.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, worshipped Maheśvara, and fasted for one night, a man shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
In that regard, whoever bestows even a mere fragment of sandalwood as a gift causes ten ancestors and ten descendants to cross over by that act. (11)
And whatever man, O Sage, shall bestow there a gift of land, even if it be only the size of a cow-hide, he shall become the sovereign of all the earth. (12)
He who shall indeed give with devotion even a single village, a single house, or even a single inch of land, he truly shall become a king. (13)
A cow, a horse, sesame seeds, clothing, a vessel with a copper milking-pail, sandals, an umbrella, and likewise excellent shoes; 14.
For those who shall give [gifts] to the Brahmins, their worlds shall be eternally imperishable. On its right side and at its back are the deities known as the Mothers.
There, that goddess who removes the misfortunes of all the worlds resides; indeed, the supreme Maṇikarṇikā should be known as the embodiment of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 16 ||
Having bathed there, whoever reverently beholds the Mothers on the back [of the mountain], he is liberated from all sins and attains his desired perfection.
Having beheld them, one should proceed on the path; for him there is no fear from thieves, nor likewise fear from rākṣasas or spirits.
Whether in his own country or a foreign land, on mountains or in forests, he has no fear of the ocean, nor indeed of evil intentions.
In all afflictions caused by malevolent planets, as well as in fears of kings and the like, one should cause a goat, or perhaps a ram, or even a buffalo, to be sacrificed.
The brahmin who performs this rite dedicated to the Goddess attains his desired fruit; [this occurs] when midnight has passed on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
He who bathes in front of the Goddess attains supreme perfection; and that woman whose sons have died, having bathed in the pool, shall be reunited with her husband.
O Sage, at the outset, one should bathe according to the rite prescribed for the Goddess using a water-pot; having bathed with this pot-bath, one must certainly not look upon the face of another.
To him a son is born, like the six-faced god; on his mother's back is a supremely meritorious and auspicious sacred site (tīrtha) of the apsarases.
O Vyāsa, by the power of this very holy site, a man who bathes there becomes endowed with beauty and good fortune, just as Urvashi did in ancient times.
Hearing this curiosity—that the husband Purūravas was obtained as that lord of the earth, the son of Ilā—Vyāsa spoke these words: || 26 ||

Vyāsa said: O great sage, tell me in detail, along with its secret significance, how the Tīrtha of the Apsarases came to be there, by what cause it was established, and at what time it was founded. (27)

How did Purūravas come to have that excellent Apsaras as his wife? Who was she, named Urvaśī, and by whom was that beautiful woman born? Tell me all this exactly as it happened, for I am filled with curiosity. (28)
Sanatkumāra said: "Where indeed Nara and Nārāyaṇa formerly performed their penance."
Indra became afraid because those two were staying at Badarikāśrama; he [sent] all the heart-stealing Apsarases, who were proud of their beauty and youth.
Those who had been commanded by Maghavan and had assembled for the purpose of creating obstacles, seeing those two there, were sporting about, overwhelmed with intoxication.
When they arrived there for the purpose of creating obstacles, the two gods then spoke: "We have no women; that is indeed the cause of our obstruction. (32)
Having conversed thus, the man said to Nārāyaṇa: "I shall indeed create one woman who is superior to them in beauty. (33)
He fashioned from the blossoms of the mango tree a woman, peerless in beauty in the world and adorned with every ornament, out of her two thighs.
Seeing that excellent woman risen up, blazing with light, they went and informed Śakra: "She is not capable of being seduced during her season. (35)
Having heard their words, Śakra went to the gods and spoke to them, bowing low in salutation and placing his joined palms upon his head.
"I am a petitioner; let favor be shown to this woman. Then the two supreme lords, the gods, gave her to Indra.
"By the power of my word, accept this Urvaśī; for this excellent woman was born from the thighs of Nara. (38)
Because of that mango blossom, this woman was remembered as Urvaśī; Puraṃdara, having taken that supreme lady Urvaśī, [departed].
Having gone to heaven, he then summoned Citrāṅgada and said: "O Citra, let her be instructed so that she becomes proficient in dance."
"Let this [art] be accomplished by applying excellent effort without delay. When Śakra had spoken thus, she was trained by him; she became proficient in dancing and became skilled in singing. (41)
Thus that beautiful woman lived there in the abode of the gods; when a great deal of time had passed, that lord of men arrived there.
The son of Ilā was the righteous-souled Purūravas by name; having attained half of Indra’s throne, he beheld the dance there.
Seeing Urvaśī dancing before Vāsava, the king, filled with desire and his heart stolen by her, did not know what to do. || 44 ||
Having summoned fortitude to his heart, he remained composed for a moment; and at that time, Urvaśī’s mind was struck by the sight of him.
Emerging from that place, the young woman, afflicted by passion and utterly overwhelmed, fell to the ground from the elevated arena.
Then, having regained consciousness of herself, she rose from the circle of the earth; she was seen by that lion among kings, who was himself tormented by the god of love.
Purūravas went to the earth, remembering her alone in his mind; and Urvaśī also, remembering that tiger among kings, returned to her own home.
Having gone to Citrāṅgada’s house, she then dispatched a messenger; she was led by Citrāṅgada at night to where Purūravas was.
Deprived of Urvaśī, heaven became empty for the dwellers of the celestial realm; yet she was brought back to the third heaven by him during the very night.
Separated from her, O Vyāsa, that king too wandered about with a vacant mind; he fell into a state of madness for sixty years.
Wandering through various sacred fords (tīrthas), he went to Mahākālavana; there, that supreme Apsaras, Urvaśī, had been taken to heaven by Gandharva.
He neither lay down nor bathed, O King, but kept crying out, "Where is Urvaśī? Meanwhile, all those celestial nymphs arrived where Urvaśī was.
Rambhā, Menakā, Pramlocā, Puñjikasthalī, Jalapūrṇā, Aśrupūrṇā, Vasantā, and Candrikā likewise [were there]. (54)
Sūryadattā, Viśālākṣī, Candrā, and Candraprabhā likewise arrived together and spoke these words to Urvaśī: || 55 ||
"Why do you weep for the sake of a mortal, O fair-hipped one of beautiful eyes? Having heard those words from them, Urvaśī spoke this speech.
A eunuch does not know the pleasure that arises from the union of a man and a woman; by this analogy, it should be understood that she has made her resolve for his sake.
Having heard her words, they consulted together with focused minds and went to the Mahākālavana forest without the knowledge of the gods.
And there they saw the king seated in the shade of a tree; having seen the king, they all became deeply overwhelmed with agitation. (59)
Seeing all those celestial women in such a state, afflicted by desire and bewildered in mind, Urvaśī laughed and spoke these words: || 60 ||
Urvaśī said: "This is that tiger among men, without whom I have become such as I am; he is Aila, named Purūravas, the world-renowned lord of the earth. (61)
While Urvaśī was speaking thus, the host of Apsaras stood for a long time in silence, their necks bowed with shame.
In the meantime, the venerable Nārada arrived there; he saw all those women who had come together with King Urvashi.
Having observed them, he then said: "Why are you making such a noise here, having abandoned the most excellent and delightful abode of Indra?"
"Choose a boon quickly, and there shall be no separation. Nārada then recounted the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha). (65)
For by bathing at this unfortunate (durbhaga) holy site, a woman or even a man attains perfect good fortune as well as all the highest enjoyments.
One who weighs oneself against sesame seeds, or salt, or even against much sugar, should do so while remaining free from deceit regarding one's wealth.

By offering jaggery or honey dedicated to the goddess Pārvatī, one becomes rich in beauty; by offering salt, one becomes endowed with a beautiful form, and by offering sesame seeds, one becomes radiant in every limb.
Through the power of this holy place (tīrtha), there is an increase in wealth by means of sugar, fullness of limbs through jaggery, and good fortune through honey.
One should feed twelve couples of the Goddess and the God; one should give a small jar, a ring for the nails, an ear-ornament, a bracelet, and collyrium.
One should likewise give a cane-staff, a bodice, two saffron-colored garments, white unguents for men, and saffron for women. (71)
One should perform this excellent vow in the month of Āṣāḍha, or Śrāvaṇa, or likewise in Bhādrapada, or on the third day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
A woman is born most excellent, just like the goddess Umā; Umā and Maheśvara should be fashioned out of gold according to one's means. (73)
Indeed, those two deities must be borne by a woman herself during the descent upon the scales; furthermore, fruits and various kinds of vegetables should be given as offerings.

Whatever is given as a gift, offered in sacrifice, or recited there shall all become ten millionfold. Thus, whatever woman performs [these acts] at that sacred site with a concentrated mind, [she gains this merit]. (75)
One who dies here goes to the world of the Gandharvas and Apsarases; of this there is no doubt. In this sacred bathing place (tīrtha), two Liṅgas are worshipped by gods and demons.

Having seen that, the couple then attained supreme perfection; especially by performing a night vigil there on the full moon day of Kārttika and worshipping with perfumes and flowers, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
Just as the Queen's separation from her own true nature is never seen, so too the separation between those two is never seen at any time.
Having done this, O Brahmin, they all then went to heaven. Thus has been described the sacred ford of the Apsarases; now another sacred ford is being told.
To the south of Pṛṣṭhadevī, indeed, the pool of Mahiṣa is said to be located; formerly, the Dānava Mahiṣa was slain by the leaders of the Gaṇas. (80)
Having bathed at that sacred ford and having worshipped the Mothers with diligence, a person is liberated from the affliction caused by ghosts, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas. || 81 ||
Vyāsa said: How did that Māhiṣa Kuṇḍa come to be, and what is the form of the Mothers? And how was the Dānava Mahiṣa slain by Rudra himself in this sacred field?
Sanatkumāra said: Mahādeva took up a fragment of a skull that was exceedingly radiant, divine, consisting of Brahmanic splendor, and as if blazing with its own luster.
Playing about, the Lord of the World indeed deluded the gods; in the blink of an eye, he, whose self is yoga, brought this world [to destruction] through his yogic play.
Having reached that most meritorious field where the Great Lord resides, the Sovereign of the Devas placed his great, divine skull at each respective spot.
The Lord, whose radiance was blazing, established [it] at the forefront of the hosts; then, seeing that which had been established by you, all those of great luster departed.
Uttering a great roar that made the ten directions resound—a sound like the agitation of the ocean or a thunderbolt by which the very sky is rent asunder—[he spoke].
At that terrible sound, the Dānava known as Hālāhala, a thorn to the gods, rushed toward that region.
Unable to endure it, afflicted by anger, that evil-souled one, invincible even to the gods and having received boons from Brahmā, assumed the form of a buffalo.
Surrounded by crores of terrible Daityas with uplifted weapons, Mahiṣa—the thorn in the side of the gods—advanced in a state of rage.
Having observed all the Gaṇas, the Lord who wields the Pināka bow said: "The Daitya Māyāvī is a leader of the Gaṇas and a thorn even for the three worlds."
"He is approaching swiftly; therefore, you must strike him down. All the leaders of the Gaṇas have taken refuge in the path of Kapāla. || 11 ||
Then the hosts of gods saw that great asura approaching, roaring with a mighty sound, whirling about with his massive arms.
They pierced him with volleys of spears, swords, and likewise with clubs; then, having stunned him with a net of arrows, they felled him to the ground.
When he had been slain, Mahādeva then spoke to the gods: "Alas! He was utterly deluded by pride; through his arrogance, he has met his destruction."
In the meantime, O Vyāsa, from that skull emerged all the Mothers—most terrifying, with blazing mouths, fierce weapons, and great strength. (15)
Having announced the Daitya to Mahādeva, those exceedingly powerful ones rushed toward that place and devoured him, tearing him apart again and again.
Therefore, those of great strength are known as the Kapālamātṛs in that sacred field; for this reason, Mahākapāla is indeed celebrated as being such. || 17 ||
In ancient times, after the skull had been established, it burst open and there arose what is known as Śivataḍāga, which destroys all sins.
Even today, that great divine lake shines forth there, renowned throughout the three worlds and frequented by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.
Whether it be water contained in a vessel, drawn up, cold, warm, or boiled, the Raudra lake purifies one here just as the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice does.
Even Brahmā, surrounded by hundreds of deities, went to that place; it was proclaimed by Brahmā himself as a ladder to the heavenly world.
Those who give up their lives here, O Vyāsa, go to the world of Rudra; blessed are those men dwelling in the Mahākālavana forest in the mortal realm.
Those who bathe in the lake Raudra, or those who drink its water, being devoted to the practice of their own dharma, behold the Lord Īśāna.
Thus, the gods who have gone to heaven constantly harbor a longing for it.

This auspicious, divine Mahākapāla destroys unrighteousness; it is worshipped by gods and demons, possesses great splendor, removes sin, is eternal, and is always difficult to obtain even from the world of the Lord of the Gods. (25)

He who, with a single-minded focus, hears this—which is praised by hosts of Siddhas devoted to austerity like the orb of the sun situated in the sky—goes to heaven, welcomed by all through its grace. (26)
Sanatkumāra said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the holy ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds, the self-manifested shrine of Maheśvara known as Kuṭumbikeśvara. || 1 ||
One who, having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule, beholds the God with a pure mind, is liberated from all sins, even those committed throughout seven lifetimes. (2)
He who [abstains from] all kinds of leafy vegetables and various tubers transcends all worlds and goes to the realm of Śiva. (3)
On the bank of that [river], one should bestow [the gift] on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, or on the eighth day; being composed in mind, he attains the supreme goal.
By a single fast alone, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, a pure man beholds me.
Having fasted on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, that sinless person who performs the binding of the turban for Maheśa shall go to heaven.
He offers camphor, saffron, musk, and sandalwood, as well as an oblation of milk-rice with ghee, to the God.
O best of Brahmins, by feeding a twice-born man along with his wife in their true form, one attains the world of Rudra for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras endures.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the sacred ford (tīrtha) of the Vidyādhara; having bathed there and become pure, one shall become a lord of the Vidyādharas. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said: O great sage, how did this sacred site (tīrtha) arise here in this field? O Brahmin, tell me out of your grace; I wish to hear it now.
Sanatkumāra said: In ancient times, there was a certain lord of the Vidyādharas named Rūpadhara; by him was fashioned a beautiful garland of Pārijāta flowers.
Having taken that garland, he went to the abode of Vāsava; there he saw Menakā dancing before Vāsava.
Then, while engaged in dancing, he gave that garland to her; Menakā, being praised in an inappropriate place, became infatuated with the garland.
Then Śakra, overcome with anger, cursed the Vidyādhara: "Go to the earth, O most sinful one! You have interrupted my dance."
"Having now been deprived of the status of a Vidyādhara due to my curse,"—when Śakra had spoken these words, the Vidyādhara replied: ||| 7 ||
O Protector, out of ignorance I have now committed an offense; therefore, O Lord, grant me your favor through your grace. (8)
Thus addressed, Śakra indeed spoke to the Vidyādhara: "Go this very day to Avantī, where the Gāṅgaṭī cave is located."
And to the north of that place is situated an excellent holy site (tīrtha), auspiciously known by the name Vidyādhara, renowned throughout the three worlds.
If one performs a bath there with devotion, one shall become a lord of the Vidyādharas; therefore, you too should diligently perform a bath in that very place.
Thus addressed by Śakra, he arrived in the region of Avantī; having performed his ablutions in that very delightful sacred ford, he remained there.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he regained his own station once more. Thus, O Vyāsa, has the auspicious Vidyādhara Tīrtha been fully described.
Whoever offers flowers, sandalwood, and ointments there shall obtain all enjoyments both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vidyādharatīrtha," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth section (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sanatkumāra said: I shall now describe the supreme Markaṭeśvara in the northern region; there is also a famous sacred site (tīrtha) there that bestows all desires.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a person shall obtain the fruit of [giving] a hundred cows; this is for the sake of pacifying boils and for the sake of children as well.
Having measured out lentils with a measure, one should grind them there; by the power of Śītalā, may children be free from disease. || 3 ||
O best of the twice-born, those men who behold Śītalā, the remover of misfortunes, with devotion—neither any evil deed nor poverty shall befall them.
And for them there is no fear of disease, nor likewise any affliction by malevolent planets.
Sanatkumāra said: Having bathed at Svargadvāra and beheld the god Bhairava, a man should perform a śrāddha ceremony right there with devotion, dedicated to his ancestors.
O Vyāsa, that man shall deliver his ancestors along with himself by means of the gateway to heaven, as he approaches the supreme abode of Rudra. || 2 ||
To the east, in front of Bhairava, Ambikā stands; by seeing her, whether a man or a woman, one is liberated from all sins.

On the Mahānavamī day, a man who has prepared an offering consisting of a goat, or a buffalo, liquor, meat, and an auspicious garland made of bilva fruit, and having offered these with devotion to the Goddess, shall attain all perfections.
Having bathed there with devotion and performed worship to Maheśvara, that man, O twice-born one, enters the abode of Rudra by way of the Gate of Heaven.
Sanatkumāra said: Having bathed in the four oceans, one should behold the auspicious Rājasthala; by the mere sight of it, a man becomes possessed of sons.
There are four oceans—of salt water, milk, curd, and sugarcane juice—which were established near that deity by Sudyumna.
