Vyāsa said: O best of sages, tell me for what reason were the oceans established near Rājasthala by Sudyumna?
This ocean known as the Salt Sea (Kṣārasamudra) has been established as a boundary for the beautiful Jambūdvīpa, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.

In Śākadvīpa, which measures two hundred thousand [yojanas], the Ocean of Milk is situated; in Kuśadvīpa, the Ocean of Curds is established at four hundred thousand; and in Śālmali, the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice is established at eight hundred thousand.
Those four oceans have been described by you as being upon the circle of the earth; how then did they come together in one place near Rājasthala?
Sanatkumāra said: In a former kalpa, there was a most righteous king named Sudyumna; his wife, of beautiful form, was renowned by the name Sudarśanā.
Having seen the sage Dālbhya, she questioned him out of a desire for a son: "O Blessed One, by what gift, bath, or ritual procedure [is this attained]? (8)
"How can a son endowed with all auspicious marks be obtained by me? O brahmin-sage, explain this to me exactly as it is, in full detail. (9)
Dālbhya said: "O daughter, in former times, those excellent oceans were ordained by the self-existent god Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, out of a desire for sons. (10)
"O daughter, when the king has performed his bath in those [waters], you will have a son; therefore, urge your beloved toward the propitiation of Śaṅkara."
By means of Dālbhya’s very words and through a marvelous narrative, she quickly dispatched her husband to the worship of Śaṅkara.
Having gone to Mount Gandhamādana, he propitiated Śaṅkara; Śaṅkara, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, being well-pleased, spoke.
"Go to Avanti, O Indra among kings; you shall obtain a splendid son. By my command, the oceans shall go to Kuśasthalī."
O King, O best of men, on that spot in the form of Meru near Śaṅkara, you shall see the oceans gathered there; entreated by you, they shall always remain there with a portion of themselves.
Having spoken thus, the omnipresent Mahādeva vanished from sight; Sudyumna, together with his wife, returned to Kuśasthalī.
Having arrived at Kuśasthalī, he beheld the oceans; seeing them near Rājasthala, he paid homage to them.
Having seen Sudyumna bowing down, all those oceans, who are affectionate toward their devotees, said: "O observer of noble vows, choose a boon."
He mentally chose a son endowed with all auspicious marks; and the king spoke again: "As long as the earth endures, so long must you remain right here, near Rājasthala. (19)
The oceans said: "We shall remain right here until the end of the kalpa."
"And a son shall be born to you, endowed with all auspicious marks; therefore, perform your bath here, for by merely bathing here [such a son] will be yours. (21)
"And here on this auspicious land, O King, we shall remain along with a portion [of ourselves]. Thus, O Vyāsa, the oceans were brought down by Sudyumna.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who undertakes a journey to them: having performed an ablution in the highly meritorious ocean known as Kṣāra. (23)
Then, O Vyāsa, devoted to his ancestors, he should perform the śrāddha ceremony and worship Mahādeva, the Lord of Pārvatī, who resides at that sacred spot.
Then one should give maṇḍakas to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; a vessel made of copper should be prepared and filled with salt.
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, along with gold, provided with the seven types of grain, made of bamboo, and wrapped in cloth.
One should diligently offer the arghya, accompanied by fruits and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Then, having gone to the Ocean of Milk, one should perform a bath as previously described.
In that [rite], milk filled in a copper vessel should be offered; likewise, having prepared it in the ocean of curd, one should give auspicious rice mixed with curd.
And having done so at the Ikṣu ocean, one should give auspicious jaggery to a Brahmin; and having performed the pilgrimage, O Vyāsa, one should indeed give a milch cow.
Thus, whoever undertakes a pilgrimage near Rājasthala shall indeed obtain auspicious fortune as well as delightful sons. || 30 ||
Upon death, he attains heaven; for as long as the fourteen Indras endure, having enjoyed the fruits of heaven for that duration, he shall thereafter proceed to liberation.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the great holy site named Śaṅkaravāpikā; this supreme tīrtha was created by the Lord while he was sporting.
Because the water used for washing the skull was cast by the God of gods into a pond, it is therefore called Śaṅkaravāpikā.
On the eighth day of the sun’s course, having bathed in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and likewise in the sequence starting from the east up to the middle of the pond; || 3 ||
O Vyāsa, one should give new water-pots filled with sacrificial food (haviṣya) and vegetables and roots to the Brahmins; hear now the meritorious fruit of that act. || 4 ||
Whatever worlds there are, both here and in the hereafter, endowed with all things, he goes to each of them and enjoys supreme sovereignty.
Those men who, full of great faith, shall proclaim this majesty, are worthy of worship even in the world of Rudra; to them, too, let there be constant salutation.
Sanatkumāra said: Then indeed, the Lord of the gods of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow whose banner bears the bull, becoming composed, praised the Sun-god, the God of gods.
The Lord of Day arrived and, being well-pleased, spoke to Śaṅkara.

Sūrya said: "Choose a boon, O Lord of Beings; I am the giver of boons and shall grant it to you. He [the Lord] said to him: "If you are indeed a giver of boons, then fulfill what is being requested by me. (9)
"Stay here in part for the benefit of all embodied beings. Having heard these words of Maheśvara, Ravi descended there.
Then, by the word of the god of gods, the immensely powerful Śaṅkara, the Sun of great splendor attained fame in that place.
Known by the name Śaṅkarāditya, he was the benefactor of the worlds; the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras were all filled with wonder. (12)
Oh, how blessed is this place where Tripurāntaka resides, and where Bhāskara also stands situated in the midst of the sacred fords!
Then all those foremost of gods, beginning with Brahmā, being satisfied, worshipped the Lord of Gods, Āditya, as well as Śaṅkara.
And those gods, having descended in beautiful embodied forms and established themselves there, spoke these words: "Those men who shall bathe here—" || 15 ||

Suffering born of old age, death, and grief does not arise for them. Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—even greater than that is obtained here from the sight of Śaṅkarāditya.
Neither diseases nor mental anxieties, nor poverty ever arise for them; rather, incomparable sovereignty is always produced for them upon this earth. (17)
Neither disease nor poverty, nor separation from kinsmen, arises, O tiger among sages, from beholding Śaṅkarāditya. (18)
Thus, in ancient times, the supreme station was indeed established by the God of gods, the wielder of the trident, under the name Śaṅkarāditya.
Sanatkumāra said: Now I shall further proclaim another, the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas); O best of sages, that supreme tīrtha was established by him under his own name. (1)
Once upon a time, O Vyāsa, Maheśvara took water from his head in a skull-bowl for the purpose of washing it. || 2 ||
Having washed [his hands], he cast them upon the ground there at that unsurpassed sacred site; it became a meritorious river named Gandhavatī, renowned throughout the three worlds.
In an instant, it became completely filled with the blood of Brahmā; bathing in it is always recommended, as spoken by the Lord himself. (4)
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the libations (tarpaṇa), all that becomes inexhaustible; for his ancestors, having become like the wind, reside on the southern bank of that river.
O tiger among sages, they remain here contemplating their own lineage, thinking: "Today a son, or perhaps a grandson, will come here into our progeny."
When indeed will he offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) made of wheat-cakes, milk-rice, or even śyāmāka and nivāra grains, combined with honey and sesame seeds?
By that offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), inexhaustible satisfaction is attained; indeed, he who, having bathed, offers a piṇḍa on the full-moon day (parvan) [attains this].
Indeed, the parents of those men or twice-born brahmins who come here as well-learned scholars shall attain satisfaction for twelve years.
They shall gratify the ancestors, and their heaven shall be eternal and imperishable; whatever gift is given there, even a mere fragment of gold—
That [merit] was declared to be inexhaustible by the self-existent Brahmā himself at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, and Puṣkara. || 11 ||
Neither at Vārāṇasī nor at Gayā will there be such satisfaction; for when the ancestors of men are gratified, they shall grant their desired boons.
Whoever shall perform a śrāddha here for the sake of a single person, all that becomes his; it is the supreme goal for the deceased. (13)
The ninth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon—all these indeed, O Vyāsa, as well as the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), [are times for fasting].
Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra; the gods, the Sun, Agni, and the deities of Brahmā; the Viśvedevas along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, humans, and animals. || 15 ||
By performing the śrāddha with faith, one indeed gratifies the reptiles, the hosts of ancestors, and whatever else is situated upon the earth—the entire world.

O best of the twice-born, every month during the dark fortnight on the fifteenth day, when the moon has waned, [if one observes the vow] under the asterisms Maitra (Anurādhā), Viśākhā, or Rohiṇī; || 17 ||

In a Śrāddha performed under the asterisms of Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), Ajaikapāt (Pūrvabhādrapadā), or Arkṣa (Uttarabhādrapadā), the hosts of ancestors attain the satisfaction earned by the performer who desires the gratification of the Pitṛs.
The Śrāddha ceremony should be performed with devotion; by it, the ancestors are gratified. Blessed indeed are those born in our lineage who possess such intelligence. (19)
And those who indeed perform the śrāddha ceremony and offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), by that offering of the cakes, our satisfaction shall be inexhaustible.

Having come here and bathed properly in these meritorious waters, a man shall indeed obtain those desires, attaining which he rejoices, surrounded by hosts of ancestors and honored by the gods as a perfected being.
A pure mind, wealth, and pure men, an auspicious time, and the prescribed rite; a worthy recipient as described, and supreme devotion—these indeed bestow upon men their heart's desires. (22)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Nīlagandhavatī," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth book (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sanatkumāra said: O honorable one, having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika and beheld the Lord Maheśvara, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
By Manu, the lord of men; by King Yayāti; by Raghu and Uśanas; and by the great seer Lomaśa. || 2 ||
By Atri, by Bhṛgu, O Vyāsa, by the wise Dattātreya, by the meritorious Purūravas, by Nahuṣa, and by Nala; || 3 ||
By bathing here, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices; this was likewise attained by King Bāṣkali when the end of the Dvāpara age had arrived.
O best of the twice-born, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices has been obtained by you, since the black-colored Liṅga was always worshipped with devotion.
Having seen and touched that deity, one obtains the fruit previously described; having worshipped the deity with devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra.
And one should give a horse that is handsome and endowed with good qualities to a Brahmin; O twice-born one, as many hairs as are counted upon it by number— [so many merits shall he obtain].
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Śiva; having descended from the world of Śiva, he shall become a sovereign ruler on earth.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Daśāśvamedha," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth *Āvantya-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sanatkumāra said: Having paid homage to the goddess Ekānaṃśā, who is renowned throughout the three worlds, and having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one shall obtain the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 1 ||

When pleased, she bestows all the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the perfection of the pill (*guṭikā-siddhi*), collyrium, the sword, the sandals, dwelling in a cave, and the elixir of life (*rasāyana*); there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Worshipped with offerings of liquor, meat, and various kinds of food, the Goddess, being pleased, shall always grant all the desires of men.
He who worships the Goddess on the Mahānavamī day with a buffalo, or with a ram according to his means, shall attain all his desires.
Vyāsa said: How was the goddess born as she who is renowned as Ekānaṃśā? I wish to hear all that regarding her who destroys every sin. (5)

Sanatkumāra said: In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, remembered his own body that had been produced in a previous existence during the night.
Then the blessed Night presented herself before the Grandfather; beholding her in a secluded place, Brahmā spoke to that goddess of the night.
Brahmā said: O Night, O Great Illusion, listen to the determination of the matter regarding that which must be done by you for the sake of the gods, O Goddess. (8)
There was a lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, an unconquered enemy of the gods; out of fear of him, all the gods who dwell in heaven were indeed terrified.
Therefore, O blessed lady, if Maheśa indeed grants a boon, he will surely become the son who shall be the end-maker of Tāraka.
She who was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and the wife of Śaṅkara, became enraged at her father, O blessed lady, due to a certain other cause.
The daughter of the snowy mountain, the purifier of the world, was destined to be; for in her absence, Hara considered the three worlds to be empty.
He will dwell for some time in a cave of the mountain Atapadhima, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas), awaiting that birth.
Therefore, he who shall become a great lord from their well-performed austerities will be the repeller of the Daitya Tāraka.
As soon as she was born, that beautiful goddess possessed but little consciousness; she was intensely distressed by separation and longed deeply for union with Hara.
The union of those two, Pārvatī and Hara, who have performed intense austerities and are perfectly disciplined, occurs; therefore, their sexual union is the cause of power.
O Brahmin, act for the sake of the gods' purpose; listen to how you must create an obstacle for those two. (17)
Then, O Mother, color her with your own form while she is in the womb; thereafter, Śarva, holding her in private, [united] with her preceded by bliss.
Thinking, "Kālī will mock me," she will then become angry and depart to perform penance; thus, endowed with ascetic fervor, she will go. (19)
He who shall be born from Śarva as a circle of light like the moon will indeed become the slayer of the enemies of the gods; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, you too must slay the Dānavas who are difficult for the world to conquer, as long as Satī has not transferred the entire collection of her virtues into another body.
"By union with him, you shall be able to slay the Daityas. When this has been done by you, O Goddess, Kālī will perform penance. (22)
And when that Gaurī has completed her vow, then Śailajā will grant you, too, the same form as hers.
Then, that one portion of yours which is innate shall become Ekānaṃśā; and joined with a portion of form, you shall become known as Umā.
O Giver of Boons, the world shall worship you as Ekānaṃśā; you who pervade all things and are the means for accomplishing all desires through manifold divisions and various forms. (25)
Oṃkārāvaktrā Gāyatrī, you alone are the expounder of Brahman; you possess a beautiful form that has been fully pervaded, and you shine in the battles of kings.
Among the Vaiśyas you are Queen Kamalā, and among the Śūdras you are their own progenitor; you are the form of the object of knowledge for the wise, and you are the refuge of all embodied beings. 27.
You are the fame of the famous; you are the prosperity of all embodied beings; you are the giver of delight to those with devoted hearts; and you are the affection of those who dwell in love.

You are the splendor of those who have performed adornments; you are the peace of those whose actions are joyful; you are the delusion of the ignorant; and you are the fame of those who sacrifice according to the proper sequence.
You are the great tide of the oceans; you are the grace of the graceful; you are the origin of all things; and you are the stability of those who adorn the world.
Thus, O Goddess, you move through the worlds in manifold forms. O Giver of Boons, those who behold you and those who worship you shall all certainly attain their desires; of this there is no doubt.
Thus she was born, being praised by Brahmā; that great goddess Ekānaṃśā should also be meditated upon with devotion. (32)
Sanatkumāra said: Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the *Harasiddhi*, which bestows perfect accomplishment—the means by which Hara attained success in winning Pārvatī.
Two powerful Dānavas were born named Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa; having uprooted the entire heaven, they arrived at Mount Kailāsa.

Having seen there the Lord of the Mountain, who held an upraised eye and an elephant-goad in his hand, and who was the Lord of Serpents with the moon and the skull-staff held in his right hand; || 3 ||
"Let the gambling proceed with just a single board, while you prattle 'O Goddess! and say 'I am your slave! (4)
When the god had thus become impassioned, those two thorns of the gods arrived; the attendants of Śiva were driven away by Nandin, and the two were forbidden entry.
Then Nandin was pierced by those two tridents; from both his left and right sides, a great deal of blood flowed forth.
Seeing Nandin, the son of Śilāda, thus struck, that goddess was meditated upon by Hara; she stood bowed before him.
"Let those two great Daityas be slain; I shall kill them!"—saying these words, he seized a terrible mallet and, out of extreme rage, struck them.
When she saw that the two Dānavas, who were proud of their strength, had been slain by her, Hara said to her: "O Caṇḍī, the wicked Dānavas have been destroyed."
"Therefore, you shall attain renown in the world by the name Harasiddhi. From that time forward, that goddess became known as Harasiddhi at Mahākāla, for she bestows the perfection of Hara.
The best of men who beholds Harasiddhi with supreme devotion obtains his desires inexhaustibly; upon death, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
He who beholds the primordial Siddhi, the Great Goddess, eternal and whose nature is the void, as Harasiddhi, obtains his desired fruit.
He who remembers the four-syllabled mantra "Hara Siddhi" shall have no fear of enemies, nor does poverty ever arise for him.
The man who worships Harasiddhi on the Mahānavamī day and offers a buffalo as a sacrificial oblation shall become a sovereign ruler upon the earth.
Worshipped on the ninth day, the goddess Harasiddhi, the beloved of Hara, is always pleased with men, O Vyāsa, and bestows unsurpassed fruit.
She is meritorious and pure, bestowing happiness everywhere; when remembered, worshipped, or seen, she grants wealth, sons, and bliss. (16)
On the Mahānavamī day, all those buffaloes and other animals that are slain go to heaven; no sin exists for those who kill them.
Sanatkumāra said: If a man, with devotion, beholds Vaṭayakṣiṇī for one month and worships her with golden flowers, his spiritual success (siddhi) shall not fail.
Thus ends the majesty of Vaṭayakṣiṇī. Having bathed at Piśācaka, especially on the fourteenth lunar day, the man who devoutly gives sesame seeds is not reborn as a Piśāca.
Whatever is given with a specific intent becomes even more inexhaustible; indeed, that family is liberated from the state of being a piśāca—of this there is no doubt. (3)
By whose name a man bathes, he is liberated from the state of a piśāca; or whoever should give here jars or water-pots along with cakes.
For him there is indeed eternal liberation; no deceased person is born in his lineage as a ghost, provided he is a devotee of Rudra with his senses subdued after beholding Śiprāguṃpheśvara. || 5 ||
A man who, having bathed, beholds Agastyeśvara with great devotion, is liberated from all sins, just as a serpent is freed from its slough.
O Vyāsa, having abandoned the abode of Yama, that man goes to the world of Rudra—he who, having bathed in the Śiprā, beholds the auspicious Lord Ḍhuṇḍheśvara.
O Vyāsa, he obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; there is no doubt about this, because in ancient times, O Vyāsa, the hand-drum (ḍamaru) was sounded here by the God.
He was proclaimed by the god as Ḍamarukeśvara by name; whatever man should behold the god Ḍamarukeśvara with devotion, [he shall attain his goal]. (9)
He shall have no fear of disease at all, and upon death, he shall go to the city of Śiva—that man who beholds the Lord of the beginningless aeons with devotion. (10)
He obtains a kingdom and heaven just like the god Purandara; O Vyāsa, he shall always be an object of envy even for the gods.
He who beholds Siddheśvara, Vīrabhadra, and Caṇḍikā shall rejoice, endowed with enjoyments, for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Having bathed in the Triviṣṭapa Tīrtha and beheld Svarṇajāleśvara, a person attains success and victory everywhere in this very life.
One should worship the God with gold; one is liberated from all sins. Having bathed, the man who beholds the auspicious Karkoṭeśvara with devotion [attains the same].
He who beholds the eternal Mahāmāyā with supreme devotion has no fear of serpents, nor does poverty ever arise for him. (15)
That man who worships Kapāleśvara with supreme devotion is liberated from the illusion of Viṣṇu and goes to the highest abode. || 16 ||
He shall be liberated from great sins even if he be a slayer of a Brahmin, having bathed at Svargadvāra and beheld the god Bhairava.
From the sight of that deity, the fruit of a hundred sacrifices shall be obtained.
Sanatkumāra said: Now I shall further describe another deity worshipped by the thirty gods, named Hanumatkeśvara, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who, having bathed in the Śiva lake, beholds Dhanumatkeśvara, rejoices in the world of Vāyu for thousands of crores of kalpas.
Vyāsa said: O sinless one, regarding that Hanumatkeśvara who was previously mentioned by you, tell me the ancient narrative concerning his former history.
Sanatkumāra said: Formerly, a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, who was a thorn to the three worlds, was struck down in Laṅkā by Viṣṇu in the form of Rāma. || 4 ||
Having slain that wicked one and taken Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, he returned to his own city together with the monkeys and the bears.
Having attained the kingdom there, surrounded by sages, at the conclusion of the discourse, Agastya, the best of munis, was addressed by Rāma.
And then he asked about the prowess of the two, Śambhu and Vātajaya; at that time, Agastya, the best of sages, spoke to the son of Daśaratha.
Just as the god Maheśvara displays valor in battle, so too is the son of Vāyu to be known as incomparable; I tell you this truth. (8)
Having heard this, Hanumān then reflected: "That which was done here by the best of sages, who is like Hara, has been witnessed directly by Rāghava."
I shall go to the city of Laṅkā to request a single *liṅga* from the illustrious lord of the Rākṣasas, the sinless Vibhīṣaṇa.
Then, having gone to Laṅkā, he spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa: "O illustrious one, give me a single beautiful liṅga."
And it was said by the Lord of the Rākṣasas: "Take this according to your liking; these six Liṅgas were indeed established by Rāvaṇa. (12)

"O observer of noble vows, O monkey, tell me which of these lingas is desired by you; previously, before the Trailokyavijaya [rite], this was promised to me by my high-souled brother. I shall grant that very thing to you this very day; this is the truth. (13)
Then Hanumān seized the linga, which resembled a pearl; "O hero, O sinless one, give me that which is seen here. (14)
Having heard Hanumān’s words, Vibhīṣaṇa then said: "O great hero, this Liṅga which you have taken was given [to me]. (15)
Indeed, it is heard in ancient lore that this very Liṅga, Dhaneśvara, was worshipped at the three times of day by one endowed with devotion to Rudra. || 16 ||
Indeed, when he was bound by Rāvaṇa, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) became liberated through the power of this Liṅga. || 17 ||
By the grace of that Liṅga, Dhaneśa, the protector of wealth, took that great Liṅga and the monkey then became healthy.
Sanatkumāra said: Having taken the Liṅga, he then set out through the clear sky and reached the city of Avantikā on the very seventh day.
Having stationed [the image] there on the bank of the Rudrasaras lake, he then performed his ablutions; he then reflected upon going for the purpose of worshipping Mahākāla.
Desiring to remove that sign, he was unable to remove it.
Then the Lord, being established there, said to that son of Vāyu: "O Hanumān, install me in this sacred field by means of your own name alone."
Moreover, it shall become famous in the world as Hanumatkeśvara; for a linga as lofty as a mountain was installed there by the son of the Wind-god.
If a man should behold the auspicious Hanumatkeśvara on a Saturday, he shall have no fear of enemies and shall attain victory in battle. (24)
Neither fear of thieves, nor poverty, nor an evil rebirth shall befall him who performs the oil-consecration at the auspicious Dhanuṣkoṭīśvara.
His diseases will dissolve away and affliction by malevolent planets shall not arise; those men who behold him with devotion will attain liberation. || 26 ||
Śrī Sanatkumāra said: Whoever should behold Yameśvara after bathing him with water mixed with sesame seeds, and having smeared him with saffron, should then worship him with blue lotuses; ||| 1 ||
One should burn black aloe-wood incense and offer sesame seeds and rice; whoever thus worships the Lord, the God who holds a trident in his hand.
Wherever one may die, Yama shall be like a father.

Thus ends the majesty of Yameśvara. Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, I shall describe the supreme sacred site, the most excellent among all holy places; it is known by the name Rudrasaras and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should behold Śiva as Koṭeśvara; he is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra. || 5 ||
Listen now to the fruit one obtains by performing a *śrāddha* at that very place: it is equal to ten horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) and a hundred *vājapeya* sacrifices.
O Vyāsa, whatever is offered at Koṭitīrtha for the sake of the ancestors obtains a fruit ten million times greater; of this there is no doubt.
All that becomes multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt. A man who, having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, meditates upon the Supreme Imperishable (Paramākṣara), [attains the same result].
O Brahmin, he who rises early in the morning and performs his bath there is indeed liberated from all sins, just as a serpent is freed by its slough.
Having beheld the god Mahākāla, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows; a man who has bathed at Koṭitīrtha and fasted for seven nights, being pure, [obtains the same].
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand cāndrāyaṇa penances; indeed, he who performs a vigil there enjoys infinite fruit.
Having performed worship with perfumes and flowers preceded by the great ceremonial bath, he who thus passes the night, fasting and with senses subdued, [attains the fruit].
One obtains the fulfillment of all desires, which is difficult even for the gods to attain; therefore, one should worship the Lord there on the full moon day of either Kārttika or Vaiśākha.
With seasonal perfumes and flowers, as well as most beautiful garments, along with camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and agallochum.
Having made equal portions, one should grind them on a stone slab; by anointing Mahākāla with this, one becomes an attendant of Rudra. 15.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, I shall diligently describe the pilgrimage to Mahākāla, which is auspicious, conducive to welfare, meritorious, and bestows the world of merit.
Having bathed in the lake of Rudra and beheld the auspicious Koṭeśvara, one should then pay obeisance and proceed to the eternal Mahākāla.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Thirty-three with perfumes, flowers, and prostrations, and having bowed down, one should then proceed to the deity Kapālamocana.
Right there, the Lord of the Gods placed his skull upon the earth; as soon as the skull was set down, an excellent Liṅga appeared there.
The place named Kapālamocana destroys all sins; there, one should indeed perform an ablution with a hundred palas of clarified butter.
O best of Brahmins, at the completion of the full period—whether by half of that, or by a quarter, provided one is free from stinginess regarding wealth—he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having paid homage, one should then go to the supreme Kapileśvara; by the sight of this deity, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
From there, one should go with a concentrated mind to the god Hanumatkeśvara; O Vyāsa, incomparable sovereignty arises from the sight of him.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, one should go to the eternal Mahādeva known as Paippala, by the mere sight of whom liberation shall be attained.
Then, endowed with devotion and faith, one should go to Svapneśvara; by the sight of this deity, an evil dream is destroyed.
From there, one should go to Mahādeva, the Lord Īśāna, whose face is turned in every direction; by the mere sight of whom one becomes the lord of the entire universe. || 11 ||
Then, having conquered anger and subdued the senses, one should go to Someśvara; by the sight of him, one is liberated from defects such as the disease of leprosy.
O Vyāsa, one should then go with a concentrated mind to Vaiśvānareśvara; by the sight of it, prosperity always arises for him in this world.
Then one should go to Lakulīśa, who holds a citron in his hand; by the mere sight of him, the state of Rudra is attained—of this there is no doubt. (14)
From there, O Great God, one should go to the supreme Gadyāṇeśvara, by the mere sight of whom all perfections (siddhis) are born. || 15 ||
Constantly entreated by the gods and worshipped for the sake of attaining success, he is therefore renowned as Abhyarthiteśvara, the Leader of Obstacles (Vighnanāyaka). || 16 ||
Then one should go to the eternal Mahākāla, who is advanced in age; by seeing him, there is no disease, nor old age, nor affliction—of this there is no doubt. (17)
Then one should go to Vighnanāśa, the Lord of Beings, who possesses supreme power; with devotion and a concentrated mind, one should perform his ritual bath with a hundred jars [of water].
And by performing a bath for its sake alone, all perfections are obtained; moreover, O Vyāsa, heaven is always attained through the mere sight of it.
Without bypassing that son [of Yama], one should then proceed to Daṇḍapāṇi; by the mere sight of whom the world of Yama is no longer seen.
Then, endowed with devotion and faith, one should go to Puṣpadanta; by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins. (21)
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should go to Guhya Mahākāla; by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from secret sins. (22)
Then, established in meditative absorption, one should go to the supreme Durvāseśvara, by the mere sight of which a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Having restrained the breath in the presence of Durvāsas and approached the great Durgā Gaurī, one should release the breath immediately thereafter.
There, one should by all means worship Ucchvāsa-vimocinī; thereafter, one should go to Kāleśvara, the Great Lord, the God of gods.
By the mere sight of whom one does not behold the realm of Yama, one should then go to Vidhīśa, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
One whose deafness does not cease merely by seeing him should indeed proclaim his own name, place of residence, and lineage. (27)
If one does not proclaim his name, that pilgrimage becomes fruitless; therefore, O Vyāsa, having sat down before the God with a concentrated mind, [one should do so].
Then, filled with devotion, he should speak after bowing down again and again: "O Maheśvara, by your grace, this pilgrimage has been successfully completed by me. (29)
"O Lord of the World, lift me up from this terrible ocean of saṃsāra! Whoever circumambulates Mahākāla according to this rite [shall be liberated]. (30)
By him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated; the fruit that one obtains by giving a hundred thousand cows to a hundred thousand brahmins—[that fruit he has obtained]. || 31 ||
Having offered that fruit to the God of gods with supreme devotion and performed a circumambulation, one should circumambulate Mahākāla.
"Śaṅkara has told me that at every step there is the fruit of a sacrifice; [there are] sixty thousand crores and six hundred crores. (33)
In this world, they become honored through the worship of Yātreśvara; he who performs such a pilgrimage is solely intent on meditation upon Śiva.
One should give a thousand-fold sacrificial fee; hear the fruit of his merit: he is liberated from the sins committed in seven births—of this there is no doubt. (35)
Having thus completed the pilgrimage and returned to his own home, the man [should feed] twenty-six excellent brahmins, equal in number to the deities of the pilgrimage.

One should feed the devotees of Śiva who are intent on meditation upon Śiva; having given them clothing along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and having obtained their permission, one should dismiss them.
Following the order of the procession, one should proceed to each successive doorway; thereafter, one should follow the instructor of Dharma, who is accompanied by all the ritual implements.
One should give a milch cow, free from any stinginess regarding wealth; thereafter, O Vyāsa, one should eat oneself, accompanied by all one's servants.
One should feed the miserable, the helpless, the poor, the blind, the disabled, and others; listen as I describe to you the fruit that is declared for this act. (40)
Having delivered a hundred lineages, including his mother and father, he, being composed in mind, rejoices in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Sanatkumāra said: He who worships the deity known as Vālmīkeśvara, remaining silent and intent on meditation, shall attain the power of poetic composition. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said: How did this Lord Vālmīkeśvara originate here, and who is he, by the mere sight of whom poetic genius is produced?
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, formerly there was a brahmin named Sumati born of the lineage of Bhṛgu; his wife was Kauśikī, endowed with beauty and youth. (3)
A son was born to him, named Agniśarman; even though he was urged by his father, he did not care for the study of the Vedas.
Then, after a long time, a drought occurred; having fallen into that calamity, he subsequently took refuge in the southern direction.
Then that wise brahmin, together with his wife and his son, reached a foreign land and a forest, where he established and took up residence in a hermitage.
Agniśarman fell into association with Ābhīras and robbers; whoever comes along that path and kills him is a doer of evil.

Memory was lost, the Vedas had departed, the lineage was gone, and the sacred tradition had vanished; then, at a certain time, by the occasion of a pilgrimage to holy places (tīrthayātrā), [he arrived].
The seven sages of virtuous vows arrived by that path; then Agniśarman, seeing them and desiring to kill them, spoke this.
"Cast off these garments, as well as your umbrellas and sandals; for you must be slain by me, as you are destined for the abode of Yama."
Having heard those words of his, Atri spoke these words: "How can the sin born of our oppression reside in your heart? We are ascetics who have set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords. (11)
Agniśarman said: "I have a mother, a father, a son, and a most venerable wife; I always support them—this is firmly established in my heart. (12)
Atri said: "Quickly ask your father and the others regarding what is earned through their own actions; if sin is being committed for your sake, let it be told to whom that belongs. (13)
If they said to you, "Do not kill living beings falsely," [then you should do so]. || 14 ||
Agniśarman said: "Never before have I been asked such words by you; it is only through your speech that awakening now arises within me. (15)
"Having gone, I shall ask them all: 'What is the nature of each, and of what kind is it? You all remain right here until my return. (16)
Having spoken thus, he quickly departed and said to his father: "By the obstruction of dharma and by the oppression of living beings... (17)
"A very great evil is seen; tell me, to whom does it belong? The father replied, 'Likewise, O mother, no demerit belongs to us here.'"
"You know what you do, what has been done by you, and what is yet to be done. Having heard those words of the two of them, the wife spoke these words: (19)
She also said, "The sin is not mine; this sin is yours alone. He spoke those words to his son, and he replied, "I am but a child. (20)
Having understood their heart and their conduct in its true essence, and thinking "I am ruined," he sought refuge with us ascetics.
Then, having hurled the black club with which living beings had indeed been slain, and having disheveled his hair, he stood quickly before the sages.
Having prostrated himself like a falling staff, he then spoke these words: "I have no mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son. (23)
"Delivered from all these [sins], I have come to you for refuge; you ought to save me from hell by granting me excellent instruction. (24)
Seeing him speaking thus, the sages then said to Atri: "By your word, his awakening has been brought about. (25)
"O Sage, let this disciple be favored by you. Having said "So be it," he then spoke to them: "Practice meditation on the Fire."

By means of this yoga of meditation and the recitation of the great mantra, you—who have committed many difficult-to-cross, most terrible sins and have been a slayer of people—shall attain supreme perfection while staying at the foot of this tree.
Having spoken thus, they all departed as they desired; and he, that yogi, remained there for thirteen years, absorbed in meditation upon Him.
And there, upon that immovable [pillar], an anthill arose; meanwhile, the sages who had returned by that path heard [the sound] there.
Filled with wonder at the sound uttered by him from the anthill, they then dug into the anthill using large stakes that had become like wood.
Seeing him, the sages raised him up with due courtesy; then that brahmin paid homage to all those eminent sages.
Bowing down before them, whose splendor was kindled by asceticism, he said to them: "By your grace, auspicious knowledge has been obtained by me today. (32)
"I am wretched; I have been rescued by all of you from being submerged in the mire of sin. To him, those most righteous ones spoke these words: || 33 ||
"O son, because you have remained in this anthill with single-minded concentration, your name shall become famous on earth as 'Vālmīki'."

Having spoken thus, the sages, endowed with ascetic power, departed for their own directions. When the chief sages had gone, Vālmīki, the best among those who practice austerity, arrived at Kuśasthalī and propitiated Maheśvara.
Therefore, having attained poetic genius, he composed the delightful poem known as the Rāmāyaṇa, which they call the very first narrative established in this world. (36)
From that time forward, O Vyāsa, the Lord of Gods became renowned in Avantī by the name Vālmīkeśvara, bestowing the gift of poetic talent upon men.
Thus has been described to you the supreme Liṅga Vālmīkeśvara, by the mere sight of which poetic genius is attained.
Sanatkumāra said: Having worshipped Śukreśvara with white flowers and ointments, and having prostrated with devotion, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 1 ||
O Vyāsa, having beheld Bhīmeśvara and worshipped him with devotion and effort, a person incurs no fear in battle, at night, in water, or in fire.
Having bathed Gargeśvara with sesame oil and worshipped him with bilva leaves, a person shall attain an increase in righteousness.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, and having bathed [the deity] with a prastha of sesame seeds and sesame water, and having worshipped with sesame seeds, one shall always obtain happiness.
Having given a thousand cows with a particularly devoted disposition, that man, liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, goes to the world of Rudra. || 5 ||
Having worshipped Kāmeśvara with ointments such as saffron and other unguents, one goes to heaven by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will; of this there is no doubt.
Having paid homage to Cūḍāmaṇi on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, a man does not go to a degraded birth; he becomes one whose intellect is fixed on righteousness.
Having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and duly worshipped Caṇḍīśvara, one is not tainted even by the grief arising from having stepped over the remains of an offering (nirmālya).
Having visited all these holy places of Maheśvara, which are meritorious, a man whose mind is purified and whose self is cultivated on this earth goes to the most delightful realm of Śambhu.
Vyāsa said: O Sage, you have described the sacred places situated in the secret realm; now tell me the extent of Mahākālavana.
Sanatkumāra said: "Just as it was previously heard by me from Brahmā himself as he spoke, that I shall now declare to you; listen as I speak."
Extending for a full yojana and adorned on its four sides with golden arches from which strings of pearls were suspended.
There the gates shine, adorned with golden pitchers placed upon them—gates featuring white lotus-shaped fronts and embellished with many jewels.
And the mighty gatekeepers, appointed by Maheśvara, shine at those gates, bestowing grace upon the worlds.
Piṅgaleśa, the youthful fire-god, stands in the east; he is fair-complexioned and accompanied by his attendants, facing toward the sacred ford.
On the south as well is the great yogin Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara; at the western gate stands Vitteśa, facing toward the sacred field (kṣetra).
Appointed indeed by Maheśa, he took his station in the western quarter; and having resorted to the northern quarter, he remained there as Uttareśvara.
That practitioner was appointed by Śaṅkara as the overseer of all affairs; those very righteous men who dwell here within the sacred precinct [were also under his care].
Those who die on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or at the conjunction of the sun and moon, go to the city of Rudra in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
Having paid homage to the five Īśānīs in both direct and reverse order, one who has fasted for a single day should meditate upon Maheśvara.
Thus, O Brahmin, he who undertakes the pilgrimage to Pañceśānī is liberated from all sins, even those committed over many lifetimes. (12)
By this very body he goes to the world of Rudra; furthermore, I shall explain to you another Pañceśānī so that it may be performed with ease.
Listen likewise as I shall proclaim that which destroys all sins: having bathed at dawn on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) with a concentrated mind in the Rudra-lake.
Having performed the śrāddha and having bowed to Mahākāla and Īśāna, the Lord, one should then reach Piṅgaleśa, bathe, and perform the śrāddha.
Then, having approached the god Gaṇeśa Piṅgaleśvara and having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should return.
Having reached Mahākāleśvara and bathed once more, with his senses subdued, he should worship the self-existent, eternal Lord of the gods.
Having observed the vow of eating only at night, he should spend the night in the northeast, meditating upon Maheśāna while laying his body upon the ground.
On the twelfth day, having bathed in the morning as before, a man should go to Kāyāvarohaṇa and worship just as he did at Piṅgaleśvara.
Then, on the thirteenth day, one should likewise worship Bilveśa in the west; and on the fourteenth day, one should worship Uttareśvara in the north.
On the new moon day, having bathed and purified himself, one should worship Mahākāleśvara with perfumes, flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings.

Having performed singing, dancing, and so forth, and having prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness; then, having completed the pilgrimage as previously described, one should return to one's own home.
One should feed five Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva, having bowed down to those twice-born ones who are embodiments of the deity and dwellers of Mahākāla. (23)
Having worshipped with gold, fine garments, and new threads, one should give a reddish-brown chariot at Piṅgalaka and an elephant at Kāyāvarohaṇa.
Having given a horse at Bilveśvara, and having given a bull in the northern [shrine], and having given a cow together with all its utensils at Mahākāla; || 25 ||
O Vyāsa, listen to the fruit of merit for one who acts in this manner. || 26 ||
Together with his paternal and maternal lineages, he rejoices in heaven upon celestial chariots that fulfill all desires, amidst the songs and dances of Apsarases.

Thus ends the majesty of the pilgrimage to Pañceśānī. Whoever performs the circumambulation of Kuśasthalī according to the prescribed rule, by him the entire earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated. (28)
But the man who beholds Padmāvatī, worships her with lotuses, and offers incense along with food offerings, shall go to the city of Brahmā upon death. || 29 ||
O Vyāsa, having worshipped a golden Śṛṅgāṭikā with flowers resembling gold with great devotion, he goes to the abode of Śiva.
But he who beholds the goddess Avantī, renowned throughout the three worlds, travels by means of a desire-yielding celestial chariot to the city of Indra.
He who worships the goddess Amarāvatī with lotuses and devotion rejoices eternally in heaven, ever delighted along with the immortals.
He who, with a concentrated mind and devotion, beholds the goddess Ujjayinī, becomes endowed with all sovereign powers and is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 33 ||
And whoever, with concentrated mind and devotion to Rudra, beholds Viśālā, is liberated from the three kinds of sins; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (34)

Thus ends the majesty of the seven kalpas. Listen, O Vyāsa, to the great tīrtha which was worshipped by Brahmā in ancient times, known as Akūreśvara, where the Grandfather (Brahmā) attained perfection.
Having performed the worship of the deity there on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, fasting, with senses subdued, pure, and self-controlled, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
A man staying at home in the morning should not speak with anyone; having beheld the god Akrūreśvara, he shall obtain the fruit of a gift of gold. || 37 ||
Thus ends the majesty of Akrūreśvara. He who, being pure, having bathed, and with senses subdued, beholds Brahmā, is liberated from terrible sin and, upon death, shall go to the world of Brahmā.
Seated in the lotus posture, Brahmā was meditating upon the supreme state when he was addressed by Vasiṣṭha and other eminent sages concerning the origins of karma.
The sages said: "The Ādityas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, as well as both the Aśvins, and the Pitṛs who are worshipped on earth by human beings throughout the worlds—" || 40 ||
The planets, the sun, the stars, the yakṣas, the elephants of the quarters, the oceans, fire, and wind—all these gods and we ourselves are proclaimed to be portions of you. (41)
O Lord of Gods, how do you meditate? Tell us all of this.
Brahmā said: There are two sciences that constitute the nature of reality, namely the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā); these two are my two forms, eternal and consisting of my embodied self.
The sages said: O Grandfather, how may we know you, the supreme and all-pervading Lord, by whose sight the highest perfection arises for us?
Brahmā said: There is a supreme sacred field of Maheśvara known as Kuśasthalī, where the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the husband of Pārvatī, was [propitiated] by me while seeking to perform a sacrifice.
Requested by that god, I was addressed by the Supreme Lord: "The Grandfather [Brahmā] has declared this field to extend for more than a full yojana in every direction. (46)

"O Lord, [the boon] was granted by me to you with the exception of Mahākālavana; he was forbidden by me there in that forest, for he was hidden out of anger. And Kapardin said there: 'We shall not come into your presence.'"
Indeed, the sacrifice was then commenced through the undertaking of Nārāyaṇa; nevertheless, the sacrifice was recognized by me by Śambhu, the God of gods. 48.
Then Kapardīśa arrived at the sacrificial enclosure for the sake of alms; he was then addressed there by the officiating priests: "Do not stay here, you loathsome one! (49)
And there he was addressed by Kapardin: "I shall go again. Having spoken thus, he indeed placed his skull-bowl upon the ground there.
The matted-haired Supreme Lord went to the Śiprā river to bathe. When Kapardin had gone to the Śiprā, it was said by the twice-born: || 51 ||

For how can a fire-oblation be performed when the sacrificial pan remains in the assembly hall? The wise have declared of old that those things which are not made of clay pans require purification. || 52 ||
That skull was lifted up by the Sadasya himself with his hand; when it was thrown away, another appeared, and when that was thrown away, yet another appeared again. (53)
Thus, O best of sages, no end to the skulls could be found; perceiving Rudra with matted hair, they came to him for refuge.
Then Maheśvara, pleased by my devotion, granted me his vision; the Lord, the Master, with a skull in his hand, spoke to me.
"Choose a boon, O Brahmin, whatever dwells in your mind. There is nothing that cannot be given by me to you; I shall truly grant you everything. (56)
"O Four-faced One, this supreme abode has been granted by me; cause it to be built according to your desire, in accordance with the four castes. (57)
To the Supreme Lord, the Bestower of Boons, who was speaking thus, I replied, "So be it," and said in that assembly, "No other boon has been chosen by me. (58)
Indeed, the city named Ujjayinī was established there at Kuśasthalī; immediately thereafter, I created the Mandākinī pool there.
O brahmins, having bathed there, one is liberated from all sins; on that [day], one should place four auspicious jars filled with wealth in the four directions.
On the full moon day of Kārttika as well as Māgha, one should cause these to be given to a person learned in the four Vedas (cāturvidya), together with sesame seeds, clothing, fruit, and cakes.
First, [he should offer] to the Ṛgveda; to the Yajurveda on the south; to the Sāmaveda on the west; and likewise to the Atharvaveda on the north.
"Having thus dedicated [the gift] to the Vedas, let my grandfather be pleased; now listen with concentrated minds to the merit that is indeed produced by this act. (63)

Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) shall likewise be attained at Mandākinī; bathing there is a thousandfold more effective, and recitation (jāpya) becomes a hundred-thousandfold more meritorious.
A gift given at Mandākinī should be known to possess ten millionfold merit; of this there is no doubt. When the month of Kaumuda arrives, one should perform the gift of a cow there.
By giving a cow made of ghee on the full moon of Kārttika, one made of sesame seeds on that of Māgha, and a cow made of water on that of Vaiśākha, one shall be liberated from sins.
Vocal, mental, and physical sin, as well as whatever misdeed arises from action—all such evil shall perish by the mere sight of the Mandākinī.
No sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to the Mandākinī is seen upon the earth; by the mere sight of it, one rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
He who performs a ritual bath in the Mandākinī and offers a śrāddha ceremony on either the new moon or the full moon day shall rejoice in the world of the ancestors.
But that man who constantly beholds the Grandfather with devotion [attains the merit] of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices. || 70 ||
This is appropriate; there is no doubt in this matter, O ascetics; this is the truth. Then, when that Manvantara has passed and the Vaivasvata Manvantara has arrived once more...
In that very same madman’s guise, Maheśvara, with his upper body remaining visible, entered the sacrificial session of Brahmā and was seen by those best of the twice-born.
Those brahmins uttered curses, while others reviled him; other twice-born men struck his penis with dust as they cursed him.
Others, arrogant in their strength, strike him with clods of earth and clubs; some, having seized his crown of matted hair, drag him away.
They indeed inquire about the practice of the vow: "By whom was this vow revealed? Since there are women here as well, how was this performed by you? (75)
If such conduct was performed by Brahmā himself, or by Viṣṇu, or even by the god Giriśa, then by whom has this evil deed been committed? (76)
"Do not mock the Lord of Gods, for you are indeed worthy of death by us today. While Śaṅkara was being struck in that manner by those brahmins, [he remained there].
Smiling, the Supreme Lord said to all the Brahmins: "Why do you strike me, as if I were mad and deprived of my senses? (78)
"You are all compassionate and established in a state of loving-kindness"—to Hara, the god who spoke thus while assuming the form of a rogue, [they replied: 79.
Deluded by the illusion of that god, those twice-born ones once again struck the one with matted hair with their hands and feet, O brahmins.
Being beaten by those brahmins, he fell into a state of extreme anger; then the Lord cursed them, saying, "You shall be deprived of the Vedas. (81)
With their hair tied in topknots, carrying clubs, they lived off the wives of others; they were devoted to gambling and prostitutes, and were abandoned by both father and mother. (82)
Neither shall there be paternal wealth nor even knowledge for the son; those by whom my remnant has been destroyed shall all be deprived of their senses. (83)
Beggars of fierce alms, subsisting on the food of others and devoid of wealth and grain, will praise themselves.
And as for those brahmins who showed compassion toward me while I was being struck there—their wealth, their sons, and their male and female slaves and so forth [shall be mine]. 85.
"And women shall indeed be born of noble lineage by virtue of my boon. Having thus bestowed both the curse and the boon, the Lord vanished from sight.
Then, when the god had departed, the twice-born, considering him to be the omnipresent Lord Śaṅkara, went to Mahākālavana, searching for him with great effort.
Having bathed in the lake of Rudra and recited the Śatarudriya, at the conclusion of the recitation, the God spoke to them with an unembodied voice: (88)
"Untruth has never been spoken by me, even in jest; how then could there be pleasure [in falsehood]? O Brahmins, I shall again bestow my favor upon you. (89)
Those Brahmins who are peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to me, and established in me—their lineage is never severed, nor their wealth, nor their progeny. (90)
Those who are devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, those who are full of devotion for Janārdana, and those who worship Brahmā and the Sun, the mass of splendor; || 91 ||
"No evil exists for those whose minds are established in friendship. Having said this much, the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World, became silent.
Having thus obtained the curse and the boon from Maheśvara, the God of gods, they all returned together to where the divine Grandfather resided.
Then, having propitiated Viriñci with their recitations, they stood before him; Brahmā, being pleased, said to them, "Let a boon be chosen from me as well."
All those best of the twice-born were satisfied by that speech of Brahmā: "O Brahmins, what boon should be requested now that the Grandfather is fully gratified? (95)
There, some brahmins said, "We shall indeed choose the Vedas"; then others said, "Let wealth and grain be chosen without hesitation."
Others said: "What need have we for wealth if the Grandfather is pleased? There are the Agnihotra sacrifices, the Vedas, and various scriptures. (97)
"May the worlds become peaceful and prosperous through our boon!"—as the brahmins were speaking thus, anger took possession of them. (98)
Then, intent on fighting for the sake of the boon, they prepared for battle; some fought with weapons, while others there were mere onlookers.
Some brahmins were indifferent, while others remained silent; seeing the brahmins thus engaged in combat, the Blessed One spoke to them.
Because the Brahmins were ill-advised and stood outside the hall, therefore the Brahmins have been driven from their very roots to the outposts as those who approach for battle.
But he who is indifferent, devoid of livelihood, and remains established in silence—his very existence shall indeed become the Vedas. || 2 ||
The third is the armed *gulma* who stands desiring to fight; he is one who is always devoted to the wives of others, to prostitutes, to gambling, and to theft. (3)
"That Brahmin shall indeed be of four kinds and devoid of a livelihood. Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed for his supreme abode, Vairāja.
Thus, O sages, this supreme field of mine is in the region of Avantī, which men here in the world call Devanagarī.
But for those peaceful twice-born ones who dwell in that sacred field, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to attain in my world.
At Kolāmukha, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara; at Vārāṇasī, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Badarikāśrama.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sāgara, at Rudrakoṭi, at Virūpākṣa, and likewise in the forest of Mitra; || 8 ||

Whatever perfection is obtained by men in this world through twelve years at these sacred fords and holy sites, that is obtained here in Ujjayinī in a single month, provided the mind is fixed on celibacy; of this there is no doubt.
O best of sages, this is indeed the most excellent of holy fords among all sacred sites and the supreme among all fields; it is always dear to me.
The greatness of the Mandākinī and the excellent origin of the sacred field have been told; O best of the twice-born, what else do you wish to hear further? (11)
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, having heard these words of Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha and the other sages then entered into supreme meditation.
Having meditated for a very long time, they set their minds on dwelling there; accompanied by their sacred fires and their wives, they departed for the Avanti region.
Having seen Mahākālavana and the great river Śiprā, as well as the cremation ground, the saline wasteland, and likewise the Gandhavatī river.
Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha and indeed having made their residence there, Ruci then became their desire as they recalled those words of Brahmā. || 15 ||
Urged by Arundhatī to depart, that great-souled one, the best of sages, spoke to his own wife.
Mahākāla, the river Shiprā, and the exceedingly pure Gati—O large-eyed one, who would not find pleasure in dwelling in Ujjayinī? (17)
That man who, having performed a bath in a great river—a rare opportunity—bows down to Mahākāla, shall not grieve over death. (18)
Even a dead insect or a moth shall become an attendant of Rudra; since this liberation is heard of there, how could it be abandoned by me? (19)
Having spoken thus, that foremost of sages suddenly took up residence right there; praising the splendor of the forest, he remained with the other eminent sages.
Sanatkumāra said: He who beholds Rāma and Janārdana at the place called Aṅkapāda in Avantī does not see the realm of Yama merely by the sight of them.
Vyāsa said: O great sage, how did those two come to be known here as Aṅkapāda? For one who has gone there does not see the world of Yama, even if he should be a slayer of a Brahmin.
Sanatkumāra said: For the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, the two gods Rāma and Janārdana, possessing divine forms and great splendor, descended into the lineage of Yadu.
