"What must be done for you by me? Tell me what should be done for you now that your son has been slain. Thus addressed, King Ugrasena spoke this to them: || 5 ||
Everything shall be accomplished, O Kṛṣṇa, for nothing is difficult to attain for you; both of you shall indeed become possessors of all-encompassing knowledge.
“You two shall indeed become accomplished in learning; go to Ujjayinī. Thereupon, Rāma and Keśava went to the brahmin Sāṃdīpani.

They both committed to memory the Vedas residing in their throats, as well as the entirety of traditional conduct, the science of archery along with its secret doctrines, and likewise its methods of withdrawal.
Within sixty-four days and nights, O twice-born one, that miracle occurred; Sāndīpani could not believe their superhuman deed.
Having reflected upon them, he then thought they were the moon and the sun arrived; thereafter, he said nothing further and went to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to bathe.
Accompanied by his disciples, the Brahmin entered Mahākālavana; at that time, those two, Rāma and Keśava, also entered together with their disciples.
Bowing to Mahākāla, he spoke to that Keśava: "Indeed, with you as their protector while remaining in human form, the gods [shall be secure]."

There was always happiness for the virtuous and for those who were ignorant; however, there was constant suffering for those people who caused pain or were always arrogant due to their strength. || 13 ||
By you two, all those kings headed by Kaṃsa have been slain; O sinless one, you must now establish the order of the sages, Siddhas, gods, and others.
Having said, "I shall do that," he paid his respects and departed; then, seeing Sāndīpani, the disciples spoke thus day after day: [15]
Whom would he not believe, since their words were so extraordinary that he himself went there to see the marvel spoken of by his disciples? (16)
Then, as those two were thus embracing, a sound arose there; when they had arrived at the house, the teacher spoke these words.
"I did not indeed recognize those two heroes born of the Yadu and Vṛṣṇi clans. Then Kṛṣṇa, having accomplished his purpose, spoke these words to Sāndīpani: || 18 ||
Delighted, he asked Rāma, "What shall I give as the preceptor's fee? Hearing those heart-warming words, the preceptor, also filled with joy, spoke.
"I desire from you a son who has died in the salt waters; for only one son was born to me, and he too was carried off by a whale. (20)
"Bring him here yourself during your pilgrimage to Prabhāsa. "So be it," Kṛṣṇa replied, and having obtained Rāma's permission, he departed.
The ocean said this to him: "The great Daitya Pañcajana, established within me, has swallowed that boy in the form of a timi fish."
Then, having slain the mighty Pañcajana who was in the form of a crocodile, he seized the conch shell situated within him—the very one who had previously swallowed him.
When Janārdana, with great ease, could not find the boy inside the belly of that crocodile from the temple of Jaleśvara, [he acted].
Thinking that he had gone to the abode of Yama, he then said to Varuṇa: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Yādavas, let a great chariot be given to me. (25)
"By which chariot the Daityas and Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, were slain by me in the city of Purā; let that chariot be given to me today. (26)
O Lord of Waters, let that chariot which was seized by the slayer of enemies and placed under my charge be returned to me, as I hold righteousness foremost. (27)

"By means of which, having conquered the King of the Dead in battle, I may see my son. Having heard this and knowing that Hari was seeking his purpose, he, with a joyful heart, gave him that unshakeable chariot in battle, [which could not be moved] by gods or asuras.
Then Hari, having beheld the chariot adorned with jewels, covered with a leopard skin and surrounded by tiger skins, [prepared for battle].
His body was adorned with various wonderful and diverse ornaments, he shone with the Garuda-bannered standard, and he was accompanied by the horses Śaibya, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Balāhaka.
Invincible by the lords of gods, dānavas, asuras, and rākṣasas, it was filled with many weapons and adorned with jewels and coral.
Resembling a thousand suns, with four beautiful faces, it was enriched by the splendor of hundreds of small bells and adorned with two chowries and a bell.
Having seen that banner of the best of bird-kings, which was as formidable in form as the fire of universal destruction, Kṛṣṇa, together with Rāma, rejoiced, his wonder having passed away.
Having performed a circumambulation and bowed down to the deities, Viṣṇu ascended his chariot, a celestial vehicle one yojana in length.

Then Janārdana, the abode of the universe, proceeded swiftly toward the direction where the realm of Yama lay; Acyuta, grasping his conch, blew it as he moved through the city filled with thousands of rays.
There, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow caused the conch to be blown; by that sound, the inhabitants of the abode of Kṛtānta were struck with terror.
The mortals within the hells, who were devoted to sinful conduct, attained happiness and became serene because of the sight of Kṛṣṇa; even the fires became tranquil.
The weapons became blunted and the various machines were shattered at that time by the sight of the God of gods.
The forest named Asipatravana became devoid of leaves, and the hell named Raurava then became free from terror.
The hell called Bhairava is not terrifying; Kumbhīpāka is without words; Śṛṅgāṭa resembles a horn; and Lohasūcī is without needles.
When the omnipresent Lord of the Universe had departed after reaching the end of hell, the river Vaitaraṇī became exceedingly difficult for men to cross. || 41 ||
Then, through the destruction of their sins, all those men dwelling in hell were liberated; having beheld Viṣṇu, the dispeller of darkness, they attained the imperishable state.
Having ascended thousands of celestial chariots on all sides and beheld the lotus-eyed Lord, they were liberated from all sins.
Then, O Sage, the entire circle of hells became empty upon the sight of that god Viṣṇu, whose nature is the universe.
Then the exceedingly fierce messengers of Kṛtānta restrained Kṛṣṇa as he was entering toward the hells to engage in battle.
The servants said: "O hero, do not bring the chariot by this path, O man! Those who seize the wives of others go to a downward state because of their sin. (46)
Even those sinful men who were commanded by Yama and were not to be released for ten million years, upon seeing you, immediately attained heaven, freed from their bonds. (47)
Having heard these words of theirs, the Slayer of Madhu, deeply moved by compassion, spoke again: "I have come for the sake of your liberation. (48)
"I am the giver of heaven to all and the warder-off of the realm of Yama; O messengers of Yamarāja, convey my words directly to Yama. (49)
Having heard these words, the messengers went quickly to Yama and reported everything that had occurred, including the liberation from hell.
Then Yama, overcome with rage, said to those servants of Yama: "Any mortal man who has arrived here is one who has violated the bounds of propriety."
"Go and restrain him; seize him and bring him here! Let this servant Narāntaka go along with his attendants. (52)
Thus addressed by Yama, that servant Narāntaka went and restrained Acyuta with fierce words.
When he did not desist, Narāntaka then became enraged; then Keśava was struck by him with exceedingly fierce arrows.
Baladeva was also struck in battle with various arrows; both of them were beaten on all sides by the terrible servants of Yama.
Taking up their two divine bows, the enraged Rāma and Janārdana struck the servants of Yama with many thousands of arrows.
Narāntaka also, oppressed by that powerful one in battle, fell down with his head split by the mace, his eyes protruding.
Then, when the heroic Narāntaka, the servant of Yama, had fallen, the army of the *kiṃkaras* became distressed and turned its back on the battle.
Being struck by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, those messengers, overcome with fear, reported to Yama that Narāntaka had been felled.
Then Yama, surrounded on all sides by his servants, went forth in a rage; then the enraged Yama said, "Never before have I been conquered by enemies."
Then he proceeds with the sounds of musical instruments—tumultuous drums and horns—as well as various *ḍamaruka* drums and Citraguptas.
The gods, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas beheld the immensely powerful Kāmapāla, the Lord of the universe, who was unshakeable in battle against Kṛtānta as he advanced.
Then all those servants, urged by Citragupta, surrounded the chariot and pierced it from every side with a flood of arrows.
And both of them struck Bala and Keśava in battle with various arrows in the fray, while Citragupta looked on.
Having torn asunder thousands of servants on all sides, Keśava—difficult to withstand in battle and protected by Kāmapāla—moved like Yama himself in the midst of the army of Death.
Then Citragupta, seeing Kiṅkara and the others shattered in battle, let out a cry of distress.

With five arrows he struck Kṛṣṇa as he approached in battle, and with eight more he hit him in the face; pierced and afflicted by the arrows, he then sat down on the floor of the chariot in distress. Seeing him thus shattered in the fray and deprived of consciousness, [the enemy was struck with fear].

Then, taking his own chariot, Kṛtānta departed while Citragupta lay fast asleep, afflicted by arrows; deprived of fame in battle and overcome with fear and agitation, he sat down, distressed and accompanied by his own troops.

The principal [forces] were shattered and the various [troops] were broken; then, hearing that Citragupta was defeated, Kāla, seeing him approaching from afar, took his excellent army, O enemy of the gods.

He fought for the destruction of creatures like the subterranean fire (vāḍava) that has begun to blaze at the end of an eon; beholding that formidable Death approaching, he covered him with arrows resembling Time itself.
Taking up his formidable staff, Kāla released it at Acyuta while the deities looked on; then that Staff of Time, the destroyer of all creatures, approached the presence of Hari.
Then the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and lords of sages were filled with supreme wonder upon beholding Rāma; and that Rāma, of infinite form, playfully seized the blazing staff of Time (Kāla).

When Kāla had seized him by force in battle and was about to release the Staff of Death (Kāladaṇḍa) once more for the destruction of Time itself, [Balarāma], quickly approaching there in the midst of the fray, then restrained Kṛṣṇa.
"Do not release [it]," the Creator said to Kāla, who wields the weapon of Time, "O Bala! By you, O hero, being powerful, this earth—the support of all moving and unmoving beings—is sustained. (74)

O God, you are borne upon the head; in this cycle of existence, there is no one equal to you. By you, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, is always carried upon your lap. O Rāma, who else is equal to you, who is capable of consuming the world? You are the creator of the world, the protector of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the lord of the world.
Even he whom you protect—Viṣṇu, the sole leader of the universe—who here is capable of praising him, and who is worthy of speaking his virtues? (77)
"Then, because we were overcome by Viṣṇu while staying upon your lap," having said this to Baladeva, they spoke these words again to Vāsudeva.
And the four-faced one, surrounded by the gods, spoke this hymn of praise: "O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Show mercy toward this terrible Time (Kāla)."
For this man does not recognize you, the approaching Viṣṇu, the sole leader of the universe, the Lord of the World, and the savior from the ocean of hell.
O Blessed One, formerly you indeed established Yama in his office; O Lord, Yama was appointed for the sake of hell for those men who commit evil deeds. (81)
Therefore, O Lord of the World, O Supreme Person, may this be forgiven; O All-pervading One, show mercy to him and speak whatever you wish to say. (82)
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa said: "O Creator, listen to my preceptor Sāndīpani; his son has been brought back by him, and thus we two have come here. (83)
"O best of gurus, let the preceptor’s fee be offered to this most excellent one; since it was indeed promised by us both, O Lord, let it be fulfilled. (84)
Having heard this, the Grandfather summoned Yama, who had been defeated in battle, and said: "Do whatever Viṣṇu tells you. (85)
Having heard that, Dharmarāja spoke thus to Viriñci: "O Blessed One, Creator of the Universe, this path was not established by you in the world."
Having reached the world of Yama, one who possesses a body is yet devoid of a body; that which goes without a body is not admitted here.
Having heard that, Brahmā himself, the all-pervading lord of this universe, the creator of the world and the heart of the world, said: "Whatever he desires, let him do. (88)
Therefore, O high-minded one, restore to the sage Sāndīpani the son whom you took from him and cast into Naraka; bring him back once more. (89)
Having heard that, Dharmarāja created for himself the form of a child born from Sāndīpani’s son.
He presented the child, endowed with beauty, to Kṛṣṇa; and that was like a marvel to all the gods.
Then, having found the son of his preceptor, the Lord, being pleased, spoke to Prajāpati: "O Brahmin, I have found the twice-born youth who is my own form."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of the World, from this day forward, those who die in the region marked by my footprints, in Avanti known as Aṅkapāda, shall not behold Yama.
In Mahākālapura, one should worship the primordial god Puruṣottama, Viśvarūpa, Govinda, Śaṅkhoddhāra, and Keśava.
Those men who behold these five deities at Kuśasthalī shall never go to the hell of Viriñci.
Likewise, by my arrival here, O Rākṣasas, may all those named Rāma be liberated from terrible sin and attain heaven. (96)
When these words had been spoken, the Creator, filled with joy, replied to Hari: "O Kṛṣṇa, may all that you have spoken be fulfilled forever."
And those who, having first prostrated before you—the primordial person, the foremost among men—shall thereafter bathe in the lake of Śiva and behold you; || 98 ||
By worshipping Mahākāla with downward-flaming [offerings], he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. Having been addressed thus, Hari took his son along with Bali. || 99 ||
Having honored the Creator and Time, Janārdana, his purpose accomplished, then ascended the chariot and blew his conch shell.
For the sake of the liberation of men who dwell in hell due to their evil deeds, they [were delivered] by the sound of the conch and by the remembrance of Acyuta.
Having ascended divine celestial chariots, they all went to heaven; that entire region became empty upon the departure of Nārāyaṇa.
Kāla, too, having received his staff from Baladeva, re-entered the city; thereafter, the Creator vanished right there.
The powerful and wise Kṛṣṇa also reached the city of Ujjayinī, accompanied by Baladeva, traveling with swift speed on a rapid vehicle.
Then the slayer of Keśin restored the son of Sāndīpani to his teacher; by this, he became free from the debt he had incurred toward him.
Thus, when Sāndīpani saw his son returned, the citizens there and the king were filled with the utmost wonder.
Considering those two heroes to be the most excellent among the best of gods, Sāndīpani honored them and spoke these words to Rāma and Janārdana.
"O two delights of the Yadu clan, as long as the world endures, your fame shall remain here in this place of mine while you both dwell within it."
I did not recognize those two heroes born of the Yadu and Vṛṣṇi clans—the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa—who had arrived for the sake of the mission of the gods.
For him there shall be no premature death, nor disease, nor an evil rebirth; indeed, having bathed here, he rejoices in the heavenly world.
Śaṅkhin, Viśvarūpa, Govinda, and likewise Cakrin—these are the four fields of Viṣṇu; Aṅkapāda is the fifth.
I shall describe their pilgrimage as it ought to be performed by the wise: having bathed in the Mandākinī and beheld Rāma and Janārdana.
Then, having bathed at Śaṅkhoddhāra, one should behold Bala and Keśava; having performed a bath there in the pool, one should worship Govinda.
Then, having seen the god of gods bearing the discus and the conch, and then having seen him with his feet marked by the sign of the wheel, one should thereafter proceed to Viśvarūpa.
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rite in the Karikuṇḍa in front of him, he should again behold Baladeva and Keśava in that same manner.
Having performed his bath in the pool, he should then worship Govinda; likewise, having beheld Cakrin and Halin, he should proceed to that Keśava.
Having bathed in the waters of the Śiprā and worshipped Keśava with devotion, a man, remaining pure, should spend that night on the Aṅkapāda mountain after returning there.
In the morning, one should feed five Brahmins of excellent vows there; a cow as a sacrificial fee should be given to the Śaṅkhin, and a horse indeed to the Viśvarūpa.
One should give an elephant to Govinda and indeed give everything to Keśava; O Brahmin, he who, having fasted on the twelfth day, worships Aṅkapāda.
Listen to the full meritorious fruit for him who performs a śrāddha with perfumes, flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings. || 120 ||
Having delivered a hundred lineages, he shall dwell for a very long time in Vaikuṇṭha with celestial chariots that fulfill all desires, and with enjoyments such as song and dance.
Having returned to this world, he is born into a pure family; he obtains an infinite lineage and shall go again to the world of Viṣṇu. || 122 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Now I shall describe another deity renowned throughout the three worlds, known as Candrāditya, who was worshipped by Candra and Āditya in ancient times.
Whoever should worship that god, who is saluted by gods and asuras, with perfumes, flowers, incenses, and various kinds of food offerings; || 2 ||
He attains the same world as the moon, the sun, and other luminaries, fulfilling all desires; he travels in a celestial chariot brilliant as the sun for as long as the moon and sun endure.

Thus ends the majesty of Candra and Āditya. Sanatkumāra said: Thereafter, one should go to Karabheśa, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the God of gods; by the mere sight of whom one is never born again in a base womb.
Vyāsa said: O Lord, I wish to hear about the god Karabheśa according to the truth; how did the god arise and become known by the name Karabheśa?
Sanatkumāra said: In ancient times, Maheśvara, the God of gods, together with the hosts of deities, sported in this forest, filled with supreme joy.
After playing for a very long time, Śaṅkara became a young elephant; and though he was Śaṅkara in the form of a young elephant, he was not recognized by the gods.
Then those gods, filled with wonder, searched for him; but when they did not see that trident-bearing god there, [they were struck with amazement].
Then, questioned by the gods, Brahmā [asked], "Where is the Lord Maheśvara? Having meditated, Brahmā beheld Hara, the master of yoga, who was concealed.
Then Brahmā, together with the gods, questioned the Leader of the Gaṇas: "O Vināyaka, Śaṅkara has not been seen by us; where has he gone?"
"Speak, salutations to you! O Lord, we shall give you sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas). Thus addressed, the leader of the Gaṇas then spoke joyfully.
"O best of the gods, this Karabha is seen as Mahādeva. Having heard these words, the gods were delighted and went toward Karabha.
"O Mahādeva, we ourselves have perceived them speaking thus"; having said this, they all went forth and stationed themselves personally in the four directions.
Having reflected thus, "How was Śaṅkara known? Maheśvara, the God of gods, became filled with wonder and then abandoned his elephantine form.
He manifested the divine Liṅga known as Karabheśvara; then all the gods, beholding it, remained prostrate in full-body obeisance (sāṣṭāṅga-praṇati). || 15 ||
From that time forward, Śaṅkara became renowned as Karabheśvara; he installed the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa) to the north of Koṭitīrtha.
He established a highly honored Karabha-liṅga, renowned by his own name; whoever, having bathed there and become pure, worships that Śiva, [attains the highest goal]. (17)
Listen now to the fruit obtained by those who offer perfumes, flowers, and food offerings; it is the merit found in all sacrifices and the fruit of all gifts. (18)
He obtains even more than that; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Then, going to Mahākāla, he shall obtain the complete fruit.
Therefore, Karabheśvara is renowned in this world as the bestower of prosperity. || 20 ||

Thus ends the majesty of Karabheśvara. Sanatkumāra said: Then Vighnanātha was worshipped by the gods with *laiḍuka* sweets; from that time forward, he became renowned as Viśveśa, the lover of *laḍḍuka* sweets. 21.
For one who worships with devotion, no obstacle arises; Vināyaka, being well-pleased, grants him all his desires.
On the fourth day, having fasted and especially bathed in the Śiprā river, one should wear red garments and worship Vināyaka with red flowers.
Having first performed the ritual bathing with water scented with red sandalwood while reciting mantras, one should smear him with red sandalwood paste and worship him.
One should likewise offer divine incense that is fragrant, O you who are fond of sweetmeat balls; as for the food offering, sweetmeat balls soaked in ghee and sugar should be presented.
No disease, fear, or obstacle shall ever arise for him; he always obtains his desired object, and upon death, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
Having descended again into the world, he is born as a lord of the earth—wise, possessed of sons, and heroic; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (27)
Thus ends the majesty of Gaṇeśa. Sanatkumāra said: He who worships Kusumeśa at Suradvāra with faith—the one saluted by gods and asuras—rejoices in the world of Śiva. (28)
He who beholds Maheśvara, the God of gods, at Jayeśvara, shall be victorious in all undertakings and goes to the world of Śiva. || 29 ||
If a human being worships the auspicious Śivaliṅga at Śivadvāra, he goes to heaven by means of a celestial vehicle and attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas. || 30 ||
Now I shall describe another excellent [liṅga], Mārkaṇḍeśvara, where the sage Mārkaṇḍeya performed most intense penance.
Having beheld that god Śaṅkara, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; with his soul purified of all sins, he becomes long-lived. || 32 ||
Listen, O Vyāsa, to that unsurpassed great place in which city that goddess Brahmāṇī resides, mounted upon a swan. (33)
She fulfills the hopes of her devotees and protects them like her own children; the Goddess is seen by those intent on peace just as a mother is.

Worshipped by Brahmā and praised by the supreme gods, that Goddess—who even before Brahmā was the bestower of perfect success—bestows all accomplishments when worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings. (35)
He who, having bathed in the Brahma-lake, beholds the auspicious Brahmeśvara, is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence and rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
Now I shall describe another unsurpassed sacrificial pool, where in former times a sacrifice accompanied by ritual fees was indeed performed by Brahmā.
The sacrificial pit that was constructed for the sake of the sacrifice is remembered as Yajñavāpī; and because a beast fell there, he is therefore remembered as Paśupati.
Having bathed in that [river] and become pure, whoever beholds Paśupati shall rescue his ancestors, O Vyāsa, even if they have entered the wombs of animals. (39)
By means of celestial chariots made of gold, jewels, pearls, and other precious materials, which go wherever one desires, he goes to the divine city of Rudra, where the Lord Maheśvara resides.
Having bathed in the Rūpakuṇḍa, a man becomes handsome; in heaven, he shall possess a form envied by the gods and Gandharvas. || 41 ||

Having bathed in the Kuṇḍa and become pure at Anaṅga, one who, being composed in mind, beholds the Lord of the gods of gods, who was formerly worshipped by Anaṅga, obtains his desired wish; upon death, he goes to the abode of Śiva. || 42 ||
Whoever performs a vigil on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha shall obtain a fruit equal to that which is proclaimed for Kedāra.
Having bathed in Karīkuṇḍa, the man who worships Viśvarūpa is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 44 ||
Having bathed at Ajāgandha and beheld the auspicious Brahmeśvara Śiva, a man instantly casts off even a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a man should worship the Lord of the Discus (Cakrasvāmin); O Vyāsa, that man is always born on earth as a universal monarch (cakravartin).
When he beholds Siddheśvara after bathing according to the proper rite, he goes to the world of Rudra by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will.
Thus ends the majesty of Yajñavāpī. Having bathed in Somavatī, the man who worships Someśvara becomes pure like the moon and rejoices in the world of Soma. (48)
Vyāsa said: There is a sacred ford named Somavatī and likewise a Liṅga named Someśvara; I wish to hear the truth of how these names came to be. (49)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to how the most beautiful Somatīrtha originated, and how this Someśvara Liṅga came to be; I tell you this truth. (50)
O Vyāsa, in former times, the divine Lord Soma, who is the supreme nourisher of the world, was a brahmin of great asceticism who served as his father.
And in Avanti, there was a highly fortunate one named Atri, a treasure-house of austerity, who performed great penance for three thousand divine years.
With his arms raised, he indeed performed penance, being entirely devoted to meditation on Brahman; then, O Vyāsa, the spiritual luster of that great-souled one ascended upwards.

From his two eyes, that splendor suddenly flowed forth, illuminating the ten directions; having seen that energy arising spontaneously from himself and surging through the ten directions, he was struck with wonder.
O Vyāsa, when all the quarters were unable to sustain it, that exceedingly unbearable energy then flowed out from the directions. (55)
Illumining all the worlds, he indeed fell upon the earth; from that, Soma was born, the cool-rayed one who is beloved by the people.
O Vyāsa, the water was produced from the Moon by that very same splendor; that river entered the Śiprā, overflowing with nectar.
Then there is the Śiprā, known as Somavatī, which bestows all perfections; by seeing the river Śiprā joined with the moon, one casts off sin. (58)
Renowned throughout the three worlds as the bestower of merit upon sinners—whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or a violator of the guru’s bed. (59)
All four are certainly liberated from sin by the mere sight [of it] here; O Sage, when the new moon and the full moon coincide on a Monday, that is the occasion.
Whatever wise person performs bathing, giving, recitation, and fire-offerings, all that becomes inexhaustible for them as long as the moon and sun endure.
Since it is held that by the offering of sesame-water and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the ancestors obtain satisfaction even at an improper time as if it were the proper time. || 62 ||
Everywhere the Siprā river is difficult to find, as are Soma, the Soma-vessel, Someśvara, and Monday; these five things beginning with the letter 'Sa' are rare to encounter.
O Vyāsa, the Śiprā, whose waters are Soma, bestows the fruit of ten million holy sites (tīrthas); it is remembered as equal to the Pitṛ-tīrtha when there is a conjunction of the new moon with Monday.

Raurava, Sūkara, Raudra, Tāla, and likewise Vinaśaka; Taptakumbha, Taptāya, and likewise Mahājvāla.

A Brāhmaṇa who sells lac, meat juices, sesame seeds, or sugarcane juice goes to the world of dogs; of this there is no doubt. || 26 ||

Having been told "So be it," Śaṅkara indeed took her hand; once, the god Śaṅkara requested his beloved for sexual union.
Having given her pleasure, she laughed while uttering his name; she then became deeply distressed and turned away from him, abandoning him.
Filled with rage and recollecting the words spoken by the god, she said: "Today I am going to the forest of asceticism in order to attain a very fair complexion."

Having bathed at Cipiṭātīrtha and bowed down to the god Śiva, O best of sages, a man never again enters a subhuman womb.
And by bathing at Vijaya and worshipping Ānandeśvara, a man is liberated from all sins and shall become victorious in the heavenly world.
Now, O Vyāsa, I shall describe another deity established at Kuśasthalī, Rāmeśvara, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Formerly, Rāma, accompanied by Maithilī and Lakṣmaṇa, arrived from Citrakūṭa and questioned the best of sages.
Rāma said: O great sage, what are the meritorious holy places (tīrthas), or what is the sacred field (kṣetra), by going to which one does not suffer separation from one's kinsmen? (13)
O Sage, I am tormented by these three: this dwelling in the forest, the death of my lordly father, and the separation from Bharata.
Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, that bull among brahmins then meditated for a very long time and spoke these words. (15)
"Well asked by you, O hero, increaser of the Raghu dynasty! My father, having entreated Śiva with devotion, obtained this sacred field. (16)
O Lord, in the region of Avanti is the city of Rāma; therein lies Kuśasthalī, which has attained fame in the world by the name Ujjayinī.
Having gone there, satisfy Daśaratha with offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍa). The Great Kāla, the preceptor of gods and demons, is stationed there.
O King, that Lord is indeed the eternal bestower of the fruits of all desired objects; when that Lord of the Universe is seen, no separation ever occurs.
Those Brahmins and the mighty king who go there attain the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara resides. || 20 ||
Having entered that very sacred ford among all holy places within the region of Avanti, he then arrived at Avanti, where the merit-bestowing Śiprā flows.
Having bathed there, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, then offered libations to his ancestors; thereafter, he set out to behold Mahākāla.
Then, an incorporeal voice was spoken by the God of gods: "O Rāghava, blessings be upon you; establish me here under your own name. (23)
"O Rāghava, I have granted you this place; do not hesitate. Then, with a joyful heart, Rāma spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
O son of Sumitrā, we have been graced by Śambhu, the God of gods; therefore, install the auspicious Liṅga named Rāmeśvara in this sacred ford.
Having heard those words, Lakṣmaṇa installed Śaṅkara; having previously seen the God, Rāma spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Come, Lakṣmaṇa, quickly bring water from the Śiprā; for I shall perform here the auspicious ritual bathing of the Lord. (27)
But Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words: "O Rāma, what will you do with Sītā? I shall not remain in the state of your servant for all time. (28)
And this [bow] is well-nourished, very firm, and stout before me; tell me truly, O Raghava, what will you do with it? (29)
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, the descendant of Raghu, stood there dejected, as did Sītā of the beautiful countenance.
Then Sītā did exactly as Lakṣmaṇa had said; having bathed and eaten, those two heroes approached Mahākāla.
Having spent the night there, he set his mind on departing; "Arise, dear son Saumitri, let us go toward the southern direction. (32)
The son of Sumitrā spoke these words: "I will not go by any means; you yourself go with this wife of yours, O lotus-eyed one. (33)
"I will not go to the forest ahead, nor to Ayodhyā by any means. To the son of Sumitrā who was speaking thus, the joy of the Raghus replied:
"How did you previously depart from Ayodhyā with me? O Rāma, I shall dwell in the forest for nine and five years. (35)
"Be heedless toward me; take me along as well, O Rāghava! O slayer of enemies, how will you remain on the path now that we are half-way? (36)
But Lakṣmaṇa said, "O Rāma, I will not go to the forest again. Perceiving that Lakṣmaṇa was distressed, Rāma spoke these words.
"Do not follow me, O son of Sumitrā; for I shall go to the forest alone. But this Sītā here is my second [companion]. Thus was Lakṣmaṇa addressed by Rāma.

Then Lakṣmaṇa, taking up his bow, rose up with a heavy heart. Having reached the boundary wall, the limit of the field, those two subduers of enemies crossed over that field boundary, and Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa: || 40 ||
"Turn back, O Saumitri, and hand over my bow. Having heard Rāma's words, Lakṣmaṇa spoke indeed to Sītā: || 41 ||
For what reason have I been abandoned? What offense have I committed? Abandoned by Rāma, I shall undoubtedly give up my life. (42)
Then Sītā said to Rāma: "O Lord, for what reason is the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, who increases the joy of Sumitrā, being abandoned by you? (43)
Rāghava, however, said to Sītā: "I shall never abandon Lakṣmaṇa; not even in a dream would I ever forsake my beloved, who is like Lakṣmaṇa. (44)
O lady of beautiful hips, you have heard before of the conduct in this field; for in this field there is no brotherly affection, as everyone is intent only on their own self-interest.
Devoted solely to their own self-interest, they do not respect one another; sons do not listen to their father, nor does a father likewise listen to his sons.
Neither does the disciple heed the word of the guru, nor does the guru attend to the disciple's service; there is no affection rooted in mutual interest, for no one is truly dear to anyone else.
Having spoken thus, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Jānakī departed; there, the joy of the Raghus installed a Liṅga under his own name.
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha and beheld the auspicious Lord Rāmeśvara, a person is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Śiva. || 49 ||

Thus ends the majesty of Rāmeśvara. Sanatkumāra said: Having bathed in the Saubhāgyaka Tīrtha and having beheld the Lord Saubhāgyeśvara, one is liberated from all sins and shall obtain supreme good fortune. (50)
Having bathed at the Ghṛtatīrtha, a man should bathe Śiva with clarified butter; then, having offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having worshipped the Goddess Yogīśvarī, who is saluted by gods and demons, one shall be liberated from all sins and attain the supreme yoga.
Having bathed at Śaṅkhāvarta, a man is freed from all sins and is born into a pure family, endowed with wealth and grain. || 53 ||
On the fourteenth day, a person seeking liberation should bathe Śiva Sudheśvara with water mixed with milk; having beheld him, one shall thereafter attain the state of liberation.
Likewise, I shall describe another sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds, which is celebrated as "Kiṃpuna" and grants liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, O Vyāsa, there was indeed a twice-born man named Sunetra; a son was born to him who is known as Viśvāvasu.
O Vyāsa, because his own father had been slain by him through the curse of Yavakrīta, he was possessed by the sin of Brahman-murder and wandered from one sacred ford to another.
Having bathed at Kiṃpuna-tīrtha, the twice-born man went to Dhārā-tīrtha; thereafter, at Kapila-dhārā, he reflected within himself.
"How have my words fallen [into error], or is the Veda itself false?"—thus he thought, and then he returned once more to Avantikā. (59)
While he was bathing again at this sacred ford, he then heard a voice: "O Brahmin, why do you meditate, by which you have become a most excellent twice-born? (60)
Indeed, you have no sin of Brahman-slaughter, for it has been destroyed by bathing at the sacred ford; go quickly to your home, O Brāhmaṇa, free from sin and at your ease.
Thus, what indeed is its greatness? Sanatkumāra said: I shall further proclaim another supreme [liṅga], Pattaneśvara; having stayed there, Maheśa beheld the city once again. (62)
The Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods known by the name Pattaneśvara, [is he who is worshipped] with perfumes, flowers, incense, and beautiful lamps.
O Vyāsa, a man endowed with devotion should always worship according to the prescribed rules; as long as the linga remains properly installed, there shall be no extinction of his lineage. (64)
He goes to the world of Śiva by means of a vehicle yoked with swans. Furthermore, I shall describe another sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Vyāsa, in ancient times the Sun-god created [this place] known by the name Durdharṣa, which is renowned as a liberator from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
There was a famous sacred ford (tīrtha) on the riverbank consecrated by the Sun; there stood a Linga, a mass of splendor, worshipped by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.
On the seventh or eighth lunar day, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on a Sunday—having bathed there, become pure, and fasted for one day. || 68 ||
Having seen Maheśvara stationed there on the bank of the Śiprā and having worshipped him with devotion, hear from me what the fruit of that is.
Having delivered his entire family of fathers and mothers, he shall go to Śiva; there, he who bestows gifts, especially cows, gold, and so forth, attains that state. (70)
That remains inexhaustible in the world as long as the moon and sun endure; likewise, I shall now describe another supreme holy site, Gopīndra-tīrtha.
In ancient times, at this place where Indra was rendered emasculated by a curse from Gautama, Śakra, overcome with shame for his impotence, entered the excellent forest.
In former times, O brahmin, he gratified Śaṅkara with fierce austerity; and by the pleased Śambhu, those marks that were upon his body [were bestowed]. (73)
Because he gave a thousand cows, he is called Gopīndra; having bathed there, one goes to heaven with prowess equal to that of Śakra.
Those who have died do not undergo rebirth on the surface of the earth; by bathing at the holy site of Gaṅgā, a man attains abundant merit. || 75 ||
One should declare the fruit [of the rite] to be obtained by bathing in the Gaṅgā on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, after having visited the Puṣpakaraṇḍa [tank]. || 76 ||
Having bathed at Uttareśvara, a man travels by means of the Puṣpaka chariot and rejoices in heaven; he swiftly delivers [his ancestors] from hell.
Having attained his desired enjoyments, he goes to heaven without a doubt; having bathed at Bhūteśvara, a man should then worship Bhūteśvara. (78)
By offering perfumes, flowers, and food oblations, one who dies shall go to the city of Rudra; moreover, having bathed in the Śiprā, a man pays homage to Kailāsa. (79)
Just as darkness is destroyed by the sun, so too is sin utterly destroyed; and he who beholds Ambālikā through the discipline of meditative absorption (samādhi) likewise attains this.
He is liberated from all sins, like a serpent from its slough; I shall now describe Ghaṇṭeśvara, who is worshipped even by the gods.
Where, having drunk the water of the well, one obtains incomparable good fortune; he who should worship the Lord of Gods with perfumes and flowers in due order. || 82 ||
He who, being pure, having bathed, and with senses subdued, beholds Puṇyeśvara, shall dwell in the world of Śiva for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Having bathed at Laṃpeśvara and worshipped Maheśvara, a man attains the status of Gaṇapati, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (84)
The mortal does not go to hell, but is honored in the heavenly world; furthermore, I shall proclaim another thing which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (85)
Having bathed there and become pure, whoever worships the Vināyaka known as Sthavira, who was formerly honored by Brahmā; || 86 ||

Listen to the fruit obtained through perfumes, incense, food offerings, and various kinds of eatables and drinks: one's desired success shall be attained, and upon death, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
A wise person should worship Pārvatī near the Navanadī; by means of perfumes, flowers, and incense, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
Having bathed at Kāmodaka and beheld Kāma, the beloved of Rati, a man shall possess a body coveted by gods and gandharvas in heaven. || 89 ||
A man who bathes at Prayāga and beholds the Lord of Prayāga transcends all worlds and is honored in the world of Śiva. (90)
Sanatkumāra said: Now I shall further describe Narāditya, the Sun-god, by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all diseases. (1)
I shall describe to you the manner in which the installation of Narāditya was performed in the past, when that battle between Raktasveda and Jaya had been averted.
The two gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, descended to the surface of the earth; they were born of Queen Kuntī and Devakī in Mathurā.
Thus they lived in the world as a lovely couple and attained supreme prosperity; from one cause Kṛṣṇa was born, and from another Dhanañjaya.
For he indeed slew all the Dānavas, beginning with Kaṃsa, in battle; thereafter, Pārtha went to heaven from Vāsava for the sake of attaining mastery over divine weapons.
When the hero, skilled in weapons, had offered the sacrificial fee to the King of the Gods, the King of the Gods praised him and indeed requested that very fee.
"Let the fierce Nivātakavacas, who dwell in Hiraṇyapura, be slain quickly by Arjuna; this shall be my teacher’s fee."
The slaughter of those evil-minded ones was vowed by Arjuna; mounting the chariot of Indra and taking up his bow along with arrows, he set forth.
Having slain them and performed that most difficult feat, Pārtha then inspired joy in all the inhabitants of heaven.
Then Śakra, his purpose accomplished, spoke these words to Arjuna: "O hero, whatever is most difficult to obtain in the world of mortals that is pleasing to you," (10)
"O Pārtha, choose the most excellent boon desired by your mind. He chose two images which had been worshipped by Brahmā himself.
When it was bestowed upon Dakṣa by Brahmā, who was filled with affection, Dakṣa also worshipped that dispeller of darkness for more than a yuga.
When a conflict between the gods and the asuras had arisen, Śakra was defeated by the Dānavas; having been deprived of his kingdom, he went to the forest.
The one-footed Śatakratu performed difficult-to-master austerity for a thousand divine years, and Dhiṣaṇa beheld him.
Having seen that king of the gods, Bṛhaspati said: "O Śakra, having abandoned the third heaven, how have you come to this forest? (15)
"O King of the Gods, knowing this—that your enemies cannot be overcome by you while staying alone in the forest—you must go quickly to the hermitage of Dakṣa."
"Ask the Lord of Creatures for those two trees produced from the Pārijāta, which Viśvakarman fashioned and which were given by Brahmā for the purpose of worship."
"And through the grace of those two who were worshipped, the destruction of the enemies shall come to pass. At these words of his preceptor, the god Śatakratu was delighted. (18)
He went quickly to where Dakṣa Prajāpati was; bowing low with humility, he requested two auspicious images.
O Vyāsa, when the two images were worshipped by Śakra for a hundred autumns, all the Dānavas met their destruction through the splendor of those two.
The two images spoke to Śakra: "Choose an excellent boon; know, O Vāsava, that we are supremely pleased by this devotion. (21)
Then Śakra, with a gratified soul, chose a boon, O best of the twice-born: "Those Dānavas of evil mind who are our adversaries—" || 22 ||
"May they all meet with destruction; this is my wish. I desire to honor you both as long as I remain Indra. (23)
Having said "So be it," those two images departed toward heaven; therefore, I pray for those two images for the sake of an indispensable purpose and for the sake of a boon.
Indra said: "Excellent, O Pārtha, excellent again! Since you are thus established here, these two images, O Pārtha, were fashioned by the high-souled Śaṅkara."
It was worshipped with deep red lotuses during the day of Brahmā; in ancient times, it was worshipped by Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the three worlds.
With fragrant blue lotuses for a thousand years, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), being composed and desiring to bring about creation, [performed worship]. || 27 ||
He worshipped the two images with lotuses and auspicious red water-lilies, thinking: "O Pārtha, how indeed will you lead me alone into the world of death? (28)
"Deprived of these two, heaven will become equal to death. Having prostrated before that Indra, who was unwilling to give, Arjuna said: || 29 ||
He said, "O Lord, I do not desire this boon. Then, O bull among sages, Śakra spoke again to Pārtha.
"O hero, taking these two, establish them in Kuśasthalī; and on the northern bank of the Śiprā, Keśava shall establish Keśavārka. (31)
"Indeed, at that place where the Destroyer of All Sins resides, establish [the deity] there, in that very Destroyer of All Sins. Then there shall be the festival of Āṣāḍhī as well as the Kaumudī."
I shall go there accompanied by hosts of Apsarases; and the Maruts shall come, as well as the clouds together with lightning.
When a mass of clouds has arisen and I am raining there, people will indeed say, "The god Purandara has arrived."
And having paid homage to the Lord Bhāskara, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, O Bībhatsu, I shall return once again just as I came. (35)
Having thus given two forms to Pārtha, O Vyāsa, Vāsava sent the son of Pāṇḍu back to the earthly realm along with his charioteer.
Nārada, for the purpose of summoning Kṛṣṇa from Dvārakā, [conveyed] that message of the King of the Gods (Indra) along with its secret meaning to Keśava.
He caused the best of brahmins to hear: "Come, O Kṛṣṇa, to Kuśasthalī, so that you may worship the Pārijāta tree fashioned by Viśvakarman."
Then, having heard those words regarding what was indeed granted by Indra both to you and to the Pāṇḍava, Śauri set out for the city of Avantī.
Descending from the sky and embracing the son of Pāṇḍu, he joyfully spoke these words, having also embraced Phālguna.
My birth has become fruitful and joy has been produced in me, O Arjuna; since my delight is incomparable, let this supreme task be performed.
Having spoken thus, O Vyāsa, the two of them then arrived at Kuśasthalī; then Kṛṣṇa, his desires fully realized, spoke to Pārtha.
"O Arjuna, having gone to the eastern direction, establish a single image; for in the forenoon, there will be an auspicious and delightful moment. (43)
"I too am going northward to establish the river, O Sage; by the sound of my conch, do you establish the Lord Ravi. (44)
Having gone to the east, O Pārtha, he then beheld an auspicious place; there Vyāsa established the Lord of Day (the Sun) in a very stable manner.
While the Pāṇḍava was meditating, "I shall install the god Arka," he [the deity] spoke to him: "Construct a beautiful place for me."
He spoke to Pārtha with that unbearable splendor; then Savyasācī, seeing that image speaking, was struck with fear.
Unable indeed to endure that splendor, he spoke these words to the god: "O Lord, where shall I establish you? Which place is pleasing to you? (48)

O Lord of Creatures, be gentle in form and beautiful to behold for all living beings! And those gods who dwell in heaven, and the nāgas who take refuge in the netherworld— [may they also be favorable]. (49)
"May the men dwelling on earth become purified by the sight of you. That god said to Arjuna: "Do not fear from the sight of me."
Then, with his right hand in the gesture of fearlessness, the bestower of fearlessness consoled him; thereafter, he assumed a peaceful and gentle form.
The god Prabhākara displayed his own splendor; thereupon the Sun said, "This very place is my immovable domain. (52)
When the auspicious moment arrived, Hari blew his great conch shell, and Nara established that Sun-god who is praised by the immortals.

Arjuna said: Victorious is the radiant one garlanded with rays, whose horses are weary, who is the abode of all worlds, and whose loud laughter resounds from the eastern horizon; by the mere chanting of his name, the bodies of men seized by the faults of abundant impurities become cleansed of sin.

O wise one, what poet would desire to fully praise the Sun, who is already extolled by sages such as Brahmā? Nevertheless, O one of excellent intellect, I shall praise him in great detail; for does a lamp not shine even when the moon has risen? (55)

What object is there that has not been composed through various artistic applications by the ancient sages, such as Dvaipāyana and others, who were praised by munis skilled in the meaning and purpose of the scriptures? Herein, the entire world appears as if its essence has been extracted by those ancient seers. (56)

Nevertheless, having reflected deeply with my intellect upon the pair of feet of the Sun, who is worshipped by the teachers of the three worlds, I shall indeed praise you with verses that possess clear meaning, sweet phonetic junctions, and diverse meters. (57)

The entire world remains utterly motionless, and various activities do not reach fulfillment, as long as you, O Lord, whose orb is as stainless as a lotus, do not rise up dispelling the darkness with your rays. (58)

The peaks of the trees do not yet shine, their clusters of blossoms closing their eyes like a forest in slumber; you awaken them, teeming with bees, only when you appear with your stainless and unsurpassed radiance. (59)

As you rise in the expanse of the sky, hosts of gods and siddhas—along with Brahmā, daityas, munis, kinnaras, nāgas, and yakṣas—all these deities worship you with their bowed heads, which are illuminated by the unsurpassed luster of the jewels in their shimmering crowns.

When you have set, the world falls into deep sleep; when you shine forth again, it awakens. Thus, O Giver of Boons, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you alone, O Blessed One, are eternally the destroyer of darkness.

O Lord, it is surely because of a lack of devotion that the undertakings of men—though endowed with energy, power, policy, and valor, and devoted to the methods of service and application—fail to yield their fruits in this world.

O You who are ever affectionate toward those who bow before You, whatever men swiftly attain by conquering their enemies in battles through chariots, elephants, spears, javelins, iron arrows, discuses, shafts, tomara-darts, and fearsome swords—all that is always encompassed by Your power.

Even when situated in the perils of desolate forests and difficult terrains—filled with bears, elephants, lions, many thorns, and thieves—even those possessed by thirst and whose minds are bewildered by great sorrow become free from the fear of death through the chanting of your glory.

You are a mass of splendor here, a refuge for those suffering from all sides; there is no other compassionate one like you in the entire world. When every form of devotion is sought, it is found in you alone; having attained you, how could the suffering of disease prevail over men? (65)

"Who is afflicted by leprosy? Where are those tormented by enemies, and who is oppressed by diseases? Who are the lame, the blind, and the dull-witted? Where is he whose feet are withered, or who is one whose actions have failed?"—having observed [the world] in this way, O Lord, you protect [beings] out of compassion from their faults. Whose other activity is so devoted to the service of others as yours is? (66)

It is said that Dharma abides in the next world when practiced; after a lapse of time, the wise grant their boons. But you, O Lord who are affectionate toward those who bow before you, when served by those desiring prosperity, bestow immediately the very fruit they desire.

The dwellings of those men for whom you are indeed a gracious granter of boons are filled with playful women whose eyes resemble those of startled female deer, and who wear beautiful necklaces, jeweled earrings, and girdles.

O Lord of the World, those men by whom you have been saluted even once, or meditated upon in such a way at the time of death—even if they were evildoers in this world, they become stainless; being purified, they attain the state of the virtuous.

Those who do not bow to you with devotion—bodies trembling with hundreds of horripilations born of the conviction that you are beyond mere logic—are impoverished; with throats and faces emaciated by hunger, they wander in the houses of others, seeking out discarded food.

You are incessantly praised with incomparable and abundant hymns by the foremost of the Nāgas, whose pairs of eyes tremble with the agitation of the waves of the ocean waters, who lick [the ground] while illuminated by the rays of their jewel-crests, and who bow their heads in prostration. (71)

O best of gods, as you travel, swarms of bees emerging from the lotuses of the celestial river, turned tawny by the pollen of golden lotuses and fanned by the winds, follow you like fly-whisks made of insects.

O Blessed One, standing repeatedly with your multitude of rays within the expanse of the ocean, you blaze for the sake of sustaining all living beings; who in the three worlds at this time is equal to you? (73)

As he stands upon the slope of the mountain of sunrise, veiled during his risings and settings, those rays of his, possessing the luster of molten gold, flash forth and mimic the brilliance of lightning.

Just as your chariot advances through the sky, rending asunder the dense masses of the darkness of clouds, so too it is perceived as if repeatedly emitting the sound of a great drum stirred by a turbulent wind.

With your rays, you awaken that lotus-pond—her eyes closed like beautiful lotuses, her girdle a row of *cakravāka* ducks and swans, and languid from the fatigue of love-play, like a passionate woman. (76)
The intensely lovely blue lotus, with its dark, trembling petals agitated by bees with long legs, shines brilliantly like a ruby colored by passion through your splendors. (77)
O bird, the sky, pure as a necklace of shimmering moonbeams and unwavering within your wings, shines exceedingly lovely; it is uniform, vast, and yet possesses a single pale-red hue.

O Giver of Boons, as long as the night, most intensely frequented by darkness, remains unpurified by your rays, so long can the praise of your virtues not be fully undertaken even by sages and seers of noble intellect who are devoted to the eternal path. (79)

You are Viṣṇu, you are the Moon, you are the slayer of Asuras, you are Ṣaṇmukha, you are the Lord of Wealth, you are Time, and you are the Creator; you are the refuge of the mountains and Malaya, you are the Fire, you are the syllable Om for the twice-born, you are the ocean here, you are the arrow, you are Rudra, you are the Primordial One, you are the cloud, you are the vows, restraints, and observances—you are indeed the entire universe.

O blameless Lord of the Cowherds, O Destroyer of Tripura, O Burner of the God of Love, O Slayer of the terrible pride of the asuras, protect me! You are the lotus-faced sovereign of the gods and the venerable preceptor of the deities; who else in the entire circle of the three worlds possesses qualities equal to yours? (81)

O Āditya, Bhāskara, Divākara, Saptasapta, Mārtaṇḍa, Sūrya, Lord of the Bay Horses, Bhānu, you whose vehicle is unwearied, you who have the form of a donkey, you who are garlanded with rays—this person seeks refuge in you, O Lord of the World. (82)

O ornament of the eastern quarter, radiant as an ear-ornament; O beloved lord of the Mandākinī, lamp of the world; O dispeller of the darkness on Mount Meru, jewel that beautifies the surface of the sky; O ruddy glow upon the face of the lady Twilight—salutations, salutations unto you! 83.

O Brahman, the Truth, the Auspicious, the Blessed One, Lord of the World, Sovereign of the celestial courtyard, praised by sages, whose form is the universe! O remover of the grief of the afflicted, protector of your servants, be gracious to me, O Blessed One, who have come to you for refuge. (84)

O Lord, since you have been praised here today by me with devotion, having placed my hands in añjali like a lotus bud upon my head, therefore, O Master, become gracious toward me; grant me a mind ever fixed on Dharma and abundant prosperity.

Salutations to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world, the cause of the creation, sustenance, and destruction of the universe; who consists of the three Vedas, who sustains the nature of the three guṇas, and whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Sūrya said: "O Pārtha of noble vows, I am now pleased by this hymn of praise; I shall diligently grant you whatever boon resides in your heart. (87)
Indeed, my sight never goes in vain; especially for heroes, there is nothing that cannot be given with effort. (88)
Arjuna said: "This alone is the boon for me, the most excellent among all boons: O Lord, O God, remain ever-present here at all times. (89)
And those men who, bowing down, shall always praise you with devotion—their wealth, grain, children, wives, and all such possessions [shall increase]. (90)
"Indeed, everything desired by my mind must be granted as a boon to me. Sanatkumāra said: Having granted him the boon, Āditya spoke these auspicious words. (91)

Having assumed a form that was universal and most terrifying, Mahādeva appeared with serpents that were exceedingly fierce, sporting, possessing sharp fangs, and overflowing with venom.

He cut him into hundreds of pieces and struck him with arrows; for even Andhaka, standing in the midst of battle, became slack and his weapons grew feeble.
His army was suppressed by Śambhu with arrows, like a lotus by bees; and it was scattered by his warriors who fought in the battle.

And seeing himself pierced by Maheśa with millions of arrows, his body shattered, he took refuge in fear and fled with great speed. || 33 ||

Bearing a great weight of fear, Śambhu wandered upon the earth with a broken heart; by whichever path the Lord went, by that very same path the Daitya followed.

The man who beholds Naradīpa stationed upon his chariot with devotion is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
O Sage, I shall now describe the chariot procession of the Lamp of Men; and I shall also declare the merit that has been proclaimed by the sages for performing it. (56)

On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Sun-god, seated upon his chariot, is indeed led through Kuśasthalī by the most excellent of the twice-born with the waving of their arms.
He who beholds the Lord of the Day (the Sun) proceeding toward the northern direction obtains the entire fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Any person who, having turned back from Keśavārka, beholds the chariot, has undoubtedly performed the pilgrimage to Śuṇḍīrasvāmin. || 59 ||
O Sage, he who pulls the chariot by pulling the rope indeed uplifts his entire lineage, including his ancestors—the fathers and grandfathers. (60)
O best of the twice-born, those self-restrained ones who behold Naradīpa as it proceeds facing southward go to the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.
One should encircle the field, the chariot, or even the deity with a thread; one attains all desires and becomes one who has performed meritorious deeds. || 62 ||
Those men who perform circumambulation of the Sun with devotion have, by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven islands.
O best of the twice-born, he who rises early in the morning and, observing silence, approaches the Sun-god through the eastern gate and pays him homage with devotion; 64.
Having entered by the southern side alone, one should worship the chariot wheel; then, having exited through that same gate and prostrated, one should proceed from there.
One should worship the Sun stationed on his chariot, taking recourse to the western gate; one should offer a fly-whisk, a canopy, a bell, and other such items. || 66 ||
At the eastern gate is Gaurī, and likewise at the southern is Aśva; at the western is said to be Gaja, and at the northern is Ratha.
But the man who indeed undertakes the pilgrimage to the Lamp of Men attains all his desires and becomes one who has performed meritorious deeds. (68)
O Sage, he who performs the circumambulation of Mahāmeru attains the auspicious heavenly realm of the Sun, Soma, Śiva, and Śakra; it is as if that very merit has been achieved by him.
Whatever fruit a man might obtain by giving a thousand cows on a hundred occasions of Vyatīpāta, or by giving a thousand horses, he shall obtain that same fruit [by this]. (70)
He who causes the ritual shaving to be performed while Naradīpa is mounted upon a chariot shall not be deprived of prosperity and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
If a mortal constantly beholds Sarasvatī for a month in a pond situated in front of the Sun, his bad dreams are destroyed.
O Vyāsa, he who beholds Naradīpa daily with devotion, having reached that supreme abode, shall be accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
Having sported together with his kinsmen, he who dies when the darkness has vanished and a brilliant light has arisen everywhere, O Brahmin, shall go to the city of the Sun.
Then, when Andhaka was struck by Maheśa with his three-pointed trident, all the gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, were filled with joy.
Then Viṣṇu blew his conch shell out of a desire for the welfare of the gods; thereupon, the sacred site known as Śaṅkhoddhāraṇa was produced.
There, O best of Brahmins, Viṣṇu is present, as is the four-faced Liṅga, which is indeed beginningless and located in close proximity to that very Liṅga.
Established upon a trident, he stands on the right side of the God; those who have conquered their senses and behold him on the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day [attain the goal].
Having exhausted the entire flood of their sins, they shall attain the supreme goal; so too shall he who offers the bali-oblation to the Yoginīs according to the prescribed rule. (79)
Having fasted on the twelfth day and bathed, he is not oppressed by anyone—neither by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, or others—having worshipped the Lord Janārdana.
Whoever should behold the god Śaṅkhin would attain the imperishable state.

Salutations to that Supreme Person, who is the manifest light of both the gross and the subtle; who is all beings, yet is not all beings; from whom the universe arises and who is indeed the cause of the universe.
Sanatkumāra said: When Andhaka was pierced by the trident, a sound issued forth from Rudra; from that, Oṃkāra arose—the Great Lord, Maheśvara, the God of gods. || 1 ||
Having bathed there and become pure, and by means of meditative concentration and self-restraint, one who beholds Oṃkāra, the Great God, is liberated from all sins.
Having slain Andhaka, the trident went into the waters of Bhogavatī. Seeing the trident of great splendor, Hāṭaka was filled with wonder and asked: "For what purpose have you come here? (3)
That spear spoke: "I have been dispatched by Śaṅkara for the sake of slaying Andhaka, that evil-doer of wicked mind."
Having pierced through it, I have come to the auspicious waters of Bhogavatī; I shall go back again to that place where Śaṅkara resides.
Having heard the words spoken by Śūla, Hāṭaka, desiring to behold the Supreme Lord, went forth with speed along the path of the trident—which was filled with many mouths, radiant, and most beautiful.
Having seen that Śūleśa Hāṭakeśvara, all the gods bowed down with their hair standing on end, like fully blossomed lotuses.
Led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, they praised him with various hymns; he who was established in Pātāla was named Hāṭakeśvara.
Having emerged by way of the path of the trident, he is therefore remembered as Śūleśvara; and there is the holy site Dhūtapāpa to the north of the God of gods.
There, that powerful lord of the Daityas was shaken by the trident; therefore, O Vyāsa, this sacred ford is called Dhūtapāpa (the Shaker of Sins).
On the eighth, the full moon, or the fourteenth day, or likewise on a Saturday, a devotee of Śiva who has subdued his senses should fast for one night.
But he who beholds Maheśvara, the God of gods, as Dhūtapāpa, is liberated from all sins, even those committed during seven lifetimes.
Having uplifted a hundred lineages, that man who beholds one who has performed the consecration in the month of Pauṣa indeed goes to the world of Śiva.
By the power of Śūleśvara, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; upon death, one goes to the supreme state by means of a thousand celestial chariots.
Thus, while this Aṃdhakaśūla proceeded as far as Bhogavatī, there arose terrible Asuras born from blood. || 15 ||

With swords in hand and possessed of great heroism, they numbered in the hundreds; being struck by those fierce beings stationed in the four directions, Maheśvara, oppressed by those evil-minded ones, then let out a lion’s roar.

By that lion’s roar, those wicked ones fainted and fell to the ground; having regained consciousness, they went toward Maheśvara, the God of gods. Then the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, were utterly terrified.
Considering them thus incurable, the gods, desiring their welfare, deliberated and then resolved among themselves: "Let us create a woman."
Having spoken thus, Brahmā brought forth the auspicious Brahmāṇī, who bears his own form, seated upon a swan, possessing four faces and four hands. (19)
And Kumāra likewise [worships] Kaumārī, who has a noble peacock as her vehicle, wears red garlands and garments, and holds a spear and a cock. || 20 ||
Furthermore, the youth [saw] Kaumārī, whose vehicle is the best of birds, who is black and has formidable teeth, and who is the mount of Dharmarāja.
She who crushes the bodies of the Daityas, who wields a staff and a mallet, who has an eye on her forehead, who is dark blue, and who is adorned with a skull in her hand.

The Lord manifested Cāmuṇḍā, who was dark-complexioned, clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with all ornaments, holding a knife and a sword in her hands, bearing a shield and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and possessing a body of skin, bones, and hair. || 23 ||
Formerly, the Mothers of the World were established near the banyan tree; therefore, they became renowned in the world as the manifest Vaṭamātṛs. || 24 ||
Having bathed there and become pure, the man who beholds the Mothers is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the Mothers. || 25 ||
O great sage, where the lion’s roar was uttered by the Lord, there stands the deity Siṃheśvara, the destroyer of all evil deeds. (26)
By the sight of that deity, one becomes as strong as a lion; and when the lion’s roar is uttered there, his body becomes bristling with joy.
There, Lord Kaṇṭeśvara is the eternal bestower of everything upon his devotees; having bathed in that sacred ford and beheld Śiva as Kaṇṭeśvara, a man [attains his goal]. (28)
"From this point on, one shall never encounter fear from planets, spirits, or piśācas. Then all those Mothers were indeed thus commanded by Hara.
"Drink quickly the blood of the fierce Andhāsura! In the meantime, O Vyāsa, [he appeared] like a blazing fire.
"O Śakra, do not fear; you shall have no fear," so said Śaṅkara. There, the supreme Liṅga Abhayeśvara manifested.
It is worshipped by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and uragas; having bathed there, become pure, fasting and with senses subdued— || 32 ||
One who worships the Lord of the Gods of gods shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; for him, no fear from spirits, ghosts, or demons exists.
He goes to the world of Śiva by means of a vehicle yoked with lions. As for the illusion of Andhaka, which arose from the Rākṣasa Rakta— || 34 ||
As the Mothers fought, that [army] quickly went to its destruction; the goddesses drank the flood of blood flowing from the bodies of the Daityas. (35)
The six attained supreme satisfaction, yet the one born from the forehead remained unsated; Śiṣṭaka, however, had his magic destroyed, and his spear and armor were shattered. (36)
The powerful Andhaka pulled the trident toward the north; though his great body was restrained, he was held back by Gaṇapa.
O Sage, because he became renowned in the world as Mahāvināyaka, a person is not afflicted by obstacles upon seeing that deity. (38)
O twice-born one, for him who worships Gaṇeśa on the fourth lunar day every month, no obstacle shall arise in this world or in the next.
Then a drop of sweat fell from his forehead onto the ground; from that was born Aṅgāraka, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Born in the region of Āvantya, the son of the Earth has red limbs; he is Aṅgāraka, red-eyed, and likewise the son of Mahādeva.
Having been praised by Brahmā with various names, he was installed in the midst of the sacrificial vessels; thereupon, the supreme holy site Aṅgāreśvara came into being.
The Linga established by Brahmā is served by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas; indeed, the man who bathes there on a Tuesday while remaining pure [attains great merit].
Having seen Aṅgāreśvara, he is then liberated from all sins; on the fourth lunar day, on a Tuesday, he should offer an arghya oblation while observing the nakta vow.
As long as four [vessels] are full, so long should they be prepared with effort; indeed, five water-pots (karaka) should be made together with a copper vessel.
They should be made of molasses and seats, provided with red garments, anointed with red sandalwood paste, and worshipped with red flowers. || 46 ||
One should have one vessel prepared there filled with sesame seeds and rice; a second with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas), and likewise a third with milk.
Having performed the fourth with *uttarī* flowers and the fifth likewise with radishes, one should present the *arghya* offering according to this procedure while reciting the mantra.
Salutations again and again to Kujā, the red-limbed one, who dwells in the midst of the planets, who resembles Kārttikeya, and who is beautiful in form. || 49 ||
O you who were born from the forehead of Śiva, O you who were born from the womb of the Earth; I have sought refuge in you for the sake of beauty. Accept this water offering; salutations be unto you!
O son of the Earth, you who possess the luster of glowing coals and the radiant glow of smooth coral, I, seeking a son, have sought refuge in you; please accept this water offering (arghya).
Born upon the earth in the region of Avanti by Śiva himself, grant me a son, grant me wealth, grant me fame; salutations be unto you! (52)
O best of sages, thus worshipped on the fourth lunar day, Bhauma (Mars) enjoys pleasures and likewise obtains sons upon the surface of the earth.
Upon death, he attains heaven for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Sanatkumāra said: When no blood remained for the Rākṣasa to drink, then Cāmuṇḍā’s mouth became filled with blood and radiant.
He was dark as the end of the world brought about by Kṛtānta, with terrifying teeth and lips; though peaceful, he blazed within the darkness, his eyes like flaming saffron filaments.
It possessed a terrible, gurgling roar and a loud, discordant howl; it was bound by the feathers of Tārkṣya and blazed with the tips of its sharp fangs.
Placing the tip of her skull-bowl at his mouth, Caṇḍī—her face flushed with rage and adorned with fierce, staff-like arms—drank the blood.
As she drank, the lord of the Daityas became emaciated in body; his eyes grew small and agitated with distress, and he was brought to exhaustion.
Thus that blind demon became one whose body was devoid of vigor, he who had withdrawn all his illusory powers and then rendered his strength exhausted.
Having encountered intense fear and being intent on saving his life, the Daitya, seeing no other refuge in the world, praised Śaṅkara.
With palms joined in reverence and his body covered in horripilation, he attained a state of pure goodness (sāttvika), having abandoned both passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
With a mind perpetually endowed with wisdom and with a pure inner self through devotion, [he worshipped] the Lord of the worlds, the God who is the sovereign of the wise.
He praised the praiseworthy and auspicious Lord, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

Andhaka said: I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, who is the creator of this entire world with its moving and non-moving beings, as well as the ordainer of what has been created; he who likewise bestows happiness and sorrow, and who is the cause of worldly existence, yet at the time of its end. || 11 ||

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, whom yogis—whose delusion, darkness, and passion have departed, whose minds are one-pointed through devotion, and from whom desire has turned away—meditate upon with their entire intellects as the one of immeasurable divine splendor.

I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, who always bears upon his head the pure crescent moon with its shimmering rays, and whose half-body is occupied by the daughter of the King of Mountains. || 13 ||

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, whose lotus feet are frequented by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, who bore upon his head the Gaṅgā as she fell from the sky with her turbulent great waves—as if she were a garland—purifying the three worlds.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who was served by the pressing of his lotus feet even as the peak of Mount Kailāsa was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who himself resembled a peak of Kailāsa. || 15 ||

I seek refuge in that Lord Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who at Dakṣa’s sacrifice likewise destroyed the eyes of Bhaga and the row of teeth of Pūṣan, and who paralyzed Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the granter of protection, by whom the sons of Diti, the sons of Danu, the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas, and the best of sages—who subsist on fruits and roots—have been repeatedly endowed with all their desired boons.

Even when this has been done, those whose minds remain attached to sense objects, though endowed with knowledge and the virtues of sacred learning, become enjoyers of happiness by taking refuge in him; I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of sanctuary. 18.

I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, the Blessed Maheśa who granted many boons to Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and Ṣaṇmukha, and who rescued Sūta from the jaws of death. || 19 ||

Propitiated by penance in a grove of the Himalayas through the smoke-vow (dhūmravrata) and austerities inaccessible to others, that Great Soul bestowed the Saṃjīvanī [mantra] upon Bhṛgu; to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, I go for shelter. 20.

For the sake of sport alone, the Blessed One created the seven worlds—adorned with various rivers, birds, and trees, together with Brahmā and named after the merits of beings—I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter. 21.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who with the tip of the nail of his lotus-like left hand forcibly severed that fifth terrible head of Brahmā, which resembled a sun-lotus. (22)

But those deluded persons who do not know you, the supreme teacher of the gods and the Lord of this world with its moving and unmoving beings—when their pride in sovereignty has vanished, they later experience torment through remorse, just as I do now. (23)

He who, being pure in action, recites this hymn, or he who, being a devotee of Śiva, constantly hears it, being always auspicious in deed within the assembly of Brahmins, goes to the unbroken realm of Śiva. (24)
Sanatkumāra said: As he was thus offering praise, the god Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident whose banner bears the bull, being pleased at the end of a full hundred years, spoke.
"O son, I am pleased; may it be well with you. You have now become pure. I grant you divine vision; behold me, free from all distress. (26)
"And whatever fruit you have desired even in your mind, I shall grant all of that; speak, O best of Dānavas! (27)
The Dānava said: "Whether it be the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Indra, characterized by return [to rebirth], all that is known to me; I do not desire even the slightest bit of it. (28)
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, grant me the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (gāṇapatya), which is distinguished, pure, and forever imperishable.
Mahādeva said: "You shall become immortal, freed from old age, and devoid of all suffering; you shall be the leader of the Gaṇas, saluted by all the worlds. (30)
The great yogin, capable of assuming any form at will, the Great Being of immense power, endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, is always dear to me. (31)
Sanatkumāra said: Then that illustrious Andhaka, having obtained boons that are very difficult to attain, became an attendant of Mahādeva and vanished right there.
When Andhaka had departed, the goddesses, beginning with Brahmāṇī, then assembled at that place where the Blessed Lord was, who had granted the boon to Andhaka.
They praised Mahādeva, and then Maheśvara was pleased; Cāmuṇḍā, comforted by Maheśa, became auspicious (Śivā).
Seeing Śaṅkara standing before them, bowing down, Brahmā and the others were also delighted and praised him with various hymns.
When those blood-drinkers were thus pacified and gladdened by Śambhu, he then spoke these excellent words for the sake of their continued existence: || 36 ||
"Since all these mighty ones have been born in the region of Āvantya, you shall therefore be known in the world as the Mothers of Āvantya. (37)
"Filled with joy in Avanti, you shall dwell there steadfastly, destroying all sins and granting boons to the worlds. (38)
Those who, being composed in mind, shall always behold [the deity] with devotion on the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, for them there will be worlds of great prosperity.
One who is childless obtains sons; one who desires wealth obtains wealth; he becomes handsome, fortunate, an enjoyer of pleasures, and an expert in all the scriptures.
He shall be honored in the world of the ancestors by means of a vehicle yoked with swans; and you must protect this city in succession, kalpa after kalpa.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods departed for Mount Kailāsa, being praised by the fierce Gaṇas and by the lords of the hosts of Daityas and immortals.

He who with faith listens to the praiseworthy proclamation of the Leader of the hosts of Asuras and Suras, goes to the eternal and lovely world of Rudra—the storehouse of all happiness—which is honored by the lords of the hosts of gods and demons. (43)
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, the greatness of the sacred field has been described by you exactly as it is—this supreme among holy sites, which increases the merit of meritorious deeds. (1)
How many sacred fords (tīrthas) are there here, and likewise how many lingas? Please tell me now, out of grace, as I am asking you.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, there are sixty thousand crores and sixty hundred crores [of lingas] in Mahākālavana; indeed, the number of lingas cannot be known.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, whatever human being is born here in the delightful Mahākālavana is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 4 ||
