The sacred fords (tīrthas) and the temples and shrines have their desires fulfilled; having bathed in them and become pure, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
All holy places of pilgrimage and all fields of spiritual attainment are meritorious; know that among them, this field and this sacred site are the most preeminent and supreme.
He who hears this with great devotion attains the supreme goal.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, you have described the entire abode of the Lord, extending for more than a yojana in every direction, which destroys the fear of worldly existence.
In whatever sacred field mortals who are of virtuous conduct and excellent character die, they shall surely dwell in the city of Īśvara, seated upon celestial chariots.
Where even worms, moths, and other such creatures, upon dying, attain the supreme goal—what other holy pilgrimage site (tīrtha) is as meritorious as Mahākālavana? || 3 ||
Therefore, O Sage, answer now this one question of mine truthfully: how was it that she became known in the past as Kanakaśṛṅgī?
O virtuous one, how did it come to be named Kuśasthalī, and how is it remembered as Avantī? How did it become Padmāvatī, and likewise, how did it become Ujjayinī?
Furthermore, O best of sages, tell us the reason for those names.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, I shall relate how it was formerly told by Virañci to Vāmadeva in the ancient Gaura-kalpa.

The Blessed Maheśa was questioned here regarding the cause of the ritual procedure, as well as from where happiness comes for those who have fallen from their own [state] and are dwelling [elsewhere].
And the attainment of heaven occurs for those who wander and act according to their own will. What region is most meritorious, most excellent, and a destroyer of sin? (9)

From what is the mind turned back so that it may arise [in tranquility] for those dwelling anywhere? Even for those dwelling in the world, there is peace both in this life and the next. O Blessed One, tell me this for the benefit of all embodied beings. (10)
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, in the beginning, in a former kalpa, that supreme [teaching] was proclaimed by Śambhu.
The Lord Grandfather, being pleased, spoke to the beloved of Pārvatī: "O Blessed One, you are the creator of all, the all-seeing Sadāśiva."
O Sanātana, you ask me about everything as if you were ignorant, regarding that place where the fire at the end of the aeon stands ablaze.
And you alone are Mahākāla; indeed, everything is known by you, O Lord—those men there who follow right conduct as well as others.
Those mortals do not remain as mere humans; they are indeed gods, there is no doubt. And when their time has passed, having died, they surely attain heaven once again.
And there stands a city, beautiful with lovely palaces and most splendid; within it shine various and diverse mansions. (16)
And palaces with golden pinnacles were constructed by Viśvakarman; the gods are always present there, as are various sacred fords (tīrthas).
All the worlds indeed go to that very city of Avantikā to behold it—the city where, in a former kalpa, I stood as well as you, O Keśava.
Likewise, the celestial sages, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Kiṃnaras, and Dānavas arrived together with Sthāṇu and Brahmā, the source of the Vedas.
In the same way, thousands of excellent women, the most beloved of the gods, flocked together to behold that most wonderful city.
And when the god Maheśvara arrived with the gods and beheld the beautiful city, he saw it thus surrounded.
With palaces richly adorned with golden pinnacles and embellished with jewels and gems, the Lord King Viśvarūpa is indeed the sole leader of the universe. (22)
There he dwells in a beautiful, divine palace adorned with jewels, being served by gods, siddhas, munis, vidyādharas, and serpents.

Then Maheśa and Pitāmaha, having come together, greeted that Lord of the Universe; honored by him with due respect according to their rank, they, along with their followers, asked about the reason for his arrival.

"Have you two come from the third heaven to the surface of the earth? Tell us, who is this companion of yours? Then those two, the lords of the lotus-born, replied: "In whatever other existence we may find ourselves, there our delight shall be."

Without you, there is no happiness for us in the abode of the gods, nor on the surface of the earth, nor even in the subterranean realm; when was the city of Kāñcanaśekhara ever established by you, adorned with houses and made variegated? (26)

Hari said: "O Lord, this [goddess], who is endowed with special qualities and is indeed a mine of all virtues, has been created by me specifically for your sake. O Ruler of the Universe, grant us both a place here—a sacred ford (tīrtha) that remains imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution."
"I grant you both your desired abode here: O Prajāpati, your residence shall indeed be to the north; O Maheśvara, you go to the southern abode, a most beautiful place granted to you both. (28)
For Mahākāla, whose flames blaze downward, stands as the Lord and the soul of the universe; the Supreme Ishvara is honored by many thousands of his attendants.
This city was created for the sake of sport by me, who desires the welfare of all beings; today, leaving my own mountain behind, it is given by me to you both.
"Since you two have uttered the words 'Hemaśṛṅga,' this city shall become famous in the world as Kanakaśṛṅgā. (31)
Thus, the first name is declared to be Kanakaśṛṅgī. || 32 ||
And where Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara remain engaged in silent recitation (japa), they eternally delight there, bestowing the fruits of all desires upon their devotees. || 33 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to how this Kuśasthalī was indeed described in former times by wise sages learned in the Vedas during the Tātpuruṣa Kalpa. || 1 ||
The entire universe, including Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, was created by the Ordainer; they were intoxicated with mutual pride and indeed hostile toward one another in battle.
The gods and the dānavas were constantly engaged in rivalry in battle, as were humans with other men, along with the siddhas and vidyādharas.
Thus, those Cāraṇas, together with the Kiṃnaras, being intent on enmity, constantly wage war with speech that is indistinct in its meaning.
And all those who were strong, together with the weak men; the beasts with the beasts, and the birds with the birds.
Thus, seeing this world to be lawless through mutual and other [conflicts], they beheld Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, the supreme Lord of all.
"I go for refuge to the Lord Hari, who removes the suffering of those seeking shelter. Having resolved thus in his mind, he meditated upon Mādhava through focused contemplation.
Then, having been meditated upon, the glorious Hari, the great yogi who assumes all forms and wields an iron staff, spoke this to the Grandfather: || 8 ||
"O Brahmin, behold me as I am being meditated upon by you through the proper practice of meditation—approaching just as you have visualized me, intent on protecting the worlds."
Then Dhātṛ, having heard this, abandoned his meditation and beheld him; rising up with a focused mind, he paid homage and worshipped him again.
Having worshipped Keśava with water for the feet, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the lotus-born Brahmā spoke these words again to the Imperishable One.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Lord of the world, this universe has been created by you; without you, O Viṣṇu, the world is not able to endure.
You alone are the teacher of this entire universe, and there is no other; from you comes this whole world, therefore, please instruct us.

The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, along with yakṣas, sarpas, and rākṣasas—having engaged in endless conflict except for you, O lotus-eyed one—they strike one another down; you alone are capable of protecting them. (14)
You are the eternal sustainer of this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, existing in the form of the Self.
Since this entire world is indeed supported by you, you are known as Upendra; because this universe is entered into and pervaded by your own abode, you are called Viṣṇu by the lords of sages.

Since you have today clothed this entire universe and are the dwelling place of all elements, you are Vāsudeva. This universe follows after you; as the All-pervading Lord, you shine as the sovereign king of the entire world without exception.

Since the entire world is indeed conformable to you, you are therefore remembered as Viśvasena; and because of the scraping away (*vilikhana*) of this world of moving and unmoving beings, and from the root *kṛ* (to act), you are therefore Kṛṣṇa.

O Lord, you have conquered the three worlds; because you are victorious over the very Creator who is himself the conqueror, you are therefore Jiṣṇu (the Victorious). Therefore, O All-pervading One, protect the world—including all the planets and the guardians of the quarters—for all time.
O King, may you be the origin of this entire world; let there be no second auspicious throne for you. Indeed, the conch shell resting in the hand of a man shines as it turns clockwise.
You possess a discus named Sudarśana; for this reason, you are praised by poets as the "Discus-bearer" (Cakrī). O Lord, you have a banner served by Suparṇa, and likewise, Suparṇa is your vehicle.

O Hṛṣīkeśa, may your horses be destroyers of the enemy, and likewise your well-tamed elephants; [may they be adorned] with crowns, neck-ornaments, armlets, earrings, bracelets, excellent necklaces, and golden threads. || 22 ||
May you become Bhīmasena, adorned with variegated garments and excellent red garlands; may you never be forsaken by prosperity, and may infinite riches be yours forever.
May there indeed be true devotion following you here; therefore, O Mukunda, be gracious to me, who am devoted to you.

Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the foremost of the dwellers of heaven, the omnipresent Lord Hara, being pleased, spoke this: "O Viriñca, show me that mandala of Sadāśiva, O Lord, which has been released by you."
"Wherever I establish the world, there shall it remain firm. Then Virañci took a handful of kuśa grass and went to the holy hermitage of Cyavana to point out a sacred site.
Then, having reached a higher plateau, the Grandfather spoke with reverence to Keśava: "O Lord, this sacred circle here originates from you; it has been abandoned by you and is eternally auspicious."

You alone are Viṣṇu, eternally worshipped by the gods and remembered by the lords of sages as that Viṣṭaraśravas; O Lord of the Universe, sit here, for you have taken refuge in Kuśasthalī in the form of the month of Mādhava.

While remaining at Kuśasthalī, the Lord Puruṣottama was thus praised by the Creator; he then sat down upon the ground strewn with kuśa grass, that Kuśasthalī frequented by gods and the lords of sages.
Then both Vidhātṛ and Puruṣottama, extending for a distance of many yojanas on all sides, gave it the name "Kuśasthalī," which became renowned throughout the three worlds.
There, the glorious Lord of the Universe, the Sovereign of All, the Creator of All, the All-pervading One, the Soul of All, and the Leader of the entire universe, ruled over the world. (31)
Thus Kuśasthalī became renowned; for it was formerly known as Hemaśṛṅgā, and because it was strewn with kuśa grass by the Creator (Dhātṛ), it is therefore remembered as Kuśasthalī.

Sanatkumāra said: Listen now to how the city of Avantī was remembered in former times during the Īśāna-kalpa, and how it was previously [established] by the gods who had been defeated by the armies of the Daityas. || 1 ||
Having gone there, O best of the twice-born, they took refuge on the peak of Mount Meru, which was covered with forests, springs, and caves, and being resolute, they performed a mantra-ritual.
Having encountered one another and honored each other in turn, all the hosts of gods went to where Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, was.
They reported everything regarding the reason for their arrival there. Having heard those words of the gods, that lord of creatures (Prājāpatya) [acted]. || 4 ||
He went together with the thirty gods to Maheśvara, the God of gods; and he too went to that place, Vaikuṇṭha, where [the Lord] indeed resides.
It constantly bestows supernatural powers and accomplishments; it is frequented by sages and celestial bards, sung of by Kinnaras, and attended by hosts of Apsarases.
By the sages beginning with Bhārgava, by the supreme celestial sage Nārada, by the leaders of the Siddhas and Gandharvas, and by the Kumāras beginning with Sanaka; || 7 ||
It was crowded with hosts of Prajāpatis and the fourteen Manus, as well as the Vasus, the Viśvedevas, and the most excellent classes of Pitṛs.
It is to be frequented by people of virtuous conduct and meritorious deeds; it is divine, adorned with celestial palaces and divine trees.
It was divine, graced with the beauty of lakes featuring stairs made of precious gems; it was filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and brilliantly radiant with the luster of jewels.

All the gods, desiring to behold Vāsudeva, went to that place free from the six waves where the birds abide; having arrived there, they began to offer praise to the God of gods, the Lord of the universe. (11)
The gods said: "Salutations to the infinite, the great one; salutations again and again to the Tortoise. (12)
Salutations to the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha, the fierce one; salutations to the one in the form of Varāha; and to Rāghava, to Rāma, the Brahman of infinite power.
Salutation to Vāsudeva, the peaceful one, the lord of the Yadus; salutation to the pure Buddha, to Kalki, the destroyer of the Mlecchas. 14.
Thus, to those engaged in praise, an incorporeal voice spoke: "Listen, O all you gods, having become single-minded. (15)
In the delightful Mahākālavana, frequented by hosts of Brahmanical sages, there is indeed a single holy city that bestows the fruits of all desires. (16)
There is a beautiful place named Kuśasthalī, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, where Hara is ever-present at the beginning or during the middle of a kalpa.
At the end of the eon, all things both stationary and moving go to destruction, as do all sacred fords and holy shrines.
All rivers, oceans, lakes, and groves; medicinal herbs, trees, and creepers; as well as mechanical devices, mantras, and all that is auspicious or inauspicious—[he knows them all]. (19)
The luminaries, the moon and the sun, and the entire world consist of Viṣṇu; likewise, their seed, their merit, and the latent impressions of the souls' karma are also He. (20)
Taking everything with him, Lord Śaṅkara remains there; for Gaṅgā consists of all holy places, and Hari consists of all gods.
The Veda consists of all sacrifices; compassion consists of all dharmas; and the Revā is the best of rivers, preeminent among those who perform meritorious deeds on earth. (22)
Therefore, O best of gods, the field of the Kurus is indeed beneficial; yet I consider the supreme sacred site of Prayāga to be ten times more so.
Therefore, Kāśī is ten times superior; Gayā is ten times superior to Kāśī; and Kuśasthalī, the bestower of merit, is said to be ten times superior to that.
Thousands of eclipses and tens of thousands of *vyatīpāta* conjunctions, even a hundred thousand new moons (*amāvāsyā*), are not worth a sixteenth part of this [moment]. (25)
A gift at the waning of the moon brings a hundredfold merit; at the two solstices, a thousandfold; at Vyatīpāta, ten millionfold; and on Rākā (the full moon), it is indeed infinite.
Therefore, this city of Kuśasthalī is indeed beneficial for the gods; for whatever gift, even a small one, is made by men here, it becomes infinite and of infinite measure. || 27 ||
"O best of gods, all that shall indeed become inexhaustible; therefore, go with every effort and do not delay! (28)
"O gods, because your merit has been exhausted, you are being afflicted by that; for this city of Kuśasthalī is indeed located in the delightful Mahākālavana. (29)
Having gone there, O sirs, perform acts such as bathing and giving on this earth according to the proper rite; through that merit, you shall attain heaven.
Having heard those words of hers, which then traveled through the sky, Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others bowed their heads to her.
O best of the twice-born, all the gods went again to that forest of Maheśvara and to the city which grants the fruits of all desires.
It was crowded with people of the four castes, frequented by ṛṣis and gandharvas, filled with meritorious people, and served by siddhas and cāraṇas.
Nowhere is a person seen who is poor yet not dull-witted, nor foolish, nor diseased, nor envious, nor afflicted by illness, nor harmful. (34)
They were givers, peaceful, and of excellent character, free from old age and disease; they were constantly devoted to their own duty, always following right conduct, and fond of guests.
Where men dwell together with women who are devoted to their husbands, there are great festivals, beautiful songs, and offerings to gods and ancestors in every house. (36)
Having seen such a city, the gods attained supreme joy; there, a sacred site is celebrated by the name Paiśācamocana. (37)

It is always to be resorted to by the meritorious and is frequented by all holy places (tīrthas). Having bathed there, recited prayers, offered oblations, and given gifts to the deities, [one attains the highest goal].
Having obtained inexhaustible merit, they returned once more to the abode of the gods; having conquered the greatly wicked asuras, they each attained their own respective stations. (39)
Those fortunate ones who perform bathing, giving, worship, fire-offerings, and libations to the ancestors in this [tīrtha], all that shall become indeed infinite.
Therefore, with every effort, this task must always be performed by the wise: namely, the protection of deities, sacred fords, medicinal herbs, seeds, and living beings. (41)
Because [the Lord] dwells there in every single Kalpa, that city is remembered as Avantī; from this day forward, this city Kuśasthalī shall indeed be known by the name Avantī.
Having spoken thus, the gods then departed for their own supreme abode; from that time forward, O best of the twice-born, Avanti became renowned upon the earth. (43)
Whoever should hear this divine, meritorious, and sin-destroying excellent discourse, or should cause it to be heard, is indeed liberated from all sins.
One without a son shall obtain a son; one without wealth shall attain wealth; [this merit is] greater than a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices and more than a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices. || 45 ||
Having constantly acquired merit, a man is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, just as the city of Ujjayinī is remembered in one *antara*, so shall I fully describe it; listen with a concentrated mind. || 1 ||
The great Daitya named Tripura, the lord of all the Daitya people, performed a most difficult penance for the sake of pleasing Brahmā. || 2 ||
Having subdued himself, he practiced exposure to the heat in the summer and service to the fire, endured the thundering clouds during the rainy season, and stayed in water during the cold season.
With withered leaves for food, subsisting on water, feeding on air, and without any support, he undertook the Gāyatrī vow, having renounced all possessions.
Thus, for a thousand years, he performed austerities that were extremely difficult to practice; when the thousand years were complete, Brahmā, being most pleased, spoke.
"O best of Asuras, choose from me whatever boon you desire; I shall indeed grant you every such boon in this world right now."

Thus addressed by Brahmā, the Daitya known as Tripura immediately spoke these words to Brahmā, who was firm in his vows. Tripura said: "O Brahmā, if you are well-disposed and wish to grant me a boon, I choose this boon: may I always be invulnerable to gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. (8)
Brahmā said: "So be it, O child; wander about free from fear on all sides. Having spoken thus, Brahmā suddenly vanished right there.
From that time forward, the great Daitya, filled with wrath and remembering his former enmity, indeed wrought great slaughter among the gods.
Having caused them to dwell there, he established three cities and mobile settlements; here all people, devoted to their respective castes and stages of life, made their abode.
That evil-minded one indeed carried out their slaughter by various means in that city, an abode of the wicked, where there were Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
They do not perform the agnihotra sacrifice, nor do they ever drink soma; O sage, people do not perform any meritorious deed whatsoever.
Devoid of the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ, no festival was seen being celebrated in anyone's house throughout the world.
There is no temple for the deities, nor is there worship of Śiva for us; there is no sacrifice, no acts of charity, and no worship of cows or Brahmins. || 15 ||
There is no person of virtuous conduct; compassion is devoid of humanity. There is neither a donor nor a benefactor, and no ascetic is to be seen at all. (16)
Thus, O Vyāsa, in that city this world had almost perished; for the Brahmins are the root of the subjects, and the Brahmins have the Vedas as their root. (17)
Sacrifices have the Vedas as their root, and the deities have the sacrifices as their root; therefore, O Vyāsa, everything has been destroyed by that evil-minded one.
By him all the hosts of gods were rendered as if slain and deprived of their vigor; defeated by him, they wander upon the earth like mortals. (19)
Having formed a mutual alliance and deliberated with focused minds, they went to that place where the stainless Prajāpati resided.
The thirty gods related the cause of their own calamity; having learned that, Brahmā, the great grandfather of the worlds, rose up suddenly.
He went together with the gods to the most excellent Mahākālavana, where the god Śiva dwells eternally accompanied by Umā.
There, where the divine city of Avanti is situated, frequented by all sacred fords (tīrthas), the four-faced Self-born One himself arrived together with the gods.
Then, having performed his bath, charity, recitation, and fire-offerings at Rudrasaras, and having worshipped Mahākāla, Brahmā spoke these words.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees! Listen, O best of deities, to this unsurpassed task of the gods.
The lord of the Daityas named Tripura, a scorner of gods and Brahmins, constantly inflicts great slaughter upon the deities. (26)
Having caused it to dwell for three days in front [of the deity], it then moves about extensively; the beings situated there meet their destruction by that evil-minded one.
Having acted thus, all creatures, both moving and stationary, were brought to destruction; the islands, villages, and cities were laid waste.
"All the hermitages of the sages and the dwellings of the ascetics [were destroyed]. Having done this, all the gods were defeated and deprived of their kingdom. || 29 ||
Just as mortals wander about, so does that evil-minded Tripura, having constantly obtained a boon from me, moves about entirely free from fear.
Therefore, with every effort, let his slaughter be considered.
Having heard these words of that Brahmā of disciplined soul, Mahādeva meditated for a long time and then spoke to that Brahmā.
Mahādeva said: "Listen, O best of gods, led by Brahmā and Śakra! I shall devise a means for victory over this evil-minded Daitya."
"Or, if you are desirous of victory for yourselves, perform penance; whatever is offered in sacrifice or given as a gift in Avantī shall all become inexhaustible. (34)
Having spoken thus to all the gods, Śiva vanished right there and went to his abode in the cremation ground, which is frequented by bhūtas and pretas.
For the sake of victory over that evil-minded Daitya Tripura, the lords of the gods performed worship there of Cāmuṇḍā.

Having then worshipped the Goddess with great sacrificial buffaloes, offerings of flowers and water for the animals, various oblations, gifts, and the propitiation of incense, lamps, and fire, he whose banner bears the bull praised her.
To the divine Durgā, the auspicious one, who delivers from the difficult ocean of saṃsāra; to her who brought about the end of Tripura, the Kṛtyā intent on the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
The virtuous Raktā, intoxicated by the fat of the Daityas, with red teeth, wearing red garments, steadfast, and adorned with red flowers. (39)
She rides upon a buffalo, is dark-complexioned, and occupies the seat of a Yakṣa; she is clothed in a leopard skin, and her flesh is so withered that she is utterly terrifying.

Having performed worship with a serene soul and remaining established in meditation, the Blessed One Bhadrā—by whom this world is sustained—the goddess Caṇḍikā, with a gracious countenance, appeared before him and spoke.
The Goddess said: "O best of gods, choose from me whatever boon you desire. I shall grant everything you have mentioned, which brings benefit to the worlds. (42)
Śrī Hara said: "O Goddess, if you are indeed pleased, grant me an excellent boon, by which I may slay the great Daitya Tripura, the thorn of the gods."
The illustrious Goddess said: "Victory to you, O Mahādeva! Accept this supreme Pāśupata weapon, given by me, O best of gods; it is the ultimate destroyer of the Daityas. (44)
And Śaṅkara, having taken the great Pāśupata weapon in his hand, [proceeded]. || 45 ||
Then Śambhu, assuming the form of Mahāḍambarika and becoming a source of terror to all living beings, swiftly emerged for the destruction of the Daityas.
Having offered praise with words, he departed, and the gods followed behind him; then Rudra indeed struck that great asura with a single arrow.
Having pierced that illusory one in three ways through a battle of illusions, Śaṅkara returned once more to this city of Avantī, which is served by the immortals.
Bestowing blessings of victory, the sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, as well as the gods, then praised him with shouts of "Victory! filled with joy.
There the Apsarases danced and the Gandharvas sang charmingly; then a most meritorious breeze blew, bringing happiness to men.
Then the cry of "Victory! arose in every house among living beings; the fires blazed peacefully, and the sounds arising from the quarters became tranquil.
Then sacrifices were performed with great festivals and abundant sacrificial fees; the gods returned once more to their own esteemed abodes.
Since the Dānava was abandoned and his fame established throughout the three worlds, therefore he was [honored] by all the best of gods and by the sages beginning with Sanaka. (53)
Indeed, the city of Avanti is named Ujjayinī, the destroyer of sins; it was formerly called Avanti, the bestower of boons for all desires. (54)
O Vyāsa, from this day forward, people on earth who reside in this city of Ujjayinī and perform acts such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts here— || 55 ||
Not even the slightest ill-deed born of sin remains within their bodies.

One seeking knowledge should dwell in Ujjayinī before Girīśa; one seeking wealth before Dhaneśa; one seeking a son before Suteśa; one seeking happiness before Dineśa; one seeking intellect before Gaṇeśa; and one seeking a beloved before Priyārthī—the one who honors those worthy of speech. 57.
O highly fortunate one, the person who always dwells in this place shall enjoy all the desires of his heart and, upon death, proceed to the city of Śiva. || 58 ||
There he dwells eternally for more than hundreds of millions of kalpas. || 59 ||
Whoever reads or even hears this meritorious narrative is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. || 60 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Now, therefore, I shall fully relate how Padmāvatī came to be; listen with respect, O Vyāsa, to this story of those who have performed great merit.
Once, a loss of all jewels occurred due to wicked beings; indeed, a decline and cessation of Dharma arose because of the evil dānavas.
Then, all the gods and demons joined together and churned the ocean; Mount Meru was the churning stick, the ocean was the vessel, and the serpent Vāsuki was the rope.
Having performed the ritual upon the back of the tortoise, they then milked the jewels; first, Lakṣmī emerged and was bestowed upon Kṛṣṇa.
Because of that, despair then arose for both the gods and the dānavas. In the meantime, Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, arrived.
By him, the quarrel arising between the gods and the Daityas was restrained; let that Padmā, born from the ocean, reside in Mahākālavana.
And at the edge of the ocean, various kinds of jewels remain; taking all of those, I shall indeed give them to you.
"Let the ocean be churned quickly; no hesitation should be made in this matter. Then those gods and asuras again exerted themselves for the sake of the nectar.
While the ocean was being churned by them, the Kaustubha jewel was obtained; after that, the Parijata tree appeared, and following that, the divine nectar (surā) was produced.
Then Dhanvantari was born, and after that the Moon was indeed born; then Kāmadhenu was born, and after that the jewel among elephants.
Then Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses; then the nectar and Rambhā; and after that, the Sāraṅga bow, from which all weapons originate.
Likewise, the conch Pāñcajanya rests in the hand of the enemy of Mura; this is the great treasure Mahāpadma, and from it comes the Hālāhala poison.
Having obtained all fourteen kinds of various jewels and taking them with them, they went to where the forest of Maheśvara was located.
Having gone there and sat down together, they held a consultation with one another; constrained by their mutual agreement, they each cried out, "Me first! Me first! (14).
A great clamor arose, and Nārada arrived once more; seeing their impurity born of the Kali age, he then propitiated Viṣṇu.
Assuming a form that causes delusion, Hari became a woman; seeing her, who was exceedingly beautiful and slender, the great asuras [were struck with wonder]. (16)
With their limbs trembling, they all fell under the power of the arrows of desire; in that interval, the Lord of the Gods gave them wine.
By means of manual dexterity, he gave the nectar to the gods. In the meantime, O Vyāsa, Rāhu assumed that very form.
Having entered among them, he drank the supreme nectar; and perceiving that, Viṣṇu quickly severed his head with his discus.
Due to the contact with nectar, the asura did not die then; O best of sages, he became known as Rāhu and Ketu in this field.
A great quantity of blood flowed forth from Rāhu’s body; in that sacred field, a great pilgrimage site was born which destroys that very defect.
Having bathed there and become pure, those who are intent on beholding Rāhu shall never experience any affliction caused by Rāhu.
One obtains one's desired object and gains the merit of donating a thousand cows; thereafter, O gods, those jewels [should be placed] in the Mahākālavana forest.
Having divided the portions and received them, they all became enjoyers of jewels; Nārada gave the gem, the lotus, the bow, and the conch to Viṣṇu.
He gave to Sūrya the seven-headed horse born from the ocean, and he presented Airāvata, the best of elephants, to Vāsava.
He gave nectar to the hosts of celestial beings, the moon to Śambhu, the Pārijāta—the best of trees—and the excellent woman Raṃbhā.
He bestowed [the cow] upon the delightful Nandana grove, the pleasure-garden of Indra; he gave the wish-fulfilling cow to the sages for the successful completion of their sacrifices.
This great treasure, Mahāpadma, has gone to the abode of Kubera; as for that poison called Hālāhala, it was not observed by anyone.
From wherever it spread forth, living beings went to their destruction; Śambhu, desiring the welfare of the worlds, bore that poison.
From that time forward, Mahādeva has been known as Nīlakaṇṭha. Having bathed in Ratnakuṇḍa, a man beholds the Blue-necked One.
Released from all sins, he shall become the enjoyer of all jewels; having obtained the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
Then all the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, took that [nectar], O Vyāsa, and spoke with their minds overflowing with joy.
Having reached Ujjayinī, we have become possessors of jewels; for by the residence of Padmā, it brings all happiness. (33)
Therefore, let Padmā dwell here forevermore, remaining steadfast; from this day forward, she shall be known as Padmāvatī. (34)
Those fortunate ones who perform bathing, giving, as well as worship, and especially the libations (tarpaṇa) for the gods and the ancestors in this [river], [attain great merit]. || 35 ||
For them there is no evil deed whatsoever, nor poverty, nor an unfortunate rebirth; indeed, they shall then deliver a hundred entire lineages from hell.
Whether seeking wealth, seeking a son, seeking knowledge, or being full of desire, wherever one may be situated, one should remember Padmāvatī. (37)
One attains all desires and that person shall become Śiva himself; O Vyāsa, such is the fruit of this name—what need is there for long-term service? (38)
Those who listen to this meritorious story and those who constantly cause it to be heard—no sin whatsoever remains for them; they shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. (39)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen attentively, O Vyāsa, to this supreme narrative that removes all sins. I shall relate exactly how this city of Padmāvatī became Kumudvatī, just as Lomaśa told it to me.
Lomaśa said: Listen, my child; I have seen a city most meritorious. Once, while on a pilgrimage, I went indeed to Kuśasthalī, that place more secret than the secret, where Hara is ever present.
Merely by the sight of whom one dispels the sin of killing a Brahmin, there the Brahmins, stationed here and there, raised the sound of Vedic recitation.
Likewise, highly fortunate sages, with concentrated minds, perform various wonderful sacrifices and the noble rites of officiating priests.
Likewise, virtuous wives of sages perform service there; ten renowned ones, equal to Viṣṇu, dwell in that very place.
For eleven Rudras have been proclaimed, and likewise twelve Ādityas; eight Vasus are well-known, and the Viśvedevas are thirteen.
The eight elephants of the quarters, the fourteen Manus, and all the hosts of Maruts, led by Indra, were also present right there.
O child, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Siddhas, and ascetics were all present right there.
Indeed, eight Bhairavas are renowned, four are the sons of Pavana (the Wind-god), six Vināyakas are proclaimed, and there are twenty-four goddesses. (9)
These are declared to be the hosts of gods, as well as the Raudra hosts; and Brahmā, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, along with Marīci, Kaśyapa, and others.
Dakṣa is the best of the Prajāpatis; Diti is indeed the mother of the gods; cows, headed by Surabhi, as well as all things stationary and moving [are his progeny]. 11.
All the sacred fords (tīrthas), rivers, and springs, as well as all the most meritorious holy sites (kṣetras) upon the earth—indeed, all of them. || 12 ||
There are seven cities, three villages, nine forests, and nine saline wastes; these fourteen are the secret gateways to liberation upon the earth.

The four oceans and various kinds of jewels; chaste, devoted wives, virtuous women, and likewise stainless Brahman-sages; as well as peaceful royal sages and Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas. || 14 ||
The Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, the Gāthās, and the Gītikā-prahelikās waited upon that God of gods, the Lord of Umā. (15)
By the mere sight of him, I became free from fever and stainless; through long austerity, I attained long life, devoid of old age and disease. (16)
Having bathed in all the sacred fords, having become pure and composed, my mind has become serene, and I have turned my back upon all sins.
Having seen Padmāvatī, who is pure and bestows the boon of all desires, where no person whatsoever is seen to be overcome by grief or disease. || 18 ||
Neither suffering, nor poor, nor foolish, nor one with uncontrolled senses, nor one characterized by mutual hostility is seen among humans or animals. (19)
They were all friends to one another and rendered assistance to one another; they were all self-controlled and tranquil, and all were instructors in sacred knowledge.
Delightful gardens, forests, and groves, as well as brilliantly white mansions arranged in rows, truly shine forth. || 21 ||
Adorned with beautiful golden jars studded with various jewels, they shine brilliantly amidst the great festivities of diverse songs and instrumental music.
There Śaṅkara always dwells together with Umā—the moon-crested one, clad in an elephant hide, whose limbs are smeared with the ashes of the funeral pyre.
It shone forever with the rays of the moon’s digits filled with moonlight; there was never a dark fortnight there, nor indeed was there a new moon or darkness.
Always in full bloom, dark-complexioned, and possessing the beauty of youth, she was seen upon the rooftops of the mansions, at the windows, at the doors, in the courtyards, and within the houses.
In mountain caves and thickets, within the darkness of caverns, and in delightful hermitages, forests, and groves; (26)
In the delightful garden ponds and in rows of halls on every side, the quarters of the sky appeared white, completely filled with moonlight. || 27 ||
And the lakes, filled with blooming water-lilies, shone like the expanse of the sky in autumn, crowded with hosts of stars.
All the rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, and beautiful pools were filled with night-lotuses, and the earth became as bright as the moon.
Because the night-lotus plant (kumudvatī) blooms at all times, this city, Padmāvatī, became known as Kumudvatī.
Those men who, with concentrated minds, perform the śrāddha ceremony at Kumudvatī, their ancestors never fall from heaven at any time.

The faithful obtain inexhaustible merit; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. Likewise, bathing, giving gifts, performing fire-sacrifices, and the propitiation of the deities [yield inexhaustible results].
Whatever action is performed there, all of it becomes inexhaustible; thus, O Vyāsa, the city became Kumudvatī, eternal.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O illustrious Vyāsa, to how this city of Kuśasthalī came to be Amarāvatī, just as Brahmā spoke to the gods. || 1 ||
Thus I shall relate in detail, O ascetic, how once that best of sages was commanded by Brahmā for the sake of creating progeny.
Mārīca Kaśyapa, that great sage, performed most difficult penance in the delightful and divine Mahākālavana. || 3 ||
With withered leaves for food, subsisting on air, his senses conquered, after a full thousand years had passed, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Listen, O best of the twice-born, to my unsurpassed words: O you of noble vows, it is because you have performed intense austerity with a specific fruit in mind.
Therefore, O dear one, may your lineage remain upon this earth with fame and sons and grandsons as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Aditi was your wife; she performed penance together with you, and therefore that illustrious lady has remained as your shadow at all times.
All these sons shall become the immortals, the ageless gods, led by Viṣṇu and Indra, who are eternally renowned in heaven.
And you too, O best of sages, shall become a sinless Prajāpati by my word; of this there is no doubt, O foremost of the twice-born.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished right there; from that time forward, O Vyāsa, she has resided in the unsurpassed city of Kuśasthalī.
Kaśyapa, together with Dākṣāyaṇī, took refuge there along with the sacred fires; from him, progeny consisting of gods, asuras, and humans increased.
From Marīci, Kaśyapa was born; from him everything is established. By means of that [nectar], the gods made the drinking of the nectar eternal, and thus they were rendered immortal.
And right there in that most excellent Mahākāla forest is the grove known as Nandana, where the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) resides, bestowing the boons of one's heart's desires.
There she constantly worshipped Mahākāla Maheśvara, as well as the most excellent Pārijāta tree and the unfading lotus.
The supreme Lake Mānasa is celebrated as Bindusaras; it is crowded with swans and cranes and frequented by gods and perfected beings (siddhas).
This is the great treasure-lake Mahāpadma, strewn with clusters of pearls and gems, adorned with the splendor of jewels, and radiant with white and blue water-lilies.
Whatever divine things exist within the sphere of the universe, all of them reside in the auspicious Mahākālavana. || 17 ||
By that very application of the self, human beings dwelling here [in this world] possess that same food, that same conduct, that same form, and that same prowess. (18)
Crowding one another, all these people on earth move about this city like immortals, resembling the gods themselves.
O Vyāsa, women equal to the celestial nymphs and eternally possessed of stable youth, as well as such an eternal city, have been seen by me on this earth.
It is eternally bestowing enjoyment and liberation upon the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas; it yields fruit over a long period of time. || 21 ||
For this was the camp of the immortals; therefore, it became Amarāvatī. Those fortunate ones who happened to have gathered here incidentally [resided there]. || 22 ||
Having performed ablutions, charity, and other rites, one beholds Maheśvara himself; for such people, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain, whether in terms of sons or wealth.
One obtains all enjoyments and, upon death, shall go to the city of Śiva; by either reciting or hearing it, one gains the fruit of the Śatarudriya.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O highly fortunate Vyāsa; this city is indeed Amarāvatī, which is celebrated as Viśālā and is sung of in all the worlds. (1)
Thus I shall fully proclaim that sacred field which was narrated by Brahmā in ancient times—the most secret of secrets, which destroys all sins. (2)
Accompanied by Umā, the God wandered alone in the forest; thereafter, all the hosts of spirits followed, as did all the gods and demons.
Wherein Viṣṇu exists in his ten forms, as well as the goddesses who are the mothers of the world, the Vināyakas, the Vetālas, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Bhairavas, and others.

The manifestations of the Kalpas and the Liṅgas numbering eighty-four, as well as the sacred fields (kṣetra), the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapāla), and likewise supernatural power (ṛddhi) and perfection (siddhi).
The ancestors, the guardians of the worlds, and those who are perfected beings (siddhas) bestowing perfection; the highly fortunate seers (ṛṣis), and the wives of the seers of pure intent.
The Kinnaras, the divine Gandharvas, the Apsarases who are excellent women, all the hosts of Maruts, and those who are the assemblies of practitioners (sādhakas). || 7 ||
The yakṣas, the hosts of guhyakas, the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—all things stationary and moving—resorted to mental meditation.
There they sat in attendance upon the God of gods, the Lord of Umā. Seeing them, the goddess Pārvatī, the daughter of the mountain, then spoke with gentle words to Śaṅkara, the refuge of the world.
Pārvatī said: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, you who are intent upon being the support of the universe! Behold these illustrious ones, meditating and taking refuge in you. (10)
O highly fortunate one, you must not neglect all these people who are afflicted by wind, rain, and heat; provide for their own welfare as well as your own.
"O Lord, fashion for me a most beautiful city, a dwelling-place suited to my inclinations, which grants all desires, for the purpose of my residence. (12)
"O Lord, this is my desire, if it pleases you. Having heard these words of Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord fashioned a beautiful city, enchanting to all living beings. (13)
Then Śambhu, with his whole being, [created] for his own benefit a divine and meritorious [city], extending over many yojanas, which was dear to the celestial beings.
Endowed with divine intentions, delightful with its celestial abodes, possessed of all divine qualities, it was vast, stainless, and auspicious. || 15 ||
It was filled with marketplaces and watchtowers where buying and selling flourished, crowded with many mansions and houses, and adorned with rows of palatial buildings.
It was constructed with walls of crystal, with floors of lapis lazuli gems, with excellent pillars of coral, and adorned with an abundance of golden ornaments.
It had a threshold of reddish gems, was adorned with door-panels, possessed golden doors, and was well-fitted with adamantine bolts.
Its ground, gates, courtyards, and inner chambers were like precious jewels; it was exceedingly beautiful with networks of bells and hung with strings of pearls.
Every house was adorned with golden pillars and banners; moreover, jars filled with jewels and gold shone resplendently in every dwelling.
There were step-wells, wells, ponds, and clear lakes, fragrant with the pollen of lotuses and adorned with water-machines.
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by flocks of peacocks, provided with water-reservoirs made of mechanical devices, and possessed of house-lakes and groves. (22)
In some places peacocks dance, and in others cuckoos warble; there are rows of forest trees laden with clusters of flowers kissed by swarms of bees.

Crowded with throngs of men and women and inhabited by those following the duties of their respective castes and stages of life, the women who had come to the interiors of their mansions stood intent on gazing [at the procession]. || 24 ||
And it shines as if with archways formed by rows of moon-garlands; thus, O Vyāsa, is this delightful city perfumed by its own yoga. (25)
There lies the beautiful city of Alakā, marked by the palace of Kubera; it is white, crowded with holy beings, and graced by birds.
There lies the divine Bhogavatī, the supreme abode of Varuṇa, crowded with fierce Nāga maidens and the wives of the Nāgas.
The excellent city of Saṃyamanī is protected by Dharmarāja; it is filled with people of virtuous conduct who are experts in performing their duties.
The delightful city of the gods, protected by Vāsava, is crowded with throngs of virtuous women and adorned by the songs of Kinnaras. || 29 ||
In former times, there were many more such delightful places, exceedingly vast in extent and most brilliantly white.
In some places, auspicious jars filled with barley sprouts served as doorways fashioned from plantain trees; in some places, Gandharvas sang, and in others, dancers performed.
In some places, young brahmins were reciting the study of the Vedas; in other places, sacrificers along with their officiating priests were performing sacrifices.

In some places they performed the ritual bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice, and in others they distributed gifts; in various places they performed the initiation ceremony, marriages, and the formal establishment of the sacred fires.

In some places there were indeed groves and sacrificial enclosures, and in others the observance of religious processions, as well as the construction of large oblong ponds, wells, and tanks according to the prescribed rites.
In some places, the reciters praise various topics of discourse, while in other places, the poets compose verses before the supreme city.
In some places wrestlers were engaged in combat, and in others actors were intent on their performances; the ponds shone with rows of steps made of jewels.
There were restless, fickle young girls, dark-complexioned and sixteen years of age, intent on carrying water, adorned with jars made of jewels and gold. (37)
Thus, O Vyāsa, this beautiful city was created by Śambhu through his yogic power (yogamāyā), destroying all sins and intended to bring about both the pleasure and displeasure [of his devotees]. (38)
It is vast, exceedingly extensive, meritorious, and the refuge of holy people; therefore, it is celebrated at all times and in all worlds. (39)
This eternal and beautiful city is known as Viśālā; whether one is situated anywhere at all, or has reached any state whatsoever, [one attains liberation].
One should always say, "It is vast"; such a city is honored in the world of Śiva. O Vyāsa, there is no city like this on earth within the sphere of the cosmic egg.

There is another [tirtha] called Viśālā, which is similar and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; if men perform the Śrāddha ceremony there at the proper time for the sake of their ancestors. || 42 ||
That [merit] becomes inexhaustible for them, and it is proclaimed in the Pitṛkalpa that this applies even to those by whom bathing, giving gifts, and so forth are performed at Viśālā incidentally.
Wherever they may go, once deceased they indeed proceed to the abode of Śiva; blessed and most meritorious in the world are those whose love is ever unshakable.

In Viśālā, the remaining fruit is such that Śeṣa is not capable of describing it; by merely hearing this narrative as it is being recited, one is instantly liberated from the sin arising from great transgressions—of this there is no doubt. (45)
Thus, O Vyāsa, the city became vast and known as Kuśasthalī; listen as I describe how it came to be in every kalpa. || 46 ||

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Name Viśālā," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth section (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 47.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen attentively, O Vyāsa, with a one-pointed mind; I have received this auspicious narrative concerning the different kalpas from the mouth of Vyāsa.
More secret than the secret, most excellent, it should never be given to just anyone—not to an atheist, nor to an ungrateful person, nor to one who is not a disciple.
O Vyāsa, this is the most meritorious and supreme narrative that removes sin; by the mere hearing of it, the defect of the kalpa does not afflict one.
The lifespan of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin is one kalpa; this remains constant throughout all the Manvantaras and through the intervals between kalpas.
Listen, O best of beings, as to how many [divisions] it is measured; the sun traverses both the human and divine day-and-night (ahorātra). || 5 ||
O best of the twice-born, listen to the calculation based on that: fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those make one *kalā*.
Thirty kalās constitute a muhūrta, and thirty of those, according to the movement of the moon and the sun, the wise call an ahorātra (a day and night). || 7 ||
By virtue of the sun's specific movement, it constantly enters into the twilight; that [period] is the day for humans, and the night is likewise of such a nature.
The fortnights, months, seasons, years, and solstices are proclaimed according to their true nature for the ancestors, the gods, and Brahmā.
The number [of years] that has been declared is such that their lifespan ends accordingly; fifteen days and nights are designated as a "pakṣa" (fortnight). || 10 ||
Two fortnights constitute a month; two months are said to be a season (ṛtu). Three seasons make a solstice (ayana), and two solstices are recorded as one year (abda). || 11 ||
By those expert in the principles of calculation, the southern and the northern [solstices] are defined; by this measure, a month consists of two fortnights.
Those who know the divisions of time understand that this constitutes a day and night for the ancestors; for them, the bright fortnight is the day and the dark fortnight is the night.
O twice-born one, here the Śrāddha for the ancestors takes place during the dark fortnight; and that which is known as a year by human reckoning, [is the period for this]. (14)

That constitutes a day and night for the gods; the wise who are skilled in the knowledge of reality have declared that the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night.
A hundredfold divine year, or indeed a thousand divine years, is recorded by the sages who know reality as a single day and night of Manu.
Tenfold a day and night is called a human fortnight; tenfold a fortnight is a month; and twelvefold those months [make a year]. (17)

A season (ṛtu) is declared by the wise who perceive the truth of reality to be the measure of the Manus; six of those [seasons] are declared to be a year, and by that [unit], the calculation is established.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of exactly four thousand years; its dawn (saṃdhyā) is of the same duration, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is likewise.
The Tretā age consists of three thousand years by its measure; its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for three hundred years, and its subsequent twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is likewise.
Likewise, two thousand years are proclaimed for the Dvāpara age; its twilight (saṃdhyā) consists of two hundred years, and its subsequent twilight portion (saṃdhyāṃśa) is likewise [two hundred].
The wise have stated that the Kali age lasts for one thousand years; its dawn (saṃdhyā) consists of one hundred years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
This number of twelve thousand years is proclaimed as the measure of a yuga. Now learn from me the calculation of the yugas according to this divine measurement.
O dear one, he then emitted this entire world, as well as the four ages: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
O best of the twice-born, that yuga multiplied by seventy-one is declared as a *manvantara* by those expert in the science of calculation. (25)
That is also declared to be the solstice; there are two solstices, southern and northern. For when the Lord of the World has arrived, Manu is dissolved therein.
Then another Manu shall exist for an equal duration of time; O Indra among kings, this is declared to be the period of one year. (27)
At that very time, an ayana was proclaimed by the sage who perceives reality; that day of Brahmā is proclaimed, and it is called a kalpa. (28)
That night is said by the wise to last for a thousand yugas; during it, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, sinks down.
O best of the twice-born, when that thousand yugas is completed at the end of a day of Brahmā, it is called a kalpa in its entirety.
Those seventy-one yugas, including the Kṛta, Tretā, and others, have been described by you; this is called the interval of a Manu (Manvantara).
These fourteen Manus have been described as increasers of fame; they are all powerful lords throughout the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
O Vyāsa, the lords of creatures—how praiseworthy is their proclamation! (33)
Within the Manvantaras there are dissolutions, and at the end of those dissolutions there are new creations; it is not possible to describe their limit even in hundreds of years.
O Bhārata, there is indeed the emission of creatures and their withdrawal; O bull among the Bharatas, the withdrawal at the end of Manvantaras is heard of in the scriptures.
There indeed dwell all the gods together with the seven sages, endowed with austerity, celibacy, and sacred learning.
When a thousand yugas are complete, the kalpa is said to be exhausted; therein all beings are consumed by the rays of the sun.
O twice-born one, placing Brahmā at their head, together with the Ādityas and their hosts, they enter the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the foremost of the gods.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the end of each kalpa; he is the unmanifest, eternal God, and this entire world belongs to him.
O Vyāsa, he alone exists, united with Maheśa; the Lord of the Universe made his dwelling in Mahākālavana. || 40 ||
O Vyāsa, dissolution does not afflict this most excellent Mahākālavana; for in every kalpa, this beautiful city of Kuśasthalī indeed remains.
Free from disease, free from fear, and changeless in age after age, these Kalpas taught by Mārkaṇḍeya come into existence.
And in this very same delightful forest, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, as well as those who are the lords of creatures—Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, and others—[performed sacrifices].
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Rudra, and others such as Bhṛgu, likewise created the worlds of moving and non-moving beings at the beginning of the kalpa, each in their proper manner.
O Vyāsa, at the beginning of such a time, when the world is being fashioned anew, there likewise occurs the manifestation of the Varāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, and the Pitṛs.
The divisions of the eons have been fully described in the auspicious Mahākālavana; eighty-four eons, O best of the twice-born, have arisen there.
O best of men, so many signs of yogis remain in the forest; yet the earth, oceans, and mountains are born again and again, and then destroyed again. (47)
This city shall indeed exist again and again; it is remembered as immovable. Therefore, it is sung of at all times and in all worlds.
O Vyāsa, it shall become renowned on earth as Pratikalpā; and those men who, being self-controlled, perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites therein— || 49 ||

For those who perform recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and ancestral rites (śrāddha) dedicated to the deities and the ancestors, there is no return to this world again, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having approached and beheld the god Maheśvara at every kalpa, they indeed bathe him for one day on the full moon of Vaiśākha.
Even those men who, exhausted by dust, happen to bathe in the waters of the Śiprā incidentally—no evil whatsoever remains for them; they dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever fruit is obtained from residing in Kāśī for thousands of Manvantaras, a living being may obtain that same fruit in a single moment during every Kalpa.
And at the end of every kalpa, that very same auspicious city existed once more; therefore, O best of the twice-born, it is renowned by all people as Pratikalpā.
And those fortunate men who feel affection for him—for them, this dissolution of the kalpa does not occur even for a moment, but passes away like a dream. || 55 ||
Whoever hears this meritorious and auspicious narrative of the origin of every kalpa, or recites it with diligence, destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Designations of the Various Kalpas," in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the fifth book (*Āvantya-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, O Vyāsa, this delightful city is eternal by name; O sinless one, I have described to you how it has arisen and become renowned in age after age. (1)
Vyāsa said: O best among the knowers of Brahman, I desire to hear from you once more the meritorious, purifying, and sin-removing narrative of the Śiprā.
The beautiful Kuṇḍa is thus described, as well as Piśācamocana; beyond that is Karkarāja, which is called the Nīlagangā.
All the Puṣkara lakes, the unsurpassed Gayātīrtha, that which is celebrated as Gomatīkuṇḍa, and likewise Dharmasara; || 4 ||

The famous pilgrimage site born of the confluence has been described, along with the auspicious account of Śani’s birth, as well as the events that took place in Cyavana’s hermitage and in the auspicious abode of the Nāgas.
At what time and in what manner does the greatness of Puruṣottama manifest? I desire to know this which dwells in your mind. (6)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O illustrious Vyāsa, to this supreme narrative that removes all sins, concerning the time when it occurred in the auspicious Mahākālavana.
"O child, there is no river on the surface of the earth equal to the Śiprā; on whose bank liberation is attained in an instant—what need is there for long-term service? (8)
In Vaikuṇṭha she is born as Śiprā; in the abode of the gods she is Jvaraghnī; at Mahādvāra she is Pāpaghnī; and in Pātāla she is Amṛtasaṃbhavā.
In the Vārāha Kalpa, she was indeed proclaimed by the name Viṣṇudehā; she is celebrated as Śiprā in Avantī, originating from the Kāmadhenu.
Vyāsa said: O best of sages, this which has been recounted by you is wonderful; you ought to tell the auspicious story of the Śiprā in brief.
Sanatkumāra said: Taking up the skull of Brahmā, the pure-souled Mahādeva wandered everywhere throughout all the worlds for the sake of alms.
Not having obtained alms, the omnipresent Lord, seeking alms, went to Vaikuṇṭha; he wandered here and there until the time for hospitality arrived.
"O Brahmin, intent on censuring the world, angry, and hungry for many days, I am focused and say: 'Give me alms; I am hungry. (14)
Then Hari, holding a skull in his hand, spoke again and again: "O Hara, please accept this alms; I give it to you."
Having spoken thus, he raised his hand and placed the forefinger upon it; then Rudra, being provoked, struck him in anger with his trident.
Then, much blood flowed from his finger; by that, the vessel held in the hand of Śaṅkara was quickly filled.
Then that stream, having overflowed, became level on all sides; in that place, the Śiprā was produced, originating from the flow of blood.
And immediately in Vaikuṇṭha there arose a river that purifies the three worlds; thus Śiprā became renowned throughout the three worlds as the best of rivers. 19.
O Vyāsa, I shall tell you how she was described as the destroyer of fever; when the Daitya Bāṇāsura fought with Kṛṣṇa in battle, (20)
The heroic lord of the Daityas, who had insulted Aniruddha, fought with his thousand arms, brandishing various weapons.
Therefore, the enraged Vāsudeva, taking up his discus with haste, severed the thousand arms with a swift-moving razor-edged arrow.
Then, his resolve shattered and his arms severed, tormented by the wounds, he turned away from his purpose and sought refuge in Śaṃkara.
Then, seeing that great Daitya arrive nearby, overwhelmed by fear, he was filled with compassion as he proceeded to the front of the battle.
Having indeed severed the thousand arms of the king of the Daityas in battle, the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the excellent destroyer of enemy armies, became enraged.
O Vyāsa, while he remained there immovable, Maheśvara arrived and indeed warded off Kṛṣṇa, showering him with volleys of arrows.
And having encountered one another, they engaged in a fierce battle with most terrible weapons and missiles that struck fear into all living beings.
Then Kṛṣṇa, desiring to slay Hara, took up the Vaiṣṇava weapon, as well as the weapon named Pāśupata, which causes the destruction of all things.
Then Śambhu, eager to take the life of Kṛṣṇa, indeed fixed [his arrow]; at that time, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose and was heard throughout all the worlds.
Then Kṛṣṇa again discharged the deluding weapon (mohanāstra) at Śiva; by that weapon, which was the divine illusion (devamāyā), Śambhu was then rendered unconscious.
Yawning repeatedly for a short while in that battle, Rudra regained consciousness and was as if born anew in that great conflict.
Then, overcome by anger, the Māheśvara fever was produced; from the surface of his forehead, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra immediately emerged.

Three-eyed and three-headed, short-statured with three feet, he has the form of a goat; he is small, matted-haired, his limbs are smeared with ashes, he is a great disease, and difficult to overcome. (33)
Having encountered Kṛṣṇa’s army, impelled by Mahādeva, he wrought slaughter among all living beings who were associated with Kṛṣṇa.
O Vyāsa, the army protected by Kṛṣṇa suddenly became turned away from the fight, broken, shattered, and afflicted by the assault of fever. 35.
Beholding her own army in such a state—yawning, afflicted by disease, shattered in resolve, and tormented by the fever of Maheśa—[he acted]. || 36 ||
Highly incensed, Kṛṣṇa unleashed the Vaiṣṇava fever; with that Vaiṣṇava fever and the Māheśvara fever [the two fevers fought]. || 37 ||
A great, terrible, and most horrific battle took place between them; after waging a vast conflict, the fever of Maheśvara was broken.
Having indeed traveled through all the worlds, he did not find peace; afflicted by him, he arrived at the delightful Mahākālavana.
Then, having plunged into the Śiprā, that most fiercely raging fever attained supreme peace upon seeing the tranquil form of Maheśvara. (40)
A devotee of Viṣṇu, having reached it, performed his ablutions; by its power, the two fevers arising from Hari and Hara were destroyed.
Therefore, at all times, she became a destroyer of fever in an instant; people who were overcome by fever attained her and were freed from their supreme suffering. (42)
And at dawn, Vyāsa, being composed in mind, bathes in the Śiprā; for him, the pain arising from fever never causes affliction. (43)
O Vyāsa, that was truly spoken then by Brahmā, Hari, and Hara.
Those men who listen to this divine narrative with one-pointed minds shall never experience any fear born from the torment of fever.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Grace Bestowed upon Jvara," within the *Māhātmya* of the Śiprā River, in the *Avantī-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the fifth *Āvantya-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sanatkumāra said: O scorcher of enemies, I shall describe to you in brief how the milk-abounding Śiprā became renowned as the destroyer of sins. || 1 ||
Long ago in the Kṛta Yuga, O Vyāsa, there was indeed a king named Damana, renowned among the Kīkaṭas, who was exceedingly wrathful.
He was a wanderer on the wrong path regarding all dharmas, a reviler of cows and Brahmins, a drinker of liquor, a stealer of gold, envious, and one who violated the teacher’s bed.
He was a plunderer of the people's entire property, a violator of others' wives, a rogue, a companion of rogues, a slanderer, and a thief in appearance.
He was a cattle-robber and a destroyer of cities; he was a captive, yet dear to those who were captives; he was contemptible and full of anger, and devoid of the Vedas and the Shastras.
He abandons the company of the virtuous, is wicked, and is fond of wicked people; he forsakes women of noble family and becomes the husband of a prostitute or a low-caste woman.
Constantly reviling the Dharma, his mind delights in unrighteousness; neither sacrifices are offered, nor are [deities] worshipped, nor are the discourses of the wise heard.
The Vedas and the sacrifices are the very form of the gods, yet they are being trampled underfoot; such an exceedingly wicked king has never existed before, nor will there ever be one again.
Once, that wicked man, wandering here and there in a terrible forest while engaged in hunting, was surrounded by hunters.
Having obtained no food at all, that wicked man, afflicted by hunger and thirst, went alone and detached to the vicinity of Mahākālavana.
The terrible night, frequented by fierce beings, had arrived there; afflicted by hunger and seeking a place to sleep, he approached the foot of a tree. || 11 ||

In some places peacocks were dancing, in some places cuckoos were warbling; in some places there were the cries of peacocks, and elsewhere it was filled with a roar like that of thunderclouds.
It is beautiful, of beautiful form, and for that reason it is called "Sundara"; O Vyāsa, it produces great merit and is the supreme remover of all sins. (19)
Where Viṣṇu, the self-controlled Śiva joined with Śakti, was ever present, they worshipped him constantly at all times and in every season.
If a person dwells at Sundarakuṇḍa for half a fortnight or even one full fortnight, his residence in Vaikuṇṭha shall certainly last for a hundred kalpas.
Even birds, insects, and moths that die there go to the abode of Śiva; how much more so, then, men in this world who have been purified by bathing there?
Those who give sesame seeds, a cow, elephants, horses, chariots, land, female slaves, male servants, gold, and various kinds of jewels; || 23 ||
O Vyāsa, I do not know what kind of fruit arises from those various gifts—such as the gift of beds and celestial palaces—that might come to them.
Listen further, O Vyāsa, to the supreme fruit of Sundarakuṇḍa as it is remembered: once, due to great sin, one falls into sinful wombs.
The Piśāca attained liberation and departed assuming the form of Śiva; having bathed at Piśācamocana and beheld the god Maheśvara. || 26 ||
One is liberated from all sins, even if one should be a slayer of a Brahmin.
Vyāsa said: Who was this one known as a Piśāca, and what evil deed did he commit, by association with which sin he attained the state of a Piśāca?
O best of the twice-born, how did this man’s attachment to the heretical paths arise? O foremost among the knowers of Brahman, I desire to learn this from you. (29)
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to this great narrative, the supreme majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha), by the mere hearing of which the destruction of all sins occurs. (30)
There was a Brāhmaṇa named Devala from the south, the lowest of the twice-born; he was always devoted to sin, greedy, a false witness, and a libertine.
One who betrays his guru, a gambler, a rogue, a slayer of a guru, one who violates the teacher’s bed, a stealer of gold, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a Brahmin, and a traitor to his master—(32)
He was a consumer of forbidden food, devoid of the Vedas and the Śāstras, a sinner who had accumulated [evil] over many births, and one cast out from all dharma. || 33 ||
A betrayer of trust, arrogant, engaged in the company of thieves, wicked, having gone to another country, dull-witted, and one who accomplishes the aims of thieves; || 34 ||
Many living beings were slain on the road by that evil-doer; that wicked man went to Magadha through association with evildoers. (35)

There was a certain Brāhmaṇa there who was self-controlled, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, maintaining the sacred fires, established in pure being, and always devoted to the rites of Brahman.
Having mounted a vehicle and set out to take his illustrious wife, who was staying at her father-in-law's house, he was killed by that very sinner.
And his wife was of noble form, endowed with beauty and grace; she was devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, firm-minded, and possessed of a pure smile.
With her husband slain, afflicted by grief and distressed by separation from her lord, that beautiful woman, having wandered lost in the terrible forest, gathered pieces of wood.
With a joyful heart, she ascended the blazing funeral pyre along with her husband; and that most wicked man [destroyed] the entire livelihood of that brahmin.

Having taken it, he set out on the road when he was seized by the king’s servants; having been bound by all of them along with that wealth, he was led to the royal palace and presented in the presence of the king.
Tied by the neck with a rope, he was cast into the hollow of a tree; then he was dragged here and there across the ground by Cāṇḍālas and Śvapākas.
By the ripening of that karma, he went to the Raurava hell; for sixty thousand years, he became a worm in excrement. || 43 ||
Then, having reached another hell by the executors of Yama’s command, he entered the terrible Asipatravana, made of iron and filled with heated arrows.
Being struck with mallets and bound with chains by the servants of Yama, he cries out while in the Kumbhīpāka hell, severely tormented in the Vaitaraṇī river.
Having thus eaten various kinds of new and fresh excrement, that sinner then attained the state of a preta for seventy-five yugas.
Possessing a massive body, a great roar, and a vast belly, with a face like a needle, he was overcome by hunger and thirst and took refuge in the desert region. || 47 ||
Then, having undergone an even more miserable state and assumed the body of a Piśāca, he became crooked, evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and naked.
He fed on food defiled by excrement and urine, leftovers, putrid, and stale; he ate the remnants from cremation grounds, was clothed in animal skins, and had three eyes.
In a broken well or pond, at a withered tree devoid of water, in a wall, a moat, or a house, in an empty dwelling, or on a riverbank; || 50 ||
He always delighted in dwelling at all the junctions [of time]; thus, after many ages had passed, he went to Mahākālavana.
Merely by residing where the beautiful Māheśvara Liṅga and the excellent Kuṇḍa are located, you were struck down by a lion.
And having caused that wicked man to be slain, he, seeking water, entered a pool; and a bone caught between his fangs fell from his mouth into the water.
By the power of that merit, all his evil was destroyed; and as soon as he died, the linga then entered into the interior of his eye.
Having abandoned his piśāca body, he entered that light which is the liṅga; from that time forth, O Vyāsa, that supreme holy site has been known as Paiśācamocana.
From that time on, the Lord became famous as Piśācamocaneśa; for as long as sins roar like elephants intoxicated with rut. (56)
Until one arrives at the Piśācamocana tirtha on the Śiprā; having bathed at Piśācamocana, become pure and composed.
Having worshipped the god Piśācamocana according to the prescribed rite, one becomes purified of all sins; of this there is no doubt.
O Vyāsa, one should cause great gifts to be bestowed at Piśācamocana; for such a person, there is never again a return from the world of Śiva.
Whoever reads or even hears this sacred story of the liberation of the Piśāca, which removes all sins, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sundarakuṇḍa-Piśācamocana Tīrtha," in the Āvantī-kṣetra-māhātmya of the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: O best among the knowers of Brahman, I desire to hear further from you: O Brāhmaṇa, when did the Nīlagangā arrive at the Śiprā-kuṇḍa?
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the great sacred site (tīrtha) which bestows the fruit of all tīrthas; having bathed in the Nīlagaṅgā, a man should worship Saṃgameśvara.
Faults arising from bad association never occur [there]. Once, in the world of Brahmā, the river Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, [arrived]. || 3 ||
Purifying the three worlds as she went, clad in blue garments and afflicted by grief, she said: "O Blessed One, what is this that has happened? What sin was committed by me in the past? (4)
"By the offense of his wicked conduct, he has been brought to this state; whatever sin exists among people on earth in all the worlds," || 5 ||
All of that of all embodied beings rests upon me; therefore, indeed, being overwhelmed by the burden, I am unable to move from this earth.
Blue-hued and discolored, she is turned away from all dharmas; whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious—(7).
Having cast [their sins] upon me, living beings here become entirely stainless; they abide in the worlds of merit which bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
O Creator, a great suffering has arisen for us, a supreme defilement; indeed, there is no happiness, no peace, no sleep, and no contentment.
O Teacher of the World, there is no eternal standing place in this world for me, who am most sinful; I have been overwhelmed by the defects arising from association with the wicked. (10)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go so that peace may come to me? What austerity, what gift, what sacred ford, and what practice [should be mine]? (11)
"O Great Yoginī, having understood this, act in such a way that I, whose limbs are smeared with sin, may regain my natural state. (12)
Brahmā said: Listen, O best of rivers, to the cause that destroys sin. In the delightful Mahākālavana, this city is indeed Amarāvatī. (13)
There flows the Śiprā, the best of rivers on earth, which is purifying; by the mere sight of it, the destruction of all sins occurs. (14)
"Go there immediately, O illustrious one, for the purification of yourself," thus was it declared by Brahmā; having heard this, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, [departed]. (15)
Having recognized that, they arrived at the auspicious Mahākālavana, located in the south-eastern quarter of Puṣkara, where the god who is the son of Marut resides.
On the northern side of the Vindhya mountains, in the excellent hermitage of Añjanī, that pure woman, observing celibacy, performed austerities together with her son.

It was frequented by hosts of Brahmanical sages and served by creatures free from enmity, amidst lakes filled with blossoming white lotuses resounding with the humming of intoxicated swarms of bees.

On the new moon day (darśa), one should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha dedicated to the ancestors; by that, his entire lineage, including himself as the hundred-and-first, is delivered.
Those ancestors born of the same lineage who dwell in hell—all of them attain a good rebirth; their worlds become eternal. || 26 ||

Having bathed, one who is intent on it should offer handfuls of sesame seeds (tilāñjali) dedicated to the ancestors; their satisfaction becomes inexhaustible, and they are glorified in the heavenly world.
Having performed the śrāddha rite, one should feed seven brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa); thus the śrāddha becomes inexhaustible and yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 28 ||
O Vyāsa, listen to another most meritorious sacred site which I shall describe to you; it is known as Dugdhakuṇḍa and is renowned throughout the three worlds. (29)
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and bestows the boon of all desires; formerly, the goddess Earth was milked by Pṛthu, who was the very embodiment of Dharma.
All milk is to be regarded as an oblation (havis) that bestows life upon all; because it was offered and deposited in this pit, it is known as the Milk Lake (Dugdhasaras).
Having bathed in the Kuṇḍa, drunk its water, and given a milch cow as a gift, one becomes completely freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth and grain.
He is born at all times and, upon death, shall go to the city of heaven; thereafter, having reached Puṣkara, he should perform ablutions, give gifts, and so forth.
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of Puṣkara.
Vyāsa said: O Brahman, who was this Vindhya mountain, and at what time did he arrive? By whom was he sent there in the past to that delightful Mahākālavana?

She who causes Kaṃsa to flee, the destroyer of the asuras, the holy one who brought down the burden [of the earth], the auspicious younger sister of Baladeva.
Born from the womb of Yaśodā, the crusher of Cāṇūra’s strength, possessing the luster of lightning, stationed in the sky, dark-complexioned, and the subduer of the black serpent.
She is the mother of Devasena, the sovereign mistress of the speech of poets, Gāyatrī for the foremost of the twice-born, and the supreme Vyāhṛti among the meters.

Aditi, the mother of all mothers; Pārvatī, the [goddess] of all women; and the youthful Jyotsnā, daughter of the Moon, who bestows the boons of all desires.

And [he bestowed] Lakṣmī, the beloved of the illustrious ones, the Yakṣiṇī worshipped by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), the shore desired by the great ocean, and the royal prosperity of kings.
The auspicious sacrificial altar of the sacrificial halls, the vessel for the oblation, the bestower of the fruit of all desires, and the supreme dakṣiṇā of all initiations. || 12 ||
Thus praised, the goddess Vindhyavāsinī then appeared in person and, with a face radiant with grace, spoke to that preeminent sage among rishis.
