"O lord of sages, the sin of killing a Brahmin arising from the Dānava has been destroyed for you upon hearing my words," he said, O lady of excellent complexion. (44)
O Lord, if you are pleased, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, may there be devotion to your pair of feet within me, O Maheśvara.

"Perform your penance and likewise your dharma; let there be no obstacle for me. Having heard those words of that high-souled one born from a jar, O large-eyed lady, I said to the sage, "It shall be so."
"The deity whom you have worshipped is the destroyer of the sin of killing a Brahmin; he shall become renowned throughout the three worlds by your name. (47)

"O Goddess, Agastyeśvara-deva is likewise renowned throughout the three worlds. Thus addressed by me, O Goddess, that brāhmaṇa remained there, adorned with the five mudrās through the grace of that Liṅga. (48)
Those men who behold that great Liṅga with devotion shall be liberated from all sins and adorned with the fulfillment of all their desires.
They shall become great-souled beings endowed with the sovereignty of their sons, and at the time of death, they go to me by means of celestial chariots that grant all desires.
And they are praised by the leaders of the Gandharvas in the eternal world of Rudra—those who always worship the god known as Agastyeśvara.
Those mortal men who have performed meritorious deeds go to the supreme state; for when the Lord of the gods is remembered, [the sins] of men born from ten million lifetimes are destroyed.
Impurity reaches its destruction; who would not bow to that auspicious one, whom a man, having bowed with devotion, serves? (53)
One is liberated from such sins as the killing of a Brahmin, which lead to rebirth in hell. || 54 ||
O Goddess, the merit that would arise from even a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices shall be surpassed by the merit obtained from this vision. || 55 ||
"What is the use of bathing at various holy fords, or what is the use of performing various acts of charity? By my grace, they shall all obtain the fruit; of this there is no doubt. (56)

Whoever, endowed with devotion, performs the worship of the Liṅga on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, or on a Monday according to their ability, shall surely deliver a hundred generations of his mother’s and father’s lineages.
And those men who, through association, perceive [the Self] as devoid of objective existence, they never at any time behold hell within this cycle of worldly existence.
O Goddess, this supreme majesty of the Liṅga has been told to you; it is the first described in the world. Now listen with diligence to the second. || 59 ||
Śrī Rudra said: Listen, O Guha, to the second Liṅga, Guheśvara, which destroys sins; by the mere sight of it, the highest perfection (siddhi) is attained. (1)

Formerly, in the Rāthantara Kalpa, in the auspicious Devadāru forest, there was a sage named Maṅkaṇaka, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; he was constantly devoted to the practice of yoga and firmly established in peace and self-restraint.
Desiring success, he performed austerities, thinking: "How shall I become perfected? How will this transformation consisting of blood go to its destruction? (3)
Having thus reflected in his heart, he commenced supreme austerity; O Pārvatī, many thousands of years passed for him.
Then, O Daughter of the Mountain, at a certain time, as he was pierced by the tip of a blade of kusha grass, vegetable juice (shākarasa) issued from his hand.
Having seen that marvel, he was struck with supreme wonder; thinking that he had attained the highest perfection, he spoke these words with pride: || 6 ||
"Aha! This is the power of asceticism; indeed, perfection has been attained by me today. There is no brahmin equal to me, for by him this perfection has been reached."

"This body is loathsome, joined with excrement and urine, smeared with marrow, sinews, and fat, and filled with flesh and blood"—yet that twice-born man, possessed of great joy, danced in that manner.
While this brahmin was dancing, the entire world—both stationary and moving—danced along with him out of passion, due to the power of that sage, O Muni.
There is no private recitation, no utterance of "vaṣaṭ," and nowhere any ritual section whatsoever.
In the meantime, all the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, were filled with wonder and said to me: "O Lord, perform that dance now! (11)
O Lord, while the sage Maṅkaṇaka was dancing, everyone danced everywhere—the entire three worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans, O All-pervading One. (12)
The mountains have shaken from their places, the rows of clouds are agitated, the peaks are crumbling, and the earth is severely oppressed.
The great rivers have become mere trickles, and the planets have strayed from their proper courses. || 14 ||
"Before the three worlds fall into turmoil and reach total destruction, restrain him; no one other than you is capable of this."
O illustrious lady, having heard those words of the gods, I went into his presence and made a solemn vow.
Assuming the form of a twice-born, I questioned that best of Brahmins: "O Brahmin, for what reason do you dance? From whence has this joy come upon you? (17)
The dancing of those whose dharma is contrary to that of the sages, out of passion for sensual desire, as well as singing and dancing, which are dear to young women; (18)
"O best of beings, O foremost of the twice-born, considering that this is a fall from asceticism for a brahmin and a lapse in virtuous conduct, for what reason do you dance so fervently? (19)
The sage said: "O Brahmin, do you not see the vegetable juice falling from my hand? For this very reason I dance; I am perfected, there is no doubt about this. (20)
O Pārvatī, having heard those words of his, I laughed excessively and struck my own thumb with the tip of my finger.
Then, at that very moment, ash as white as snow emerged; O large-eyed one, the proud brahmin was addressed by me with a laugh.
"Behold, O Brahmin, the abundant ashes that have issued from my thumb; yet I do not dance, nor do I feel joy, for I am equal to a sage. (23)
Having seen that great marvel, the best of the twice-born was ashamed; and seeing such fortitude, he was struck with supreme wonder.
With palms joined in reverence and a mind filled with wonder, he said: "I consider no other god to exist except you, O bull-bannered one. (25)
No other being in the three worlds possesses such power; therefore, O Lord of Gods, forgive what was performed by me out of ignorance.

Dancing is an act contrary to the virtuous and causes the depletion of austerity. O Lord, the merit accumulated over a long time through difficult penance has been suddenly lost by me through this dancing. (27)
Having heard those words of his, I said to that best of the twice-born: "Choose a boon—blessings upon you—I am pleased, O best of the twice-born. (28)
"O best of Brahmins, by means of this knowledge, what desire of yours shall I fulfill? (29)

The sage said: "O Lord, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, if you are pleased with me, let such a course of action be ordained so that there shall be no loss of my ascetic merit."
O Pārvatī, being pleased, I said to that brāhmaṇa: "O brāhmaṇa, may your penance increase; go to Mahākālavana."
There always resides the meritorious cave that originated seven kalpas ago, situated to the north of the deity Piśāceśvara.
There you shall see an auspicious liṅga that has existed for seven kalpas; by the mere sight of it, your austerity will attain increase.
Sin arising from desire and anger, accompanied by greed and delusion, as well as that born of envy and malice—such evil goes to destruction.
Having heard my words, O Goddess, that brahmin who had mastered the Vedas, and having heard the rule prescribed by me, that twice-born man then [acted accordingly].
Having emerged and become resolute, and having paid homage again and again, he went to the cave located in the most excellent Mahākāla forest.
There he beheld that supreme Liṅga, which increases the power of asceticism; indeed, from the sight of the Liṅga, he became resplendent like twelve suns.
In the meantime, O Goddess, it was said by the gods in the sky: "The secret Liṅga born of the cow dung has indeed been seen by Maṅkaṇaka."
Success, so difficult to attain, has been achieved by the twice-born simply through the sight [of it]; therefore, O Goddess, he shall become Guheśvara on the surface of the earth. 39.
Those who behold Guheśvara endowed with supreme devotion shall encounter no obstacle to their dharma or their asceticism.
Whoever shall behold [it] on the eighth or the fourteenth day, the ancestors of that embodied being will go to the world of Brahmā.
Whoever comes here and beholds [the deity] with diligent effort shall uplift themselves and twenty-one generations of their kin.
Even one who has committed thousands of sins, if he shall behold [it], goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells. (43)
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife—all these shall go to complete destruction by the mere sight of that Liṅga.
Whatever impure karma has been accumulated over hundreds of millions of births, all of that shall go to destruction by mere touch; it is not otherwise.
For even those embodied beings on the surface of the earth who are burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka), upon reaching the Liṅga, they are liberated from all their transgressions.
Having spoken thus, O Goddess, that divine sage Maṅkaṇaka, the twice-born, established a holy hermitage and remained right there engaged in ascetic penance.
O Goddess, this power that destroys sins has indeed been told; by hearing it or even by reciting it, one is liberated from all sins. (48)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Guheśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Rudra said: The third is Ḍhuṇḍheśvara, which bestows the fruit of happiness and heaven; it is a Liṅga that removes all sins and destroys the evil deeds of men. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in former times there was a leader of the Gaṇas named Ḍhuṇḍha on Kailāsa; he was lustful, of wicked conduct, and his senses were afflicted by vices.
He went to the world of Śakra by chance, out of curiosity, to where Raṃbhā was dancing before Śakra, displaying her art.

He beheld various beautiful and auspicious postures (bhāvas) such as those involving the gaze and the hand; the technical formations (karaṇas) such as the needle-piercing (sūcīviddha); the hand-gestures (hastakas) such as the banner (patākā); and likewise the dance accompanied by the hands and following the rhythm (laya) and tempo (tāla).
Śakra, together with the thirty gods, his eyes fixed upon her face, became truly joyful at heart, with the hair on his body and his face bristling with delight.
In the meantime, O Goddess, Ḍhuṇḍha was deluded by her charm, by the power of lustful passion, and by the inevitability of what was destined to happen.
By him, Rambhā, who was fond of the stage, was struck with a cluster of flowers; and Vāsava, seeing that injustice toward the Gaṇa, cursed her.
"Fall into the world of mortals; you have caused the destruction of the spectacle," thus was the Gaṇa cursed by Śakra of immeasurable splendor, O Goddess.
Having fallen into the world of men, unconscious and with his senses overwhelmed, disoriented and deprived of courage, he lamented again and again.
"Alas! I have obtained the fruit of injustice through an act performed out of delusion; therefore, a wise man must practice righteous conduct."
By relying upon the path of logic, may my success be achieved. || 11 ||
Having spoken thus, he performed austerities on Mahendra, the best of mountains, as well as on Śrīśaila, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāriyātra, and in the abode of Yama.
O Goddess, when he was not yet perfected, he then went to the great bank of the Gaṅgā, as well as to the Yamunā, the Candrabhāgā, the Vitastā, and the river Narmadā.
Having reached the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kauśikī, Śāradā, Śivā, and Carmaṇvatī, and having bathed there, he abandoned all ritual activities.
Holy fords are useless and asceticism is useless, since the fruit of pilgrimage has not been obtained by me, though I have wandered through the lands of action seeking my heart's desire. (15)
In the meantime, O Goddess, an incorporeal voice spoke, consoling the leader of the Gaṇas: "Go to Mahākālāyana."
Of all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist on earth, beginning with Prayāga, Mahākāla is distinguished as that which always grants spiritual perfection (siddhi).
There resides a most meritorious Liṅga that accomplishes all goals; it is situated in the presence of Piśāceśvara—worship it with haste. 18.
"By the grace of that Liṅga, you shall once again go to the realm of Śaṅkara, which is accessible to the radiant ones but always difficult for sinners to attain. (19)
Having heard those words from the sky at that time, the Gaṇa then arrived with joy in the most excellent Mahākāla forest.
There he beheld that auspicious Liṅga which bestows all prosperity; filled with supreme devotion, he worshipped the Lord of Gods.
Then, O daughter of the Mountain, a voice issued forth from the center of the Liṅga: "O child, I am truly pleased with you; what desire shall I grant you?"
Ḍhuṇḍha said: "O Lord of Gods, O you who are affectionate toward those who seek refuge, if you are pleased, may my devotion to your lotus feet be forever unwavering. (23)
If Maheśvara is pleased, grant him this boon quickly.
And those men on the surface of the earth, O God, Supreme Lord, who behold you—may they be instantly liberated from sin. (25)
O illustrious lady, having heard the speech of Ḍhuṇḍha, the Liṅga said: "Furthermore, those who shall worship me with supreme faith will always and forever be free from sin. (26)
They shall obtain supreme desires and become the best among the Gaṇas; adorned with all ornaments, they shall be worshipful in all the worlds.
Having thus obtained the boon, Ḍhuṇḍha spoke again with palms joined in reverence: "May this Liṅga, renowned by my name, remain forever established in the world. (28)
"Let it be so," was declared by the pleased Liṅga, O Pārvatī; from that time forward, the supreme deity became renowned as Ḍhuṇḍheśvara. (29)
By the mere sight of whom, men always attain perfection. || 30 ||
Those who worship the supreme deity Ḍhuṇḍheśvara with devotion—their sins accumulated since birth shall perish at that very moment. (31)
He alone is a man of merit in this world, he alone is dear to me, who beholds with devotion the supreme Liṅga Ḍhuṇḍheśvara.
Whatever merit shall arise from even a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, that will be exceeded by the mere sight of Ḍhuṇḍheśvara. || 33 ||

Whether mental, verbal, or physical, whether arising from secret acts, manifest or unmanifest, and even that which was committed through casual association—all of that shall quickly perish by the sight of Ḍhuṇḍheśvara. (34)

O Goddess, having been addressed thus by me, that leader of the Gaṇas, Ḍhuṇḍha, was established through the majesty of the Liṅga; he went to my own realm and shone together with the Gaṇapas, becoming most dear to me. || 35 ||
This sin-destroying power has been told to you, O Goddess; by hearing it or even by reciting it, one is glorified in my world.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Ḍhuṇḍheśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mahādeva said: This fourth deity, famous in Avantī, is Ḍamarukeśvara; when that Lord of the World is beheld, sin goes to its destruction.
Formerly, in the Vaivasvata Kalpa, there was a great Asura named Ruru. His son was the mighty-armed and very powerful Vajra; he possessed a massive body, sharp fangs, and was terrifying. || 2 ||
Because of that, the gods were displaced from their respective offices in the abode of the Thirty-three.
Then they took that wealth of theirs and went from there to Brahmā; Brahmā, too, became agitated with fear, his senses overwhelmed.

Knowing him to be invincible even by all the gods together, that one of great strength, once they had fled, slaughtered those brahmins who were performers of sacrifices and practitioners of austerity, as well as others who followed the path of dharma—that evil-minded one.
O Goddess, at that time the surface of the earth was devoid of Vedic recitation and the utterance of "vaṣaṭ"; with its sacrifices and festivals lost, it became senseless and cried out in lamentation.
Then all the gods and the great sages were deeply distressed; having assembled together, they deliberated on a plan for the destruction of that evil-minded one.
Then, O Goddess, while they were thus reflecting, a body suddenly appeared before them all, enveloped in a mass of splendor.
Therefore, a divine lotus-eyed Kṛtyā arose, illuminating all directions on every side with her own splendors.
She said to all the thirty gods: "O Suras, for what purpose have I been created? Let the task that must be performed by me be announced quickly."
Then all the thirty gods, having heard her auspicious words, related to her in full the conduct of Vajra.
Upon hearing this, that goddess laughed again and again with a loud, boisterous laugh; as she laughed, lotus-eyed maidens emerged from her.
Holding nooses and goads, fierce, with faces encircled by garlands of flames, they set the moving and the unmoving world in motion with their howling and roars.
O Great Goddess, they all went to where the great asura Vajra was; a tumultuous and terrifying battle then ensued between him and them.
The intermediate quarters were pervaded by various weapons and missiles discharged from all sides; with their entire armies fully equipped, they fought fiercely in the battle.

Then a battle commenced between that goddess and the enemies of the gods. Then, seeing the host of Mothers angrily crushing the great asuras and his own army turning its back in retreat, Vajra unleashed a magical illusion (māyā).
It is called Tāmasī, difficult to overcome, by which young maidens are deluded. || 17 ||
Then, while that place had become shrouded in darkness, the goddess, overwhelmed with fear, arrived together with them at the supreme Mahākālavana.
There, Hara, bearing the skull, remained stationed in the form of a linga, having perceived that the host of Mothers had vanished through the power of his illusion.
Then Vajra, having learned of the thirty gods, arrived at that place surrounded by his own army, together with the goddess.
O Goddess, surrounded by hundreds of millions of chariots in the divine Mahākālavana, he, enraged, spoke these words throughout the forest.
"Today I shall slay the gods along with that most wicked woman, together with the maidens who were lost through the power of the illusion of darkness."
In the meantime, at that time, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived eagerly at Mandara, which possesses beautiful caves.
He related to the gods the defeat of the gods by Vajra.
"O Lord, O Great God, the gods have been struck by the son of Ruru with his thunderbolt in the Mahākālavana; therefore, go there, O Maheśvara! (25)
O Supreme Goddess, having heard the words of Nārada, I then quickly departed from Mandara, assuming a most terrifying form.
Surrounded by hosts of serpents that were flickering, extremely fierce, and terrifying, he saw before him the great army of the Dānavas, which was inspiring fear.
O illustrious lady, Mahākālavana has been besieged on all sides by the Asura Vajra, the son of Ruru, who is difficult to withstand.
Then, having arrived and struck him with my fierce ḍamaruka drum, the army of that evil-minded Vajra was suddenly rendered unconscious.
O Goddess, by the sound of the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), the supreme Liṅga then arose, piercing the earth and enveloped in garlands of flames.
Then, O lady of beautiful hips, a great flame issued forth from a single part of that linga, pervading the entire cosmic egg.
But from another part of the Liṅga, a great wind arose.
Driven by a wind accompanied by a mass of blazing flames, that army was consumed by the discus and reduced to ashes.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, paid homage to that mighty son of Ruru.

By the majesty of this deity, the exceedingly powerful Vajra was consumed along with his army; therefore, he shall become known in this world as Ḍamarukeśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (35)

Since he was born upon the surface of the earth by the sound of the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), this god shall therefore become the most excellent of those worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. (36)
Those who, having seen him, shall worship the god Ḍamarukeśvara, they all shall become liberated from suffering and freed from feverish distress.
Whatever fruit is obtained from performing a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa penances according to the rules, that same fruit one attains by worshipping Ḍamarukeśvara.
Even men devoted solely to sin, if they should happen to behold the Liṅga Ḍamarukeśvara situated in this place with devotion—even by chance—[are purified]. || 39 ||
Those devotees who shall praise the famous Liṅga known as Ḍamarukeśvara will certainly go to the eternal world of Rudra. (40)
Freed from mental sins, they shall go to the supreme state; by beholding it, men shall obtain the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeyas, and the fruit of a thousand cows. (41)
The steadfast man who goes into battle after having beheld Ḍamarukeśvara shall conquer his enemies and, at the end, be glorified in the world of Rudra. || 42 ||
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power has been narrated to you; when praised and glorified, it bestows the fruit of all desires. (43)
Śrī Rudra said: O Pārvatī, know the fifth deity to be the Lord of the beginningless kalpas; he is the eternal remover of all sins and is always proclaimed as being without beginning.
O Goddess, in the beginning of the former kalpa, this liṅga emerged when there was neither fire, nor sun, nor earth, nor directions, nor sky.
Neither wind nor water, neither sky nor moon nor planets; neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas [could perceive it]. || 3 ||
Therefore, O Daughter of the Mountain, this entire world of moving and unmoving beings has arisen from this *liṅga*, and by means of time, it returns to dissolution within this very *liṅga*.
From this source have emerged the lineages of the gods, sages, and ancestors; as well as the Manvantaras, the genealogies, and the accounts of the deeds of those belonging to the lineages.
As many creations as there are, and likewise as many dissolutions; as well as the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, and the forests.
The worlds beginning with Bhūrloka, as well as the seven Pātālas that are remembered, and likewise the course of the sun, moon, planets, lunar mansions, and luminaries; || 7 ||

Therefore, O fair-faced one, everything visible and invisible arises from this *liṅga*. That which is the beginningless cause, called the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), is what the great seers call the subtle, eternal *puruṣa*, whose nature consists of both being and non-being. (8)
It is eternal, imperishable, ageless, immeasurable, and dependent on nothing else; it is devoid of smell, form, and taste, and is free from sound and touch.

Without beginning or end, the source of the world, the origin of the three qualities (guṇas), and imperishable; it is described by the great seers as a sign (liṅga) that is incomparable and unknowable.
At the end of the dissolution, this entire divine realm came into being through him in its entirety.
I am awakened upon the earth, the beginningless source of the universe, the cause of all, whose nature is inconceivable, the supreme, and beyond all action.
Having quickly revealed both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, the Master of the Universe, agitated them by means of his supreme yoga.

Just as a fragrance causes agitation merely by its proximity, even though it does not actively assist the mind, so too is that Supreme Lord; He is declared to be the beginningless God who is intent upon being the cause of the universe.
O Pārvatī, when the Pradhāna is agitated by that Liṅga, there arises the support of the worlds, renowned as the Brahmāṇḍa. || 15 ||
In that egg from which the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—was born and into which it dissolves, even its end cannot be found.
He alone is the agitator who was previously the object of agitation, the lord of the earth; through contraction and expansion, he is established in the state of primordial matter (pradhāna).
Once born, that Lord of the World, though devoid of qualities, assumes the quality of passion (rajas); having attained the state of Brahmā, he proceeds with the creation while experiencing it.
In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds through the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva); then, attaining the state of Viṣṇu, he performs protection through righteousness (dharma).

Then, having withdrawn the entire universe into himself through the manifestation of the quality of tamas in the form of Rudra, he who is both endowed with the three qualities and yet devoid of qualities rests within the three worlds.
Just as one who previously sows, one who guards the field, and one who reaps are designated by those respective names, so too do [the selves] attain the states of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the state of Rudra, he even withdraws them; and in the state of Viṣṇu, he protects them all—these three states are remembered as his constant condition.
Rajas is Brahmā, Tamas is Rudra, and Sattva is Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World; these alone are the three Vedas, and these alone are the three Puruṣas.
Indeed, in age after age, he is always sung of as beginningless by the gods, the ancestors, the hosts, and the perfected ones; therefore, he is the Lord of the Beginningless Kalpa.
O large-eyed one, Mahākālavana has always been known by that name ever since the dispute between Brahmā and Keśava arose. || 25 ||
"I am the elder, I am the elder, because of being the cause of creation at the beginning of the kalpa"—then a divine, unsupported voice arose from the sky.
"In Mahākālavana, there is a Liṅga known as Kalpeśvara; whoever sees its beginning or its end shall become a lord—of this there is no doubt, nor should any dispute be raised. (27)
Then, O Goddess, Brahmā went swiftly to the infinite world above, and Viṣṇu went to the world below at his word.
Neither the beginning nor the end was seen by Brahmā or Keśava; then, filled with wonder, the two praised one another.
Having offered various hymns from the Vedas while standing before him, they said: "There is neither beginning nor end, nor is any kalpa perceived here. (30)
Therefore, from this day forward on the surface of the earth, this place shall become renowned as the supreme Mahākālavana, beginning with that name.
Even that mortal who is possessed of the five great sins and is evil-minded shall go to Śiva upon seeing the auspicious Ādikalpeśvara Śiva.
May there always be auspiciousness for those whom you have come to behold; blessed are they in the world of mortals who have sought refuge in you.
O Lord, whatever merit is obtained by men through ablutions at all sacred fords, all of that—and even more—is attained simply from the sight of you. (34)
So long do they fall into this worldly existence, which is filled with pleasure and pain; so long, O Lord, is the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra not seen.
When the evil of men is exhausted, then there shall be a vision of you.

Whether he be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—even a man who associates with such persons and commits great sins—he too goes to the supreme abode from which there is no return. (37)
O Lord, by worshipping you, one obtains that same fruit which is gained through the Aśvamedha sacrifice and that which is gained through the Rājasūya sacrifice. (38)
Those men are beasts in this world; their birth is useless, by whom Mahādeva—the Lord Śiva, the sovereign of beginningless kalpas—has not been seen. (39)
Having spoken thus, O lady of beautiful countenance, the divine Keśava and Brahmā took their positions to the left and right sides of that Liṅga.
This sin-destroying power has been recounted to you, O Goddess; by the mere hearing of which the supreme state is attained. (41)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Anādikalpeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O illustrious lady, know that Svarṇajvāleśvara is the sixth [liṅga] here; by the mere sight of it, one becomes wealthy in this world. || 1 ||
O Goddess, while I was sporting with you in my palace, a hundred divine years passed as I was solely absorbed in the essence of amorous delight. || 2 ||
Then, O illustrious lady, Vahni was impelled by all the gods into my presence; thereupon Vahni arrived for the sake of the three worlds.
Then, as I was sporting, I cast my own semen into the mouth of the Fire-god; being scorched by it, the Fire-god then went to the Gaṅgā. || 4 ||
Having gone there, Agni discharged his extremely difficult-to-restrain seed; nevertheless, O Pārvatī, the fire was still scorched by the remainder of that seed.
Then, O beloved, by the residue of his virility, there arose a divine and beautiful golden mountain, blazing with intense heat, unbearable and difficult to withstand.
O Pārvatī, having seen the first offspring born from Agni, the Asuras, Suras, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras were overcome by greed.
Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, humans, Rākṣasas, and birds rushed forward in great agitation, desiring to seize the gold.
On account of the gold, a great clamor arose among those crying "This is mine!", and through ignorance, a life-threatening conflict broke out.
Then, O illustrious lady, seizing their principal shields and various weapons, they roared with loud cries along with the gods.
The Asuras together with the Asuras, humans with humans, Gandharvas with Gandharvas, and Kinnaras with Kinnaras. || 11 ||
The spirits fought with the spirits, the Rākṣasas with the Rākṣasas, and the Vetālas with the Vetālas in a most dreadful battle.
The son hates his father, and the father likewise his son; the wife kills her own husband, and the husband likewise his beloved wife.
A son kills his mother, and a mother destroys her son; thus, a firm bond of enmity arose on account of the goldsmith.

Everything belonging to both the gods and the asuras was exceedingly terrible and vast; sharp and massive spears fell by the thousands, along with javelins with very keen points and various other weapons.
O Great Goddess, for the sake of gold, they vomited much blood.
Swords, spears, maces, and double-edged swords fell upon the surface of the earth; and heads were severed by fierce battle-axes in that dreadful combat.
With their limbs smeared with blood and having slain one another, they lay prostrate like mountain peaks covered in mineral ores.
A terrifying cry of "Alas! Alas! arose by the thousands as they cut one another with weapons for the sake of the gold.
As they struck one another in battle with iron clubs, nooses, and fists as hard as thunderbolts, the sound reached as if it were touching the heavens.
"Cut! Pierce! Run! Strike him down upon the head!"—such most terrible sounds were heard there on all sides.
Thus, while that tumultuous and most terrifying battle was raging, O Goddess, the earth trembled and the gods, including Indra, were struck with fear.
The oceans were agitated and the mountains shook; for his sake, the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—was distressed.
The sages, headed by the Vālakhilyas, and the gods led by Śakra, placing Bṛhaspati at their head, went to the world of Brahmā along with the women.
With their heads shattered and gasping for breath, they related in full detail the entire account of the destruction of the three worlds.
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, reflected upon them and came into my presence together with them.
When I questioned them all, they said: "By whom have these been shattered? By whom have you been afflicted with weapons and missiles? From what source has this fear come upon you? (27)
"And who is that wicked Dānava by whom we have been so greatly tormented? O Goddess, all of that was told before me by those overwhelmed with fear. (28)
Then those gods, headed by Brahmā, told me the cause of their fear.
"Through greed and for the sake of gold, we have all been destroyed; the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, has been afflicted. (30)
Having heard these words of theirs, O fair-faced one, I understood that a terrible quarrel had indeed arisen among them for his sake.
And he by whom the destruction of the three worlds was indeed suddenly brought about—those who would give up their lives for his sake call him a slayer of a Brahmin.
But the son of Agni is the slayer of a Brahmin; for whichever person dies with him in mind, his body shall become variegated and subject to transformation.
For there will undoubtedly be relics (dhātus) in his body; incomparable suffering is observed, such as cutting, burning, grinding, and friction. (34)
In the meantime, Vahni, having observed his son’s conduct and knowing my anger, became truly afraid on account of his son.
O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, having been propitiated by Agni for the sake of a son, he came into my presence together with Suvarṇa.
"O God Śaṅkara, this son of yours must be protected by you; O Supreme Lord, let him be placed in your own treasury. (37)
O Mahādeva, when you are pleased, this is to be attained; there is no doubt in this matter. O Goddess, let it be granted by your will to whichever person soever.
Having heard these words of him, whose face is like that of the gods of the ancestors, I agreed, saying "So be it," out of greed, O illustrious lady. (39)
Out of affection, O son of Fire, I then placed him on my lap; out of affection indeed, I kissed him on the head and embraced him again and again.
"I grant you a boon, O highly fortunate one; choose an auspicious one. I am indeed well-pleased; obtain whatever desire you wish. (41)
I command you, and thus you shall attain the highest good; there exists upon the surface of the earth a place that fulfills my desires.
O son, the auspicious Mahākālavana remains imperishable even at the time of dissolution; there itself, to the south of Karkoṭaka, the Liṅga is situated.
O son, it removes great sins and bestows splendor upon sight; by the mere sight of it, you will have fulfilled your purpose.
Through this purifying [rite], one shall become meritorious and difficult to attain; a man who is of low birth becomes of noble birth, and one who is stained becomes stainless. (45)
"By your grace, he shall become both deformed and handsome; likewise, his gifts, vows, and religious observances shall be fully perfected. (46)
O observer of noble vows, through your gift, your sacrifices, fasts, pilgrimages, and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) shall all become perfectly complete.
And you shall exercise sovereignty over all jewels; indeed, you will be beloved and desired by the gods and by the worlds.
Thus addressed, O Great Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, that meritorious one of divine form became indeed stainless and enveloped in garlands of flames. 49.
The Liṅga said: "O Suvarṇa, by good fortune, by good fortune! From this day forward, you shall indeed attain fame on the earth by the name Kāñcana."
"O son of Agni, you must always remain by my side; your fame shall become imperishable throughout the three worlds. (51)
Thus addressed by the Liṅga, O Goddess, the son of Fire became exceedingly pure; his body enveloped in flames, he attained a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Then, a brilliance was obtained through gold, filled with garlands of flames; therefore, O Goddess, Śiva became renowned as Svarṇajvāleśvara.
O Goddess, for him who worships that Śiva as Svarṇajvāleśvara with devotion, there arises victory, a powerful kingdom, sovereignty, the capacity for charity, and endless sons and grandsons.
Whatever sin a man commits, whether knowingly or unknowingly, he washes away that which arises from his body by the mere sight [of this]; there is no doubt in this matter. (55)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by offering funeral cakes at Gayā, that fruit is said to be twofold through worship; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Whatever fruit is obtained from the correct recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred thousand times, that same fruit one attains by praising Svarṇajvāleśvara.
Whatever merit is obtained by giving all forms of gifts according to the prescribed rites, one attains that same fruit simply by reciting this; of this there is no doubt. (58)
Those who worship Svarṇajvāleśvara on the fourteenth lunar day are always honored by Lakṣmī, who fulfills their desires.
O Goddess, this Liṅga is protected by the thirty gods as well as by various kinds of Gaṇas; no one knows it, being deluded by my Māyā.
"O Goddess, by my grace, that supreme Liṅga is seen; this has been told to you in full. Listen now to something else, O fair-faced one. (61)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Svarṇajvāleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, Triviṣṭapeśvara is the seventh [liṅga]; by the mere sight of which that heaven (triviṣṭapa) is obtained.
Formerly, O Goddess, in the Vārāha Kalpa, the stainless celestial sage Nārada went to heaven, desiring to see Śatakratu.

There, in that delightful pleasure grove, resplendent with wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), which was everywhere filled with breezes pleasant to the touch and fragrant with the scent of flowers; (3)
Resounding with the sounds of lutes and flutes, frequented by gods and celestial musicians (gandharvas), and illuminated by diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, moonstones, and other gems.

In that auspicious realm, whose qualities were beyond comparison with worlds such as Brahmaloka, he beheld the Lord of Gods, Śatakratu, seated there and being joyfully praised by the gods, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras.
O Goddess, having been questioned by Vāsava, the great sage Nārada recounted the majesty of Mahākālavana.
The Mahākālavana forest is delightful, ever-granting bliss, auspicious, worthy of service, meritorious, pure, and the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Those people who behold the auspicious Mahākālavana acquire merit; it is certain that their sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed.
The Lord himself dwells here, surrounded by hosts of all living beings; therefore, it is declared by the wise to be the most excellent among the chief sacred fords (tīrthas).
On earth, Naimiṣa is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins; the supreme sacred site of Puṣkara is said to be ten times more meritorious than that.
Prayāga, which fulfills all desires, is said to be ten times more meritorious than that; and Amareśvara, which is renowned, is said to be ten times more meritorious than that.
The holy Prācī Sarasvatī is remembered as ten times more meritorious than that; the Gayākūpa is declared to be ten times more distinguished than that.
Therefore, O Goddess, Kurukṣetra is ten times superior to that; likewise, Vārāṇasī is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra.
Ten times superior to that is the excellent Mahākāla, which excels it; O Śakra, the Mahākālavana is indeed the ornament of the three worlds.
Sixty thousand crores and six hundred crores of Liṅgas are present there, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Indeed, nine crores of Śaktis dwell in that sacred field.

Even worms, insects, and moths that die there during the sacrifice go by means of divine celestial chariots to the eternal world of Rudra; having heard this wonderful majesty from Nārada, the best of the gods [was moved]. (17)
Accompanied by all the hosts of gods, Vāsava, filled with joy, arrived in haste at the illustrious Mahākālavana. || 1 ||
Having seen such a delightful and auspicious Mahākālavana, which is superior even to heaven and is remembered as imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution; || 19 ||
And there were various palatial mansions, beautiful and made of gold; and hundreds of towers adorned with jewels, rubies, and corals from the earth.
Having seen such a delightful and supreme Mahākālavana, with its wonderful archways fashioned from diamond, sapphire, and ruby, resembling pure crystal; || 21 ||
All the gods, filled with joy, praised Nārada, the highly wise celestial sage by whom this story was told.
We shall not go to Kailāsa, nor likewise to Meru; we shall not go to Mandara, nor shall we go to Triviṣṭapa.
This is the most excellent Amarāvatī, and this is the auspicious Bhogavatī; this is the world of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and likewise the world of Viṣṇu.

In the meantime, O Goddess, the triple heaven became empty. Perceiving himself to be the cause of that emptiness, and having reflected upon it again and again, he resolved to depart, casting off his own body.
"Having abandoned me, all the gods have gone to Mahākālavana; I too shall go to that very place where those gods have gone. (26)

Having spoken thus, he arrived at that very moment in the excellent Mahākāla forest; out of curiosity, he then beheld there on the earth-ground a most preeminent and beautiful holy site (tīrtha), surrounded by those gods.
At that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O you who are worthy of the triple heaven, establish me by your own name to the east of Karkoṭaka and to the south of Mahāmāyā. (28)
Thus addressed by the God of gods, he, with a heart delighted and fixed upon Him, installed the deity named Triviṣṭapeśvara after his own name.
Having worshipped with auspicious flowers, O lady of beautiful countenance, he said this: "From this day forward, the earthly realm shall attain renown by this name."
But those who behold you with effort, even if they are doers of evil deeds, shall go to the supreme abode, adorned with divine ornaments.
And on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, or especially at the time of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), whatever man performs worship endowed with devotion— || 32 ||
Mounting a supreme celestial chariot that moves at will, adorned with jewels, and resembling the rising sun, he shall dwell in my presence.
What is the use of various gifts that have been given, or what is the use of various sacrifices that have been performed? Those who behold you with devotion shall obtain all their fruit.
Whatever desire men shall contemplate while worshipping me, the attainment of that very wish will come to pass; of this there is no doubt. (35)
Furthermore, having seen that supreme Malliṅga, the thirty gods spoke again: "The blessed Triviṣṭapa has installed this Lord, the God. (36)
Those fortunate ones who shall worship the god who is the lord of the three heavens, their divine residence shall become imperishable in the three heavens.
Having spoken thus, he worshipped the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga once again; then, together with Triviṣṭapa himself, he returned to his own abode.
This power that destroys sins has been told to you, O Goddess; by hearing it or even by reciting it, the imperishable world of heaven shall be attained.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Triviṣṭapeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 7 ||
Śrī Rudra said: O Pārvatī, know that the eighth is indeed named Kapāleśvara; by the mere sight of it, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
Formerly, in the Vaivasvata kalpa, when the Tretā age had arrived, I performed a sacrifice at the divine Mahākālavana, the beloved abode of Pitāmaha.
When the Brahmins were seated and the sacrificial fire was being offered oblations, I assumed the garb of a Kāpālika and went to that assembly.

O Goddess, he was covered in tattered rags, shaven-headed, and carrying a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga); his limbs were smeared with ashes from funeral pyres, he was deformed with a distorted face, holding a skull in his hand and adorned with ornaments made of skulls.
Then all the brahmins, seeing me in the form of a rogue carrying a skull, became enraged and reviled me with shouts of "Fie! (dhik).
Repeatedly mocked with cries of "Pāpa! Pāpa! and "Go! Go!", how indeed can a fire sacrifice be performed when a Kāpālika has arrived before them?
"It is proclaimed in the Vedas that those who are free from skull-bones are pure; yet this sacrificial altar here belongs to one who indeed carries human bones."
"O best of the twice-born, listen to what I have said to you brahmins: you are all compassionate, pained by the suffering of others. (8)
The virtuous should always practice compassion toward all embodied beings; indeed, the Brāhmaṇa is said to be a friend to all living creatures.
"I am a Kāpālika Brahmin, my body adorned with ashes; having undertaken the Kāpālika vow, I wander upon the surface of the earth. (10)
I constantly propitiate Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, by means of a twelve-year vow for the destruction of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"O twice-born ones, this world-renowned destroyer of sins has indeed been commenced by me for the sake of expiation; being purified, I shall go to a happy state. (12)
Having heard my words, those best of the twice-born said: "O lowest of men, you who speak thus are indeed most exceedingly sinful. (13)
Adorned with skulls and especially censured by the Brahmins, Mahādeva was not invited to the great festival of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
In that sacrifice, the Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Gandharvas, and the Kinnaras all assembled. || 15 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu; Kubera, the oceans, the rivers, and all the lakes as well. || 16 ||
The Suparṇas, the mountains, and the Nāgas were all summoned to the sacrifice, as were their followers and wives, along with Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas.
Having thus addressed Mahādeva, who was adorned with human bones, the highly fortunate Brahman-sages and the stainless celestial-sages [departed]. 18.
Knowing me to be impure, how can you deign to speak? Grant me entrance, for especially are you a slayer of a Brahmin.
When I was addressed thus by the Brahmins, I then spoke these words: "Wait for a moment; having eaten, I shall go again. (20)
When these words were spoken, O Goddess, I was then severely beaten with clods of earth, sticks, feet, and fists again and again.
Then, laughing and casting it upon that altar strewn with darbha grass, I vanished like a lamp inside a skull; I was not perceived by those best of the twice-born.
When I had vanished, that skull was thrown outside the pavilion; then, O illustrious lady, another one of the same form appeared there.
In this way, hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions were cast there and born; then they were filled with wonder.
Then all the wise ones said: "This was not the deed of anyone else, except for the great god Mahādeva, who has the Gaṅgā and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (25)
Then, having been praised individually by the brahmins with various hymns of praise, they performed oblations in the fire with the Śatarudriya mantras.
Then, O Goddess, out of compassion for the twice-born, I was pleased and said: "O Brāhmaṇas, let a boon be chosen by all of you, whatever is desired in your hearts. (27)
Then those brahmins said: "O Lord of the World, because your killing was performed out of ignorance, we have thereby committed the sin of killing a brahmin. (28)
"O Lord, grant us your grace so that the sin of killing a Brahmin may be destroyed; we choose this boon indeed, for no other boon is desired. (29)
Then, in the presence of those twice-born ones, he spoke this: "Where on the earth you have piled up that heap of skulls."
There, the primordial Liṅga had remained concealed due to the reversal of time; O Brahmins, behold that Liṅga which grants liberation from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
O best of Brahmins, even I myself committed the sin of killing a Brahmin in the past, while severing the fifth head of Brahmā, which was fierce with its splendor.
From that, the sin of killing a Brahmin arose within me, which is exceedingly difficult to endure; likewise, a skull became stuck to my hand, which is also extremely unbearable. (33)
Then, being burned and indeed pervaded by the sin of killing a Brahmin, I set out on a journey for my own sake in order to quickly destroy it. || 34 ||
He went to all the sacred fords, yet he was not liberated from the sin of killing; consequently, sorrowful and deeply tormented, he found no happiness anywhere. (35)
In the meantime, an incorporeal divine voice spoke: "O Lord, go to Avanti yourself; why do you grieve in vain? (36)

O Lord, you have created the meritorious Mahākālavana, where Rudra stands with a skull in his hand, a sight most wonderful; how is it that you do not know this sacred field which destroys even the greatest sins? (37)
In that field, O Lord of Gods, behold the great Liṅga situated in the vicinity of the elephant-form; by its power, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed. || 38 ||
Then, having heard those excellent words, I quickly arrived; there I beheld a great liṅga held in the hand of Kapāla.
O Brahmins, that skull then fell from my hand onto the ground; I gave it the name "Kapāleśvara Deva" (the Lord of the Skull). || 40 ||
"O Brahmins, behold that god known as Kapāleśvara; by the mere sight of him, you shall become stainless. (41)
Then that Liṅga was seen by them, surrounded by many skulls; they became fulfilled at that moment from the sight of that Liṅga.
Therefore, he became renowned on earth by the name Kapāleśvara. O Great Goddess, those who worship the one known as Kapāleśvara— || 43 ||
O Goddess, those men who have performed meritorious deeds go to the supreme state; even a man who has committed a terrible sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, [attains it]. (44)

That sin goes to dissolution by the mere sight of this Liṅga. Whatever sin has been accumulated through action, mind, or speech, this Lord, when worshipped on the fourteenth lunar day (Caturdaśī), destroys it.

O fair-faced one, even those who perform worship incidentally shall attain whatever desires they may have, however difficult they may be to obtain—sovereignty, incomparable righteousness, long life, and freedom from disease.
He shall obtain incomparable freedom from rivals and whatever else there may be; even those men who are exceedingly sinful and devoted to cruel deeds [shall attain this].

O my beloved, those who behold the God according to the prescribed rule for a year shall become sinless lords of hosts (Gaṇeśas) dear to me; having cast off their bodies, they behold my beloved abode. 48.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the deity Kapāleśvara has been told to you; now hear about Svargadvāreśvara.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kapāleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Rudra said: O Pārvatī, know that the ninth Liṅga is Svargadvāreśvara; O Goddess, it removes all sins and bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. || 1 ||
O Goddess, when those sisters, Aśvinī and the others, arrived at Kailāsa, the most excellent of mountains, they were filled with wonder upon seeing you.
"O Queen, we have been invited to a sacrifice by our father with great affection and full of high honor, together with our wives and our retinues. (3)
"O large-eyed one, were you forgotten, or was it my father’s forgetfulness? For what reason has he not invited you?"
O Pārvatī, having heard those words of theirs, you then released your life-breaths through yoga in their presence out of a sense of contempt.
Then, tormented by grief, they went to where Prajāpati was and related the entire event exactly as it had happened before Dakṣa.
Having heard those harsh words, Dakṣa said nothing at all.
O Goddess, when I saw that you had met your death upon the ground, my attendants were then indeed dispatched for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice.

Then those fierce hosts, by the hundreds and thousands—deformed, terrifying, and formidable, possessing great strength and various weapons—advanced and released showers of arrows while uttering dreadful cries.
Then all the hosts of gods—the Vasus together with the Bhāskaras, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas—possessed of great strength, stood with bows in their hands.
Having set out for battle, they released sharp arrows; then, having come together, the Pramathas fought with the gods, discharging showers of shafts like clouds pouring down torrents of rain.
Among them was one named Gaṇa, the very powerful Vīrabhadra; he struck Śakra in the heart with his trident.
But he, rendered unconscious by that blow, sat down; then the elephant Airāvata was likewise struck on the frontal globe with a fist.
Struck suddenly by him, that lordly elephant, uttering terrifying cries and seized with fear, rushed toward the sacrificial enclosure.
In the meantime, the gods were turned away by him; thereupon, they sought refuge with Viṣṇu, the sole leader of the universe.
Then, seeing all the dwellers of heaven routed by the Gaṇas, Viṣṇu, overcome with anger, quickly released the Sudarśana [discus].
Then, as Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus rushed toward him with great speed, he suddenly opened his mouth and placed it within his belly.
O Goddess, when that discus—indeed the infallible slayer of Daityas—was then swallowed, the enraged Nārāyaṇa rushed toward Vīrabhadra.
Seizing him by the feet, he struck him on the ground at a great distance; then, as he was being beaten upon the earth with a mace, Sudarśana—

Accompanied by a gushing forth of blood, that [weapon] emerged from his mouth; yet, O Goddess, Vīrabhadra, the best of the Gaṇas, having obtained a boon from me, did not meet his death even though he was struck with the mace.
Then all the Pramathas, afflicted by the power and strength of Viṣṇu, suddenly reached with great difficulty the place where I was stationed, O Goddess.
Upon seeing me with the spear in hand, Viṣṇu vanished; so too did Indra, along with the thirty gods, the ancestors, and the brahmins.
Then, his soul overwhelmed with fear, he vanished from sight; thus, when the sacrifice had been destroyed and the host of gods had perished, [the Lord acted].
"O Goddess, I have then appointed a host at the gate of heaven; O Lord of the hosts, no entrance must be granted to the gods. (24)
The gates must be guarded with great effort according to my command; whatever deity is seen must be slain, without a doubt. (25)
From that, the destruction of the world arose, and heaven was conquered by the gods. || 26 ||
When the gate to heaven was blocked, Śakra and the other gods, overwhelmed by fear, went to the world of Brahmā and consulted with one another again and again.
Everything regarding the closing of the gate of heaven was told before him: "O Grandfather, the gate of heaven is pervaded by the hosts of Maheśvara. (28)
"Since the doors have been barred, entry has become difficult; by what means shall we go to such a heavenly world? (29)
"O Grandfather, no joy arises for us without heaven. (30)
Having heard these words spoken by them, Brahmā then declared: "The god Śaṅkara, Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, is to be propitiated. (31)
He is worthy of praise, worship, and salutation; he is the agent of creation and destruction. O gods, heaven is difficult to attain without his grace.
He is the protector, the creator, and the capable one; he is our supreme refuge. He alone is to be propitiated, and he is considered the most worthy of worship. (33)
Therefore, with every effort, go for refuge to Śiva. I shall tell you the means; listen with full attention. (34)
O Śakra, accompanied by the thirty gods, go quickly at my command to the delightful Mahākālavana, to the east of Kapāleśvara.
"O Vāsava, there exists the supreme Liṅga at Svargadvāra, fashioned by Mahādeva for the sake of compassion toward the worlds. Worship it quickly; it will grant you your desire."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the thirty gods were exceedingly delighted; O Great Goddess, they then arrived at Mahākālavana.
They beheld an excellent, meritorious liṅga that grants access to the gate of heaven; by the mere sight of it, the gate of heaven was thrown open.
O illustrious lady, all have gone to the heavenly world as before; seeing the gods free from fear, I was then addressed by the Gaṇas.
"And having been commanded by me, all you foremost of hosts, turn back! How can that which was promised by myself become false? (40)
"The god who bestows the gateway to heaven has been seen by the gods; there is no doubt about this, for it was told by Virañci in the delightful Mahākālavana. (41)
The hosts of gods, headed by Śakra, immediately went to the gate of heaven; from that time forward, Śiva became renowned as Svargadvāreśvara (the Lord of the Gate of Heaven). 42.
It shall attain renown in the world of mortals as the bestower of the heavenly realm. || 43 ||
Those men in this world who behold Śiva, the Lord of the Gate of Heaven, indeed go to the heavenly realm by virtue of worshipping the Lord of the Gate of Heaven.
Those who behold the god Svargadvāreśvara even incidentally shall have no fear, even for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Goddess, the merit that is proclaimed to come from a thousand horse-sacrifices is surpassed by the merit gained from worshipping Svargadvāreśvara. (46)
Whatever sin was previously accumulated over thousands of previous births—that sin goes to dissolution by the mere glorification of this Liṅga. (47)
O Goddess, those men who with devotion behold Śiva as Svargadvāreśvara on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, or on a Monday, have entered my very body and shall not be born again.
When that single liṅga is worshipped, ten thousand crores of other liṅgas situated within it are also worshipped here, O Bhava.
By touching that linga, by chanting its name, and likewise by worshipping it, people go to heaven with ease and obtain their desires as they wish.
Whether unwillingly or willingly, those who behold [this] day by day—even they, meritorious and highly fortunate, indeed go to the heavenly world. || 51 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Svargadvāreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 9 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Pārvatī, know that the tenth is named Karkoṭeśvara; by the mere sight of whom one is never overcome by poisons.
And the serpents were cursed by their mother because of their failure to obey her word: "Since my words were not carried out by you in this sinful deed. (2)
"For the fire will indeed consume you at Janamejaya’s sacrifice; having heard this curse from their mother, the serpents were then terrified of death. (3)
O illustrious one, all have gone to their respective places for the sake of livelihood; O beloved, the remainder has gone to the Himalaya mountain to perform penance.
The serpent named Kambala went to the world of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and then Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Nāgas, went to Maṇipūra.
Kāliya, overwhelmed by fear, was submerged in the waters of the Yamunā.
Thus, O illustrious Susmitā, all those serpent-kings went to Kurukṣetra to perform austerities, O glorious one; and likewise, the serpent Dhṛtarāṣṭra went to Prayāga, my dear.
The lord of elephants, Elāpatra, went to the world of Brahmā; having prostrated before him, he spoke while she remained seated upon her mother’s lap.
"O Lord, we have been cursed by your wife while she was enraged in your presence; why was she not restrained by you at the time of the curse?"
Brahmā said: "Your mother was not forbidden by me because of the power of her future karma; for there will indeed be a snake-sacrifice for King Janamejaya."
And you, my child, at my command, go quickly to Mahākālavana, endowed with devotion, for the sake of pacifying all the nāgas.
Propitiate the Lord of Gods in the presence of Mahāmāyā; there, by the grace of the God of Gods, you shall attain perfection.

Having gone there, O Goddess, Karkoṭaka himself, with a concentrated mind, propitiated the God while standing before Mahāmāyā. Then, O illustrious lady, the Lord of Gods was pleased with him and granted him a boon.
Those who are venomous serpents, cruel, of sinful conduct, and full of virulent poison—their destruction shall come, but not that of those who walk the path of dharma.
"I am pleased with your devotion today; attain union with me. Then, O beloved, the serpent Karkoṭaka shall be dissolved into that deity."
Thereafter, the god Maheśvara is renowned as Karkoṭakeśvara; by the mere sight of him, diseases go to their destruction.
That man who, endowed with devotion, worships that deity, shall attain sovereignty and deliver a hundred generations of his lineage. || 17 ||
The diseased is freed from disease, and the suffering one is liberated from suffering; by the mere sight [of him], one immediately becomes rid of all sins. || 18 ||
And those who behold Karkoṭakeśvara with regularity shall attain all their desires and, in the end, dwell in my city.
Those who behold [it] on the fifth, the fourteenth, or on a Sunday—serpents shall never cause affliction to their family.

Even a woman who is unfortunate shall always obtain good fortune; a pregnant woman obtains a son who is free from disease and an ornament to the family; and the seizing spirits of children perish, so that there shall be no fear of untimely death.
Whatever desire a devoted man may contemplate in his mind, he attains that very thing, even if it be difficult to obtain, by beholding Karkoṭeśvara.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Karkoṭeśvara has been told to you; now hear about the supreme Siddheśvara.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karkoṭeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "O Goddess, know that the eleventh auspicious Liṅga is Siddheśvara; it is located near Vīrabhadra and bestows all spiritual perfections."
Formerly, in the Devadāru forest, disciplined brahmins endowed with yoga performed austerities out of rivalry for the sake of attaining supernatural powers. || 2 ||
Some subsisted on vegetables, others were without food, and still others lived on leaves; some used their teeth as a mortar, while others crushed their food with stones.
Some were devoted to the heroic posture (vīrāsana), while others were devoted to inhaling smoke; some stood on their heads with their feet upward, and some remained in the open air under the clouds.
Others, with concentrated minds, perform the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances; yet even after hundreds of years, they do not attain the supreme perfection.
Afflicted by suffering, they reflected: "How will success be achieved? Success is not obtained here even through difficult penance."
Thus, the scripture formerly sung by the sages has become useless; everything is obtained through austerity, for this world has its root in austerity.
Eye-salve, a medicinal pill, the power of traveling in sandals, the perfection of the sword, dwelling in a cave, the wish-fulfilling gem, and whatever else is desired.
Thus those perfected ones (siddhas), filled with supreme indignation, cast aside that dharma of austerity and fell into a state of atheism (nāstikya).
At that very moment, however, an incorporeal voice spoke, consoling those Siddhas like a mother her own biological son: || 10 ||
"Do not despise us, for the Veda is indeed authoritative upon the earth. Neither penance nor dharma is to be censured; hear now the reason for this. (11)
"O you whose wealth is penance, success shall not be yours here; for that penance performed out of rivalry by those desiring success has been done in vain. (12)
From desire comes the loss of austerity, and from egoism comes pride; likewise, from anger, greed, and delusion [these] arise—of this there is no doubt. (13)
He who, free from rivalry and devoid of desire and anger, performs action with a pure disposition, enjoys the fruit of austerity.
He who is permeated by latent impressions (vāsanā), whose mind is one-pointed and composed, who is a believer and full of faith—he enjoys the fruit of austerity. || 15 ||
The man who always regards the wives of others as his own mother and the wealth of others as a clod of earth enjoys the fruit of austerity. (16)
O Brahmins, in such a person as this, the perfection of asceticism is seen; and you all, out of rivalry, have likewise performed what is difficult to achieve. (17)
Therefore, even in a thousand years, success will not be achieved, unless my word is carried out with a mind free from conceptual construction.
Having gone to Mahākālavana, all of you, with concentrated minds, should propitiate the Lord of Gods, who eternally bestows spiritual perfection.

By the sight of that God, the highest perfection is attained; even Sanaka and the others, who were devoted to yoga, having approached the God and worshipped Him with devotion, reached supreme accomplishment. (20)
Formerly, King Vasumata attained the very rare perfection of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi) merely by beholding this Liṅga, through its power. || 21 ||
The high-souled Haihaya, the son of Kṛtavīra, obtained the power of traveling by means of sandals as well as a thousand steeds.
In former times, the power of invisibility was attained by Anūru; likewise, through the vision of this Liṅga, the Siddha obtained the perfection of gold, foot-ointment, elixir, and collyrium.
Having heard the words from the sky, those Siddhas, filled with wonder and endowed with joy, arrived at the most excellent Mahākālavana.
And they beheld that supreme Liṅga which bestows all accomplishments; by the sight of that Liṅga, they attained the highest perfection.

From that time forward, he became renowned among the gods as the supreme Siddheśvara. O Goddess, for those men who behold the supreme deity Siddheśvara, no accomplishment (siddhi) shall be difficult to attain upon this earth.
Even those devoid of devotion who go to Siddheśvara by chance will become fully perfected; they will certainly attain success, of this there is no doubt.
He who, though joined with great sins, should remember Siddheśvara, will certainly become perfected, endowed with knowledge and sovereign power. || 28 ||
But he who, by means of constant discipline, beholds the supreme deity Siddheśvara, shall attain within six months whatever desired perfection (siddhi) may exist in his heart.
Especially on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, whoever beholds Siddheśvara shall behold my own abode.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth shall obtain wealth; a seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge; and a seeker of a wife obtains a wife. (31)

O Dear One, he who worships on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on a Monday, and during an eclipse, having delivered a hundred generations of his paternal lineage as well as himself, rejoices in my world for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras lasts.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the god Siddheśvara has been recounted to you; now hear about Lokapāleśvara.
Śrī Hara said: O Goddess of the gods, know that the twelfth is Śiva, the Lord of the Guardians of the World; by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins.
O Goddess, in ancient times, thousands of Daitya hosts of exceeding prowess emerged from the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
By them this earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, has been pervaded; all their hermitages have been destroyed, and likewise, the sacrifices have been demolished.
Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas were indeed devoured; and the sacrificial fire-pits were filled with dust as well as honey.

All the water-pots were shattered, and earthen vessels and the like were reduced to powder; the place was devoid of Vedic recitation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and it was bereft of the sounds of *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
And the goddess Earth was made to suffer, her sacrifices and festivals destroyed; then the world-protectors, terrified, went to Mādhava for refuge.
With palms joined in reverence, they all spoke, afflicted by hunger and made miserable: "O Lord, we have fallen into exhaustion, deprived of our share of the sacrifice. (7)
In the past, we were protected by you from Namuci, Vṛṣaparvan, the terrible Hiraṇyakaśipu, Naraka, and likewise from Mura.
Likewise, O best of gods, protect us; a great danger has come upon us.
Having heard those words of theirs, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace then departed; O Daityas, they had entered the abode of Varuṇa.
Having gone forth from there at night, O Goddess, they slaughtered the best of the twice-born—ascetics who had been initiated and were devoted to their religious vows.
Then, O beloved, having gone to heaven, Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, was conquered; likewise, Dharmarāja was subsequently conquered in the southern quarter.
Then, having gone to the western direction, the Lord of Waters was utterly defeated; and in the north, O Goddess, Dhanada was likewise utterly defeated by those Daityas.
Then, becoming distressed, they sought refuge in Viṣṇu; O Goddess, Viṣṇu then declared a remedy to the gods.
Having gone to Mahākālavana, the gods, concentrated and full of devotion, should propitiate Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, the benefactor of the world.
Success shall be yours there through his grace. || 16 ||
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor, those guardians of the world set out for the auspicious Mahākālavana.
At that moment, they were hemmed in right there by the weapon-wielding Daityas; having been lost again, they arrived once more where Lord Janārdana was.
They described how the three worlds had been besieged by that most fierce one; those guardians of the world were then addressed repeatedly by Nārāyaṇa.
Having become observers of the vow, adorned with skull-bowls, carrying khaṭvāṅga staffs, peaceful, and embellished with the five mudrās. || 20 ||
With all your limbs adorned with ashes and resplendent with small bells, having undertaken the great vow, go together with Brahmā to the excellent Mahākālavana, wearing anklets bound upon your feet.
Then, O Great Goddess, having heard the speech of Kṛṣṇa, those guardians of the world arrived, having assumed the form of Kāpālikas.
There he beheld a great and wondrous Liṅga, a mass of splendor, which was praised again and again with various hymns by the guardians of the world.
Then, from that linga, a flame of fire issued forth, by which all those Danavas were burnt and reduced to ashes.
Having understood the majesty of the Liṅga, they, being composed in mind, bestowed a name upon it; that supreme, radiant Liṅga was served by the guardians of the world.

"He shall attain fame on the surface of the earth by the name Lokapāleśvara. Having spoken thus, all the gods, surrounded by the world-protectors (Lokapālas), returned to their respective divine abodes with joy, just as before. (26)
O Goddess, those men who behold Śiva, the Lord of the Guardians of the World, shall become fully endowed with all prosperities in birth after birth. (27)
Neither poverty, nor disease, nor untimely death shall befall them; rather, incomparable sovereignty always arises for them from the mere sight [of this]. (28)
Whatever desire one may have in view when they behold [the deity], all that is fulfilled for them; and upon death, it becomes their supreme goal.
O Goddess, by worshipping the Lord of the World-Protectors, one obtains that same fruit which is obtained from the Aśvamedha sacrifice when it has been properly performed.
He who beholds Śiva, the Lord of the World-Guardians, even by chance, rejoices eternally in the heavenly world together with the World-Guardians.
Those men who, with devotion, behold [the deity] on the day of the sun's transit, on Monday, especially on the fourteenth day, on the eighth day, and during the two solstices; || 32 ||
Thus, they become invincible to their enemies in battle here; having died, they go by celestial chariot to the world of Śakra, which is very difficult to attain.

In due order, they go to the world of Varuṇa and that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) as they please; then again they go to the world of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which is very difficult even for the gods to attain.
O Goddess, this power which destroys sins has been told to you; it is rare and supremely secret. Now, listen to [the account of] Kāmeśvara.
Hara said: Know, O Goddess, that the thirteenth *liṅga* there is Kāmeśvara; by the mere sight of which auspicious good fortune arises. (1)
O Pārvatī, as Brahmā was meditating while desiring progeny, there arose a great mass of beauty, possessing the radiance of the sun, lovely and adorned with divine ornaments and decorations. || 2 ||
Having seen him—supremely divine, beautiful, adorned with good fortune, inconceivable, and unknowable—Brahmā then spoke to him.
"Who are you, and for what reason have you come here? Speak, O one with the form of Manmatha, for you appear like Kandarpa himself. (4)

Having heard the words spoken by Brahmā himself with respect, he said: "O Prajāpati, O highly fortunate one, I have been created as a portion [of you] by your desire for creation; command me, what shall I do? (5)
Brahmā said: "Those Prajāpatis who were created by me with the desire for creation were not capable of creating progeny; they desired that they might obtain happiness."
"You are the leader in the creation of beings; this world is dependent upon you. By my command, O Kandarpa, perform a manifold creation."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, O Goddess, Smara vanished from sight; he had been cursed by the enraged Brahmā: "You shall surely meet your destruction."

"Because my word was not heeded, [you shall be consumed] by the fire arising from the eye of Bhava. Having heard that terrible curse, Kandarpa, overwhelmed with fear, bowed down before Brahmā and, humbled with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, toward me who have no other refuge; for the anger of masters does not reach its full intensity toward those who have sought their protection.
Brahmā said: "O high-minded one, because your devotion toward me is incomparable, therefore twelve places have been granted to you."

Indeed, [the mind of men is captivated] by the side-glances of amorous women, as well as by their tresses of hair, their hips, breasts, and navel, the roots of their arms, and the sprout-like lower lip.

In the springtime when the cuckoos warble, during the moonlight, and at the arrival of the clouds, I have bestowed the two months of Madhu and Mādhava, together with their power, for the sake of desire.
Women are composed of nectar, blessed, and the cause of essence in this world; they are the repositories of pleasure and were created for the sake of progeny.
The entire world has been thus brought under control by these excellent women; for how can a man whose mind is attached to women possess any sense of self-respect? (15)
Moreover, even when they had gained self-control, the very women who were objects of their respect became the cause of destruction for the ancient enemies of the gods. (16)
For women alone are the source of fear for the gods, such as Indra and others; and even for a man who has obtained his livelihood through women, there is danger from every side. (17)
Defeat prevails and terrifying helplessness arises; for one whose mind is conquered by women, the emergence of calamities is easily attained. (18)
Thus addressed by Brahmā and dismissed, O blessed lady, Manmatha was given the Puṣpaka chariot, a bow, and likewise five arrows.
Endowed with passion and delight, the mind-born god whose banner is the fish, wielding his bow, mocks the three worlds together with his companion.

[He should honor] the learned, ascetics, heroes, the wise, and those who have conquered their senses; as well as the gods and the hosts of ancestors, who know the proper time and the nature of auspiciousness.
[He saw] the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras; the worms, insects, and moths, and the fourfold assembly of living beings.

"An effort has been made on my behalf after reflecting again and again; yet it is heard that Lord Śaṅkara is difficult to overcome in the three worlds. Who, other than me, is capable of agitating that deity? (23)
Having spoken thus, he arrived where I was established in asceticism, accompanied by Rati and his friend Garva, and supported by Madhu.
Then Kama beheld me, my matted locks and mane as tawny as a heap of saffron, slightly sleepless due to some cause, and adorned with ornaments made of the king of serpents.
Gazing with eyes directed straight ahead toward the tip of the bridge of the nose, one should then take hold of that which has the form of a lower lip, as a mere support.
Passing through the aperture of my ear, Madana entered my heart; tormented by desire for the sake of Rati, I called you to mind. (27)
The divine cultivation of samādhi, which takes the form of direct perception of the objective, brought about my stainlessness at that very moment, O Pārvatī. (28)
O Goddess, I have indeed fallen into a state of madness, a transformation consisting of passion; yet, relying on fortitude, I have rejected it with great effort. (29)
I have seen the god of love within my own heart, acting as an adversary; I shall burn him who dwells in my body through the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
If a yogi should enter a non-human womb, he should perform concentration on the external fire and, once it is established within the body, burn [the obstacle] away.
In the meantime, that Madana, who is difficult to perceive and whose body consists of desire, being intensely tormented, emerged in a state of misery.
Then, having gone to the foot of a mango tree, the fish-bannered god, whose friend is spring, released an arrow named Mohana.
And that arrow, having reached my heart by way of sport, I then became enraged, O Goddess, and opened my third eye.
By a spark from his eye, while the inhabitants of heaven were crying out, Kandarpa—the one who inflates the pride of lovers—was swiftly reduced to ashes. (35)
When Kāma had been consumed by fire, Rati, devoted to her husband and overcome by grief, lamented, afflicted by intense sorrow. (36)
