"Alas, my Lord! Alas, my life-breath! Alas, my Master! Why do you abandon me? O Lord, why do you forsake me, who am devoted to my husband and whose very life is my husband? (37)
As she was lamenting in this manner, an incorporeal voice spoke: "Do not weep, O large-eyed one; by the grace of Śiva, the God of gods, this husband of yours shall rise again."
Then, O Goddess, beloved, at that moment I was entreated by you: "O Supreme Lord, this Kāma has been consumed by your wrath. (39)
"O Lord, by whom indeed has creation been destroyed upon the surface of the earth? O God of gods, show mercy; grant a husband to me, who am wretched. (40)
Then, O Goddess, I spoke to that Rati who was speaking piteously: "By this Madana, my mind has today been made to tremble. (41)
"Therefore, let his limb which was burnt by me be restored to life through your grace; today, this limb of his has been burnt by me with the fire of my third eye. (42)
Therefore, he shall wander among living beings as one truly bodiless; for even though he is bodiless, he will worship the Liṅga in Avantī.
Out of compassion for the gods, I rendered him bodiless; then, commanded by the deities, Kama went to Avanti.
Having gone there, even though he was bodiless (Anaṅga), being endowed with a spirit of devotion, he beheld the supreme Liṅga that bestows the fruits of one's desires.
The gratified Liṅga declared: "O Kāma, you shall obtain every desire; even though you are bodiless, you will become powerful—of this there is no doubt. (46)
He shall obtain birth from the womb of Rukmiṇī through union with Kṛṣṇa; he will become renowned in the world by the name Śambarasūdana.
"O Kāma, although he was already satisfied by you with your mind alone, even without your body, therefore I shall forever attain renown by your name. (48)
Those who behold you as Kandarpa, endowed with supreme devotion, attain an eternal state that bestows perpetual bliss. (49)
O Manmatha, those who behold you shall become long-lived; their form shall be beautiful, and their lineage shall be stainless.
They shall possess sovereignty, supreme enjoyments, and women endowed with divine arts; they shall have healthy progeny—of this there is no doubt. (51)
Those men who behold me with devotion on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra shall indeed attain the world of the gods and rejoice there.
The Yakṣas, the lords of the Gaṇas, and the Siddhas, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, shall go to the world of Rudra in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
Thus addressed by the Liṅga, O Supreme Goddess, Kāmadeva also established a hermitage there in the vicinity of that Liṅga.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of Kāmeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear the glory of Kuṭuṃbeśvara hereafter.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kāmeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 13 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know that the fourteenth deity is named Kuṭuṃbeśvara; by the mere sight of whom the increase of one’s lineage occurs. (1)
O Goddess, when the Ocean of Milk was churned by the gods and asuras in the past, then there emerged a poison that was difficult to restrain and unbearable.
A fierce poison consisting of *kālakūṭa*, terrifying with its flames, burns the world together with its gods, asuras, and humans.
Then all the hosts of gods, along with the asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, being terrified by the flames of poison, sought refuge in me alone. || 4 ||
"O fair-faced one, I have been praised with various hymns; this has been said [by you]: 'An effort was made for the sake of nectar, yet death was obtained, O Lord. (5)
A task intended in one way was rendered otherwise by destiny; indeed, out of greed, they began to churn the ocean of milk excessively.
O Lord, when the Kālakūṭa poison arose and by whom the world of moving and non-moving beings was consumed, fear born from that Kālakūṭa arose within us.
O Lord of the World, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, grant protection for the benefit of all people, so that no dissolution may occur.
O illustrious lady, having heard the words of those thirty gods, I assumed the form of a peacock out of compassion for the deities; I then held that most terrible poison called Kālakūṭa in my throat.
Seeing my form, you were terrified and suddenly fled; because you avoided me like a poisonous tree that should not be approached, I became sorrowful. (10)
The Gaṅgā was seen by my side, joined by a multitude of rivers; and she, O Goddess, was addressed by me with reverence and preceded by hymns of praise. || 11 ||
O Gaṅgā, purifier of the world, carry the Kālakūṭa poison swiftly to the great ocean; no one other than you is capable of bringing it there.
Gaṅgā said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, I have no power to carry you; for you are of fierce form, difficult to serve, and you would surely burn me—of this there is no doubt. (13)
Then the Yamunā was addressed, but Sarasvatī was not capable; likewise, various other rivers were summoned by me one by one. (14)
"O Goddess, those [rivers] were unable to bring the poison named Kālakūṭa; therefore, I summoned Śiprā, who originated from Brahmā. (15)
"O Śiprā, my daughter, go to the Mahākāla forest at my command, taking the Kālakūṭa poison with you before the presence of Kāmeśvara. (16)
"The supreme Liṅga exists; unite yourself with that Liṅga. When I had spoken thus, the supreme portion of Brahmā replied: (17)
"O Lord, at your word I am setting out without a doubt; yet this Kālakūṭa poison is surely difficult to touch and will surely devour me. (18)
"I shall become unfit for service due to association with the wicked. Then I spoke again to Śiprā, the destroyer of sins: || 19 ||
O lady of beautiful smiles, whatever holy places exist in the world of mortals, in Pātāla, in the heavenly realm, and indeed in the intermediate space, they are all meritorious.
"All of them, having come for the sake of service at my word, will carry out your command; go, daughter, by my permission. (21)
Thus addressed, Śiprā then took the Kālakūṭa poison and arrived, O lady of excellent hips, at the place where the unsurpassed Liṅga was located.
That poison, known as Kālakūṭa, was cast upon the top of the Liṅga; from that, the Viṣaliṅga was born, seen as the bestower of death.
O Goddess, whether it be an animal, a bird, or even a human, whoever beholds that Śiva dies at that moment from the sight of that deity.
Then, the ascetics who had come there to undertake a pilgrimage to the sacred ford, upon seeing that deity, all died at that very moment.

Then, O Goddess, the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! Hearing that great sound of lamentation, O Pārvatī, those best of the twice-born were restored to life by me with a mere glance.
Bowing down, the brahmins praised Māma with various hymns. Then I said to those brahmins, "Choose an excellent boon."
Bowing down, they said: "O Goddess, O Śaṅkara, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, these subjects are being destroyed by this Liṅga, O Lord. (28)
"O Lord of the World, protect them indeed; for this, O Master, is our boon. O Goddess, out of compassion for the worlds, I have made this vow. (29)
This Linga will undoubtedly bring about security and health; O Brahmins, because it descended from the body [of Śiva], it will come here of its own accord.
Then this god Lakulīśa shall become touchable; he will undoubtedly bring prosperity to the family. || 31 ||
"He shall attain fame in the world by the name Kuṭuṃbeśvara. Having been told this by me, O brahmins, they remained right there engaged in ascetic penance.
Then, by my command, Lakulīśa ascended that linga, creating wonder in the world and likewise establishing his fame throughout the land.
O illustrious lady, those who behold the one known as Kuṭumbeśvara will undoubtedly experience prosperity for their family and household.
He who performs the Darśa sacrifice on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina will have many sons and great wealth; of this there is no doubt.
He attains great prosperity and is also liberated from diseases; with all his desires fulfilled, he rejoices in my world.
Those who shall perform its viewing, its touching, and likewise its worship—all of them, their desires fulfilled, go to my abode.
In its vicinity, however, is a river joined by ponds and wells; by the mere sight of which a man is liberated from sin. (38)
Having bathed on a Monday or a Sunday, or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, he who beholds Kuṭuṃbeśvara with a concentrated mind [attains his goal]. (39)
O Goddess, he obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; this which I have spoken is the truth. (40)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Kuṭuṃbeśvara has been recounted to you; now listen to [the account of] Indradyumneśvara.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kuṭuṃbeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 14 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know, O beloved, that Indradyumneśvara is the fifteenth Śiva; by the mere sight of whom glory and fame are produced.
O Goddess, in ancient times there was a king, Indradyumna, the lord of the earth, by whom this world was protected like a father protects his own biological son.
Then, having seen many sacrifices on earth accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, that high-souled one indeed went to heaven, which bestows the fruits of all desires.

Then, having fallen from heaven with his fame lost upon the earth, that lord of men suddenly fell to the ground, his merit exhausted; and as he lay fallen, overwhelmed by intense grief, he began to reflect.
The fruit of an action performed here that is experienced in heaven is not something else; it is that very same fruit which is experienced by one remaining on the earth.
Therefore, that fault is considered to reside therein, and from that comes his downfall; from that downfall, however, great suffering and remorse arise.
In this world, those who possess fame become partakers of heaven; for the sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth. As long as that sound exists, so long is the man said to live.
Whosoever, whether living being or deceased, has ill repute proclaimed concerning them in the world, he falls to the lowest worlds for as long as that report concerning him continues to be recited.
Therefore, one should be of virtuous conduct, for otherwise there is a fall to the earth; having adopted a most wicked way of life, one might only increase one's fame.
In this matter, I highly praise supreme fame, which brings about heaven; for even by the gods that supreme fame is desired. (10)
As long as the imperishable fame of men remains upon the earth, their bodies indeed become endowed with a mass of splendor.

For them there is no sweat, nor foul odor, nor even excrement or urine; the King and the Ordainer in heaven have declared this to be their definition. Adorned with various ornaments, they are carried away in celestial chariots.
Having reflected thus, O fair-faced one, King Indradyumna, desiring heaven, then went to Himavat, the best of mountains.

Where the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya performed intense penance, [the king], having seen him and bowed his head repeatedly with a full prostration (aṣṭāṅga), questioned that rishi of celebrated vows with humility.
O knower of dharma, the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas are known to you, as are the various royal lineages and the eternal lineages of the ṛṣis. (15)

"O best of the twice-born, there is nothing in this world unknown to you. I wish to hear this; let it be told by you in its true essence: how is eternal fame produced in the world, and is it from the fruit of austerity? (16)

Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Ah! I shall tell you that for which you desire fame: as long as your fame remains established upon the earth, so long shall you dwell together with the gods. Therefore, O knower of dharma, go quickly to the supreme Mahākālavana."
To the left of the deity Kalkaleśvara, there is a sin-destroying Liṅga; worship it there with diligence.
By merely worshipping him, you shall obtain supreme fame, as well as eternal heaven, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (19)
Having gone there, he worshipped that liṅga which has thus been described; then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, being filled with joy, praised him.
Seated in their celestial chariots in the intermediate space, they spoke these words to the lord of men: "Your fame has become stainless through the worship of this Liṅga."
From this day forward, O Indra of kings, this Liṅga shall certainly attain fame in this world by your name as Indradyumna.
Those men who worship the god Indradyumneśvara shall be liberated from all sins and [travel] in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
They shall go to heaven joyful, being praised by the celestial sages; furthermore, nothing whatsoever in this world shall be difficult for them to obtain.
Those who shall behold [it], whether out of greed or even through casual association, for them there will arise fame, renown, merit, and likewise righteousness. (25)

There shall be no falling from heaven for them as long as fourteen Indras endure, those who will perform worship especially on the fourteenth day; they shall always deliver their maternal and paternal lineages.
Having spoken thus, O beloved, all the gods, after worshiping the Liṅga with great effort, returned to heaven together with Indradyumna.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Indradyumneśa has been told to you; O beloved, let another be heard.
Īśvara said: Know, O Pārvatī, that the sixteenth is named Īśāneśvara; by the mere sight of which sovereignty arises for men. (1)
O Goddess, in former times all the gods, the highly blessed sages, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, were indeed oppressed by Tuhuṇḍa.
Indeed, the entire forest known as Nandana came under his control; having conquered Airāvaṇa, the lord of elephants, he stationed him at the gate.
The lord of the Dānavas seized the horse named Uccaiḥśravas and prepared to bring about the destruction of all the celestial women.
Out of fear of her, the path to heaven indeed became obstructed; and the gods, deprived of their authority, entered into a consultation. || 5 ||
At that time, the great sage Nārada, who knows the proper occasion, arrived with his ministers, wandering about and endowed with great splendor.
Then, saluted by the gods and honored according to the prescribed rites, he was informed of the events as they had occurred and of Tuhuṇḍa’s conduct.
Then they questioned Nārada, the best of sages, regarding the mantra: "O one of great intelligence, tell us; you know everything in every respect. (8)
"O Great Sage, O best of divine seers, when such a time has arrived, what ought to be done? There is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you."
Having relied upon meditation for a moment and slightly closing his eyes, he spoke the means that destroys all suffering.
"Let those who are distressed go quickly to the delightful Mahākālavana; stationed behind Indradyumneśvara himself, worship the supreme Liṅga known as Īśāneśvara. (11)
Formerly, indeed, in the Īśāna-kalpa, by the sage Īśāna—who was truly learned in the Vedas and devoted to the study of the Vedas—the highest position was obtained upon the head of Śaṅkara.
Indeed, by the mere propitiation of him, one's heart's desire is obtained. || 13 ||
Having heard the words of Nārada, the gods, their minds filled with joy, went to where the great Liṅga was located, and they all offered hymns of praise.
O Īśāneśāna, O Īśāna, O Tatpuruṣa, salutations be unto you! Salutations to Vāmadeva, O Mahāghora, O Sadyomukha, salutations again and again! || 15 ||
O three-eyed one, O Bharga, O Mahādeva, O beloved of Umā, salutations again and again! Salutations to Śiva, salutations to Bhīma, salutations to Sarva, salutations again and again! (16)
Salutations to Śambhu, salutations to Rudra, Virūpākṣa, salutations again and again! By you, O God, all creatures—including gods, asuras, and humans—are sustained. (17)
O Maheśvara, the immobile beings and the mobile creatures that move about, as well as Brahman, the Vedas, and all that is to be known, have been created by you.
O Goddess, the sky is your head; the moon and sun are your eyes; the wind is your breath; and the fire is your imperishable splendor.
Your arms are all the directions, O Lord, and your belly is the great ocean; your thighs are the mountains, and your feet are considered to be the earth.
Indra, Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, the gods, asuras, and great serpents stand before you in humble prostration, praising you with various hymns.
All beings in the world are pervaded by you, O Lord of the World; when you are pleased, the entire universe is pleased, and when you are angry, there is great fear.
You alone are the remover of fears, O slayer of enemies; the destruction of the powerful asuras has been accomplished by you.
O Lord, you did not attain supreme nirvāṇa through your strides; for you are the creator and the transformer of all beings here in every respect.
Having propitiated them, they all paid homage to it from every side. In the meantime, O Goddess, [a voice] arose from the midst of the Liṅga.
A great flame enveloped in smoke, by which that Dānava Tuhuṇḍa—the son of Muṇḍa—was consumed, surrounded as he was by his army.
And they attained their respective offices through the power of this Liṅga; and the gods, being delighted, proclaimed the name of this very Liṅga.
It is our firm conviction that he possesses the nature of sovereignty; therefore, he shall become renowned throughout the three worlds as Īśāna.
And for those who fully propitiate the one known as Īśāneśvara, fame, fortune, constant success, and joy shall be theirs. (29)
Constantly honored by the gods and by hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, they shall go joyfully to the heavenly world in radiant celestial chariots.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and maidens obtain their desired objects of longing; of this there is no doubt. (31)
The man who, established in self-restraint, correctly practices this vision, shall suffer no loss anywhere for as long as a hundred lifetimes may last. (32)
O illustrious lady, those who behold the one known as Īśāneśvara day after day shall be capable in all their undertakings at all times.
Thus, O Goddess, has the sin-destroying power of the deity Īśāneśvara been described to you; now let the story of Apsareśvara be heard.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Īśāneśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Know the seventeenth deity to be the renowned Apsareśvara, by the mere sight of whom people shall obtain their desired objects. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in the forest named Nandana, which is endowed with all objects of desire and resounds with the songs of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras.
It was filled with parrots, cuckoos, ruddy geese, chakoras, and ospreys; it was a place comparable to the divine realm, an ornament of the third heaven.
Seated there, the enemy of Vṛtra and the eldest of the gods were attended upon; Rambhā danced before him, manifesting various modes of dance.
Then, having become distracted in mind due to some lapse of memory through negligence, she was seen by Vāsava indeed to be devoid of proper rhythm and tempo.

The best of gods became enraged and indeed pronounced a curse upon her: "Forgetfulness is a human trait; it is never seen among the divine. Therefore, go to the world of mortals as one devoid of luster."
Then, due to the agitation caused by Indra’s wrath, that apsaras fell to the earth, motionless, distraught, and weeping piteously and profusely.
Lamenting piteously, she said: "What evil deed have I committed? Have I not performed pure austerity? Why has the god not been propitiated? (8)

Then the entire host of Apsarases, accompanied by their circles of friends, arrived where Rambhā had fallen, O fair-faced one; the company of Apsarases was tormented by the burning fire of grief for her.
Just as a lotus-pond does not shine at all when it is asleep under a cloudy sky, so too Rambhā, devastated by the curse, never shines again.
O lady of beautiful countenance, Rambhā was seen surrounded by her circles of friends by the celestial sage Nārada, who was filled with wonder in his inner soul.
Why are the Apsarases suddenly seen overwhelmed with grief? And why does this Rambhā weep so piteously again and again? (12)
And having approached, he asked: "O excellent Apsarases, why are you dejected in countenance and distressed? Tell me respectfully. (13)
And they related that ancient account to him; having heard it there, the sage Nārada became absorbed in meditation.
He diligently spoke a beneficial expedient for them: "Let all the Apsarases go to the most excellent Mahākāla forest."
Worship the Lord of Gods, the Liṅga that accomplishes all aims, which was worshipped in a former aeon in the presence of the Goddess Pṛcchā.
"By my word, Urvashi obtained Pururavas as her husband; likewise, having heard the speech of Narada, the Ganas assembled. (17)
In the beautiful Mahākālavana, out of a desire to worship the Liṅga, Rudra himself was pleased by their devotion and granted them a boon.
"O Rambhā, you shall obtain good fortune and the heavenly world, O illustrious one; O highly blessed lady, you will certainly become the beloved of Jiṣṇu. (19)

Therefore, go to Triviṣṭapa, having been honored by this Saṅgha; for in former times, you were propitiated by the Apsarases out of a desire for heaven, and thus you became renowned as the Lord of the Apsarases (Apsareśvara) and attained fame throughout the three worlds.
Those who shall propitiate the Lord of the Apsarases with devotion will have all their desires fulfilled in age after age.
O illustrious lady, for those who shall urge others in this world to see [the deity], neither displacement from their station nor separation shall occur, even in their dreams.

What is the use of gifts, what is the use of austerities, and what is the use of sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees? By merely touching [it], one obtains a kingdom, and then heaven and liberation in succession. (23)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the god Apsareśvara has been told to you; now let the [power] of Kalkaleśvara be heard.
Śrī Śiva said: Know the eighteenth deity to be the renowned Kalakaleśvara; by the mere sight of whom no quarrel ever arises. (1)
It pacifies all suffering, liberates from all evil, subdues diseases, serpents, fire, and thieves, and bestows one's desires. (2)
"O Goddess, a quarrel arose between me and you in the past; O auspicious one, listen with a focused mind as I relate it in detail. (3)
O lady of excellent complexion, when you were the daughter of the Snowy Mountain, O beloved, you were then married by me according to the prescribed rites.
And when the marriage was completed with you, O fair-faced one, she indeed became known by the name Mahākālī, being similar to you even in complexion.
Resembling a blue lotus, with dark and curly hair, you indeed sat then in the midst of the auspicious pavilion of the mothers, O you whose splendor is like black collyrium.
"O Kālī Sundarī, my beloved, sit beside me; O slender-limbed one, you of white luster shine like moonlight upon my dark body. (7)
Like a female serpent dwelling upon a bright sandalwood tree, you are like the night in the dark fortnight; may you remove the defect of my sight. 8.
"O Goddess Girijā, O lady of beautiful smiles, having been addressed thus by me, you then spoke these words to me with a faltering voice: (9)"
But when you dispatched the highly fortunate Seven Sages, who have mastered the Vedas, on my behalf, why did you not tell me for what purpose? (10)
At that time, you even entreated my father, the King of the Himalayas, with great effort on my behalf; why then do you not say the same to me now, O Kālī? (11)
Even though you said out of dejection, "O Nārada, go for my sake and quickly entreat Pārvatī," why did you not say that to me at once: "Is Kālī not [Pārvatī]? (12)
This worldly verse is true; it does not arise in vain: every person is overcome by the dullness they have created for themselves through their own actions. 13.
One who seeks must inevitably suffer the cutting off of the head; yet, having performed very long and arduous austerities, I have made this request of you.
For me, this is indeed a certain humiliation at every step; yet, O Dhūrjaṭi, I am neither crooked, nor fierce, nor uneven.
"You are not of noble birth, you are of vain conduct, neither wicked nor envious; yet you are known as 'the poisonous one,' for it is evident that faults have taken refuge in your hands. (16)
"Born of no noble lineage, of vain conduct, and always possessed by envy, I do not steal your eyes; you yourself are the one who destroys them. (17)
"May the Lord Āditya, who consists of twelve forms, recognize you! O shameless one, I have not uprooted the teeth of anyone. (18)
The divine Pūṣan, the twelve-fold maker of day, knows [the truth], since you revile me with your own faults because of this headache in your head. (19)
"As for what he said to me—that I am known as Kṛṣṇa and Mahākāla—even so, O Hara, I shall declare to you this preeminent renown."

You ought to forgive him after hearing this for the sake of illustration and not out of hatred; for as long as a deformed man does not see his own face in a mirror, [he remains unaware of his true state]. (21)
One considers oneself more handsome than others only so long as one does not behold one's own face distorted in a mirror. (22)
Therefore, one recognizes this [Self] alone as the Self and not another person, [fearing] a man fallen from truth and righteousness as one would a base venomous serpent. (23)
"O Goddess, even an atheist is terrified by this, how much more so a believer?"—when you said this to me, O Goddess, I raised a great clamor. (24)
O Girijā, you who do not know yourself, O Mṛḍā, you who consider yourself a scholar: it is true that even when praised with all his limbs, he remains just like his father.
Hardness and pain arise from the elements in many ways; crookedness and unfitness for service come from all of them, as if from the frost.
"O Goddess, though you were addressed by me in this way, you spoke these words once again; nevertheless, everything has indeed been transmitted [to you] through association with the wicked. (27)

From the serpents comes the state of having many tongues; from the ashes, the absence of affection; from the moon, the turbidity of the heart; and even from the bull, the quality of being difficult to comprehend.
Your fearfulness arises from dwelling in cremation grounds, and your nakedness is not out of modesty; your ruthlessness comes from the skull-bowl, and your compassion has long since vanished. (29)
Thus, at that auspicious time, a fierce and terrifying quarrel broke out; as it proceeded in this manner, the three worlds trembled.
The gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas were terrified; then, from that [sound], a tumultuous roar arose, piercing the earth and becoming a liṅga.
From the center of the Liṅga there arose an auspicious and bliss-bestowing voice, which indeed comforted the gods and the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then the lords of the gods gave him the name Kalakaleśvara; thereafter, he became renowned on earth by the name Śaṅkara.

O lady of excellent hips, for one who worships that god Kalakaleśvara with devotion, neither Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, nor Vināyakas shall cause distress to the Brāhmaṇa, and no quarrel shall arise in his home.
By such a sight, his wife becomes virtuous, beautiful, fortunate, dear, possessed of many sons, and endowed with great wealth. (35)
Those who behold the god Kalakaleśvara on the fourteenth day shall experience neither sorrow, nor old age and disease, nor likewise untimely death.
And no fear of enemies shall arise for them, O daughter of the mountain; the world shall be imperishable, O Goddess, as long as fourteen Indras endure. (37)
This power that destroys sin has been told to you, O Goddess; by the mere hearing of it, there is well-being both in this world and the next. (38)
Īśvara said: O beloved, the nineteenth is Nāgacaṇḍeśvara; by the sight of whom one is liberated from the sin incurred by stepping over sacred offerings (nirmālya).
Now I shall describe in detail its auspicious power; listen with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess, for it is the destroyer of all sins. (2)
In ancient times, the celestial sages, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas were seated in the Sudharmā assembly hall, recounting auspicious stories.
In the meantime, Śakra respectfully questioned the divine sage Nārada, the seer of pure vows, who had arrived at the Goddess’s side.
Having seen him endowed with discipline, devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), wearing a girdle, deerskin, and a loincloth, and adorned with the handle of a lute; || 5 ||
By you all this triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ, has been seen—being produced, already produced, and undergoing dissolution by the thousands.
There is no one equal to you in this world, except for the single Supreme Lord—the unmanifest cause of the universe, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being.
Since you have been fully gratified by me through yoga, austerity, and devotion, you perceive the entire three worlds clearly in every respect.
Therefore, I wish to ask you; please tell me with certainty about that most excellent field on earth, which is purifying and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having heard this and reflected upon it, Nārada then pondered; after reflecting for a long time, he spoke these words. (10)
O King of the Gods, the merit of the unsurpassed king of sacred fields has been remembered; Prayāga is praised as the most excellent field among all fields. (11)
Therefore, O Vāsava, the field of Mahākāla is said to be ten times more meritorious; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation even by its mere sight.
Having heard this and having praised that sage, the thousand-eyed one, seated in his celestial chariot along with all the hosts of gods, proceeded with haste.

Standing in the intermediate space together with the gods, the victorious one beheld the sacred field filled with lingas so densely that there was not even the space of a finger's breadth between them.
Sixty-six billion [deities] dwell in the delightful Mahākālavana; how could their discarded offerings (nirmālya) ever be transgressed? (15)
"A great fault certainly arises from stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya)," having reflected thus, O Goddess, those delightful beings returned once more to heaven.

Fearing the defect of using discarded flower offerings (*nirmālya*), those gods did not enter the sacred field (*kṣetra*). In the meantime, O Goddess, the foremost of the Gaṇas arrived, seated upon their celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
Being sung to by various groups of Kinnaras with diverse songs, and being praised by Cāraṇas and gods as he proceeded toward the heavenly world; || 18 ||
"Who is this blessed one of great asceticism seen with wide-open eyes? Blazing with splendor, he is being attended by celestial nymphs. (19)
All the immortals asked: "O mighty-armed one, who is this host resembling Rudra? Where is he going, so joyful in spirit and with a smiling face? (20)
Then, questioned by all the gods whose minds were filled with wonder: "Who are you, O tiger among men, and what meritorious deed was performed by you? (21)
Then, O Goddess, all was told in its entirety before the gods; Mahākāla, the Great God, was worshipped with devotion and praised.
Delighted, he granted me the status of a Gaṇa, which is very difficult to attain, and certainly bestowed upon me the auspicious name Nāgacaṇḍa.
The immortals respectfully asked that best of the Gaṇas: "O Nāgacaṇḍa, did you indeed drop the *nirmālya* there?"
"In the meritorious Mahākālavana, you have traversed while wandering; for there is no movement possible there, since it is crowded with *liṅgas*. (25)
Then he explained the means before the gods: "O lords of the gods, there stands a Liṅga that bestows all fruits. (26)
The deity Īśāneśvara stands in the northeastern quarter; by the mere sight of him, one does not go to a state of evil-doing. || 27 ||
Whatever great sin arises from stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), all of that goes to destruction by the sight of that Liṅga. || 28 ||
Then all the hosts of gods, highly fortunate ones, came once again to Mahākālavana, and Mahākāla was worshipped. || 29 ||

Just as that Liṅga was seen to cause the destruction of all defects, by the mere sight of it—even through such acts as stepping over the *nirmālya*—the defect of the gods was destroyed; therefore, they gave it this name.
It was told to us by that wise Nāgacaṇḍa: "Therefore, the narrative known as Nāgacaṇḍeśvara shall become famous in the world. (31)

Having given him this name, those gods departed for their supreme abode in heaven. Whatever people shall worship Śiva as Nāgacaṇḍeśvara, the sin arising from stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) shall perish for them.
Those who behold the god Nāgacaṇḍeśvara day after day—their sin, whether committed through ignorance or knowledge, is destroyed; it is not otherwise.
By the mere sight [of it], one attains joy, bliss, well-being, health, and a beautiful form for seven births; of this there is no doubt. (34)
Through the chanting [of the name] of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara, one attains all desired objects, even those difficult for the gods to obtain; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara has been recounted to you; now listen to that of Pratīhāreśvara.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, O beloved, know that Pratīhāreśvara is the twentieth; by the mere sight of whom one becomes wealthy in this world. || 1 ||
O Goddess, because of Dakṣa’s wrath, you formerly gave up your life-breaths; thus, O beloved, you were born on the Himālaya mountains and have been recovered by me once again.
And then, O Goddess, sexual union was commenced by me together with you; a full hundred divine years passed in delight, O Goddess, as I was overcome by passion and tormented by the god of love. (3)
Then, having observed Mahārati, the gods, headed by Vāsava, with their minds deeply agitated, held a consultation at the appropriate time as was fitting.
For a hundred divine years, that god Rudra remains on Mount Mandara, in its beautiful caves, constantly engaged in amorous dalliance with Gaurī.
If a son were to be born from these two who possess such excellence of seed, then the entire three worlds would perish because of him; of this there is no doubt.
We are certainly not capable of bearing even his splendor; therefore, let that deed be performed by which our passion may be pacified.
Thereupon, Bṛhaspati—the preceptor and leader of the gods, possessed of great splendor and having reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras—perceived a means.
"Let all the thirty gods go into the presence of Śiva; let the Lord himself be informed, for he will not perform that deed."
Having thus resolved, O Goddess, those gods then departed quickly; they stood at the auspicious gate of Mount Mandara, filled with wonder.
"Nandī, the lord of the Gaṇas, stands vigilantly at the gate; O Goddess, I remain here performing that pleasure together with you."
Then, thinking that entry into my presence was difficult for the gods, those deities remained there reflecting.
Agni spoke these auspicious words before them: "Assuming the form of a swan, I shall go into the presence of Śiva. (13)
Having deceived the doorkeeper, he did exactly as described; O lady of pure smiles, he spoke into my ear while in the form of a swan.
The gods, Indra and the other immortals, stood restrained at the gate; having heard those words of his, I then came to the door.
And so, from where have you come, and why do you pay me homage in due order? I have seen those gods; what shall I do for you? (16)
They said, "Let this most dreadful carnal union be abandoned. O Goddess, I did exactly that, and they returned once more to the third heaven.
Then Nandin was cursed by me: "Go quickly to the world of mortals! Thereupon, fallen by that curse, he then descended to the earth.
With a heart gasping for breath, dejected, and his eyes agitated by grief, Nandin lamented thus, rolling upon the ground out of sorrow.
"I have certainly been deceived by Agni, and especially by Vāsava. What evil deed did I commit in some previous life? (20)
The world-protectors saw that host fallen into such a state and asked him: "O Nandin, from where does this great lamentation come? (21)
Nandin reported everything in their presence, and they then described the means [to achieve it], which was Mahākālavana.

Then, O Goddess, having heard those words, that attendant Nandin, his body covered in horripilation, went to Mahākālavana; assuming the form of a skull-bearer (kapālika), he worshipped [the Lord] according to the prescribed rites.

Then, O beloved, a bodiless voice emerged from the Linga: "Your release from the curse has occurred because of the excellent devotion of the gatekeeper. He was then worshipped with great devotion by Nandin, the gatekeeper.

From that time forward in this world, O Goddess, I have described to you the power of Pratīhāreśvara, the Lord of the Lords of Gatekeepers, which bestows the most desired fruits upon all people. || 25 ||
Those who worship Śiva as Pratīhāreśvara with devotion shall never suffer displacement from their station or separation [from loved ones], even in their dreams.
Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes, whether it be small or great, all of that goes to destruction through the worship of Pratīhāreśvara. (27)
Whoever shall remember in their mind Śiva, the Lord of Gatekeepers, his entire lineage will undoubtedly go to heaven. (28)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pratīhāreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Know that the twenty-first is named Kukkuṭeśvara, by the mere sight of which one does not obtain birth in the womb of an animal.
There was a king named Kauśika who was always born as a cock; he was seen during the day, adorned with all kinds of ornaments. || 2 ||
The earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, was pervaded by him; through the power of his past karma, he obtained a kingdom free from all thorns.
The wife of that lord of the earth was renowned by the name Viśālā; she was endowed with beauty and charm, and possessed of the sixty-four arts.
Accompanied by her, that best of kings ruled his kingdom; she was the king's beloved, dearer to him even than his own life.
O Pārvatī, at times there was no sexual union with her; she remained constantly distressed due to the absence of pleasure.

As time passed in this manner, Viśālā—the one who knew the cries of all beings and possessed large, wide eyes—became afflicted with love while in the company of the king; she beheld a pair of insects distressed by the quarrel of the bodiless god of love.
Thus propitiating her, the insect said repeatedly to his beloved: "O beautiful one, endowed with grace and good fortune, I am your slave."
Favor me, who am tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, according to your desire; with my head bowed low, I have offered this salutation with joined palms to you. (9)
"There is no woman like you to be found anywhere in this world; you are like one of golden complexion, devoted to me, and possessed of a lovely smile. (10)
"Why are you angry with me, who am so wretched, O sweet-spoken one? Tell me, O auspicious lady, why do you stand there with a face full of wrath? (11)
In great anger, she said to him: "Why do you speak to me in vain? O lowest of insects, driven by lust, you gave the powdered sweetmeat to another while abandoning me, your own beloved! (12)
"I shall not do this," the insect said again and again; "I touch your feet with truth—be gracious to me who am prostrate before you. (13)
Having heard those words, the ant then became joyful and offered herself to Kāmana. (14)
Seeing that great marvel, the queen lamented: "Fie on my kingdom! Fie on my beauty! And fie on my youth today! I have not been desired by my beloved; I shall die, without a doubt. (15)
Having lamented thus in many ways and sighing again and again, the large-eyed woman, like one distraught, went to the hermitage of Gālava.
Seeing that seer seated there, whose source was asceticism and who was firm in his vows, she, with her body bowed low and her mind tormented by grief, spoke.

O Brahmin, this single doubt revolves within my heart: although my husband is submissive to me and possesses both beauty and charm, I do not know what the cause is that our union does not take place. (18)

O observer of noble vows, he who formerly went to the kingdom of women, conquered them all in battle, and brought back eight excellent women from among those beautiful ones—why is it that he no longer desires them? (19)
There are indeed horses and elephants, as well as infinite wealth and grain; for every person on earth abides by my command.
"O best of the twice-born, by what ripening of karma has this firm youth of mine become useless, such that the king finds no pleasure in it? (21)
"It is seen during the day, yet it is not seen at night; is this the result of actions performed in this life, or perhaps something pertaining to the next world? (22)
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me how to avoid misdeeds. Having heard those words of hers, Gālava spoke these words: || 23 ||
Listen, daughter, to what occurred in the past which was done by this king out of childishness, O knower of dharma, when he could not be seen at night. (24)
That son of Vidūratha, your husband, is certainly a meat-eater, delighting in faults, with a mind attached to sensual objects. (25)
Many cocks were devoured by that prince. || 26 ||
As he was eating in this manner, many years passed by. After a long time, King Tāmracūḍa asked his ministers, "For what reason do the cocks no longer come here? (27)
Then it was reported by someone that the wicked-souled Kauśika, the son of Vidūratha, had eaten all the chickens without any cause, O King. (28)
Then Tāmracūḍa, filled with rage, uttered a curse upon the evil-minded Kauśika: "A terrifying disease that causes destruction shall befall you. (29)
From that time forward, the prince grew weaker day by day; though treated with medicines, he was overcome by disease and suffered intensely. || 30 ||
Then, driven by some desire, he went to the hermitage of Vāmadeva; overcome by the disease of consumption and his mind longing for death, he bowed down again and again and questioned Vāmadeva.
"O Blessed One, by what sin does my body waste away day and night, even though it is being nourished by me with various kinds of meat? (32)
Then Vāmadeva said to him: "Cocks have been eaten by you; indeed, you have been cursed by Tāmracūḍa, the king of cocks. (33)
"Go to him alone for refuge; he will tell you the means. Thereupon, the prince went into the presence of Tāmracūḍa.
And having seen that Tāmracūḍa, with great devotion and palms joined in reverence, he spoke while bowing down: "Protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (35)
"O Lord, out of ignorance and for the sake of nourishment, these chickens were eaten; O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive this offense of mine, a wretched man. (36)
Then Tāmracūḍa said to her: "O King, because you have made this request, when your day arrives, you shall attain manhood. (37)
The teacher and protector of the worlds, the king who wields the scepter and is the lord, shall become a cock at night, deprived of all enjoyments. || 38 ||
Therefore, O daughter, he is not seen, having entered the state of an animal. || 39 ||
Having heard these words of the high-souled Gālava, that large-eyed lady, having honored Gālava, the best of sages, asked with supreme devotion: "How indeed may there be an end to the curse? (40)
Gālava, having perceived it through diligent meditation, related [the matter].

In the Mahākāla forest, there is a Liṅga that grants liberation from birth as a bird; it is situated in the eastern part of the deity Jvāleśvara. Merely by beholding it, the end of the curse will come to pass.
Having bowed down to the best of sages, she returned in great haste to where that tiger among kings was staying, piercing various kinds of deer.
With her eyes wide open, that beloved woman with tremulous glances was beheld by him and gladdened with various kinds of tender nectar-like words.
Then, at that time, the king said to that deer-eyed woman: "O beloved, tell me, what must be done by me now? (45)
She said, "O Great King, today I am going with you to the meritorious Mahākālavana, which destroys all evil deeds. (46)
Having heard those words of hers, the king, filled with joy and hurrying, was then led by her to the vicinity of this liṅga.
Then, O Pārvatī, having worshipped that Liṅga which grants liberation from birth as a bird, the king remained right there together with his beloved.
On that night, the cock did not become as it usually was; by the grace of Śiva, he assumed a divine and captivating form. (49)

Kāma was utterly defeated by him of incomparable splendor through his form; thereupon, overcome with wonder, the king reflected: "Who is this whose power it is that I have been released from such a difficult-to-overcome curse? (50)
The king questioned his beloved, whose face was like the full moon: "How shall I be released from this curse? By what meritorious deed? (51)
Then, with joy, she related in detail the entire account of whatever Gālava had said regarding the release from the curse.
"O King, you have been liberated from the curse by the power of this Liṅga; having propitiated that Liṅga once more, enjoy pleasures on earth for a long time."
Praised by the hosts of gods, the king went to heaven together with her; from that time forward, that liṅga became known by the name Kukkuṭeśvara.

O Goddess, that which is renowned in this world as bestowing the fruits of all desires—those who shall worship it under the name Kukkuṭeśvara will not go to the womb of an animal, nor shall there be any separation [from their loved ones]. (55)
Furthermore, there shall be no falling into hell for men, nor suffering, nor the fear of old age; there shall be no untimely death, nor any hardship. (56)

Those who behold the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga on the fourteenth lunar day shall become endowed with beauty and good fortune in age after age; and whatever ancestors of theirs may reside in hell, [they shall be liberated]. (57)
And those who have entered the womb of animals, or those who have gone to the state of beasts, or even those who have attained the state of trees—for them there will be liberation. (58)
Śrī Viśvanātha said: Know that the twenty-second is named Karkaṭeśvara; by the mere sight of it, one is no longer seen to be born from an animal womb.
In former times, during the Bṛhatkalpa, there was a lord of men named Dharmamūrti, a friend of Śakra, by whom thousands of Daityas were slain.
By whose splendor the moon, the sun, and others were rendered lusterless, and by whom subjects were protected after slaying enemies in battle. (3)
Capable of assuming any form at will and undefeated in battles, he had a wife named Bhānumatī, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
The king's chief queen was dearer to him than his own life; she shone like the goddess Śrī in the midst of ten thousand women.
The king was never released from his thousandfold kingship; once, having gone to a solitary place, he, his mind filled with wonder, questioned his own priest, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
"O Blessed One, by what dharma is my splendor unsurpassed? And why is my vast radiance seen to be so difficult to endure? (7)
Vasiṣṭha said: "Formerly, O protector of the earth, you were born of the Śūdra caste, possessed by many vices along with this wicked wife of yours."
Dwelling there for very many years with a wicked heart, his soul overcome by great anger, he was always speaking harsh words.
O King, you have always been a stealer of the property of Brahmins, always a reviler of the Vedas, always envious, and always a betrayer of trust.
Then, having met his death at the appointed time, he reached hell; there he was severely scorched in a copper frying pan for fifteen years.
In Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, and the one known as Mahāraurava, [the sinners] are made into many subtle fragments, each the size of a sesame seed.
O King, having been torn apart on the blade-leafed tree and cast into the crucible by the wise one, he was brought down to the earth for the sake of purifying his remaining sins. (13)
O King, having assumed the form of a crab, Yama [placed] you in the famous lake of Śiva within the excellent Mahākālavana forest.
Whatever has been given, recited, performed, offered in sacrifice, or whatever worship of the gods has been done—all that action becomes inexhaustible in that famous lake.
Then you were cast there by that future meritorious karma; O protector of the earth, you remained stationed there for five years.
Once, having gone slowly to the riverbank to play, you were spotted there by a crow and seized by its beak.
Having flown into the path of the sky, he was struck violently by you; beaten then by the forceful kicks of your feet, he was greatly pained.
You were released from the beak of the agitated crow in the temple of the Goddess to the east of Svargadvāra, which bestows great merit.
"Cast down by Śiva and tormented by the thrusting of his beak, you have quickly died there in the presence of the god Parameṣṭhin."
Having cast off that worn-out body as far back as that previous crab-form, at that very moment he possessed a divine body adorned with celestial ornaments.
By the power of that liṅga’s majesty, he became a lord of the Vidyādharas, being honored by the lords of the Gaṇas while traveling in a celestial chariot that moves at will.
As you were proceeding to heaven, respectfully questioned by the hosts of gods: "Who is this great-souled one who goes joyfully through the divine path from the sky? (23)
Then, all the hosts of Rudra previously related to the gods the entire account in detail, concerning his liberation from the state of being a crab.
"O lords of the gods, this power of that Liṅga has now manifested. And it was immediately declared by the gods: "By the power of this Liṅga... (25)
"Since the bliss of heaven has been attained by one who was released from the womb of a crab, he shall therefore become known in the world by the name Karkaṭeśvara."
From that time forward, this deity has been known by the name Karkaṭeśvara; O King, you have enjoyed great pleasures in heaven according to your desire.
You have returned to this earth and obtained a kingdom free from all thorns; all of this has now come to pass for you through the majesty of that Linga.
Therefore, O King, quickly worship the Liṅga with great devotion; by the word of Vasiṣṭha, you shall then attain the power of recollecting your past births.
That king then remembered his own past karma; having gone back once more to that liṅga, he worshipped it with great effort.

O Pārvatī, those who always worship with devotion the one known as Karkaṭeśvara attain dissolution in that Liṅga along with their own bodies; having enjoyed pleasures on earth for a long time, they go to the supreme goal. || 31 ||
Listen to the fruit of merit for those who regularly behold the god Karkaṭeśvara on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day. || 32 ||
Upon death, they go to my city, accompanied by seven times three generations of their kin, in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble the radiance of the sun.
There, O Goddess, they indeed dwell for hundreds of millions of kalpas, being served by divine and great enjoyments and thousands of charming women.
At the end of that time, they indeed reside for that same duration in the abode of Viṣṇu, served by various Vaiṣṇava enjoyments and by thousands of women.
Having reached the world of Brahmā from the world of Viṣṇu, they rejoice once more; after enjoying various kinds of pleasures, they then proceed to the supreme state.
The merit that is obtained from ten horse-sacrifices is the fruit of a pilgrimage; now hear about Meghanādeśvara, the deity of Karkaṭeśvara.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Karkaṭeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 22 ||
Śrī Hara said: O Goddess, hear now of the twenty-third [liṅga], Meghanādeśvara, by the mere sight of which all perfections (siddhis) are attained. || 1 ||
O Great Queen, security and prosperity, as well as timely rains, depend upon the king; so too do the subjects, diseases, death, and fears. (2)
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all rooted in the king; the king is the cause of righteousness.
O Pārvatī, in this world there was a king named Madāndha; he was wicked, shrouded in egoism, and a thorn to the gods and brāhmaṇas.
O beautiful lady, due to his fault at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, a terrible twelve-year drought occurred in the world.
The thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain; the Lord became adverse. Even at the end of the night, nothing could be seen, much less the various kinds of clouds.
At that time, the rivers had their floods diminished and were in some places hidden; sacrifices, Vedic recitations, and auspicious rites of the vaṣaṭ-call had ceased.
Agriculture and cattle-rearing were abandoned, as were trade and commerce; the land was strewn with skeletons and bones, filled with men crying out in lamentation.
The cities were mostly empty, the villages and dwellings were burnt down, and they were destitute of cattle, goats, horses, and buffaloes, devouring one another.
Having completely abandoned their hermitages, O Pārvatī, the Brāhmaṇas, overwhelmed with grief, wandered here and there; they died or perished.
All creation, both mobile and immobile, was completely uprooted; in the meantime, the gods, led by Śakra, were overwhelmed with fear.
They went for refuge to Janārdana, the God of gods and the worthy protector, to the enchanting White Island (Śvetadvīpa) on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
It possesses auspicious qualities beyond compare with worlds such as Brahmaloka; it is eternally blissful, peaceful, and its radiance is equal to ten million suns.
Its palaces, couches, and seats were arranged according to one's own desire, and it was illuminated by diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, moonstones, and other gems.

O Goddess, having performed a prostration with eight limbs before that sun, which was free from all diseases and endowed with the fear of old age and death, those gods then spoke this hymn of praise, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (15)
You are Brahmā and Rudra, and Maheśvara, the best of gods; you are the creator and the transformer, the inexhaustible source of the worlds.
And thus, O Lord, you are supreme truth and supreme austerity, as well as supreme purity, the supreme path, and the supreme sacrifice.

"They call you the supreme office of the Hotṛ priest, the supreme abode, and the Supreme Puruṣa. O lady of beautiful countenance, having been thus praised by them at that time, the God of gods [spoke].
Then Kṛṣṇa said to the gods, "O deities, what shall I do for you today? Thus was Lord Hari requested by them, who were tormented by the drought.
"O Lord, let a means be told by which satisfaction and anger may arise. Having reflected through meditation, Keśava spoke.
"Go, all you thirty gods, to the auspicious Mahākālavana; there is a rain-inducing Liṅga there which was formerly installed by the clouds."
Indeed, all the clouds that bring rain are present within that very linga; by the majesty of that linga, there shall surely be rain.
O Goddess Pārvatī, having heard those words of Vāsudeva, the gods are located in the northeast of the lord of the gatekeepers.
They arrived at Mahākālavana, where the supreme Liṅga resides; having beheld the beautiful deity, they praised him with supreme devotion.
Salutations be to the Great Lord; salutations to the Infinite One who wears a garland; salutations to the one whose form is radiant; salutations to the one endowed with beauty.
Salutation to Yoga, salutation to the Veda; salutation to you with tawny matted hair; salutation to the one whose body is infinite knowledge, salutation to the embodiment of the Lord. || 26 ||

Salutations to the one with the brilliant, loud laughter; salutations be to you, the wearer of the crest-lock (Śikhaṇḍin). Salutations be to you, Śaṅkara; salutations be to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow.

Salutations to the Ender, to the One who exists in all possibilities; let there be salutations to you, the Three-eyed One. Salutations to you of manifold forms; salutations to you whose form is inconceivable.
Salutations to you whose body is Yoga; salutations to you, O All, at all times! O Lord, the entire world has perished, being tormented by drought. (29)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, protect us who have come to you for refuge with a good rain! In that interval, clouds appeared, possessing the luster of the charcoal from the full moon day.
Emerging from the center of the Liṅga while sounding the vault of the sky, they then rained down upon the earth, striking one another with great force.
Everything that had come into being became lusterless, and nothing could be discerned; moreover, the ten directions shone as if enveloped by a mass of darkness.
Satisfied by the majesty of that God of gods, all those excellent deities attained supreme joy, as if they had drunk the nectar of immortality.
Then, as he dispelled the darkness, the clouds vanished; cool breezes blew, and the ten directions became tranquil.
The luminaries of pure radiance circumambulated the Moon; the planets became free from conflict, and the rivers, too, were perfectly tranquil.
The great sages were free from sorrow, and the Gandharvas sang melodiously; by the power of this Liṅga, the entire creation was restored once again.
Having worshipped with devotion, the gods gave this linga its name according to its true nature; seeing the greatness of this linga, the gods were exceedingly pleased.
"It shall be known everywhere by the name Meghanādeśvara. O beloved, the narrative of Meghanādeśvara has thus been told by me to you."
By its power, men on earth shall become successful in their aims; through the sight of this Liṅga, there shall be a rain of all desired things.
Performing the ritual bathing of the Liṅga for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of kalpas, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O Pārvatī, wherever the power of Meghanāda is recited, there shall be excessive rain upon the surface of the earth.

Īśvara said: O highly fortunate one, Mahālaya is auspicious and consists of twenty-four [tattvas]; it encompasses the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
O Lord, I have heard that [this world] was produced, sustained, and pervaded by you alone—the pure, all-pervading Great Self. (2)
All the sages, exceedingly joyful, silent, and immutable, speak of the cause of this Great Lord of the three worlds. || 3 ||
By you all this triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ, was created; being produced, already produced, and being dissolved by the thousands.
The birth, maintenance, and destruction of the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, sages, cāraṇas, and serpents have been witnessed by you again and again.
O Lord, staying where do you create this world of moving and unmoving beings? By your grace, you should explain how it is that you withdraw it through your divine play.
Who is this Mahālaya, established in the form of a fierce planet, within whom you have held the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ?
"Thus was it asked by you, O Goddess; I have related it to you previously. Now I shall speak further; listen with a one-pointed mind. (8)
O beloved, at the end of the dissolution, the elements such as earth and the rest were held together in a single location within the great abode in Mahākālavana.
Therein lies my supreme abode, Mahālaya, which is auspicious, possesses incomparable qualities, and transcends all worlds such as the realm of Brahmā; it is the source of my ultimate bliss.
The supreme Liṅga, consisting of Brahman, resides there eternally; within that Liṅga, indeed, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.

Therein reside the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and Viṣṇu is likewise established right there; O Goddess, everything is presided over within the interior of the Liṅga. From that Liṅga was born the Great Self (Mahātmā), possessed of great intelligence.
O Pārvatī, the ego (ahaṃkāra) consisting of the elements is Viṣṇu and Śambhu; intellect (buddhi) is Prajñā, Dhṛti, Khyāti, Smṛti, Lajjā, and Sarasvatī.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all.
From this, the five great elements—the constituent signs—namely earth, wind, space, water, and light, indeed dissolve away. (15)
Land, water, and likewise space, as well as the fourfold birth—namely, from an egg, from a sprout, from sweat, or from a womb. (16)
The fourfold mark of birth is observed in this very linga: austerity, ritual action, merit, and likewise vow and charity. (17)
From that sign, the states of rajas, sattva, and tamas are born; in that [sign], the eternal Brahman, the light of truth, is heard.
That which is the unmanifest cause, subtle, consisting of both being and non-being, from which the Grandfather was born—the one Lord, Prajāpati. (19)
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and also the two Aśvins; the Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and likewise the Pitṛs. || 20 ||
Water, heaven, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and the directions; likewise the year, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and day and night. || 21 ||
And whatever else has come into being, all that is witnessed by the world; whatever is seen here, at its end it dissolves back into her.
Therefore, it is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mahālaya; it is situated to the south of the god Muktīśvara.
The man who worships that Mahālaya Liṅga as the form of Rudra shall always be a conqueror of the three worlds and possessed of fame.

O highly fortunate lady, when the supreme lord is worshipped with supreme devotion at the meritorious Mahālayeśvara, all the gods are indeed well-worshipped here, because he himself is worshipped by them.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mahālayeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 24 ||
Śrī Hara said: O beloved Pārvatī, know that the twenty-fifth deity is Muktīśvara; by the mere sight of whom liberation is attained.
Long ago, O highly fortunate lady, in the Rathantara Kalpa there was an excellent brahmin named Mukti, who was self-controlled, had conquered his senses, and was firm in his vows.
Near Mahākāla, however, is the unsurpassed Muktiliṅga; in that delightful Mahākālavana, he dwells, intent upon yoga.
Thereupon, having conquered his appetite for food, he performed penance for thirteen years; once, he went to the great river for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Having bathed there in the holy Śiprā, which is dear to the learned and destroys great sins, the Brahmin, while chanting prayers, saw someone approaching before him.
He saw a hunter with a great bow in his hand, red-eyed and very terrifying, speaking with the desire to kill and wishing to seize the bark garments.
Seeing him, the Brahmin was agitated out of fear of the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, that twice-born man remained right there.
Seeing him, the hunter, in whom Hari had entered, stood before him as if terrified; casting aside his bow and arrow, he then spoke these words.
The hunter said: "O Brahmin, I had come here desiring to kill you; but now, upon seeing you of such great splendor, my mind has returned to its natural state."
O Brahmin, thousands of brahmins and tens of thousands of women were slain by me, a householder, for the sake of my livelihood. (10)
My mind has never once experienced distress; now, I desire to perform ascetic penance in your presence. (11)
"You ought to show favor by granting me instruction. Thus addressed, that brahmin did not offer any reply.
Thinking, "This is a slayer of a Brahmin and an evildoer," that bull among Brahmins remained right there as a hunter, even though he had not been told to do so.
Having bathed, he immediately returned to the vicinity of the Mukti-liṅga; accompanied by the twice-born, O Goddess, he beheld the eternal Lord.

At that very moment, having assumed a divine body, he merged into that liṅga. Witnessing that great miracle, O lady of beautiful countenance, the brahmin Muktin suddenly reflected within himself: "Liberation has been attained! (15)
"By me, a hunter joined with evil and devoid of meditative concentration, this most difficult austerity has nevertheless been practiced. (16)
"The supreme form has not been attained, nor indeed is liberation obtained. Having reflected thus, that bull among Brahmins, out of dispassion, entered into the water and performed extensive penance.
Then, after some time, O virtuous lady, it is said that a hungry tiger came to that river and prepared to attack him.
While a tiger was about to seize the Brahmin moving within the water, the twice-born man uttered these words: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa! (19)

Even the tiger, having heard the mantra, gave up his life-breaths at that very moment; O Goddess, he became a beautiful man, wearing divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and enriched by the splendor of divine decorations.
He said, "O best of the twice-born, by your grace I shall go to that place where the eternal Viṣṇu resides, having been freed from the curse and restored to health. (21)
When this was said, the brahmin asked, "Who are you, O bull among men? He replied, "O Indra among kings, I am Pratāpin in my previous birth."
Known as Dīrghabāhu, he was proficient in all dharmas; I know the Vedas and various treatises as well. (23)
"I know what is auspicious and inauspicious; I am the omniscient one upon this earth. I have no need for brahmins whatsoever; what purpose do brahmins serve? (24)
On one day, all those brahmins, filled with anger, gave him an invincible curse: "You shall become a cruel tiger. (25)
"O best of the twice-born, through my insult of the Brahmins, I have become a terrifying eater of flesh; behold the reversal of time! (26)
Thus was I addressed in the past by those Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas: "O bull among the twice-born, this Brahma-curse, which is difficult to withstand, has been incurred by me. (27)
Then, O sage, all those brahmins were deeply propitiated by me with a voice faltering with emotion, O twice-born one, as I prostrated before them. (28)
I know the splendor of the brahmins and the great fortune of those wise ones, by whom the ocean was made undrinkable with its salt waters through their wrath.
In the same way, among those sages of radiant austerity whose souls are purified, the fire of whose anger has not even today been extinguished at Kaṇḍaka.
Due to his contempt for the Brahmins, the evil-minded and cruel great Asura Vātāpi was digested upon encountering the sage Agastya. (31)
In another instance, the fire was made to consume everything by Bhṛgu; and in ancient times, Śakra was made to have a thousand female organs by Gautama.
Keśava was born in ten ways from the most difficult-to-cross Vedic lore; and by the propitious Vālakhilyas, Garuḍa was made the lord of birds.
The two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, were made drinkers of the Soma by the high-souled Cyavana after he had paralyzed the thunderbolt.
By the grace of Dattātreya alone, Kārtavīryārjuna obtained a thousand arms, which are otherwise extremely difficult to attain. (35)
In ancient times, the inhabitants of heaven, including Indra, were protected by Vasiṣṭha; for happiness, fame, longevity, glory, and strength originate from the Brāhmaṇas.
And all the lords of the Lokāloka mountains, headed by the Brāhmaṇas—these indeed are the Soma-kings, the masters of happiness and suffering. (37)
When enraged, those who possess direct perception could reduce this entire world to ashes; indeed, many such powers of those who speak of Brahman are heard of. (38)
And anger is vast and immediate; it brings about its retribution instantly. Due to my anger toward the best of the twice-born, I went to the torments of hell. (39)
One should always protect one's prosperity from anger, one's wealth from envy, one's knowledge from honor and dishonor, and one's self from negligence. (40)
"O best of Brahmins, whatever sin I have committed out of ignorance, through royal pride, or by fate, you ought to forgive me as one who has come to you for refuge. (41)
Then all those brahmins, being satisfied, joyfully said this to me: "Whenever anyone shall stand before you at the time of your sixth meal," (42)
And for some time, O lord of men, he will be a meat-eater, until that best of the twice-born has bathed in the meritorious waters within the Śiprā.
When you have entered into the water and say, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," you shall be released from me when I am in the form of a tiger seeking to seize you.
Thus you have spoken; this mantra, "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," was heard by me from you, and its fruition has now arrived.
O you of noble vows, by your grace I have been born with a divine body; O Blessed One, I have become one who has achieved his life's purpose through the sight of you.
"Accept a boon from me, and whatever doubt is in your heart, speak that as well, O best of the twice-born; I shall fulfill everything for you. (47)
I am eager to attain freedom from debt by granting you instruction. || 48 ||
Having heard these words of that one with a divine body, the twice-born man, his lotus-like face blossoming with supreme joy, spoke.
Today my knowledge has borne fruit; today my austerity has borne fruit; today my tongue has borne fruit; today my eyes have borne fruit for me. (50)
"O King, you have heard what was proclaimed: embodied beings behold that which was previously within their own bodies today as the form of a tiger, O best of ascetics. (51)
If I am worthy of your grace, and if you deign to do this, [grant me] a body consisting of light, eternal and of the nature of Brahman. (52)
I wish to hear the cause that has long resided in my heart: O illustrious one, how is liberation attained through effort by one who desires liberation? (53)
Even though he was devoted to the practice of yoga for thirteen years, he did not attain that supreme wonder despite his difficult asceticism.
"Even by that hunter, liberation was attained in an instant; a doubt has arisen in me regarding this—tell me clearly, what is the cause? (55)
Having heard those words of his, he then spoke these words: "I shall tell you the supreme secret, the mystery characterized by liberation."
O sage, by worshipping Mahādeva, liberation—which is otherwise very difficult to attain—is swiftly achieved; this has been stated by the ancient, high-souled, and wise ones. (57)
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Brahmin, and exert yourself according to the truth; by my command, O best of the twice-born, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
When I was cursed by those brahmins, they were greatly propitiated by me; out of compassion for me, they said, "O King, your liberation shall come to pass. (59)
"Mahākāla desires liberation, and Muktibrāhmaṇa, the best of brahmins, exists there endowed with ascetic power; he will ask you a question."
Then you shall speak of the Muktīśvara Liṅga in front of him; thus, liberation shall come to both you and that Muktīśvara.
For previously marked karma does not leave the embodied being; this law has been observed by the Creator through the manifold workings of karma. (62)
Having heard these words of his, that brahmin, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, rose up from within the water and then spoke these words.
"By good fortune you have come, O King; by good fortune we have met. Men such as you, who show the way to liberation, are rare in this world. (64)
Having spoken thus, O large-eyed one, the king and the brahmin went together to the Muktiliṅga to behold the eternal Lord; and having seen the God, they were filled with joy. (65)
At that very moment, both of them, together with their bodies, attained dissolution into that liṅga. O Goddess, such is this majesty of it that has been described by me to you.
Liberation occurs from the touch of this Liṅga, and not otherwise. Those who always worship the eternal Mukti-liṅga with devotion—even one joined with sin—goes to the supreme goal. (67)
O fools, what is the use of austerities, what is the use of gifts, and what is the use of religious observances? Perform the vision of the Mukti-liṅga, which bestows liberation.
Neither the hosts of gods, nor the asuras, nor the great seers know me, O large-eyed one, in my supreme form which is stainless like the luster of a gem. 69.
Even Prajāpati himself does not know my supreme form directly; nor does Viṣṇu, nor the foremost of the thirty gods—how much less others, O beloved, such as the sages? (70)
O illustrious lady, this very splendor seen here in the form of a *liṅga* is indeed what Śuka and these other gods meditate upon.
O Goddess, let the yogis, purified through many births by my grace, enter my body which bestows liberation. (72)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Muktīśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 25 ||
Īśvara said: Know, O Goddess, that the supreme deity Someśvara is the twenty-sixth; by the mere sight of whom a man becomes free from blemish.
O Goddess, in the kalpa known as Vārāha, the highly fortunate Atri, the mind-born son of Brahmā, became a Prajāpati.
His son was Soma, and from Dakṣa’s side there were twenty-seven daughters who are celebrated as the Dākṣāyaṇīs.
For they are to be considered the wives of Soma, yet Rohiṇī is the best among them; we have heard that Soma frequents her alone and no other.
The others, having arrived, spoke exactly as it had happened in the presence of Dakṣa; then Dakṣa, having approached him, said, "He did not do it."
O beloved, when Dakṣa remained there despite being forbidden, he became enraged; in his fury, he cursed Soma: "Be quickly hidden from view! (6)
Thus cursed, Soma indeed vanished at that time; and Soma cursed Dakṣa, saying, "You too shall become [a beast]."
Having abandoned this manifold state, he attained this eternal body of water; therefore, Dakṣa, though the son of Brahmā, is also celebrated as Prācetasa.
Thus, having vanished due to the curse of Dakṣa, Soma departed; and the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, together with the ancestors, approached Brahmā at the Vairāja abode of Brahmā.
Having prostrated before him again and again, they said: "O Blessed One, you are the self-existent primordial creator of all beings. (10)
"O creator of the offerings to gods and ancestors, protect us who have come to you for refuge. Having heard the words of the gods and understood them, the divine Lord of Creatures [replied]. (11)
He consoled the gods with well-composed words of water: "O thirty deities, the fruit of that man's karma must necessarily be experienced."
"The Lord God Viṣṇu himself will bring about the end of the curse. Having heard these words of the lotus-born one, the gods, their distress gone, approached Viṣṇu, the protector, for refuge.

Accompanied by Brahmā, O Goddess, they offered praise with concentrated minds: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Creator of the universe! Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa. (14)
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, the gods have come to you for refuge; for you are our supreme object of meditation, and you are indeed our supreme teacher. || 15 ||
For you indeed are our supreme deity, O best of gods, even among Brahmā and the others; yet Soma has vanished due to the curse of Dakṣa, O Janārdana.
"O Lord, without Soma, the medicinal herbs have perished upon the surface of the earth. Having heard those words of theirs, Viṣṇu spoke these words: || 17 ||
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you fearlessness. I shall undoubtedly restore the lost moon quickly. (18)
Having spoken thus and dismissed the lords of the thirty gods, the Blessed One, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, suddenly called Soma to mind.
When he was not approached even though remembered, Janārdana, the ancient Puruṣa, the God, became enraged and spoke this to Brahmā: || 20 ||
"Let the ocean of the jar be churned by the gods and the hosts of asuras; when the great ocean is being churned, the moon shall come into existence once again. (21)
"There you shall obtain the nectar and various kinds of jewels. O Pārvatī, having heard those words of Vāsudeva, [they departed].
Having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope, the gods began to churn the ocean, the reservoir of waters.
And formerly, O Goddess, for the sake of Soma, the Asuras and Dānavas likewise approached the face of these two with great envy, as did the king of the Nāgas.
All the gods stood together where the tail was; therefore, indeed, wherever the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa was, there they were.
Lifting up the head of the serpent, he cast it down again and again; indeed, as the ocean was being churned, a great sound arose.
There, various aquatic creatures, crushed by the great mountain, met their destruction by the hundreds and thousands.
O Goddess, when that [ocean] had been churned with effort by Keśava, the moon—cool-rayed and radiant—was born with a serene soul. (28)
O illustrious lady, the gods, humans, and ancestors, as well as trees and medicinal herbs, all depend for their livelihood upon that very moon. (29)
Then, seeing that he had been born, the Blessed Keśava said: "O Candra, protect these subjects; become the eldest of the world."
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, Soma—who had previously perished and entered the dense forest—set out to protect the subjects.
In his presence, Nārada quickly related everything; having heard the words of the high-souled celestial sage Nārada, [he spoke]. || 32 ||
Then Soma, afflicted by Dakṣa’s curse, vanished; O Goddess, he went for refuge to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
