Having gone there, he spoke according to the curse with a faltering voice; having heard the words of Pūrvacandra, Brahmā spoke these words: || 34 ||
"This is my first son, who has been severely tormented by the newborn Moon; what more can I do? (35)
And Viṣṇu has granted firm strength to this Moon; therefore, I shall go there where the Lord Janārdana resides.
Seeing that slayer of Madhu, Brahmā said to Viṣṇu: "O Lord of the World, this Moon has been created by me at your command. (37)
"O Lord, he has indeed been tormented by the new moon,"—having been addressed thus by Brahmā, O Goddess, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, related the account before Brahmā again and again. (38)
Brahmā also, for the sake of the former Moon, bowed down and stood with palms joined in reverence, praising Viṣṇu, who is saluted by the worlds.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, salutations to Viṣṇu, salutations to Jiṣṇu, salutations again and again; salutations to Vāmana, to Govinda, salutations to Ananta, salutations to Acyuta.

Victory to you, O Govinda of great majesty; victory to you, O Viṣṇu; victory, O Padmanābha! Victory to you, O Primordial One, Lord of the mace-bearer; victory to you, O Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe! 41.
O Goddess, having been thus praised at that time by Brahmā, the creator of the world, he looked toward Soma who was standing nearby and spoke these words.
"Go, O Soma, at my command to the most excellent Mahākālavana; to the north of the Muktiliṅga is a supreme Liṅga that bestows liberation. Worship it with diligence, and it will grant you a body. (43)

Thus addressed by Vāsudeva and by Brahmā again and again, O Great Goddess, he came to the most excellent Mahākālavana; and having seen the Liṅga, O lady of virtuous vows, he praised it with this hymn.
Candra said: Salutations to the God of gods, the three-eyed Great Soul, whose eyes are reddish-brown and who wears a crown of matted locks. || 45 ||
Salutation to Mahādeva, who wields the trident, who is possessed by spirits and vetālas, who is endowed with a terrifying loud laugh, and who is the matted-haired Sthāṇu. || 46 ||
Salutations to the one who destroyed the teeth of Pūṣan, likewise to the destroyer of Andhaka, to the excellent dweller on Kailāsa, and to the one who is like all the gods.
Salutations again and again to Bhairava, whose form is formidable and whose hair stands erect; who is terrifying with flames of fire and who dispels the dharma of the Kali age.
Likewise, salutations to the destroyer of the forest of wood, who wields a sharp trident; to him who wears a bracelet and a serpent-king as a neck-thread, the wielder of the spear.

Salutations to the one with a fierce staff in hand, and to the one whose mouth is the submarine fire; salutations again and again to the one known through the Vedānta, O embodiment of sacrifice! || 50 ||

Salutations to you, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the cause of fear to the world, the Lord of the Universe, the divine one who is both gross and subtle, Śambhu, the one with matted hair, the formidable one, and the God of all gods. || 51 ||
O Goddess, having been thus praised at that time by the invisible Candra, Mahādeva, in the form of a Liṅga, being pleased, then spoke these words: || 52 ||
"I am pleased with this hymn; speak, O Soma, what you desire. Whatever you long for, I shall accomplish it all for you; of this there is no doubt. (53)
Soma said: "O Lord, if I am worthy of your grace, and if you are pleased with me, O Lord—by your splendor, your radiance, as well as by your form and your beauty. (54)
"O Maheśvara, by your grace I wish to make my own abode," [he said]. "So be it," [replied] the Liṅga at that very moment, O night-stalker (Rajanīcara).
That was obtained by the Moon-king through the grace of this Liṅga, O Maheśvarī, because the God of gods was propitiated by Soma.
Therefore, he became renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Someśvara; O Great Goddess, those who worship the supreme Lord Someśvara [attain the highest state].
O beloved, those mortal men who have performed meritorious deeds go to the supreme state; so too does the man who beholds the Someśvara Liṅga with devotion.
Freed from the sufferings of birth and other afflictions, that person merges into me; those men in this world are but beasts—what fruit is there in their living? (59)
And by those who have neither seen nor worshipped the Lord Someśvara in this most terrible cycle of existence, which is agitated by the fear of birth and disease; (60)
Somesvara alone is to be worshipped, for he is the destroyer of leprosy; he alone is a man of merit in this world, and by him his entire lineage is adorned. (61)

He by whom Someśvara has been worshipped is the support of all the worlds. Having worshipped Someśa even once with a bilva leaf, a man—liberated, enjoying [divine] pleasures, and free from affliction—shall dwell for a long time in my world.
O Goddess, O beloved, those men who worship the Someśvara Liṅga with devotion using golden flowers attain the supreme goal.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Someśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Anarakeśvara.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Someśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" section of the fifth book, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 26 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Goddess, the twenty-seventh [liṅga] is known as Anarakeśvara; by the mere sight of it, how could there be hell even in a dream? (1)
Long ago in the Kali Yuga, O Goddess, during the aeon known as Vārāha, when a turbid time had arrived and the Truth (Satya) had gone to dissolution.
People have become lawless, supportless, homeless, and atheistic; even those belonging to the castes and stages of life deceive one another.
The brahmins do not worship the gods; they perform despicable acts. Having become overcome by greed and delusion, these men are attached to sensual desires.
Bound by enmity, they became intent on killing one another; they ceased performing sacrifices and Vedic study, and were deprived of the offering of funeral cakes and water.
The Brahmins will eat all kinds of food and be devoted to falsehood; at that time, they will mostly sell their merchandise using fraudulent measures.
O beloved, men are seen with grey hair at the age of sixteen; the decline of the lifespan of human beings occurs very quickly indeed.
Men and women who have become such through their sins fall into the hells in succession, according to the weight of their transgressions.
Some have their heads split open with axes, others are sawn apart; their eyes are plucked out with tongs glowing like fire.
They are pierced by sharp iron spikes heated with fire, tormented by mountain peaks, and ground to powder by cruel mountains.
They are cast into heated cauldrons and burned in heaps of fire; others, face-downward in impure filth, are crushed by the one who wields the staff.
Bound with iron chains and hanging head-downwards, they cry out in extreme misery as they are whirled around in the air.
Men are devoured by worms, bees, sharp gadflies, and likewise by mosquitoes, as well as by merciless birds with iron beaks.
Some, mangled and afflicted by thirst, run about seeking water; they are made to drink their own urine by the fierce ones and are further agitated by blows.
And by whichever limbs men commit fallen actions on earth, those very same limbs are purified by them when they have reached the place of torment.
Those who look upon their guru, the gods, or Brahmins with an angry eye, and those who gaze at the wives of others with a wicked look—their eyes are split open and pulled out with iron spikes.
Then their ears are filled with iron pegs; furthermore, they are torn out with weapons and again with heated spikes.
Those by whom the censure of a guru, or of friends, deities, or virtuous women has ever been heard, are swiftly impaled with iron spikes.
The tongue is split into hundreds of pieces by iron-tipped instruments glowing with the color of fire; furthermore, it is filled with sharp, needle-pointed spikes driven in by gusts of wind.
Those men who, devoted to speaking ill of others, repeatedly address their preceptor or even their mother with harshness—[their mouths become thus]. (20)
He cuts off the limbs of those wicked men who destroy the flowers and leaves in a grove prepared for the sake of the gods. || 21 ||
And for those evil-minded ones by whom the wife of another was embraced, there shall be an iron woman, glowing with the color of fire, upon their chests.
They are also stationed and even slain by the fierce servants of Yama; and women are embraced by men made of heated iron.
Then, having reached the end of their time, they are cast along with other men into a house of iron with a bed of blazing fire.
Whatever sensation is observed here in this world within the body, the pain in the limbs of men shall indeed be a hundred times greater than that. || 25 ||

Other men are devoured by crows, scorpions, and vultures; being burned, they lament in distress, crying out "O brother! O father! Again and again they speak thus in agitation, yet they truly find no peace.
O Pārvatī, they undergo sufferings that are unbearable; in this way, they certainly experience the pain of torment. A highly fortunate man named Nimi beheld the path of Yama.
Fierce, terrifying, and difficult to traverse, it is filled with those of evil deeds; it is shrouded in darkness and overgrown with hair like moss and grass.
It was permeated with the foul odors of flesh and blood as its mire, and was surrounded on all sides by a blazing flame of fire.
It was assailed by downward-facing karkoṭas and vultures, and surrounded by needle-mouthed pretas as large as the Vindhya mountains.
With trees, blood, and flesh, with severed arms, thighs, and hands, and with mangled bellies and palms scattered here and there; || 31 ||
It was filled with the foul stench of corpses, inauspicious, devoid of enjoyments, and surrounded on all sides by the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana).
He saw the ground strewn with burning sand and various iron slabs, as well as the bodily torments of those who have committed evil deeds.
Perceiving that foul odor, he spoke to that man, saying: "How much further must we travel? Thus he spoke.
"What region of the gods is this? I wish to know this. Thus addressed, the messenger of Yama, staff in hand and blazing like fire, showed him the path ahead and said, "Come this way! (35)
Again, that king, filled with humility, spoke to that servant: "O man of Yama, tell me, what evil deed have I committed? (36)
"Indeed, by me, though a righteous man, this calamity has been brought about; I am known by the name Nimi, born in the lineage of the Janakas. (37)
Born in the region of Videha as a perfect protector of men, he has established the four castes in righteousness and has been protected by me.
Just as in former times, Manu, who was preeminent in righteousness, performed many sacrifices here; likewise, I have protected the earth in accordance with dharma through numerous sacrifices.
I did not abandon the battle, nor did I turn my back on a guest; nor did I harbor any longing for the wives, wealth, or possessions of others. (40)
"How have I come to this most dreadful hell?"—when asked thus by Nimi, the servant of Yama, though cruel himself, bowed down and spoke these humble words. (41)
The man said: "O Great King, it is exactly as you have said; there is no doubt in this matter. However, a very small sin was committed, and I am merely reminding you of it. (42)
O King, that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which was prescribed for the śrāddha but was not given by you—having been forgotten through negligence—it is the fruit of that very action. (43)
"O King, this alone is your sin; no other whatsoever exists. O Vaideha, come for the enjoyment of merits! (44)
Having heard this, the royal sage Nimi then said to the messenger: "I shall go, O follower of the gods, wherever you will lead me. (45)
I ask you something regarding the truth; you ought to explain it as it truly is: why are these crows with adamantine beaks stealing away the eyesight of men? (46)
Furthermore, their eyes indeed become like that again and again; O Lord of Messengers, tell me what loathsome deed was committed? (47)
Their tongues are likewise torn out as they are born anew; they are split apart with saws—why are these beings so deeply afflicted? (48)
"Why are these men, deprived of their senses, tormented day and night? These and other tortures of evildoers are being seen; tell me in detail for how long they shall endure. (49)
The man said: "O protector of the earth, regarding that which you ask me—the arising of the fruit of sinful actions—I shall explain it to you here in brief, exactly as it is. (50)
For a person experiences merit and demerit in alternation; as one enjoys them, whether it be merit or even demerit, they go to exhaustion.
But without experiencing [the results of] enjoyment, O Indra among kings, a human being does not cast off merit or sinful karma; this which has been declared is the truth. (52)
Thus, these great sinners, dwelling within the various hells, exhaust their most terrible [karma] through agonies day and night. (53)
Whether in the state of a god, a human, or an animal, one undoubtedly experiences pleasant and painful results arising from merit and demerit, born of virtuous and non-virtuous deeds. (54)
O King, this has been recounted by me to you in brief, concerning the liberation from the fruits of one's own actions for both the meritorious and the sinful. (55)
"Therefore, come, let us go elsewhere, as you have just now seen. Then, placing him in front, the king prepared to depart. (56)
Then, indeed, all the men dwelling in the place of torment cried out: "O King, show us favor! Stay for just a moment; for the breeze that touches your body refreshes our frames. (57)
O tiger among men, O lord of the earth, show compassion; [this [gift] removes from one's limbs all burning heat, pain, and afflictions in their entirety. 58.
Having heard these words of theirs, the king questioned that messenger of Yama: "How is it that these men feel such joy while I am present? (59)
What great meritorious deed have I performed in the world of mortals, by virtue of which this vision of Prahlāda’s mother has arisen? Let that be declared.
The man said: "The famous Anarakeśvara at Mahākāla was seen by you on the fourteenth day of the month of Āśvina; such is the fruit of that [act]."
Then, the breeze that comes into contact with her body is refreshing; O King, it does not afflict those who have committed sinful deeds with their torments. (62)
The king said: "If that torment does not afflict her in my presence, then, O gentle-faced one, I shall remain here as immovable as a pillar."
The man said: "Come, O lord of kings, let us go; enjoy the pleasures earned by your own merits, for you shall not undergo the torments of those who perform evil deeds."
The king said: "Neither in heaven nor in the world of Brahmā is that happiness obtained by men which is found in bringing relief to an afflicted creature; such is my conviction. (65)
Therefore, I shall not depart as long as these beings, who dwell in hell and are so deeply afflicted, do not become happy through my presence. (66)
If many others are to obtain happiness while I am suffering, then I have obtained everything; therefore, depart without delay.
The man said: "This Dharma and Śakra have both come here to lead you away. You must certainly depart from this place; therefore, O King, let us go. (68)
In the meantime, Dharma, together with Śakra, said: "O Nimi, knower of the supreme dharma, the hosts of gods are pleased with you. (69)
"Come, come, O tiger among men! Enough has been done by you, O Lord. Success has been attained by you, O King, as well as imperishable worlds. (70)
And you should not harbor anger; listen to my words, O Lord: hell must necessarily be seen by all kings. (71)
I shall lead you to heaven, for I have been properly worshipped by you; ascending this excellent, stainless celestial chariot, let us go today.
Nimi said: "O Dharma, thousands of men are being tormented here in hell; they cry out with the plea 'Save us!'—it is for this reason that I do not depart from me. (73)
Indra said: "By their own actions, these evildoers have reached hell; however, O King, you too must go to heaven by virtue of your meritorious deeds. (74)
The king said: "O knower of dharma, do you or Śakra, lord of Śacī, know of any merit superior to mine? You ought to tell me that auspicious thing. (75)

Dharma said: "On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, O mighty-armed one, you beheld the highly renowned god, the lord of those who have no hell, the bestower of heaven, in that most excellent Mahākāla forest. (76)

And the merit of yours that is superior to that has no measurable number; O King, enjoy the merit earned by your own actions as you please. Let all these denizens of hell exhaust the fruits born of their own karma.
The King said: "How will men feel longing for the company of the virtuous if no excellence arises in them even in my presence? (78)
Therefore, by whatever good deed there may be that is particularly distinguished, let the sinners who have come to the torments of hell be liberated from them. (79)
Dharma said: "O King, you previously beheld the Lord of Anaraka; indeed, grant to these [beings] even a fraction of the merit produced thereby. (80)
By the power of that merit, they shall be liberated from these hells; when he had done so, they were then released from hell.
Then Dharmarāja, accompanied by Śakra, said to Nimi: "O lord of the earth, you have thus attained this most excellent station."
And behold these denizens of hell liberated from their evil karma; then, O lord of the earth, a rain of flowers fell upon him.
And having placed him upon a celestial chariot, Hari led him to the heavenly world; those who were there, having been sinful, were now fallen from their torments.
By the power of that god, O beloved, they went to the heavenly world; therefore, the god is well-known as Sadeva Anarakeśvara. || 85 ||
Praised by all the hosts of gods, he alone who delivers one from hell is truly virtuous; by him alone is a lineage purified. (86)
The sin arising from hundreds of previous births is dissolved for those men who constantly behold the Lord, the Sovereign of the Unfallen (Anarakeśvara). (87)
O Daughter of the Mountain, those who rejoice at the sight of the God are also liberated from sin and go to my abode. (88)
By the sight of that liṅga, a man swiftly leads ten thousand families of both the past and the future to my world. (89)
That fourteenth day of the dark fortnight which is conjoined with Śivayoga is declared to be dear to him; it destroys all sins.
And those men who come there and fast before the god, the Lord of Hell, are liberated from the sins born of a hundred lifetimes.
Whatever evil has been accumulated through action, mind, or speech—that the Lord washes away when he is duly worshipped on that lunar day.
This sin-destroying power of the god Jaṭeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear of his supreme majesty.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Anarakeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The illustrious God of Gods said: Know that Jaṭeśvara is renowned as the twenty-eighth; by the mere sight of whom a human being becomes liberated. || 1 ||
Formerly, in the Rathantara Kalpa, there was a lord of the earth named Vīradhanvā; he was righteous, illustrious, and renowned throughout the world.
Once, O fair-faced one, having gone to the forest for the sake of deer, he, overwhelmed by anger, slaughtered herds of deer with his bow.
O Goddess, he went to that place where the five brothers of noble vows, the sons of Saṃvarta, were staying in the form of deer.
Once, having seen five young fawns in the forest—just born and still breathing—they were filled with curiosity.
There, they each seized one [of the fruits], but they died, being exceedingly distressed; thereafter, all five of them went indeed into the presence of their father.
Seeking an expiation, they then spoke these words concerning the killing of the deer to Saṃvarta, who was surrounded by his assembly.
"O Lord, as soon as they were born, five deer were killed by us unintentionally; therefore, let an expiation be ordained for us. (8)

He said: "One attains purity once the expiation has been performed. However, he who bestows an expiation without having studied the Dharmaśāstras may himself become purified through that expiation, while the sin shall go to the one who gave it. (9)
The twice-born who are established in the Dharmaśāstras and wield the sword of the Vedas—whatever they may say, even in jest, that is remembered as the supreme Dharma.

Whatever flaw there may be in the observance of celibacy, whatever flaw in the recitation of prayers, and whatever flaw in the performance of a sacrifice—all these become flawless when rectified by Brāhmaṇas.
When the deities of the earth utter the words "It is flawless," every sin is destroyed and the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is attained.
While Saṃvarta, the best of the twice-born and most excellent, was speaking thus, the sages headed by Bhṛgu, Atri, and Aṅgiras arrived.
For their sake, those sons of Saṃvarta, distressed and bowed with devotion, related exactly what had occurred again and again.
They also spoke of the Dharmaśāstras as they were truly ordained, and the penances as they were prescribed according to the divisions of place and time.
A child who is less than sixteen years old, or one who is eighty years of age, as well as women and those who are ill, deserve only half of the prescribed expiation.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin, an expiation should be prescribed; such is the established law. (17)
Now, having donned deer skins and maintained your vows, practice for five years; thereafter you shall become pure.
Thus addressed, those youths, who lived according to the nature of deer, entered the forest undisturbed, meditating upon the eternal Brahman.
Then, when that year had passed, King Vīradhanvan came to that place where they were roaming in the form of deer.
And they too, subsisting on the manner of deer, were seen by the king at the foot of a certain tree, standing there engaged in silent recitation; for they appeared to him as deer.

Thinking that those expounders of the Veda had been pierced by night-stalkers, they died; and seeing those Brahmins of rigid vows dead, the king, trembling with fear, went to the hermitage of Devarāta.
There, the king asked, "O great sage, the murder of a Brahmin has occurred for me. Having related the matter from beginning to end, including the killing, the lord of men spoke. (23)
With his soul overwhelmed by intense grief, that seer, who was like a god, wept as the best of kings lamented in extreme distress.
He said, "Do not fear, O King; I shall remove your sin, just as the earth was submerged in the netherworld called Sutala. (25)

Just as he was lifted up by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, in his form as the Boar, so too will that Lord Janārdana himself deliver you, O Indra among kings, who are overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus addressed, King Durita then spoke these words.
"What is the use of this lusterless and evil-minded twice-born man? This lowest of brahmins is not even able to rescue himself. (28)
Having spoken thus, he struck him with his very sword; seeing the brahmin dead, the king was defiled by rage.
In that very forest, O Goddess, deluded by a multitude of sins, he killed Kapilā, the milch-cow with her calf belonging to Gālava.
Afflicted by hunger and afflicted by thirst, through childishness, delusion, and recklessness, a cruel intellect arose and his sin became matted together.
With his sins having become matted locks, he wandered in the dense forest; once, he was carried far into the great forest by a horse.
In that place, teeming with tigers, lions, and elephants, and frequented by deer and śambaras, the king, being alone, released his horse beneath a tree.
Then he slept there fearlessly upon the kusha grass; meanwhile, hunters were wandering about, and seeing him sleeping so without fear, [they approached]. (24)
Those hunters went quickly to inform their master; directed by him, they set out to seize them.
Then, from the body of the king, a white woman adorned with ornaments arose; taking up a discus, she struck down the Mlecchas.
Having slain the Dasyus, that goddess vanished right there.
Then the king, released by her, woke up at that very moment; seeing the Mlecchas slain, the monarch reflected: || 38 ||
In this very forest, the most terrible killing of a cow and the killing of a Brahmin have occurred; how has this succession of sins been incurred by me, a cruel man? (39)
Having reflected thus and sighing again and again, he mounted that very horse and went to the hermitage of Vāmadeva.
The sage Vāmadeva beheld the king in such a state; afflicted by his matted locks of sin, he was then filled with suffering. (41)
Vāmadeva said: This very tiger among men, King Vīradhanvan, born of the Lunar dynasty, has fallen into a miserable state.
"I shall rescue this king, the best of men"—having thus reflected, the brahmin Vāmadeva, a man of great asceticism, then replied to the afflicted protector of the earth, Vīradhanvan. (43)
"O King, O protector of the earth! I am known as Vīradhanvan, the son of Vidūratha, renowned throughout the three worlds. (44)
In a previous birth, while living as a hunter in the forest, he killed deer; then, one night, he performed a rigorous vigil beneath an āmalakī tree.
In the bright fortnight of Phālguna, there is the auspicious Āmalakī-ekādaśī; when it is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the circumambulation of Jāmadagnya on that day.
In the past, you witnessed with wonder the worship performed by the people; moreover, a fast was undertaken involuntarily, and there was a vigil during that [festival]. (47)
By her power, O King, he became a monarch of great strength and prowess; protected by her, he has now been saved from the hosts of mlecchas in the forest.
All your enemies have been slain; by that very act you shall attain auspiciousness. Yet, as a ripening of past karma, the sin of killing a Brahmin has come upon you.
"O King, by the power of my asceticism and by the strength of my yoga, I have perceived that your body has become matted with a mass of sins. (50)
Now I shall protect you; listen to my supreme words.
Thus addressed by the sage Vāmadeva, that lord of the earth, having bowed down and become composed, questioned him again and again.
"How shall my sins arising from [the killing of] cows and Brahmins be removed? You ought to show me favor by granting instruction. (53)
Having heard those words of his, the great sage Vāmadeva recounted the majesty of this Liṅga, O illustrious lady.
"Go to Mahākālavana, O Great King, by my command; there dwells even the God of gods, the world-pervading Jaṭeśvara. (55)
And he is recited in all the Vedas as the destroyer of the sinful assembly; he is situated to the north of the god Anarakeśa.
Having heard those words of Vāmadeva, the king went with great haste to the most excellent Mahākālavana.
Having seen there the God of gods, Jaṭeśvara, who is worthy of worship by the world, the lord of kings again offered praise with supreme devotion.
Salutations ever to you, Śiva; salutations again and again to the one whose body is the universe. Salutations to the divine and secret one, whose physical form is the hidden vow.
Salutations to Jaṭāya Rāma, who acts by means of his illusory power; salutations be to the one of manifold forms, salutations to the one whose form is dark-blue.
Salutation to Bhoga, to Dhūmra; salutation be to the one whose self is the sky. Salutation to the mass of fire; salutation to you, O source of purity! 61.

Homage to the sun that dispels the great darkness; homage to you, the slayer of enemies! Homage to the one who has reached the further shore of saṃsāra, whose body possesses a divine form! Homage to the golden-hued one; homage to the subduer of the deluded!

Homage to the one of beautiful form, worshipped by the gods; homage to the one of diverse forms, who is beyond primordial nature. Homage again and again to the one who is independent of form; homage, homage to you, the dark-hued and beautiful one.
Thus praised then, O Goddess, Mahādeva Maheśvara, his entire body encircled by matted locks, emerged from the midst of the Liṅga.
With his entire body smeared with ashes, his arms resplendent with the coils of serpents, his form resembling a mass of snow, he was as pure as the silver mountain.
The omnipresent Lord was adorned with matted locks resembling strings of pearls, and was encircled by those that were tawny, formidable, and grotesque.
That Lord Jaṭeśvara is beautified by rivers in the form of serpents, bound to the hoods of the lords of serpents, and colored white, yellow, and so forth. || 67 ||
She spoke these words to the king, O daughter of the mountain: "O Indra among kings, I am pleased with this hymn; I have been gratified by you."
Indeed, your accumulated sin has been dissolved by the mere sight of me; therefore, go with joy to my supreme and eternal abode.
Thus addressed by the God of gods, King Vīradhanvan went to the supreme abode, which is free from burning and dissolution.
O beloved, being praised by hosts [of celestial beings] while traveling in a chariot that moves at will, he was liberated from the multitude of his sins by beholding the Lord with matted hair.

Therefore, this deity is proclaimed by the name Jaṭeśvara. O lady of beautiful hips, for those who behold Jaṭeśvara with true devotion, their sin is instantly reduced to matted hair and perishes at that very moment. (72)
O Goddess, those who always worship Jaṭeśvara, the God of gods, shall possess strength, power, and good fortune.
And whatever other gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or humans shall worship the liṅga according to the rules with a spirit of devotion; || 74 ||
They too shall obtain whatever desires are most difficult to attain—sovereignty, incomparable righteousness, long life, and freedom from disease.

One shall obtain unrivaled sovereignty and whatever else there may be; even those sinners of cruel deeds who have taken refuge in the Liṅga will become liberated from their sins and freed from all feverish distress.
Those who behold Jaṭeśvara with devotion day after day shall become endowed with righteousness, wealth, and good fortune.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one who suffers is liberated from suffering; moreover, by the mere sight [of it], one immediately becomes cleansed of all sins. (78)
O Pārvatī, those who shall read the majesty of Jaṭeśvara, or those who shall listen to it with devotion toward me, being self-restrained and endowed with faith; || 79 ||
They shall obtain all desires and find an excellent state in my city; even that woman who is unfortunate shall always attain good fortune.
A pregnant woman obtains a son who is free from disease and adorned with Vedic learning; the malevolent spirits that seize infants perish, and there shall be no fear of untimely death.
This great [rite] is auspicious, life-prolonging, and the supreme refuge for those who desire dharma; it brings to an end the terrible fear born of evil dreams and that born of sin. (82)
Whatever ill-eaten food or contact with wicked people might cause a short life, it is destroyed without a doubt upon hearing the narrative of the Liṅga. (83)
Whoever recites this auspicious narrative of Jaṭeśvara during the ancestral rites (śrāddha), that śrāddha shall become inexhaustible and increase the satisfaction of the ancestors. || 84 ||
This power of the god Jaṭeśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear of the auspicious Rāmeśvara. || 85 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jaṭeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Hara said: O beloved, know that the twenty-ninth deity is Rāmeśvara; by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Formerly, O Goddess, in the Tretā Yuga, there was Rāma, the best among those who bear arms; he was a hero endowed with all virtues and devoted to his father.
Rāma himself was born from the womb of Reṇukā; he was indeed Viṣṇu descended due to the most difficult-to-overcome curse of Bhṛgu.
Once, having been commanded by the sage Jamadagni, he said this to his son Vipula: "O son, cut off your mother's head."
Having heard the words of his father, as well as those of his brothers and his mother, Rāma cut off their heads; then Jamadagni granted him a boon.
O Bhārgava, you shall be unconquerable by all the lords of the earth; you will become the destroyer of them all before long.
"Take this firm axe, my son, which has arisen from the flames of fire; by means of this sharp weapon, you shall thereafter become renowned."
Then, after some time, King Kārtavīryārjuna was born in the lineage of the Haihayas, renowned for his thousand arms.
But the evil-minded one slew Jamadagni for the sake of Kāmadhenu; seeing his father slain, Rāma, filled with rage, spoke this: || 9 ||
"Now let the three worlds behold my eternal prowess; and let that evil-minded killer of a Brahmin, born of Kṛtavīrya, also see it."
I shall cut off the thousand arms of him by whom my father—who was always devoted to virtuous deeds—was slain; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, his eyes red with rage, he overpowered Kārtavīryārjuna on the ground as he cried out again and again, treating him according to his will.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, with his sharp battle-axe, cut off his entire thousand arms along with his kinsmen.
O beloved, he struck down the king as he stood upon his chariot and slew him; by him, the earth was rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
Having indeed rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas, that mighty Bhārgava performed a horse sacrifice for the destruction of all his sins.
In that sacrifice of great giving, the descendant of Bhṛgu, being pleased, bestowed the earth as a sacrificial fee upon Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
The high-minded one, the best among chariot-warriors, gave white horses of Varuṇa’s lineage, a chariot, inexhaustible gold, cows, and lordly elephants.
Even then, at that great horse-sacrifice, the highly illustrious one’s slaughter of many living beings did not cease.
Thus, indeed, in the Purāṇas and in all the various Āgamas, the expiation for those who have killed a person who trusts them is heard as follows.
The sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed by the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or else by twelve years [of penance], if only one such act has been committed on earth.
Furthermore, by me, a cruel man, many living beings have been slain—those who were trusting, those who were heedless, and even those still in the womb, again and again. (21)
"Women, the elderly, children, and especially my mother"—thus filled with sorrow, Rāma fell into the deepest despondency.
Having reflected for a moment, O beloved, he went to Mount Raivataka and performed severe penance there for many groups of years.
Nevertheless, the slaughter arising from the many living beings did not cease; then Rāma went to Mahendra and likewise to Malaya.
Having wandered across all the mountains on the delightful and holy Sahya, Himālaya, and Badarikāśrama, he went to the Narmadā river for the purpose of bathing.
The Yamunā, the Candrabhāgā, the Gaṅgā that flows through the three paths, the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, and the supreme, auspicious Carmaṇvatī.
The Viśālā, Kapilā, Durgā, Gambhīrā, Gomatī, Śivā, Godāvarī, Daśārṇā, and likewise the meritorious Bhīmarathī. || 27 ||
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara; Aṭṭahāsa, Prabhāsa, Kedāra, and Amareśvara.
Although he had completed his pilgrimage, Bhārgava, afflicted by grief, reflected: "Surely the majesty of sacred fords is no longer seen upon this earth at present."

"The sin of killing a Brahmin has not left me; my dharma has been rendered fruitless. That which is proclaimed in the scriptures regarding the auspicious acts of visiting holy places and giving gifts is false. If this were true, how could it be that I have perished and [this] has come to pass? (30)
At that very time, Nārada, the bull among sages, arrived at that place where Rāma was stationed.
With a dejected face and miserable, reflecting again and again, Rāma, seeing him in such a state, then replied to Nārada.
"O Nārada, divine sage, listen to my supreme words: O best of the twice-born, my mother was previously slain at the command of my father."
Due to the defeat of my father, kings have been slain by me upon the earth; the wombs of women have been torn open, as well as children, the elderly, and women. (34)
The worlds were struck down incessantly by Viśoka, who was merciless; afterwards, compassion arose in me as I beheld the next world.
The horse sacrifice has been performed, and gifts have been given in many ways; I have bathed in all the sacred fords and at all the springs.
On the mountains, penance was performed, oblations were offered, and prayers were recited incessantly; for the sake of destroying the sin of killing a Brahmin, what have I not done here? (37)
But the sin of killing did not depart; therefore, everything was in vain. || 38 ||

Having heard these words of his, the venerable sage Nārada reflected for a long time and then replied with speech that was both beneficial and true: "O Rāma, why do you not now remember yourself as Hari? (39)
You yourself previously declared that in the Mahākālavana field—the supreme and most excellent of all fields—there is a great liṅga that destroys the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa. (40)

"O highly fortunate Rāma, Jaṭeśvara exists there, bestowing all spiritual perfections; you have already descended [to earth], so go there without delay. Having heard Nārada’s words and remembering that unsurpassed sacred field, [he departed]. (41)
Then, O Goddess, he went quickly to Mahākālavana; there he propitiated the Liṅga, and consequently the slaughter was destroyed. Then, O Goddess, being pleased, I emerged from the midst of the Liṅga.
"I shall grant whatever desire you wish," said the son of Jamadagni as I spoke; thereupon Rāma, with his neck bowed low in devotion, replied. (43)
"May my devotion to your lotus-feet always be vast; O Maheśvara, if you are pleased, grant me this boon today. (44)
O Pārvatī, having been addressed thus by him who was well-pleased, I then granted him his desired boon: a state that brings renown. (45)
From this day forward, the god shall be known by your name; thus he will be celebrated in the three worlds as Rāmeśvara. (46)
Those who worship the supreme deity Rāmeśvara with devotion—their sins accumulated from the very beginning of birth perish at that very moment. (47)
That man alone is meritorious and worthy of worship in this world and the next, who beholds with devotion the Lord Śiva as Rāmeśvara. (48)
Those who rejoice in the sight of the God as well as His worship, they too, being liberated from sin, go to my abode. (49)
Furthermore, even that terrible sin which is equal to a thousand killings of Brahmins—that evil is dissolved through the worship of Rāmeśvara. (50)
That fruit which is difficult for Brahmins to attain through sacrifices such as the Vājapeya is obtained with ease simply by beholding Śrī Rāmeśvara.
Those heroes who, facing the enemy on the field of battle, are slain for the sake of cows and Brahmins, attain a destiny even superior to theirs by beholding the auspicious Rāmeśvara.
By him the worlds are always conquered, just as the three worlds were by Rāma, who constantly beheld with devotion the auspicious Liṅga Rāmeśvara. 53.
This power of the god Rāmeśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Cyavaneśvara.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Rāmeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Viśvanātha said: O Goddess, know that the thirtieth is Cyavaneśvara; by the mere sight of whom, one does not suffer a fall from heaven.
O Pārvatī, the son of the great seer Bhṛgu, named Cyavana, that great sage, having become like a pillar, performed penance while abstaining from food.
On the delightful bank of the Vitastā, it is said that for many groups of years, a certain Brahmin lived enveloped by creepers and accompanied by an anthill.
After a long time, O Goddess, he was completely covered by ants; thus that wise one was enveloped on all sides like a lump of clay.
The righteous Śaryāti, accompanied by his family and filled with joy, arrived at that region to sport in the excellent forest. || 5 ||
He had four thousand women as his wives; however, he had only one daughter, fair-browed and known by the name Sukanyā.
Surrounded by her female companions and adorned with all her ornaments, she, while wandering about, saw the two eyes of Bhārgava within an anthill.
Then, out of curiosity and with her intellect deluded, she said, "What indeed is this? and pierced his eyes with a thorn.
Pierced by her in the eyes, he experienced supreme agony; consequently, the army of Śaryāti was overcome with excrement and urine.
Then, when the passage for excrement and urine was blocked, the king was greatly distressed; thereupon, the king, filled with rage, replied in a faltering voice: (10)
Who has committed an offense here today against the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu, who is constantly devoted to austerity, aged, and especially prone to anger? (11)
"Whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly, tell us this without delay. All the soldiers said to him, "We do not know of any harm we have done."
Then that protector of the earth, deeply distressed, himself repeatedly questioned his own circle with both gentle and stern words.
Seeing her father distressed, Sukanyā then said to him: "I saw something with a most beautiful luster within an anthill."
"Like a firefly, that which was well-known to me has been pierced by him nearby. Having heard this, Śaryāti quickly approached the anthill.
There, with palms joined in reverence, that lord of the earth requested Bhārgava—who was advanced in asceticism as well as in years—for the sake of his army.
O Brāhmaṇa, whatever offense has been committed against you by this girl out of ignorance, I give this very daughter of mine to you, who is firm in her vows.
"O best of the twice-born, please accept her as your wife; be gracious. Then Cyavana Bhārgava spoke thus to the king.
"O Lord of the Earth, if you accept her in this way, I shall forgive [this offense]. The lord of the earth then gave his daughter to that Cyavana. (19)
Having accepted that maiden, the Blessed One was indeed pleased; once his favor was obtained, the king then returned to his realm along with his army.
Having obtained a husband who was an ascetic, the blameless Sukanyā also constantly attended upon him with affection, through austerity and self-restraint.
Then, after some time had passed, the two beloved Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, beheld Sukanyā, who had performed her ablutions and was uncovered.
Seeing her, whose limbs were beautiful like the daughter of the King of the Gods, they approached her and said, "To whom do you belong, O most radiant one? (23)
That highly fortunate woman, devoted to her husband, spoke thus to Śaryāti’s daughter, who was indeed the wife of Cyavana.
Then the two Aśvins, laughing, spoke to her once again: "Why, having become such as this, do you [desire] a husband worn out by old age? (25)
O auspicious lady, having cast aside here the aged Cyavana—who is excluded from the enjoyment of desires—you should choose one of us two. (26)
"Do not spend your youth in vain for the sake of a husband who merely resembles a divine being. Thus addressed, Sukanyā spoke this to the two Aśvins: || 27 ||
"I am devoted to the god Cyavana; do not suspect me thus. Then they both spoke to her again: "We two are the best of divine physicians. (28)
"We shall make your husband young and endowed with beauty; on this condition, O slender-waisted one, invite us. (27)
Having heard their words, she spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu; and having heard that, Cyavana said to his wife, "Let it be done."
They said to that princess, "Let your husband enter the waters. Thereupon, Cyavana, desiring beauty, quickly entered the water.
O beloved, at that time the two Aśvins also entered the lake; then, after a moment, they all emerged from that lake.
All of them possessed divine forms, were young, and wore celestial earrings; they were dressed in identical attire and increased the delight of the mind.
They all spoke together: "O auspicious one, O lady of excellent complexion, choose one of us as your husband, for this is our desire. (34)
Having observed them all standing there, assuming identical forms, the goddess, having deliberated with her mind and intellect, chose her own husband.
Having obtained his wife and his desired youth and beauty, the highly effulgent Cyavana, filled with joy, spoke these words to the two Nāsatyas: || 36 ||
That I, though endowed with beauty and possessed of youth, have been made old by you two, and yet have obtained this wife. (37)
"Therefore, I shall out of affection make you both drinkers of Soma; this is the truth, there is no doubt, even as the King of the Gods looks on. (38)
Having heard that, their minds filled with joy, the two gods departed for heaven; they performed a sacrifice for the sake of the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, who were worthy of the Soma.
For these two physicians of the gods are indeed censured for that deed; if you yourself shall offer Soma for their sake, [they will be purified]. (40)

"I shall strike you with my thunderbolt, which is of terrible form and most dreadful. When he had spoken thus, that descendant of Bhṛgu, looking at Indra with a smile and perceiving Vāsava to be powerful, reflected quickly.

I shall propitiate the god Mahādeva Maheśvara, whose servant is Śakra, under whose control the gods follow, who is capable as the protector of the world and the cause of its creation and destruction. || 42 ||
Having spoken thus, O Goddess, Cyavana went to Mahākālavana. There, the Liṅga of the god Rāmeśvara, situated to the northeast, was worshipped with faith by that high-souled Cyavana. 43.
Rudra, being pleased with him, granted him freedom from fear even of the thunderbolt; however, Bhārgava paralyzed the arm of that one as he was about to strike.
By the power of this Liṅga, which was pleased by his propitiation, in that interval a flame issued forth from the center of the Liṅga.
Scorched by her and blinded in an instant by the smoke, all the hosts of gods, deprived of their senses, spoke with faltering voices. (46)
"O slayer of Bala, let these two Aśvins be made drinkers of Soma. Having heard the words of the gods, Śakra, afflicted by fear, then replied to Cyavana with his neck bowed in salutation: || 47 ||
"O Bhārgava, from this day forward these two shall be drinkers of Soma; therefore, I tell you all this as the truth. (48)
"O ascetic, let there be no anger toward you regarding this hospitality; this is the power of this Linga, that I have been rendered lusterless. (49)
Therefore, O Goddess, it shall attain renown on earth by your name, since it was propitiated by the high-souled Cyavana. (50)

This indeed became renowned throughout the three worlds as Cyavaneśvara. Those devotees who shall worship the Lord of Devas, Cyavaneśvara, their sins accumulated since birth perish at that very moment. || 51 ||
The man who constantly beholds the one known as Cyavaneśvara shall be liberated from birth, suffering, old age, and disease, and shall attain final liberation. || 52 ||
Whatever desire a man may contemplate in his mind as being dear to him, he attains that very thing, however difficult it may be to obtain, by beholding the Lord Cyavaneśvara.
Those who behold the god Cyavaneśvara with constancy, O beloved, go to my world after casting off their bodies.
He who hears this meritorious, auspicious narrative that removes all sins—that virtuous soul goes to the supreme divine abode; of this there is no doubt. (55)
O illustrious lady, even one who is devoid of devotion and devoid of ritual action, if he beholds [the deity] by chance, attains a meritorious state that is accessible only to yogis.
Those who worship the god Cyavaneśvara with various kinds of flowers, having crossed over the ocean of worldly existence, go to the supreme state. || 57 ||
This sin-destroying power of the god Cyavaneśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear of Khaṇḍeśvara, O Śivā.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cyavaneśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Lingas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O beloved, know that the thirty-first deity is Khaṇḍeśvara; by the sight of whom, the fasts, vows, and other observances become complete. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in the Tretā Yuga there was a king named Bhadrāśva; after his name, the region became known by the name Bhadrāśva.
Once, the most excellent Agastya, having come to his house, said: "I shall dwell in your home for seven nights."
The king, bowing his head to him, said, "Please be seated. His wife was named Kāntimatī, who was most beautiful.
Her splendor became equal to that of the twelve suns; she had a hundred co-wives, O lady of excellent complexion.
Day after day, those beautiful-eyed women always performed their tasks like female slaves, trembling with fear due to the power of Kāntimatī.

Seeing her thus, with her eyes fixed upon his face, and beholding the queen in such a state, exceedingly beautiful, Agastya, filled with joy, exclaimed: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! (7)
On the second day as well, having seen the queen of great splendor, he thought: "Aha! This entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been robbed by this woman."
Thus Agastya spoke upon seeing the queen on the second day; and having seen her again on the third day, he spoke thus once more.
"Alas, these fools do not know the supreme majesty of the Liṅga in the sacred field of Mahākālavana, situated to the east of Cyavaneśa. (10)
"Since these partial vows become complete through the sight [of you], on the fourth day, raising his hands, he spoke again: 11.
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! Excellent, O Bhadrāśva of noble vows! Thus [you spoke] on the fifth day, and likewise again and again on the sixth."

Seeing him dancing on the seventh day, the king, accompanied by his wife, spoke to him with a heart full of wonder: "O Brāhmaṇa, what is the cause of your joy, such that you are engaged in this dancing? (13)
Agastya said: "O King, you are a fool, and your ministers are great fools! Oh, how deluded is the family priest, since they do not know my intention!"
"Even such kings as these are born by whose sight [one is purified]. Thus addressed, the king then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, we do not know your intention at this moment; please tell us, O illustrious one, if you are disposed to show us favor. (16)

Agastya said: This queen was formerly a maidservant of a Vaiśya named Haridatta in the city of Vaidiśa; you were indeed her husband, and by the power of the Khaṇḍavrata, you have been born as a laborer.
And that Vaiśya, having gone to Mahākāla, worshipped the god Maheśvara in various ways with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 18 ||
Having honored them, [he said], "Until you return home, may you two be our protectors. Then, after a long time, both husband and wife died.
By that merit, your birth occurred in the house of Priyavrata; and this wife of yours was formerly the female servant of a Vaiśya.
"Through the connection with another's merit, this excellent land was obtained; 'The kingdom, the wife, the son, and the virtuous one'—these were the words spoken by me. (21)
O protector of the earth, by the majesty of that god, I see you performing various sacrifices, renowned among hundreds of kings.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, that which was previously spoken by me to you is indeed true.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Kumbhayoni, the lord of the earth resolved to go to Mahākālavana; then, accompanied by that great sage, he set out together with his inner apartments.
The lord of the earth again beheld with faith the Liṅga described by Agastya, and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites together with his wife.
Then the god of immeasurable splendor, being pleased, said to the king: "May your penance be according to your heart's desire, as well as enjoyment and sovereignty."
Having established his lineage, power, good fortune, long life, and freedom from disease, as well as a kingdom without rivals, he shall thereafter attain heaven.
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, he went to his own realm; then, having made his kingdom free from thorns, O beloved, he departed for heaven.
O Goddess, by the power of this Liṅga, the multitude of partial vows observed throughout many lifetimes became complete.
Therefore, the god Khaṇḍeśvara is renowned throughout the three worlds. O Goddess, those men who behold the auspicious god Khaṇḍeśvara— || 30 ||

Indeed, their partial vows (khaṇḍavrata) quickly become complete; whatever deficiency was committed in penance, in the vow, or in charity—all that reaches fulfillment through the sight of Śrī Khaṇḍeśvara. (31)
Having beheld the god Khaṇḍeśvara, O Goddess, one is liberated from the obstacles of sin committed through the actions of mind, speech, and body over seven lifetimes.
Having beheld the god Khaṇḍeśvara, one attains the fulfillment of all duties; O beloved, his misfortune arising from seven births is destroyed.
O lady of excellent complexion, when the god Khaṇḍeśvara is worshipped, all the gods, including Indra, become satisfied and grant boons.
O beloved, those who indeed worship the god Khaṇḍeśvara with faith, especially with various meritorious ablutions and fragrant substances; || 35 ||
Through incense, lamps, prostrations, recitations, and various kinds of hymns of praise, they all became endowed with their desires, possessed of splendor, and united with sovereignty. (36)

Embodied beings are born long-lived, of virtuous conduct, and stainless; their state is exceedingly excellent, free from sorrow, eternal, and imperishable. By the grace of Khaṇḍeśvara, they are so born—of this there is no doubt. (37)
And these—Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Kuvera, Agni, and the others—have attained supreme perfection through the worship of Khaṇḍeśvara.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Khaṇḍeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear indeed of Pattaneśvara. || 39 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Khaṇḍeśvara," in the *Caturaśītiliṅgamāhātmya-khaṇḍa*, within the fifth section (*Āvantyakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Know that Pattaneśvara, the thirty-second most excellent Lord, renowned throughout the three worlds, bestows spiritual perfection upon men. || 1 ||
O Goddess, formerly on Mount Mandara, which possesses beautiful caves, while I was sporting with you, I was once questioned by you while we were staying in private.
For what reason have you abandoned Mount Kailāsa, so delightful, white as pearls and stones, and as pure as a conch shell or the rays of the moon? (3)
It resounded with the songs sung by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras; it was always covered by flowering trees and adorned with groves of plantain trees.
Then [he beheld] that place, crowded with cuckoos, ruddy geese, chakoras, and ospreys, resembling the world of the meritorious and serving as an ornament for heaven.
In the empty Mahākālavana, overgrown with various shrubs and creepers, crowded with lordly elephants, wild elephants, tigers, lions, and śambara deer; || 6 ||
It was adorned with bears, monkeys, jackals, insects, and other creatures; it was graced by peacocks, snakes, cats, mice, and the like.
O Lord, how was this dwelling made? This is a source of curiosity for me.
Thus questioned by you, O Goddess, on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, I, being well-pleased, have described my city to you, my beloved.

The delightful Mahākālavana is a supreme source of happiness even greater than heaven; it is situated within a forest on an excellent sacred field, a seat of the cremation ground (śmaśāna-pīṭha). || 10 ||

Know, O Daughter of the Mountain, that this city possesses incomparable qualities; for such a city-god has indeed never been seen in the three worlds, one who rivals the abode of the gods through his skill in song and instrumental music. (11)
In the meantime, O illustrious goddess, the divine sage Nārada Muni arrived at Mandara, desiring to see me.
For the sake of diversion and out of curiosity for your benefit, I have asked you: O great sage, where was the time spent by you, numbering as many eons?
In which hermitage did you accumulate the store of ascetic merit? Which sacred fords did you visit, and where did your long-standing delight reside? (14)
"O best of sages, tell me of that wonder which was seen before. Thus questioned by me, O Goddess, the great sage, the son of Brahmā, related the account of the city with great care.
Having wandered extensively through many sacred fords and shrines, as well as various ports, countries, and cities.
O Mahādeva, while wandering for the sake of travel in the delightful Jambūdvīpa, I beheld the supreme king of cities, which always bestows great joy.

Its arrangement is fashioned according to one's own will, and it is constructed as if from hundreds of palaces; it brings about the attainment of the fruits of desire and wish, bestowing an ineffable happiness. (18)
Enveloped by breezes pleasant to the touch and fragrant with the blossoms of all seasons, it resounds with the sounds of lutes and flutes, bringing great delight to the mind. (19)
Illuminated by diamonds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, moonstones, and other gems, he is free from the fear of old age and death, and is devoid of all diseases.
Served by Śakra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, the Ocean, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśa, they indeed dwell throughout the seven meritorious worlds, both above and below.
O Maheśvara, even those gods who are ever-joyful long for that city, where peaceful and high-souled beings dwell.
They illuminated the quarters of the sky, were self-controlled, and possessed the splendor of the sun and Vaiśvānara; they wore divine garments, were steadfast, and bore crests upon their heads.
The Brahmins were meritorious devotees of Maheśvara; the Kṣatriyas were intent upon Hari; the Vaiśyas were seekers of liberation established in austerity; and the Śūdras were long-lived.

He is of radiant form, and he is of red appearance; he is yellow, and in some places he is other than white. He possesses a name, and yet he is devoid of a name; he is invisible in form, and he is visible in form. || 25 ||

In some places he has eyes like a thousand suns; in some places he possesses the radiance of a single sun; in some places he excels even the moon; and in some places he is as brilliant as a finger-ring.
Birth, death, old age, disease, and various other miseries—all these go to dissolution when the Lord of Pattana is pleased. (27)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Pattaneśa has been recounted to you; now hear about Ānandeśa.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Pattaneśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 32 ||
Śrī Hara said: Know that the thirty-third deity is Ānandeśvara, the Lord; he is meritorious, the destroyer of sins, and the constant bestower of all prosperity. (1)
Formerly, in the Rathantara Kalpa, there was a lord of the earth known as Anamitra, a sovereign ruler over the entire surface of the world.
A king whose soul was dharma, a great-souled one whose wealth was valor, he shone like the imperishable sun, surpassing all living beings. || 3 ||
He was impartial toward enemy, son, and friend, and was a knower of the duties of others; he married Giribhadrā, the daughter of the mountain, who was of excellent complexion.
She was exceedingly dear to him, even more precious than his own life. He had a son named Ānanda, who was wise and devoted to knowledge.
As soon as he was born, she cradled him firmly in her own lap; embracing him with deep affection, she cooed to him again and again.
Having been born with the memory of his former lives, he sat upon his mother’s lap; he then laughed, and his mother, becoming agitated, spoke these words.
"I am afraid; what is this, my child, that there is a smile upon your face? Has an untimely awakening occurred, or do you see something auspicious? (8)

Thus addressed, he said to his mother: "Everyone seeks their own interest. Do you not see that a female cat wishes to lead me away? And here is a second one, a 'born-stealer,' who has become invisible."
And because of your love for your son, O Mother, you thus strive for your own purpose; alas, having coaxed me over and over again many times, you embrace me.
Out of affection and agitation for the newborn child, even these women have arrived; hear now the reason for this laughter as well. (11)
The greedy female cat, intent on her own interest, gazes at me; likewise, this second one, who carries off newborns, has become invisible.
But you desire from me a fruit that is to be enjoyed gradually; you do not know me at all, nor indeed have I ever done you any favor.
The association of fools lasts no more than five or seven days; nevertheless, you feel affection for them and constantly embrace them with love. (14)
"O child, O dear one, you speak falsehoods to me by saying 'tateta'. Hearing these words of her son, the mother, filled with anger, spoke this: || 15 ||
"O child, I do not embrace you out of affection for the sake of doing you a favor; rather, I have renounced my own self-interest, which shall henceforth reside in you. (16)
Having spoken thus, she abandoned him and departed from the maternity chamber; then that Jātahāriṇī seized the child who had been cast aside.
Having then carried away that child who remembered his former births, O beloved, she placed him upon the bed of Haiminī, the wife of King Vikrānta.
Considering him to be his own son, the powerful king performed the naming ceremony, and he became renowned by the name Ānanda.
The son of Vikrānta and the twice-born Bodha was named Caitra by him, and he was consecrated with Vedic mantras.
The night-stalker then devoured the third son of Bodha; at that time, Ānanda, though he remembered his past lives, had already undergone the sacred thread ceremony.
"Permitted by the preceptor, perform the salutation; first, attend upon your mother. Having been thus addressed, he spoke these words: || 22 ||
"Which of my mothers is to be saluted—she who gave me birth or she who protected me? Having heard Ānanda's words, the Teacher spoke these words: [23]
"O highly fortunate one, this is indeed your mother, the daughter of Janaka; she is the chief queen of Vikrānta, known by the name Haiminī. (24)
Ānanda said: "She is the mother of Caitra, and this Caitra has been consecrated with Vedic mantras by Brahmins in the house of a twice-born; I am the son of Giribhadra. (25)
The Guru said: "Then who are you, and who is this Caitra spoken of by you? Thereupon, he related the previous events from the beginning.
The Guru said: "O child, an exceedingly profound and great danger has arrived. Due to delusion, I know nothing; my intellects wander in confusion. (27)
Ānanda said: What occasion for delusion is there here, since the world is established in this manner? O brahmin-sage, who is whose son, or who is not whose kinsman? (28)
Therefore, O Guru, it is a wonder how the cycle of existence here destroys the cycle of existence for living beings, since their minds are struck down by great delusion. (29)
The daughter of the wicked and unbearable Brahmaputra was born on earth as Jātahāriṇikā; she devours the children. (30)
Indeed, two mothers were obtained by me in this very birth; furthermore, having become one who remembers his past lives, two mothers were obtained. (31)
"Therefore, I shall perform penance; let Caitra be brought here. Then the king, along with his wife and kinsmen, was greatly amazed.
Therefore, turning away from possessiveness, she consented to him; and he, having brought back Caitra, made his son fit for the kingdom.
Having honored that Brāhmaṇa whom he had protected with the affection for a son, Ānanda also performed penance in the auspicious Mahākālavana forest.
To the west of the god Indreśvara is an excellent liṅga; he indeed worshipped it with devotion through difficult penance.
Then, O lady of pure smiles, the God spoke to him as he was performing penance: "For what purpose do you perform such intense austerity, my child? Tell me."
"You must become the sixth Manu; go and do that. Enough of your asceticism; through that [act], you will attain liberation. (37)
Thus addressed by the God of gods, the high-minded one said, "So be it. O Goddess, that Manu became equal to Brahmā and possessed great fame.
He begot sons through the worship of this Liṅga; then the gods gave it the excellent name Ānandeśvara.
O Goddess, since Ānanda attained a perfection that is very difficult to obtain, therefore let this well-known name Ānandeśvara be beheld.
O large-eyed one, those who behold the Lord Ānandeśvara shall become endowed with sons and grandsons upon this earth.
For those men whose sin arising from hundreds of millions of births has been exhausted, that devotion arises through the vision of Ānandeśvara.
At that very moment, a person is liberated from birth, death, old age, and the like, when he beholds the Lord of Gods known as Ānandeśvara.

I have described the vision of Ānandeśvara, which grants liberation to men; the god Ānanda, the supreme Liṅga that bestows both heaven and final emancipation. O large-eyed lady, this most excellent Liṅga is worshipped here by the gods.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the deity Ānandeśvara has been recounted to you; now listen to [the account of] Kaṃthaḍeśvara.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ānandeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Hara said: Know that the thirty-fourth deity is indeed Kaṃthaḍeśvara; by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins.
Formerly, there lived on the beautiful bank of the Vitastā a Brāhmaṇa named Pāṇḍava, who was greatly oppressed by poverty.
Abandoned by his kinsmen as well as by his wicked wife, he possessed only a single ragged garment which held all his wealth and affection.
Therefore, being gratified by him in the mountain cave as he desired a son, I also said, "O large-eyed one, you shall have a son."
A son was born to him from the midst of his patched garment; that very garment, both cold and warm, became the clothing for that son.
And that was obtained through my grace, O fair-faced one; furthermore, a boon was granted by Rudra regarding Kaṃthā.

Then, when the sixth year had passed, he contemplated the investiture with the sacred girdle (mauñjībandha). Having invited all the sages and propitiated them again and again, and having paid obeisance to all the seers, he honored them with devotion.
The girdle was also bound for him with fruits according to his means; then all those sages, having been propitiated again and again, spoke to him.
"O best of sages, please grant your blessings to this son; may this son of my son live for a long time."
Having heard that, they all remained silent and gave no reply. When they did not speak in response, the best of sages himself reflected through meditation that his son was surely short-lived.
Having realized this, the sage suddenly fell into a state of delusion; afflicted by grief and pained by affection for his son, he lamented.
Vāḍava said: "How is it that my son has been granted such a short lifespan by Maheśa himself? For in the past, a boon was granted to me by Rudra when he was pleased."

"A son equal to me in prowess shall arise for you from within a patched garment; yet, having given birth to him, you will falsely declare him to be short-lived, thus making the word of the Three-eyed One come false. (13)
Seeing his father distressed, the sage remained silent at that time; then the boy suddenly spoke words that increased his joy. (14)

"Abandon now this fear, you who are despondent on my account; I shall strike down the King of the Dead, whose own efforts have been frustrated. Listen to my words, O world-protectors together with your Lord: this is my solemn vow for the sake of conquering the Lord of the Ancestors. (15)

Having propitiated Śaṅkara through most rigorous austerities and through devotion even to my own father, I shall destroy Death’s hope for victory. Father, why are you all so agitated by excessive despondency? I shall immediately bring that Lord of the Ancestors under my own control.
I go for refuge to Rudra, the Great Lord, the supreme deity who is never separated from Umā; let all the sages listen from every side: for one such as me, there is no defeat by death. (17)

Having propitiated the feet of the Blue-throated Lord through fierce austerities, I shall soon lead Death away; those whose eyes tremble at the nectar of Kaṇṭhāja’s words, their bodies bristling with hair standing on end.
The sages questioned that child: "How do you know Rudra, the Supreme? We have been worshipping him for a long time with fierce austerities and a multitude of vows. (19)
"Nevertheless, we do not know Maheśa; how was he known by you, a mere child? O son, our hair stands on end with joy and wonder as we truly desire to hear about him. (20)
Where and how was Maheśa, the Great Lord and the sole sovereign of the world, known by you? (21)
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, that boy related the account to the daughter of the mountain.
While I was playing here, a Siddha who bestows success approached me; perceiving that my lifespan was short, he spoke these words out of affection. (23)
"Go, my son, at my command to the excellent Mahākālavana; there, to the south of the Ānandeśvara Liṅga, is a Liṅga. (24)
Worship him quickly; you shall become long-lived. Through his imparting of instruction, knowledge will be perfectly attained from Maheśvara.
"O lords of sages, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that there is no other god in the worlds; therefore, this very day I shall go to the auspicious Mahākālavana."
"I shall worship the Liṅga; let this despondency be abandoned here. Having heard those words of his, the great ṛṣis [departed] along with him.
And the father, O Goddess, as well as all those who had assembled, were struck with wonder; the boy propitiated the God with the desire to slay Kāla.
Then, O daughter of the mountain, a voice issued forth from the middle of the Liṅga: "O child, I am pleased with you; what desire shall I grant you? (29)
The boy said: "O God, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased with me, may those who behold you be liberated from the rags of sin and become long-lived. (30)

Having heard the words of the child, O illustrious lady, it was declared regarding the Linga: "Those who shall worship me, endowed with supreme faith, they will forever be free from old age and death. (31)
O best of Gaṇas, they shall obtain the highest desires and become worthy of worship in all the worlds, adorned with every ornament. (32)
Having thus obtained the boon, Kaṇṭha stood before him with palms joined in reverence; he was addressed by the gracious Liṅga: "O you of noble vows, choose yet another boon."
This boon is indeed difficult to obtain in this world even for gods, dānavas, and guhyakas; since it has been brought down by me, there is nothing that cannot now be given to you.
O Mahādeva, if a boon is to be granted once more by you, as spoken by the child: "O God, may your fame in the three worlds on earth be known by my name. (35)
"Let it be so," was declared by the gratified Liṅga, O Pārvatī; from that time forward, the Lord of Gods became renowned as Kaṃthaḍeśvara, by the mere sight of whom a man becomes long-lived. (36)
He who beholds that Linga, the Lord Kaṇṭhaḍeśvara; || 37 ||

O Gaurī, freed from the wretchedness of sin, he shall attain liberation. That Liṅga is meritorious, conducive to fame, worthy of being sung, and the destroyer of sins; it purifies all transgressions through the chanting of my name. (38)
Those men in this world are unfortunate, and their birth is useless, by whom that Lord Kaṇṭheśvara has not been seen at Mahākāla. (39)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Kaṃthaḍeśvara has been narrated to you; now hear about Indreśvara.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kanthaḍeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 34 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Goddess, the thirty-fifth deity is the unsurpassed Mīndreśvara, which bestows great siddhis and destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin.
There was a Prajāpati named Tvaṣṭṛ; his son was Kuśadhvaja, who was devoted to his own duties, self-controlled, and struck down by Vāsava.
Hearing that his son had been slain, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Prajāpati, became enraged; plucking out a single lock of matted hair, he spoke these words: || 3 ||
Today let the three worlds, together with the gods, behold my prowess; and let that evil-minded Indra, the slayer of Brahmans, also see it.
"By him, devoted to his own duty, my son was struck down! Having said this, with eyes red with anger, he offered that matted lock into the fire.
Then Vṛtra rose up, enveloped in garlands of flames; he was massive in body, possessed of great fangs, and had the luster of a heap of crushed collyrium.
Indraśatru, of immeasurable soul and augmented by the splendor of Tvaṣṭṛ, grew day by day, possessing great strength and reaching the range of an arrow-shot.
Seeing the great asura Vṛtra for his own destruction, Śakra suddenly reflected: "What deed might now be well-done? (8)
In the meantime, Vṛtra, the best among the powerful, arrived; there he beheld Vāsava together with the gods, O lady of beautiful countenance.
The Daitya Vṛtra, possessed of a massive body, waged a fierce battle, tumultuous with various weapons and missiles, and crowded with the clashing of hosts of warriors.
The surface of the earth was stained with blood from shattered and split armor, while it was impassable due to a multitude of severed lotus-like faces and hand-buds.

It was a place where throngs of headless trunks were joined together, where the celestial armies were struck down, and where the limbs of warriors were adorned with abundant, glittering ornaments scattered about.
In that most terrifying battle, having pierced through the gods along with the Guhyakas, [the sky] had its quarters reddened by the surging billows of blood.
Having bound Vāsava, he indeed went to the heavenly world; O lady of beautiful countenance, he ruled his kingdom without fear and without rival.
Then, when Devendra had been bound, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati came to that place where Śatakratu was held captive.
Having seen Śakra in such a state and having greeted him with blessings, he released him from his bonds and then spoke these words.

This is not the favorable time for you now, O Lord of the Gods; for a very great effort has been observed, as well as a coalition of the enemies of the gods. Indeed, all the foremost and mighty Asuras there have been seen by me.

"It is my opinion that even each one of them individually would be capable of conquering you. O Śakra, never before has such a gathering of the enemies of the gods been seen or even heard of as has now been witnessed. (18)
Having heard the words of Bṛhaspati, Śakra was filled with agitation; after reflecting for a moment, he said, "O Bṛhaspati of great intellect! (19)
"Tell me now, O Bṛhaspati, what should be done in this matter? In a few short days, many powerful Dānavas and that mighty Vṛtra will come into my presence. (20)
Having heard these words of Śakra, Bṛhaspati said to him: "O Śakra, go at my command; let a remedy be applied quickly."
O Vāsava, in the delightful Mahākālavana, to the south of Khaṇḍeśvara, there exists a Liṅga that bestows all prosperity.
"Therefore, propitiate him with diligence; he will grant you that desire. Having heard Bṛhaspati's words, Śakra departed with great haste.
O Goddess, having beheld that unsurpassed Liṅga in Mahākālavana, he immediately offered praise with his neck bowed in devotion.

Salutations to the God of gods, to Śaṅkara, and to the Bull; salutations eternally to the one who is desirable, to the multiformed one, to him whose sacred thread is a serpent, to the most excellent one; salutations to you, the granter of all desires. (25)
You alone are the primordial creator of progeny; you alone are Time who destroys all beings. You alone are the Lord of Waters, the Lord of Beings, the Lord of Wealth, and you alone are the Fire.

You alone are the moon and the sun, you are the wind; you are the creator, the ordainer, the supreme and ancient one. You are the reservoir of waters, you are Varuṇa; you are the best of mountains and the lord of serpents. You are Ḍiṇḍi, Mahākāla, and the bull; you are Vināyaka and the most excellent of the Guhyakas.

Having heard this praise thus uttered, Śatakratu was addressed by the Liṅga: "Go, O Śakra, at my command; strengthened by my splendor in battle, you shall slay Vṛtra, O destroyer of enemies—of this there is no doubt. (28)
O Pārvatī, by the majesty of that Liṅga, he slew Vṛtra in battle with the foam of the waters, while the enemies of the gods looked on.
Having slain the Dānavas afterwards with ease, he who was fierce in battle then spoke to the gods: "Vṛtra has been killed in the great war."
"By my prowess, you have attained the sovereignty over the three worlds. Thus addressed by Śakra, those gods were filled with wonder.
By the majesty of this god, the great asura Vṛtra was slain; and the sins residing within his body were brought to destruction by the mere sight [of him]. || 32 ||
Since the Great Lord, the God of gods, was propitiated by Indra, he shall therefore become renowned on earth by the name Indreśvara.
By the sight of this Linga, even sinners shall go to the beautiful city of Indra, freed from all their transgressions.
The man who constantly beholds the one known as Śrī Indreśvara shall be liberated from all sins and will rejoice in heaven for a long time. || 35 ||
