Whoever worships with devotion this Liṅga propitiated by Indra shall go indeed to the supreme abode for four divine Kalpas.

By him who has properly worshipped the god Indreśvara with devotion, all of us—Viṣṇu and the others, including Indra—as well as the sages and the guardians of the worlds, have undoubtedly been worshipped. (37)
Thus addressed from all sides by the gods, including Śakra, Vaikuṇṭha, and others, the Lord, accompanied by them, then went to heaven.
This power of the god Indreśvara has been described by you; now, O Pārvatī, listen to [the account of] the god Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Indreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Hara said: Know Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara to be the thirty-sixth Lord; by the mere sight of whom a man becomes possessed of a son.
There was an ascetic named Mṛkaṇḍu, born of the lineage of Brahmā and perfected in the study of the Vedas; yet he remained childless.
He reflected upon the matter of a son, thinking, "How might a son be born? For it is recited in the Vedas: "For one who is sonless, how can there be the higher worlds? (3)
"Therefore, I shall perform penance so that a son may be born to me. Having reflected thus in many ways, he went to the Himalayas.
And he, whose self was purified through meditation, made his dwelling for the sake of asceticism; subsisting on air, subsisting on water, fasting entirely, and standing with his feet upwards.
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits; eating only leaves, or one or two leaves; and many other such austerities as these. || 6 ||
That sage remained there for exactly twelve years; yet, O Goddess, I was not satisfied by that difficult penance.
Then, having understood his intention, I was informed by you at that time: "This great sage is indeed performing a severe penance for the sake of his son. (8)
Illuminating the mountain with his splendor and drying up the reservoirs of water, he agitated the inhabitants of heaven by means of his exceedingly difficult asceticism.

All the oceans were agitated, as were the moon and the sun; the sages fell into a state of confusion, and heaven and earth trembled. O Lord, there will undoubtedly be an untimely dissolution of the world.
"O lady of beautiful hips, I said to that sage Mṛkaṇḍa, 'Let a son indeed be granted to him,' for he desires a son not born from a womb."
O large-eyed one, he is inexhaustible like another thousand-eyed Indra; he has the luster of the moon, a face like the moon, and is as beloved to the world as the moon.

"O Goddess of gods, this great sage Mṛkaṇḍu desires a son who is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus, whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus, who has broad and beautiful hips, and who is adorned with lovely earrings. (13)
Furthermore, O Goddess, you who are affectionate toward those devoted to you, have said out of compassion: "You do not grant a son to the sage who is performing severe penance. (14)
How are you, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, praised by the wise? Who indeed would go for refuge to you, the source and origin of the worlds? (15)
"You cause all the Daityas to be utterly overwhelmed by all the gods; O Lord, O mine of compassion, I have been honored by you for a very long time. (16)
No one else would grant me such an excellent boon out of compassion; for you, O Lord of the entire world, are the sovereign, the creator, and the ruler. (17)
The Lord, the Master, the Great Sovereign, compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees—the Lord of All, who has been praised—what desired object would he not grant to the Brahmin? (18)
O Śiva, by my word, grant him a son—he whose sins have been destroyed by austerity and whose self is now realized in Brahman.
O Goddess, O Gaurī, daughter of the Mountain, whose eyes are like trembling lotus petals—I have described you with auspicious words and syllables of affection. (20)
O Mother of Skanda, O you whose face resembles the orb of the full moon; O slender-waisted one, whose luster is like that of refined gold.

"You have said, 'O lady who moves with the gait of an elephant, I shall carry out your word. You are success (*siddhi*), you are the practitioner (*sādhaka*), you are the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and you are the action (*kriyā*) that relies upon its performance. (22)
O beautiful one, you are Māyā, Śrī, Dyuti, the illustrious Śraddhā, Ruci, and Asaṃtati; having displayed manifold honor toward me alone, O lovely lady. (23)
"You shine with various forms, having deluded the entire world; yet you have also spoken, O Goddess—let my word be carried out."
O Maheśvara, let a boon now be granted to this sage, a Brāhmaṇa whose every limb has been emaciated by ascetic penance.
I too have said, O large-eyed one, "Listen to my words: let this best of Brahmins go to the excellent Mahākāla forest. (26)
To the east of Pattaneśvara, O large-eyed lady, there stands an excellent Liṅga that bestows sons and destroys great sins.

Having heard my words, you also spoke to that best of the twice-born: "O most excellent of sages, go to Mahākālavana for the sake of a son; by propitiating the Liṅga there, you shall obtain an excellent son. (28)
Urged by you, the Brahmin, having resolved "so be it," departed full of supreme hope and desiring a son. (29)
Having seen there that great liṅga, which bestows sons and destroys sins, he served it with devotion through difficult penance.
Then, after some time, O beautiful woman, I emerged from the midst of the linga along with you; and that best of the twice-born was addressed by me.
"Know that I am Śarva; tell me, what shall I do for you? We two were pleased with you in the past, and your conduct has been understood. (32)
"O Brahmin, whatever boon you desire, I grant it to you today," said I, being pleased; and the sage, having been addressed by me, was struck with great wonder. (33)
Bowing down, that best of sages, joyful at heart, said: "O lords of gods, for the sake of offspring, what could be unattainable for me?"
Then, O Goddess, I said to Mṛkaṇḍa, the best of sages: "Your son shall indeed be born of no womb; he shall be human, endowed with sovereignty and knowledge, long-lived, all-knowing, and wise. (35)
In the meantime, O Goddess, there appeared the great ascetic, the son Mārkaṇḍeya, the great sage whose soul is supremely devoted to dharma.
As soon as he was born, that righteous-souled one remained right there engaged in austerity; he propitiated the God, who, being pleased, then granted him a boon.
"O best of the twice-born, since I have been gratified by your asceticism as soon as you were born, I shall therefore attain renown through your name."
O best of Brahmins, those who behold me endowed with supreme devotion attain the eternal state that bestows perpetual bliss. (39)
Those who go there by chance shall always be free from suffering; indeed, those men, having propitiated the God of gods, will rejoice.
The three-eyed lords of the Gaṇas and the Siddhas, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, shall always belong to those men who are my devotees. (41)
Those who shall worship me with charming and fragrant flowers will become long-lived and forever free from suffering.
When this was said by that Linga, Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic, remained right there in Mahākālavana and performed penance. || 43 ||
The power of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara has been described, O Goddess; now hear the majesty of the god Śiveśvara. 44.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Hara said: Know that the thirty-seventh is the infinite Śiveśvara; by the mere sight of whom all prosperities are born.
In ancient times, during the Brahma-kalpa, there was a king named Ripuñjaya who, devoted to the protection of his subjects, resided in the delightful Mahākālavana.
Having performed worship of the gods, observances, charity, meditation, Vedic study, hospitable rites, and the protection of subjects, he knows nothing at all.
He protected his subjects as if they were his own children; those subjects flourished in happiness, being free from old age and death.
O beloved, the city of Mahākāla is pervaded by his very splendor; its inhabitants possess sons, are rich in wealth and grain, and are endowed with all their desires.
In the meantime, O Pārvatī, while he was ruling the earth, O Goddess, Mahākālavana—my own city marked by me—was such that he found no pleasure anywhere else to go except for Ujjayinī. || 6 ||
Then I thought of Gaṇeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas known as Śiva; he arrived at that very moment and said, "What shall I do?"
I too said to Gaṇeśa: "Go, my son, to my beloved Mahākālapura, for it is indeed occupied by King Ripuñjaya."
Thus addressed by me, O Goddess, he replied, "So be it," with palms joined in reverence; his face beaming with joy at my command, he departed for the world of mortals.
"O Goddess of pure smiles, I am well-pleased with you, O auspicious attendant; for a capable servant of a lord who is endowed with both practical skill and wisdom is indeed rare. (10)
Then that monk, possessing many medicinal herbs in his form, took a drum upon his shoulder and spoke these words: || 11 ||
Who is seized by spirits or poison, or afflicted by various ailments? Who suffers from what most terrible disease that I might bring to pacification? (12)
"Whoever is childless shall become possessed of a son by relying on the power of my mantra. I am a physician who knows all methods and bestows all desires. (13)
Having heard his words, the people, filled with curiosity and accompanied by the elderly, children, and women, approached him.

He destroyed even their most difficult-to-conquer disease; and they, being greatly delighted, performed a magnificent worship for him with gold, jewels, garments, wealth, grain, villages, cities, and other such things.
Thus he dwelt there for fourteen years, watching for a weakness in the king, yet he found no such opening.
Oh, how exceedingly difficult it is for this king! Oh, he is the refuge of the world! Oh, this hero is a treasury of splendor, invincible, and possessed of great intelligence! (17)
While he was thinking thus, the auspicious Gaṇa Śiva, appearing in the form of a mendicant, remained concealed within the dense thicket of creepers in the dilapidated garden.
In the meantime, however, the queen of that King Lokavrata was Nirjarā, who was dearer to the king than even his own life. (19)
Peerless in beauty in the world, that queen was childless yet desirous of a son; having heard [the teaching], she took refuge in a monk, even though she had many co-wives. (20)
Knowing him to be the granter of all desires, the beautiful woman, full of curiosity, sent her own female companion named Sunandā to the king of the nāgas.

In the monastery of the monk, she remained vigilant within the guarded inner apartments; and having encountered the monk there, she then reflected upon the city and spoke to the monk, who was intent on his thoughts and engaged in begging for alms.

Having prostrated and joined her palms in reverence, free from distress for the sake of her purpose, she said: "O Blessed One, the queen of the king—who is dearer to him than his own life—is barren and desires a son; thus, the goddess wishes to see you in secret. (23)
"You are generally a mine of compassion who grants the desires of your subjects. Having heard this, the attendant of Śiva, finding an opening, spoke.
The monk said: "O blessed lady, what is this perverse talk of yours? You say, 'Go to the house of the king unrecognized. A reckless man would be seen in the city unrecognized. (25)
Thinking thus, O auspicious lady, go quickly back to your own inner apartments; I shall not come there until the king’s word is fulfilled.
Having heard those words of the monk, her mind agitated, she went quickly to the inner apartments and reported that matter to the queen.

Having heard her friend's words, the dejected queen said to her: "Sunandā, what means is there by which the king might be moved to bring the mendicant here quickly, before he departs for some other place? (28)
Sunandā, who spoke with propriety, addressed her with skillful words: "You are the beloved of that king, dearer to him than his own life. (29)
Therefore, manifest your own mental instability to the king; for that reason, the king will carry out your word.

At that very time, the king, longing for a sight of the queen, went to the inner apartments and beheld his beloved in a state of distress. Then the king, his heart moistened with affection, questioned her.
The king said: "O Queen, what is this? You speak as if despondent; by what sorrow are you broken, and who has committed such an offense against you? (32)
Having heard the king's words, the queen spoke these words: "O King, I have no sons; because of that, I have no peace. (33)

For those who are deprived of sons, play leads only to suffering. Childless people are wretched in the world; they are miserable, being bereft of sons. And for one without a son, there is no refuge, especially for one devoid of both daughter and son.
Happy in this world are those people who embrace their own young son, adorned with dust, as he speaks with indistinct syllables. (35)
For this reason, I have reached a state of supreme world-weariness; indeed, I have now seen a means for the sake of my son.
A monk has arrived here, eternal and possessing a divine form; his power is heard to be unimpeded regarding all things. (37)
O King, by the grace of that monk, we shall become mothers of sons; there is no doubt in my mind regarding this matter, for women and children alike seek refuge in him. (38)
Having heard her words, the king went to the ruined garden together with his beloved, and there he beheld that mendicant.

As soon as the king saw the mendicant who had assumed the form of a *liṅga*, he beheld a truly great marvel; bowing with devotion, the lord of the earth worshipped that *liṅga* in the form of a mendicant according to the prescribed rites.
"I am sonless," he said this: "Blessed is this queen of mine; O God, you who are Śiva, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), grant me a son. (41)
Thus addressed by that lion among kings, the mendicant, who had assumed the outward signs [of a monk], then replied to the protector of the earth: "O King, you shall have a son. (42)
From that time forward, that high-minded king, together with his wife, joyfully sought refuge in that god with his whole being.
By the majesty of the God of gods, a son was born who was exceedingly powerful, righteous, illustrious, a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, and preeminent in virtues. || 44 ||
Then, O Goddess, out of curiosity I came from Mount Mandara; having seen the Gaṇa in the form of a Liṅga, as well as the king and his servant.

And by my power of yoga, O Goddess, I indeed created a city for myself, illuminated by the luster of various jewels and frequented by various perfected beings (siddhas). That auspicious and eternal abode was then granted by me.
O lady of excellent complexion, to the north of the deity Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, from that time onwards, this god has been known as Śiveśvara. || 47 ||
Those who shall constantly worship the unsurpassed Śiveśvara will have all their sins shaken off and shall become the foremost of the Gaṇas.
Having understood that the world is heavy with children, I shall bestow supreme knowledge upon those who behold Śiveśvara at the time of their death.
Considering liberation to be extremely difficult to attain and worldly existence to be most terrifying, one should serve that Lord Śiva, for he is the cause of non-rebirth.
Whatever mortal, even in any state of life, should take refuge in that Śiveśvara, he attains that goal which is indeed attained through sacrifices and gifts. (51)
The mortal who, being self-restrained and pure, causes this narrative to be heard, or reads it, or causes it to be read, shall be liberated from all sins.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the god Śiveśvara has been recounted to you; now hear about Kusumeśa. || 53 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Śiveśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 37 ||
Īśvara said: Know, O Goddess, that the thirty-eighth deity is named Kusumeśvara; he bestows heaven and destroys even the greatest of sins.
Formerly, O large-eyed one, when the Vaivasvata Kalpa known as the Vārāha had arrived, I came from Kailāsa after manifesting myself.
O Pārvatī, while I was sporting with you and with the dice in the delightful Mahākālavana, a great sound arose.
And having been questioned, O Goddess, upon hearing that most unbearable sound, I have related to you the origin of that sound.
These lords of the Gaṇas sport in the midst, and among them is the Gaṇa Vīraka, who is exceedingly adorned with flowers and is very dear to me.
O Goddess, that very same Vīraka—who was once struck down for the sake of flowers and now is honored with heaps of blossoms—is always the giver of joy to me.
O lady of beautiful countenance, you who are the repository of various wonderful qualities and are worshipped by hundreds of lords of the Gaṇas, having heard my words, you have also spoken thus.
O Maheśvara, without merit the lotus-face of a son is not seen; yet for me, there is longing even for such a son as this.
"When shall I behold such a son who bestows joy? Having heard your words and having laughed again and again, I said, "O Pārvatī, this Vīraka is now given to you as a son. (9)
Let this very son be the giver of joy to your eyes; let Vīraka have his purpose fulfilled by you, his mother, being honored with flowers.
"Having heard my words, Vijayā was sent by you [with the message]: 'Hara has given me a son; O Vijayā, bring him here quickly. (11)

Vijayā said to the leader of the Gaṇas, who was standing in the midst of the host: "Come, Vīraka! Out of fickleness you have provoked the Lord; why were you so excessively deluded by a passion for dancing like one who is mad? (12)
Thus addressed, trembling with fear yet adorned with flowers, he then approached your presence slowly, followed by Vijayā.
O Goddess, seeing Vīraka adorned with flowers and trembling with fear, you summoned him with words of sweet syllables.
"Come, come! You have been born as my little son; you, Vīraka, have now been granted by the God. Having spoken thus, she placed him upon her lap and kissed his sweet-voiced cheek.

Having smelled him on the crown of his head and rubbed his limbs, she adorned him with divine ornaments herself—with tinkling bells, waist-bands, anklets, and excellent sets of necklaces, armlets, and golden coins set with fine gems. (16)

Then, being pleased, she performed the rite of bodily protection for him with soft, variegated, and beautiful sprouts born of divine mantras, as well as with his pure ashes mixed with white mustard seeds.

Having spoken thus and placed a garland upon his head, radiant with streaks of yellow orpiment, he said: "My child, go now and play with the Gaṇas; remain vigilant and gradually engage in the activities of childhood. (18)

He too [dwelt] for a moment on the Gaṇḍaśaila mountain, crowded with Siddhas and filled with clusters of gems; for a moment at the foot of a tree thick with spreading creepers and swarms of bees; and for a moment amidst rows of blossoming Tamāla trees and wandering swarms of bees.

For a moment he sports in water with very little mud, for a moment in a cluster of lotuses, and for a moment in a beautiful, stainless grove of trees; indeed, the playful child Gaṇeśādhipa, who brings joy to the gods, frolics about.
While Vīraka and his host were thus sporting, the twilight enveloped in darkness arrived; then, O beloved, I was informed by you.
"O Śaṅkara, let sovereignty be granted to this son of mine; let him have half of your body, the status of Gaṇeśa, and the position of a world-protector before all others. (22)

O Lord, [this] state as a *liṅga*, its imperishability, and this divine station so difficult to attain, are being venerated by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, as well as by Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, the Ādityas, the Lokapālas, and the lords of lords. || 23 ||
While being praised by these very high-souled hosts, he was adorned by me with various auspicious flowers.
"O large-eyed one, let him therefore become famous by the name Kusumeśvara. I also said this to my beloved Vīraka: || 25 ||
Listen to the sweetness of the songs of the Gandharvas, which is equal to my own power, divine, and always attended by the lords of the Gaṇas; it is like nectar. 26.
Behold the enchanting song of the Kinnara women; behold this continuous dance of the host of Apsarases. (27)

O fair-faced one, Kusumeśa is surrounded by Vidyādharas; O Goddess, it was especially by me that the Lord of the Pramathas was first brought to the state of being Kusumeśvara when he was adorned with flowers. (28)
O large-eyed one, a place was granted to the north of the Śiva-liṅga; a highly esteemed boon was bestowed, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
O Gaṇapa, for those who shall behold you under the name Kusumeśvara, no sin arises, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
Those men who shall worship Kusumeśvara with flowers, having reached my abode, will rejoice, freed from all suffering.
Even that mortal who beholds you with a concentrated mind for a single day shall be liberated from all sins and go to my world.
He who worships Kusumeśvara with devotion using flowers shall attain the supreme station, from which a return to this world is difficult to find.
O Goddess, having been nourished by such excellent boons, this Kusumeśvara has fulfilled his purpose; through the Liṅga, the Gaṇa has attained the state of lordship.
This power of the god Kusumeśvara has been told; now hear that of the god Akrūreśa immediately thereafter. (35)
Hara said: Listen to the thirty-ninth [deity], Akrūreśvara, by the mere sight of whom a noble intellect arises in men. (1)
O lady of excellent hips, in the beginning of the eon, it was by you alone, in your supreme form as Śakti, that the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were created.
Then, you were praised by the gods, along with the Kinnaras and Mahoragas; meanwhile, your various hosts performed circumambulations.
Some performed prostrations and others offered hymns of praise; at that time, Bhṛṅgiriṭi alone did not perform a prostration.
Having adopted a cruel disposition, he was exceedingly arrogant with pride.
"The Great God is but one; what need have I for this woman? When he does not come to your side, then you may speak as you please. || 6 ||

"Why do you not perform worship, circumambulation, or praise? You are my devotee, dependent on me; you have been made my son by me. O Gaṇeśa, being such as you are, why indeed do you behave with such fickleness? (7)
Having heard this, Bhṛṅgiriṭi became enraged and said to you with pride: "O Pārvatī, I am not your son; I am the son of Śaṅkara. (8)
He alone is my mother and he alone is my father; thus, day and night, I go for refuge to the Supreme Lord.
O Pārvatī, you yourself are indeed established as his very refuge; if I pay homage to you, then I pay homage to all the Gaṇas.
O timid one, having heard these words of Bhṛṅgiriṭi, you, being enraged, spoke this to that lord of the Pramathas, Bhṛṅgiriṭi.
Having become my son, why do you speak such discourtesy to me? For a son, skin, flesh, blood, and entrails are derived from his mother. (12)
O Gaṇapa, the collection of nails, teeth, and bones, as well as the penis, speech, and the head, and likewise the semen—this body is indeed paternal.
Having heard this, Bhṛṅgiriṭi immediately, by the power of yoga, cast off all flesh and indeed every portion belonging to the mother.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful thighs, he—whose nails, teeth, bones, and nose were [mutilated]—formed a cruel resolve, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
"Abandoning you, he came into my presence, afflicted by grief. Then, O beloved, the attendant Bhṛṅgiriṭi was cursed by you at that time."
"Since a cruel intention was formed by you, who are of wicked mind, you shall undoubtedly go to the world of mortals. (17)
O Goddess, having been addressed thus by you, the Gaṇa Bhṛṅgiriṭi likewise fell to the world of mortals, like a meritorious man at the exhaustion of his merit.

Having gone to Puṣkaradvīpa, he whose self was purified by austerity remained there for ten padmas of years standing on one foot with his arms raised upward; indeed, the world was scorched by his difficult penance.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śakra, together with the thirty gods and we ourselves, O lady of beautiful hips, approached her presence.
Then, having approached him, I spoke before him: "Enough with this cruel asceticism that brings about the destruction of the world! (21)
While you remain thus, even the three worlds have become unconscious; therefore, withdraw this great and terrible ascetic power that torments the world.

"O son, let Pārvatī be entreated; she will grant you a boon. Through her grace, your liberation from the curse shall indeed come to pass. Having been addressed thus by him, O Maheśvarī, you were then entreated with devotion and respect by the Gaṇa Bhṛṅgiriṭi, who was bowed low in humility.
"O large-eyed one, you have been told by me: 'Go, my son, at my command; in the beautiful Mahākālavana, there you shall become Akrūra. (25)

Furthermore, you shall regain Kailāsa, which is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas; there, before Aṅkapāda, is the great Liṅga that endures through seven kalpas, by the mere sight of which auspicious wisdom arises.

Even those who are ungrateful, atheists, cruel, and betrayers of trust; those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and those who have fallen under the power of a curse—even such men enjoy heaven by the mere sight of that Liṅga.
Having adopted a cruel resolve and having slain Kaṃsa, the slayer of Keśin, accompanied by Baladeva, abandoned that city of Mathurā.
Having gone to Mahākālavana and gratified Maheśvara, he attained the state of Akrūra and acquired eternal fame. || 29 ||
Having heard your words, the attendant Bhṛṅgiriṭi then agreed, saying "So be it," and went to Mahākālavana; there he propitiated the God with difficult penance.

In the meantime, O Goddess, you arose from the middle of the Liṅga, having made half of my body your own, with one half adorned by a mass of matted hair bound by the lord of serpents and the other half adorned by a braided braid.
One half was adorned with leafy creepers and decorated with crescent moons, while the other half was bound with pearl necklaces and encircled by serpents.
Then, O Goddess, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, having witnessed that great calamity, reflected in his heart: "This was performed by me out of ignorance."
Umā and Śaṅkara indeed possess one eternal body; they are a single, indefinable form that appears divided into two. (34)
O Pārvatī, as he was thus reflecting with his mind bowed in devotion, you said to him: "I am pleased; choose a boon, my son. (35)
He said: "O Mother, O Great Goddess, if you are pleased with me, my cruel disposition has departed through the majesty of this linga. (36)
"May this deity become famous by the name Akrūreśvara. O Goddess, you are said to be the sole cause of all states of being. (37)
You are the personified accumulation of merit; you are the refuge for those who cultivate virtue. You alone are the father, the mother, the friend, and the kinsman—the supreme cause.
Make this most meritorious place, which destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, and which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, granting all desired objects. (39)
"And you then spoke with sweet words, 'So be it. O child, I shall first perform that which is most dear to you."

"O son Kanakaprabha, for your sake there is nothing difficult for me to do. However, those men who, even by chance, behold the deity named Makūreśvara in this place—even if they are devoted to sin—they too shall certainly and inevitably become Gaṇas equal to you. (41)
Those men who shall praise the name of this Liṅga with devotion, being liberated from mental sins, will go to the imperishable heaven.
That man who, having bathed according to the prescribed rules, performs worship, shall be liberated from all sins and attain the solar orb.
Indeed, longevity, health, sovereignty, and whatever desire is wished for here shall be attained; moreover, by touching [this place], a human being will obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having bathed in the Mandākinī pool, whoever worships the Lord Akūreśvara with various flowers—even if he is struck down by great sins—[is purified]. (45)
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, being sung of by Gandharvas for the duration of four kalpas, he too shall go to heaven.
Thus addressed, O Goddess, that host approached my presence; having been liberated from the curse by you, have they forgotten you, O fair-faced one? (47)
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Akrūreśvara has been recounted to you, O Goddess; now hear about the supreme Kuṇḍeśvara.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Akrūreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 39 ||
Īśvara said: Know the fortieth [tīrtha] to be Kuṇḍeśvara; hear now about it, by the mere sight of which the supreme, true goal is attained. || 1 ||
"I have been informed by you, O Goddess, on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves: 'I wish to see Vīraka; where has my dear son gone? (2)
"O large-eyed one, I said: 'In the midst of the waters within the supreme Mahākālavana, he performed an exceedingly rigorous penance. (3)
Accompanied by the sages, wise and radiant like the sun, let us go there with our attendants to see him, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Having heard my words, you then urged me: "Arise, O Śambhu, let us go; mount the bull quickly."
"O Goddess, as soon as I remembered Vīraka, my breasts became full with milk; I have remembered the eternal Bull, who is the embodiment of Dharma. (6)
Having understood my thought, he approached my side; then I mounted upon that very bull together with you.
At that very moment, he set out swiftly with various hosts of attendants; you, clinging to the shoulder of the bull, proceeded with great speed.
For I was firmly embraced by her arms, which were adorned with tinkling bracelets; and you became frightened at that time when I was pressed against her excessively.
"O large-eyed one, that bull was then dragged away by my attendants; seeing it being dragged so swiftly, she then spoke out in fear. (10)
"O Lord, I am now exhausted, terrified by this speed; therefore, O All-pervading One, I wish to rest upon the slope of this mountain. (11)
"I shall go on foot for a moment, for this great mountain is treacherous; having heard your words, 'Very well,' was spoken by me, O beloved. (12)
O lady of beautiful hips, rest for a moment at the foot of this mountain so that you may dispel your fatigue, while I depart with speed.

"We shall search for that path where your happiness lies. This Kuṇḍa, the leader of the Gaṇas, shall dwell near you; he has been appointed by me as a servant who remains under the power of your command. (14)
Having spoken thus, O Goddess, and having stationed the protector of the Gaṇas there, I ascended to the mountain peak like the sun ascending the Udaya mountain.
Then Avalokita beheld that exceedingly beautiful great mountain; on this excellent mountain, [he thought], "This is delightful, this is delightful. (16)
Ten years have passed while I was beholding this lord of mountains; then, O Goddess, you wondered, "Where has the destroyer of Tripura gone? (17)
Surely Mahādeva does not know that I am tormented by love and deprived of sexual union; having abandoned me, where does he dwell so free from fear? (18)

Though the bodiless god of love has departed somewhere with Hara, he torments me by remembering our enmity, even as he has fixed his arrows; alas, seeing me looking on and lamenting again and again. (19)
Then Kuṇḍa, the leader of the Gaṇas, perceiving your state of mind, spoke in an elevated voice: "O Goddess, do not be despondent. (20)
"Come, here is your husband; do not let your heart be troubled. Having heard these words of Kuṇḍa, O lotus-faced one, [she replied: 21.
"Afflicted by suffering, you said, 'O Kuṇḍa, I do not know Śaṅkara; where has Śiva gone, and what does he do during this long time? Show me Mahādeva! Thus was he addressed again and again. (22)
O fair-faced one, when I was not shown by him [the attendant] through that pit, then, O Goddess, I—the protector of the Gaṇas—was cursed by you in your anger. (23)
"Go to the world of mortals, because Hara has not been told [of this]. In the meantime, O Goddess, I have arrived in your presence. (24)
"O Goddess, when questioned by you, 'Where have you gone, leaving me behind? on that desolate and inaccessible mountain, I shall therefore give up my life. (25)
"O Lord, what did you do after going ahead of this mountain? Having heard your words, I have related everything exactly as it happened."
O highly fortunate lady, this mountain is most difficult to assail and is impassable from all sides; yet, for the sake of your welfare, I have surveyed a path.
"O slender-waisted lady, by which path shall we proceed with confidence? O Goddess, this group of attendants has been made despondent and distressed. (28)

"You too have said, O Mahādeva: 'The Gaṇa Kuṇḍa has been cursed by me because he did not carry out my command; yet my word is never in vain. Therefore, by my order, let him go to the auspicious Mahākālavana. (29)
Where you stand facing north, having assumed the form of Bhairava, there stands before you a Linga that always grants all desires.
By the mere sight of him, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas; indeed, that deity shall become renowned as Kuṇḍeśvara. || 31 ||
Thus addressed by you, O Goddess, he approached you again and again; then, at your command, he was sent forth with these words: "Go to Kuṇḍa by my order."
"O son, by quickly propitiating the Liṅga in Mahākālavana with haste, your fame shall become eternal throughout the three worlds. (33)
Having been addressed thus, he arrived at that very moment; seeing the eternal Liṅga before the Northern Śiva, he worshipped it with devotion.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis, as well as the yakṣas and apsarases, arrived by the thousands.
Then, at that very moment, I arrived there together with you, surrounded by my hosts; having seen the pool and Gaṇeśa, who was intent upon the worship of the Liṅga.
"O son, we have spoken with reverence of one who is devoted to meditative absorption and dhyāna; Pārvatī is pleased with you—pray for an excellent boon. (37)

"An imperishable state has been attained by you through the sight of this Liṅga. From this day forward, this deity shall become renowned on earth by the name Kuṇḍeśvara, for he always bestows all prosperity. (38)
The man who beholds Kuṇḍeśvara, who is indeed beginningless, with devotion, shall obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices; it is not otherwise.
Whoever shall worship the Liṅga Kuṇḍeśvara with devotion, for him there shall always be the entire fruit of giving and the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas). (40)
By always touching Kuṇḍeśvara, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices and a hundred agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Those who behold [the deity] in the morning with devotion, having performed their observances according to rule, will joyfully attain their desired perfections; of this there is no doubt. (42)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Kuṇḍeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear about the supreme Luṃpeśvara.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Kuṇḍeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 40 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Pārvatī, know that the forty-first Lord is renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Luṃpeśvara.
In a region crowded with hosts of barbarians, there was a lord of the earth known as Lumpādhipa, whose prowess was equal to that of Mahendra.
He had a beloved wife named Viśālā; she was endowed with the virtues of youth and possessed a beauty peerless on earth.
Desirous of battle, that king questioned the best of the twice-born.
Then it was reported by someone that there was a Sāmavedic Brahmin in the hermitage; O mighty-armed one, O best of kings, fight with him.
Then that king set forth together with thousands of Mlecchas—Tuṣāras, Barbaras, Luṃpas, Pahlavas, and likewise with packs of dogs.
Surrounded by cruel bandits and his senses agitated by anger, he then arrived at the holy hermitage of the sage Sāmagas.
The sage was honored by him with offerings such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and seats; in the meantime, the king beheld the sacrificial cow.

She suddenly made a request, but it was not granted by the sage at that time; having violently disturbed his hermitage, he carried off the sacrificial cow and destroyed the entire forest while that brahmin looked on.
Seeing the cow being driven away and the calf exceedingly distressed, the brahmin spoke these words: "O King, do not commit such a rash act! (10)
As the best of Brahmins was speaking thus, the wicked Luṃpa, overcome with anger and surrounded by wicked men, struck him with sharp arrows.
Lamenting repeatedly, "O son! O son! like one who is helpless, the king killed the Brahmin Sāmaga and went to his own home.

In the meantime, the son arrived with sacrificial fuel in his hand; seeing his father, the brahmin, then fallen under the power of death—innocent and high-souled as he was—he lamented, deeply distressed.
"By whom was this despicable deed committed against my father, who, being old and not fighting, was struck down with hundreds of sharp arrows? (14)
Having lamented thus piteously in many ways, he performed all the funeral rites for his father according to the prescribed rules.
Taking up water, he quickly cast it into the fire, burning his father; he also pronounced a most terrible curse upon that lord of Luṃpa.
"May that evil-minded and ill-behaved man by whom my father—a learned man devoted to his own duty—was slain, contract the disease of leprosy. (17)
In the meantime, O fair-faced one, King Luṃpādhīśa was afflicted by leprosy and became unable to walk.
Due to the power of a Brahmin’s curse, he became even more afflicted by his ailments; desiring death out of world-weariness, he sorrowfully gathered pieces of wood.
Then, as he was about to prepare the funeral pyre, Nārada arrived; he was indeed honored by that king who was overwhelmed with grief.
Then that Luṃpa questioned Nārada, the best of sages: "O divine sage, suddenly a disease of leprosy has come upon me; because of it I am exceedingly tormented, and it does not find any relief. (21)
Why does one increase through medicinal herbs? You ought to explain this; for there is nothing in this world or the next that is unknown to you. (22)
Having heard those words of the lord of Luṃpā, Nārada related everything regarding that most difficult-to-overcome curse of Brahmā.
Then the king, together with his wife, entreated Nārada: "O Blessed One, how shall this curse of mine, so difficult to overcome, come to an end? (24)
Thus addressed by Lumpa, O illustrious lady, the venerable sage Nārada out of compassion spoke to him and his wife.
O King, in Mahākālavana there exists a supreme liṅga that removes leprosy; it bestows all prosperity and destroys sin. (26)
And on the beautiful bank of the Śiprā, to the east of Keśavārka, go there, O lord of kings; you shall become endowed with splendor.
Thus addressed, that Luṃpa indeed arrived with great haste at the beautiful Mahākālavana, which is frequented by hosts of great sages.
Having reached that place adorned by the Śiprā river, which was like heaven itself, the king entered it with joy upon seeing the unsurpassed Liṅga.
Having bathed in the holy waters of the Śiprā, which destroy even great sins, he indeed became divine in form upon the sight of that Liṅga.
O Pārvatī, by the mere sight [of it], the king was freed from leprosy and indeed liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; he became one who had accomplished his purpose.
Having stayed there for one night, that lord of the earth, together with his wife, rendered the highest honor to the ascetics.
Then, benedictions were pronounced by those high-souled ascetics, who possessed divine knowledge, were divine themselves, and shone with the splendor of the sun and fire.
O lotus-faced one, a name was then given to that Liṅga: "Since this god, the destroyer of leprosy, was worshipped by Lumpana, he shall become famous on the surface of the earth as Lumpeśvara. (34)
Those who, having bathed in the meritorious waters of the Śiprā, worship the supreme Liṅga Lumpeśvara with devotion, shall go to the highest state.
Whatever desirable and beloved objects they shall mentally pray for, they will obtain them through the sight of the Lord of Lumbinī; of this there is no doubt.
Even one who is burdened with great sins, if he beholds the Lumpeśvara Liṅga with a concentrated mind, shall become equal to a god.
The cow-killer, the ungrateful person, the matricide, the violator of the guru’s bed, the one who practices evil deeds, as well as the brother-killer and the father-killer; || 38 ||
By beholding Lumpeśvara even once, one is liberated from all sins; when worshipped, he burns away the evil accumulated over seven lifetimes.
Having spoken thus, all the sages honored him with joy; the king, freed from the disease of leprosy, returned to his own realm.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the god Lumpeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear of the supreme Gaṅgeśvara.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Luṃpeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 41 ||

Śrī Hara said: Now hear of the forty-second deity, Gaṅgeśvara, by the mere sight of whom one obtains the fruit of all holy places (tīrthas); it is the support of the eternal, the station of Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe. || 1 ||
The goddess Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths, having issued forth from his foot, entered the nectar-source, Soma, the receptacle of the waters.
Then, purified by contact with the rays of the increasing sun, she fell upon the summit of Mount Meru and there divided into four streams.
Falling from the edge of the slopes of Mount Meru’s peak, that illustrious river, her waters scattering, fell down without any support.
Flowing with its waters evenly distributed among the Mandara and other mountains, it became known there as the Sītā and proceeded toward the Caitraratha forest.
And having flowed away from that, she went to Aruṇoda, the best of rivers.
In the same way, on the southern side of Gandhamādana, there is the one called Alakanandā; having reached the forest at the foot of Meru, she flows into the Nandana grove, which delights the gods.
Having flooded Lake Mānasa with her great force, she then went to the beautiful mountain-king Triśikhara.
And from that [place], O beloved, all the mountains were flooded at that very moment; having flooded them, she reached the great mountain Himavat.
O Pārvatī, when Gaṅgā was held by me right there within my mass of matted hair and was not released, she then became enraged with me.
She caused my limbs to overflow, O lady of beautiful countenance; and I, O illustrious one, restrained her in anger within the midst of my matted locks.
There she performed austerities for many hundreds of kalpas; indeed, I was propitiated by Bhagīratha through fasts and hymns of praise.
Then, O Goddess, the Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, was released by me; having reached Mahākāla after flooding the Northern Kurus. (13)
The Ocean’s queen was born, dearer to him than his own life; Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, was then wedded by the Ocean. Together with her, the Ocean, the lord of rivers, took his delight. || 14 ||
Then, on one occasion, the gods were worshipping Brahmā; likewise, O Goddess, the Ocean went to the eternal world of Brahmā together with Gaṅgā for the sake of a vision during that great festival.
Then Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, approached the Grandfather; her garment, bright as the moon, was blown upward by the wind.
Then the hosts of gods suddenly cast their faces downward; but the royal sage Mahābhiṣa, free from fear, beheld the river.
Then, having understood his disposition, he was rebuked by Brahmā and told: "Having been born among mortals, you shall regain the higher worlds once again."
Then, O illustrious lady, the enraged Ocean cursed Gaṅgā: "Since you have become attached to another, forsaking me, therefore you shall go to the human world. (19)
"In that world of short lifespan, you, being miserable, shall experience suffering. Having heard that terrible curse, Gaṅgā spoke these words: || 20 ||
Why indeed was I cursed in the assembly of the gods despite being innocent, for I am devoted to my husband, my very life is my husband, and in the ultimate sense, I am one with my husband? (21)
But because her garment was blown away by the all-pervading wind through negligence, Brahmā then replied to that river, the purifier of the world: 22.
"O Great River, O Goddess, because you were cursed for the sake of the Vasus by the Ocean regarding a destined matter, therefore go now quickly. (23)
In the delightful Mahākālavana, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, there exists an excellent Liṅga on the southern bank of the Śiprā.
He brings about all accomplishments, is meritorious, and destroys all sins; propitiate him with diligence, and he will grant you what you desire.

Having heard the words of her grandfather, the river that flows through the three paths was pleased and said: "Going there is my desired wish, since my friend Śiprā is also dear to me—she who is meritorious and the destroyer of great sins."
Having thus reflected in her mind, the divine celestial river then arrived at Mahākāla and beheld the supreme liṅga.
Then she worshipped her with divine milk according to the prescribed rite; having seen her friend Śiprā there, the two of them embraced one another.

From that time forward, she became known as Śiprā, flowing toward the east. The god Gaṅgeśvara himself became renowned throughout the three worlds, for he was propitiated by Gaṅgā and grants the fruits of one's desires.
Then Gaṅgā, the river of the gods, was joyfully praised by the celestial Gandharvas, as well as by the Vālakhilya ṛṣis and other sages.
The ocean arrived there, and that great river was honored; then Gaṅgā was told by the Liṅga, "Stay here with a portion of yourself."
In that vicinity, as long as the earth remains, it shall be a place of great merit; and the ocean has accepted [the proposal], saying, "So be it, exactly as you have said."
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā departed, yet she remained there in a portion of herself; O beloved, he who, having bathed in the waters of the Śiprā, beholds Gaṅgeśvara—
For him, the fruit of giving a thousand cows arises; there is no doubt in this. He likewise obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as the fruit of all dharmas.
O Goddess, one indeed obtains continuously and perfectly the fruit of all sacrifices, as well as the fruit of all gifts and the fruit of all yogas. (35)
In that regard, O fortunate lady, whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) there are on earth—Dharmāraṇya, Phalgutīrtha, Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and Gayā—[are all present here].
Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Kedāra, Amareśvara, the Candrabhāgā, the Vipāśā, the Sarayū, the Devikā, and the Kuhū; (37)
The Godāvarī, the Śatadru, the Bāhudā, and the Vetravatī—all these rivers are indeed joined here with the Gaṅgā. (38)
Indeed, O Pārvatī, all the hidden holy fords (puṇyatīrtha) and fields of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra) abide there in their entirety, yet as mere fractions [of their original power]. 39.

He who beholds these with a concentrated mind obtains their fruit; having bathed, he beholds the god Gaṅgeśvara—this which I have spoken is the truth. Therefore, O Goddess worshipped by the Gaṇas, this place is proclaimed as the most meritorious.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Gaṅgeśvara has been told to you; now hear about the supreme Aṅgāreśvara.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gaṅgeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Śiva said: O Daughter of the Mountain, know that the forty-third [tirtha] is that by the mere sight of which all forms of prosperity arise. (1)

In the first kalpa, O fair-faced one, he was born of old from my body as Vakrāṅga, with a reddish complexion, fierce and resembling glowing embers; held by me upon the earth, he became renowned as Bhūmiputraka (the Son of the Earth).
As soon as that son of massive body and terrifying aspect was born, the goddess Earth trembled, and the gods, including Indra, were struck with fear.
The oceans were agitated and the mountains shook; everything, including the gods, asuras, and humans, was oppressed by that very [force].
O beloved, the Vālakhilya sages and the gods led by Śakra, placing Bṛhaspati at their head, went to the world of Brahmā.
Having prostrated before the Grandfather (Brahmā), they spoke with heavy sighs, recounting in full detail the entire account of the destruction of the three worlds.
By him alone, born from the body of Hara, as soon as he was born, the three worlds were effortlessly overwhelmed, oppressed, and likewise devoured.
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, reflected together with them and came into my presence.
When they were all questioned by me, "For what reason are you overwhelmed by fear? Why are your hearts filled with gasping breaths? From whence has this dread come upon you? (9)

O Goddess, overwhelmed by fear, they all related everything before me: "O God of gods, O Lord of the world, [this world], including the gods, asuras, and humans, has been tormented and even devoured by that which was born from your own body. (10)
Having heard these words of theirs, that best of speakers, being summoned by me out of compassion for their welfare, came into my presence and spoke.
"O Lord, let an order be given; what shall I do? he asked. "Do not drag this world [into existence]," I told him again and again. (12)
"Since you were born from the dust of my body, you are called Aṅgāraka; for the constant welfare of the worlds, you have been made Maṅgala by me. (13)

"This child has been given by Gaurī and presented before you by the Queen, who desires her husband's welfare and was urged by the minister's request. (46)
Having heard what the queen said, she placed the infant, who possessed the luster of the young moon, before Vikaṭā and returned home.
Then that goddess Vikaṭā, having summoned the yoginīs, said: "Quickly take this infant before the assembly of Mothers."
"Carry out their command and protect him with great effort! At these words of Vikaṭā, the Yoginīs and Khecarīs [protected] him at that very moment.
Brāhmī and the other Mothers traveled by way of the sky to where that child, radiant as the sun, was; having bowed down to the assembly of Yoginīs, they [approached] him.
Placing it before the Mothers, they spoke the words uttered by Vikaṭa: "Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhikā, Kaumārī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā. (51)
Then, having seen that beautiful boy sent by Vikaṭā, they simultaneously asked these words: "O boy, who is your leader? (52)
When he was questioned by the Mothers with the words "And by the Mothers," and he said nothing at all, then the host of Mothers spoke to the circle of Yoginīs.
"This one, marked with the great signs, is fit for kingship; O Yoginīs, he must be led back to that very place without delay. (54)
The great goddess Pañcamudrā dwells there, bestowing all desires; by serving her, the glory of nirvāṇa is not far off for men. (55)
For this child, who has been dwelling in that sacred seat for sixteen years, supreme perfection shall come to pass through the supreme grace of Rudra.
Thus, by the word of the Mother, he was immediately brought back to the presence of the five mudrās in an instant by the yoginīs from the assembly of Mothers.
Having reached that great seat (pīṭha) and come here from the heavenly world, he performed extensive penance in the meritorious Mahākālavana.
Through his exceedingly intense austerity, with his senses and mind perfectly steady, Umādhava became pleased with that prince.
Śaṅkara appeared before him in the form of a Liṅga and said, "I am pleased; choose a boon, O prince. (160)
He himself beheld before him a Linga composed of all light, which had arisen from its great grace, piercing through the seven netherworlds.

Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground, he praised Dhūrjaṭi with hymns composed through practice in previous births, being well-pleased by the deities devoted to Rudra; and with the hair on his body standing on end from joy, he prayed for a boon.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, if a boon is to be granted to me, then you should remain here forever, removing the affliction of worldly existence.
O Śambhu, residing in this liṅga, fulfill the desire of your devotee, even without the performance of mudrās and the like, and even without mantras, O All-pervading Lord.
"Those who are devotees of this Liṅga through their actions of mind, speech, and body—upon them you must always bestow grace; this is my boon. (65)
Having heard that boon, the Lord in the form of the Liṅga said: "O hero, let it be as it has been spoken by you, the son of a Vaiṣṇava. (66)
"O Hero, I shall bestow upon my devotees in Avanti this Liṅga named Vīreśvara, after your own name, which shall indeed grant all their desires. (67)
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, muttered in prayer, praised, or worshipped here becomes inexhaustible for the devotees; of this there is no doubt. || 68 ||
But you, having attained a supreme kingdom difficult for all other monarchs to obtain, and having enjoyed vast pleasures, shall attain perfection in the end.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Vīreśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now listen to that of Nūpureśa.
The illustrious God of Gods said: Know that there is one more than seven, known by the name Nūpureśvara, by the mere sight of whom all perfections (siddhis) are attained. || 1 ||
Formerly, in the Rathantara Kalpa, there was indeed a group named Nūpura; they were eternally devoted to Rudra and adorned with the five mudrās.
Once, having arrived at the assembly hall of Kubera, he remained there to witness the great festival performed by the Apsarases.
And other women danced there, for Urvashi, the best among women, as well as Rambha, Tilottama, and Mena, danced filled with joy.
Then, having witnessed their dance, the leader of the Gaṇas, truly afflicted by the arrows of Kāma, began to dance in their midst.
Then, dancing with joy and tormented by the arrows of love, he struck Urvaśī on the chest with a cluster of flowers.
Then Urvaśī, having been struck with a cluster of flowers, became enraged and went for refuge to the god Dhanada, the granter of all desires.
There, Dhanada spoke, his mind agitated by anger.
"Since you, afflicted by lust, have indeed caused the destruction of the stage, therefore, O sinful man, fall into the world of mortals!"
And due to the curse of Kubera, he descended to the surface of the earth; afflicted by great sorrow, he lamented: "What has been done by me, a sinner? (10)
Having lamented most bitterly, O Goddess, he then went mentally for refuge to you, the Supreme Sovereign and bestower of boons. 11.
Then the Supreme Goddess, having become manifest and being pleased, spoke with affection to the Lord of the Gaṇas, who was bowed in devotion upon the earth.
"Go, my son, at my command to the auspicious Mahākālavana; there exists the Prācīsarasvatī in the form of a pond. (13)
To its south, my son, there exists a supreme Liṅga; having bathed in the pond, worship that Liṅga with devotion. (14)
"She shall be known as Prācī, and that Lord of Gods shall become famous by your name. Having been addressed thus, O Goddess, Nūpura went to Mahākālavana.
"O Goddess, impelled by you, go there for the sake of fame. Thus addressed, the divine Nūpura, being delighted, joined his palms in reverence. (16)
He beheld there that beautiful Mahākālavana, frequented by gods and Gandharvas, and within it, that Linga served by gods and Gandharvas. || 17 ||
There, the eastern Sarasvatī stands in the form of a pond; having bathed in it, Nūpura then worshipped the Lord.
Then the God, with a gracious soul, replied to Nūpura: "Excellent, Nūpura! May it be well with you; may you attain prosperity at all times. (19)
"He shall become the beloved of the goddess Pārvatī and of Śaṅkara. Having been addressed thus by that Liṅga, O dear one, Nūpura [attained his goal] at that very moment.
Resembling the risen sun and possessing a splendor equal to fire, he was born as a mass of radiance, difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to behold.
O lady of beautiful countenance, having witnessed such power, the gods said: "Oh, the majesty of the Liṅga! Behold this wonder upon the earth! (22)
And through the sight of the Nūpura, the desired perfection (siddhi) was attained; therefore, from this day forward, the Lord became renowned upon the earth.
He who is known by the name Nūpureśvara is the eternal bestower of all desires; those who, having bathed in the pond, shall behold him with concentrated minds [shall obtain their wishes].
Those who shall perform worship endowed with a spirit of devotion to Nūpureśvara Rudra go to the supreme state; they all dwell in joy until the dissolution of all beings.
Birth, death, old age, disease, and various other miseries immediately go to their dissolution when Nūpureśvara is worshipped.

O lady of auspicious eyes, that pond is indeed equal to the Gaṅgā; O lady of virtuous vows, born from the body of the lord of mountains, know this to be Prayāga, where the confluence of the Vitastā and the Yamunā occurs. (27)
O Goddess, Somatīrtha is then the destroyer of all sins; by bathing there, O Goddess, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 28 ||
And he who, having bathed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, worships Nūpureśvara, shall indeed deliver a hundred ancestors on both his mother’s and father’s side.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the deity Nūpureśvara has been recounted to you; now hear about Abhayeśvara.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Nūpureśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 47.
Śrī Rudra said: O beloved, know that the forty-eighth [chapter] is that by the mere sight of which there shall be no fear of rebirth.

At the conclusion of the first Kalpa, O lotus-eyed one, during the Pādma Kalpa, when the moon, sun, and stars had perished, and the earth and heaven had vanished, Brahmā indeed reflected: "How shall creation come to be? (2)
Then, from the two eyes of that great-souled one, whose form was thus agitated, a thick drop of tears fell from his left eye.
From that drop of tear was born the Dānava named Hārava, who had sharp fangs, a massive body, and a luster like a heap of crushed collyrium.
Born from the leading forth of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he became renowned as Kālakeli; his body was black, exceedingly tall, with large fangs and hair standing erect.
With a terrifying face, wicked, resembling Yama and difficult to approach, he had the appearance of a heap of black collyrium, held a noose in his hand, and was fearsome.
Then those two Daityas, having come together and made their agreement, rushed forward in a state of excitement, desiring to kill Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, overcome with fear and fleeing in all directions, wandered about; there, in the exceedingly deep water, he beheld Him of immeasurable luster.

Beholding that Person clad in yellow garments and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, Brahmā then fell into a state of supreme terror and said: "Who are you that lie here while this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been destroyed?"
Then Viṣṇu said to him: "I alone am thus the father of the universe, the creator of the world, the destroyer of the world, and the ordainer of the world's maintenance. (10)
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds, the lotus-born Brahmā then replied: "I am the creator in the three worlds. (11)
"The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, has been created by me. In the meantime, those two Daityas, arrogant in their strength, arrived there.
Seeing the two of them desiring food and overcome by hunger, Brahmā, his sprout-like lower lip trembling, spoke this to Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals. (13)
If you are said to be some cause for this world, then you ought to slay those two terrible asuras now.
Having heard that, Viṣṇu then understood their mutual distress and said: "Rest for a moment; afterwards, there shall be a duel."
Having spoken thus and made their pact, those two Daityas, arrogant in their strength, rushed forward with great haste to slay Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, seeing those two Dānavas invincible in battle, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were overcome with terror, drenched in sweat and trembling.
They spoke to one another words appropriate to the place and time: "What indeed should be done? What task should belong to me or to you? (18)
"A terrible danger has arisen; what is to be done by us two in this situation? Seeing that death was imminent, Brahmā spoke to Keśava. (19)

"Go quickly, O Kṛṣṇa, to the supreme Mahākālavana, which is said to be imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution; there protection will be found. I shall go there; you too, O Keśava, go there. (20)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa indeed went along with him; they both reached Mahākālavana, yet Maheśvara was not seen there either, as they wandered for a period of ten thousand years.
Then, having seen that divine linga made of flames to the south of Nūpureśvara, Brahmā and Viṣṇu themselves requested the Lord: "O Master, grant us freedom from fear."
"O Lord of Gods, become our refuge; we are tormented by the two Dānavas. Then, O Pārvatī, protection from fear was granted by that Liṅga.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) heard the roar of those two Dānavas; trembling with fear, he addressed the Lord who supports the trembling Liṅga.
"O beloved, this very Death, bringing terror, is approaching us swiftly; 'Let fearlessness be granted,' O Goddess—this was said by Kṛṣṇa at that time. (25)
Having heard the words of Brahmā and Keśava, who were afflicted by fear, those two gods were placed within his belly by him in that form.
By those two, the entire world was seen, including the sun, the moon, and the mountains; together with the hosts of Siddhas and Gandharvas, and filled with rocks, palm trees, and creepers.
O Goddess, it is joined with the ocean as its pedestal, resplendent with various castes and stages of life, together with the subterranean realm (Pātāla), and possessing serpents and great trees.
Together with the arrangement of the seven worlds and including the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, those two emerged again from that belly, filled with wonder.
O Pārvatī, seeing the two Daityas reduced to ashes by that Liṅga, they, filled with supreme devotion, praised the Supreme Liṅga.
The Linga, being pleased, said: "What shall I give to you both? O gods, this vision of me is unfailing and exceedingly difficult to obtain. (31)
Then Brahmā and Viṣṇu requested a boon: "If a boon is to be granted to us, then become the bestower of fearlessness upon men. (32)
And for those who shall worship you and sacrifice to you with concentrated minds, and who shall constantly remember you—you shall be the giver of fearlessness to them. (33)
"You shall become renowned on earth by the name Abhayeśvara; those who behold you with devotion shall have their purposes fulfilled. (34)
There shall be no fear whatsoever, nor likewise any falling into saṃsāra; there shall be no separation from wealth, sons, or wife. (35)
A woman who is suffering and unfortunate, whoever shall behold [it], will undoubtedly become endowed with good fortune and happiness; and a pregnant maiden shall obtain a handsome husband. (36)
Whatever desire men contemplate while beholding you, they shall attain every such wish; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Having said, "It shall be so," O Supreme Goddess, the two gods Brahmā and Viṣṇu were dismissed by the Liṅga and departed for their own abodes.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Abhayeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now let the account of Pṛthukeśvara be heard.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Abhayeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Listen to [the account of] Pṛthukeśvara, the forty-ninth lord of gods, by the mere sight of whom a man becomes a sovereign ruler of the whole earth. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in the lineage of Svāyambhuva there was indeed a king named Aṅga; he married Mṛtyu’s daughter, Sudurmukhā.
A son named Vena was born, an atheist and a defiler of the Dharma; he was a stealer of the property of gods and Brahmins, and a ravisher of others' wives. || 3 ||
O Goddess, having been cursed by the twice-born, he met his death at that very moment; and from the churning of his thighs, the Mleccha tribes fell forth.

Born from a portion of his mother’s body, he possessed the luster of a mass of black collyrium; born from a portion of his father’s body, he was righteous according to the best of the twice-born. Pṛthu, of celebrated valor, was produced from the right hand after it had been churned.
Having been consecrated by the brahmins and having performed most difficult austerities, that king attained sovereignty through the great boon of Viṣṇu.
Seeing his subjects deprived of Vedic study, devoid of the *vaṣaṭ* call, and destitute of wealth, crying out in distress, the king then became sorrowful.
He desired to milk the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
In the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived; seeing Pṛthu overcome with anger, he spoke these words: || 9 ||

O King, do not give way to anger that would lead to the destruction of the three worlds; know this to be my view: that various crops have been swallowed by this earth, and all food has been devoured. (10)
Then, at the words of Nārada, Pṛthu became enraged; he desired to burn the earth along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
He discharged the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra), by which the earth was then scorched; afflicted by fear, she assumed the form of a cow and approached Pṛthu.
Being struck by him, she spoke these words to the king: "O best of kings, I am a cow who has come to you for refuge. (13)
O protector of the earth, out of reverence, make me your calf and milk me.
Having heard those words of hers, that best of kings milked her, making the Himalaya the calf and [yielding] radiant jewels and crops. (15)
The subjects born were fair-faced, and a great festival commenced; rites such as sacrifices and gifts began, preceded by auspicious ceremonies.
Then the king reflected: "I have committed this sin; for it is said that women are not to be slain, nor is a cow, nor likewise a twice-born man. (17)

"Under the delusion that this Earth had assumed the form of a woman, she was slain by me; and now the thought of killing a cow has arisen—alas, what a succession of sins! Therefore, having prepared a funeral pyre, I shall enter the fire without a doubt. (16)
While Pṛthu of immeasurable splendor was reflecting thus, the venerable sage Nārada arrived there once again.
O beloved, seeing Pṛthu thus dejected and lost in thought, the wise Nārada said, "O King, what is this? (20)
Then he said: "O Brahmin, this sin has been committed by me; a woman who should not be slain was killed, and my mind was set upon the slaughter of a cow. (21)
"To what worlds shall I go after having committed such a most dreadful deed? I shall die, there is no doubt; I am a slayer of a Brahmin, a man of sin. (22)

"O twice-born one, rescue me from this suffering by instructing me in my duty. Having heard those words of his, Nārada recounted the supreme majesty of the Liṅga, which pacifies even the greatest of sins.
O King, in Mahākālavana, to the west of Abhayeśvara, there exists a Liṅga that destroys great sins; go there immediately, O King, and you shall become purified. || 24 ||
Having heard the words of Nārada, Pṛthu went there; and upon seeing the beautiful Liṅga, he became free from sin at that very moment.
The lord of the earth became resplendent like twelve suns.

Then, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, a name was bestowed upon him by those dwelling in the intermediate space: "Since he shall be worshipped by Pṛthu on the surface of the earth, from this day forward this deity shall be renowned as Pṛthukeśvara. (27)
And those who shall behold the Lord of Gods, the Lord Pṛthukeśvara, they shall have all their desires fulfilled upon the surface of the earth.
Whatever sin arises for men, whether through ignorance or even through knowledge, that sin shall quickly perish by the sight of Pṛthukeśvara. (29)

Whether verbal, mental, or physical, whether arising from secrecy or committed openly, whatever sin has been committed even through association—all that shall quickly perish by the sight of Puthukeśvara. (30)
Those who worship the god Pṛthukeśvara with devotion shall properly attain sovereignty both in the world of men and in heaven.
Having enjoyed sovereignty over humans and gods upon the earth, they shall go to the supreme abode of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Having spoken thus, Pṛthukeśvara was honored by the hosts of gods; Pṛthu then ruled the earth with its cities and its mountains.
This power of the god Pṛthukeśvara, which destroys sins, has been recounted to you, O Goddess; now hear indeed of Sthāvareśvara.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Pṛthukeśvara," within the Greatness of the Eighty-four Liṅgas, in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 49 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Listen attentively, O Goddess, to the fifty-first Lord, by the mere sight of whom the affliction of planetary influences does not arise. || 1 ||
Saṃjñā, the daughter of Viśvakarman, was the wife of Ravi (the Sun). Being unable to endure her husband’s splendor, Saṃjñā once quickly created a shadow-form of herself.
She was told with great respect: "Stay right here in the presence of the Sun; even when questioned, you must not speak of my departure for the Sun. (3)
Having spoken thus, Saṃjñā then departed for her father’s abode; meanwhile, the Lord of the Day, thinking that this second woman was indeed Saṃjñā, begot a son who was named Śanaiścara.
When he was born, fear seized the gods, asuras, and humans alike; as soon as he was born, the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, were overwhelmed.
Indra too, terrified with fear, went for refuge to Brahmā and, with a faltering voice, related the account of the son of the Sun.
The wheel of Rohiṇī was shattered and the circle of constellations pervaded; as soon as he was born, the three worlds were overwhelmed by the son of the Sun.
Having heard the words of Vāsava, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, suddenly summoned Sūrya and spoke these words: ||| 8 ||
"O Bhānu, let a boundary be established; let this legitimate son of yours be restrained. The three worlds, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ, have been overwhelmed by his splendor."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Ravi spoke thus: "This son of mine is incurable; let him be restrained by you yourself."
Behold my two feet, burnt by you with ease through a mere glance; even Brahmā, terrified with fear, went to Hari in his mind.
Having heard the words of Sūrya, Hari arrived at that very moment; and having heard the words of Brahmā, the frightened Kṛṣṇa spoke this.
"Go to where Maheśvara, the God of gods, resides. At Kṛṣṇa's word, they all came into my presence. (13)
O Pārvatī, the entire account of the son of the Sun was related by me; and as soon as it was remembered, the son of the Sun arrived at that very moment.
I saw one with downcast eyes, crooked-limbed and dark in appearance; having steadied myself and offered salutations, I addressed him very slowly. (15)
"For what purpose have I been remembered, O God? Grant me your command, Śaṅkara! I abide by your instruction; tell me, what shall I do? Command me. (16)
O Pārvatī, having been addressed thus by that son of the Sun at that time, I strictly restrained him, saying, "Do not afflict the three worlds."
He said, "Give me a place, as well as drink and food. O large-eyed lady, I gave him an excellent place for the sake of worship. (18)
O child, residing in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, afflict human beings for thirty months in succession; therein you shall attain satisfaction.
The eighth, the fourth, and the second house situated from birth—even if located in the twelfth house—shall always be unfavorable for you. (20)
Whether he be the eleventh, the sixth, or one who has reached the third stage, he will become most worthy of honor among men; therefore, worship shall be performed for him. || 21 ||
The fifth and the ninth are indeed neutral, while the seventh is always situated in the state of becoming (bhava) for a human being engaged in karmic activities.
You shall receive exceedingly great worship from the planets at all times; your course shall become stable, and you are declared to be the most excellent of those who receive boons.
Therefore, you shall be known as Sthāvara on the surface of the earth, because you, Śanaiścara, are superior among the planets by virtue of being situated in a zodiacal sign (rāśi).
Therefore, you shall forever be known on earth by the name Śanaiścara; your form will resemble the temple of an elephant's cheek, and you shall be equal to my own throat.

For by color you shall indeed be named Asita on the surface of the earth; among the planets, your gaze shall be downward and your motion slow. When pleased, you grant a kingdom; when enraged, you indeed take it away in an instant.
Gods, asuras, and humans, as well as siddhas, vidyādharas, and serpents—struck by your fierce gaze, they shall go to their destruction; it cannot be otherwise.
"By your grace, they shall attain their heart's desire, which is otherwise very difficult to obtain; furthermore, I shall grant you another secret and enchanting place. (28)
The supreme Mahākālavana is said to fulfill the heart's desires, to be meritorious, difficult even for gods and dānavas to attain, and imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution. 29.
Go there at my command, to the west of Pṛthukeśvara; whatever liṅga exists there shall be known by your name.
This fame of yours, moreover, will surely endure throughout the three worlds.
Thus addressed, O Goddess, Sthāvara, the observer of my command, then went swiftly to the beautiful and auspicious Mahākālavana. 32.
Having seen that very liṅga right there, he obtained a most beautiful location; that liṅga became famous in the world by the name Sthāvareśvara.
Then, O Goddess, Śani said: "Those who here, with devotion, behold this Linga known as Sthāvareśvara, which has been worshipped by me—for them, my affliction shall never arise."
And whoever beholds me on my day according to the prescribed rule, I shall undoubtedly pacify all of his afflictions. (35)
I shall constantly burn away the suffering caused even by other planets; and for him, there shall be no fear of me, even in a dream. (36)
Neither the grahas, nor the piśācas, nor the yakṣas, nor the rākṣasas can cause obstacles for him when I am pleased; of this there is no doubt. (37)

On the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on Saturdays, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise during the solstices (ayana), those men who behold the Sthāvareśvara Liṅga with devotion shall attain imperishable and eternal residence in heaven.
Those men who regularly observe my vow here do not possess any evil deed, nor do they suffer any calamities arising from evil deeds. (39)
There shall be neither poverty nor separation from loved ones; for one desiring a son, I shall always grant the fruit produced by a son.
I bestow wealth upon the destitute, as well as fearlessness upon those afflicted by fear; and for one who desires heaven, I grant heaven and whatever else is desired. (41)
Having spoken thus, Śanaiścara worshipped the Liṅga once more; having worshipped it with auspicious flowers, he remained right there with devotion.
This power of the god Sthāvareśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now listen to [the account of] Śūleśvara.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Sthāvareśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 50 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, know that the fifty-first Lord is the deity Śūleśvara, who destroys all diseases.

O fair-faced one, when the first aeon had begun for the sake of sovereignty, there was a most terrible war between the gods and the dānavas, while Jambha was the lord of the Daityas and Śacīpati was the lord of the gods.
Thereupon the gods were defeated and the Daityas became victorious; then Andhaka reached Mount Mandara and dispatched a messenger to me.
That messenger, evil-minded and full of pride, spoke loudly to me: "O Śaṅkara, listen to my words; I have been commanded by Andhaka."
"Give me Gaurī for the sake of a wife; let this Mandara mountain be abandoned. If this is done, you will have achieved your purpose; otherwise, there is no other way for you. (5)
I was addressed by that messenger on the great mountain along with you; having smiled for a moment, I spoke these words.
"Go, messenger, by my command, and speak quickly to Andhaka: 'Come here, engage in battle, and having conquered her, take this Sundarī away.'"
Thus addressed, the messenger departed, conveying my words to him. Then the Daitya Andhaka, seeking battle, arrived at Mandara accompanied by his ministers and a fourfold army.
Then, a fierce battle took place between him and me for a long time; subsequently, Andhaka’s formidable chariot was shattered and split asunder.
