Then, O Goddess, the enraged Andhaka leaped down from that chariot; seizing my chariot with great force, that powerful and mighty Daitya fought with me, though he was struck by me with a trident.
That great asura, impaled upon my trident, was held by me in the mid-air; while he remained thus impaled on the trident, that wicked one was whirled around by me.
Then a great flood of blood flowed from his limbs; for every single drop of blood, there appeared a Dānava equal to it.
O Goddess, they arose by the millions, and I was again afflicted by them; O beautiful lady, I remained there reflecting, "What should be done? (13)
And by me was created Durgā, red-toothed and most terrifying; then, by her, the blood of Andhaka was drunk in great variety.

When that [liquid] was drunk—first the yellow and then the red—the other goddesses did not rise; rather, those lords of the Dānavas who had previously risen were swiftly struck down by her with that very same excellent trident, meeting their destruction at that very moment.
With a joyful heart and palms joined in reverence, Andhaka said to me: "May I always have devotion toward you; for a vision of you is difficult to obtain. (16)
"I have been struck down by my own master; who indeed is more blessed than I? For I have been pierced through the chest by your spear even from the sky. (17)
I go for refuge to you, who cause the projection and distraction of volitional constructs, who set in motion the activities of the world-ages, and who possess a thousand faces and heads. 18.
I go for refuge to you, the Lord of the daughter of the mountain king, whose abode is on the peak of the mountain king, and who has made Mahālaya your dwelling place.
O beautiful one, when I was thus praised by the Daitya who had been impaled on the trident, compassion arose within me, and then Andhaka was made a Gaṇa.
And that excellent trident, O Goddess, was then joyfully addressed by me: "Come, O Trident! The wicked Daitya Andhaka has been slain by you in battle."
Being well-pleased, I grant you the supreme, most excellent station, which is not attained by the gods, nor by the Gandharvas, nor even by the great seers.
"Thus, even by those whose sins have been destroyed, I am attainable only after they have worshipped me. Then Śūla, having bowed with his neck bent low, spoke to me.
If you are pleased, O Blessed One, and if you have compassion for me, then tell me of that supreme state wherein my mind may be purified from the other sin born of association with the wicked. (24)
Then, with a heart embraced by compassion, I instructed him [to go] to the delightful Mahākālavana, which bestows exceedingly meritorious fruits. (25)
In that place is this Liṅga, which brings us [the fruit of] attainment and bestows grace upon the world; worship it with diligence to the east of Pṛthukeśvara.
Having heard my words, he departed with haste; there he beheld that Liṅga, which bestows manifold fruits.
Furthermore, the trident beloved of Śaṅkara was seen by him in its embodied form; having manifested with many faces, it filled his mind with wonder and joy.
Embraced by him with great affection, he was asked again about his welfare; then, while suffering from a sharp pain, he recounted the slaying of the wicked Andhaka.

Strongly impelled by my Lord for the sake of your purification, I shall go into the presence of Śiva, purified by the sight of you. From this day forward, you shall attain fame in the world of mortals by my name.
Therefore, because of the sight of you, there will be even more; I choose this. What is the use of bathing in various sacred fords, or what is the use of performing various acts of charity? (31)
Those who shall behold you with devotion will obtain every fruit.
Any person who, endowed with devotion, shall perform worship for you on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, or on a Tuesday, with great reverence; || 33 ||
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot that moves at will, adorned with jewels, and resembling the rising sun, he shall wander about in joy.
Those who, constantly afflicted by fear, perpetually tormented by diseases, or intensely distressed by miseries, shall utter your name—they shall have no fear in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. (35)
But those men who, even by chance, shall behold you devoid of worldly attachment, they shall not fall into saṃsāra nor into the most dreadful hell.
Having spoken thus, he diligently embraced the Liṅga with that trident.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Śūleśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Oṃkāreśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śūleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" of the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Viśveśvara said: O Goddess, know that the fifty-second Lord is named Oṃkāreśvara, whose fame exists throughout the three worlds.
O Goddess, in the first eon known as Prākṛta, I first produced from my mouth a person of tawny (kapila) appearance.
Then that divine person appeared, asking, "What shall I do? When told by me, "Divide yourself," he vanished from sight.
Like that of a lamp extinguished in nirvāṇa, his destination was not perceived; therefore, the thought arose in him: "How is the self to be analyzed? (4)
As he was thinking thus, there arose from it a four-faced being, possessing the form of the three letters and sounds, and bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life.
Known by the names of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and consisting of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, he then pervaded all the worlds with his vast powers.
"Oṃkāra"—this was the name bestowed upon him by me out of grace; and thus he was adorned with those noble words spoken at that time.
From the heart of that God, the Vaṣaṭkāra arose—the supreme Goddess of the meters, consisting of twenty-four syllables. || 8 ||
She has six bellies, three feet, and is characterized by five heads; the goddess standing nearby is situated there at her side.
Gāyatrī is sweet-spoken, and Sāvitrī is world-renowned; that Oṃkāra has been proclaimed by me along with Gāyatrī, O Pārvatī. By my command, perform a manifold creation together with her.
Thus addressed, he became three-peaked and assumed a form resembling gold; by my command, he brought forth creation from his own body.
Formerly, the hosts of gods, the thirty-three deities, as well as humans and sages, were established through the authority of the Vedas.
For those who have entered their bodies, there shall be a recurring manifestation, just as the sun is constantly subject to rising and setting. || 13 ||

Having withdrawn all the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and pannagas, into himself by means of the syllable Om, the Blessed Lord Oṃkāra became the master of the universe, with the entire world contained within his own womb.
O Daughter of the Mountain, at the end of the kalpa, he who is unmanifest and eternal emitted all beings; this entire world belongs to him.
He who is indeed the creator, the transformer, and the great destroyer; the Vedas are preceded by Om, and sacrifices are preceded by Om.
Knowledge is preceded by the syllable Oṃ, and austerity is preceded by the syllable Oṃ; he who is known as the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū) is that Brahmā, the lord of the worlds. (17)
He is to be known as Vāyu; he is the omniscient creator of progeny. Likewise, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the two Aśvins [are he]. || 18 ||
The lords of progeny, the seven great seers, the Vasus, the Apsarases, the Gandharvas, and the Rākṣasas; || 19 ||

Then the Daityas, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and various Bhūtas; the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and others on earth; and all four-footed creatures belonging to the animal kingdom—[all these were present]. 20.
Having brought all mobile beings and whatever else is designated as living, in its entirety and without exception, he has come into my presence.
Having bowed down and become composed, he spoke these words: "O God, O Maheśvara, by your grace, the creation has been accomplished by me. (22)
"Grant me the supreme station so that my fame may become eternal. Having heard the words of Oṃkāra, I replied, O fair-faced one: || 23 ||
This divine Mahākālavana is my beloved place; it is eternal, immutable, imperishable, auspicious, and the source of all prosperity.
There your fame shall be eternal; of this there is no doubt. It is situated to the east of the god Śūleśvara.
This Liṅga, originating from the three kalpas, shall attain fame by your name; it shall be known as Oṃkāreśvara throughout the three worlds.
O Goddess, having been addressed thus by me, Oṃkāra, with a joyful mind, beheld that liṅga there and became absorbed into that liṅga.
From that time forward, the twice-born utter the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning of all things in the Vedas for the sake of merit and for the sake of auspiciousness. (28)
O Pārvatī, ever since the syllable Om entered into dissolution, listen to the extraordinary power of the Liṅga as it is being described by me. (29)
O Goddess, whatever merit is proclaimed to be gained during thousands of Yugas, hundreds of Vyatipātas, and thousands of solstices—that merit is surpassed by the sight of Oṃkāreśvara. (30)
Whatever fruit is obtained from studying all four Vedas, a fruit even greater than that is said to come from the vision of Oṃkāreśvara.
Whatever merit is gained by practicing celibacy throughout one's entire life, that merit is said to be surpassed by the sight of Oṃkāreśvara.
O Goddess, the merit that comes from subsisting on cow-dung and the merit that comes from fasting—greater than both of those is the merit obtained from the sight of Oṃkāreśvara. (33)
The merit that is proclaimed for worship has no measurable limit.
What is the use of sacrifices rich in great wealth, or what is the use of austerities so difficult to perform, when one obtains that very fruit simply from the sight of the syllable Om? (35)
By worshipping, or even by touching, praising, or likewise hearing of the god Oṃkāreśvara, men shall become recipients of liberation.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Oṃkāreśvara has been told to you; now hear of the supreme Viśveśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Oṃkāreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 52.
Īśvara said: Know that the fifty-third is the well-known Īśvara, renowned as the Supreme Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) throughout all the worlds. || 1 ||
In former times, there was a king named Vidūratha in Vidarbha; he ruled his kingdom without any thorns, accompanied by ten thousand women in his inner apartments.
Then, having gone out on a hunt, he killed by mistake an ascetic who was wearing a black antelope skin, peaceful, and meditating upon the eternal Brahman.
Deluded by fate, he mistook the Brahmin for a deer in the great forest; as a result of that karma, at the end of his life, he went to the Raurava hell.
Having experienced that terrible torment there for the duration of his own lifespan, he returned here to the mortal world and became a venomous serpent.
O beloved, he too, out of anger, bit the Brāhmaṇa on the foot; struck by the staff, he also met his death at that very moment.
Having fallen from hell, Siṃha became a most dreadful being in his second birth; he devoured a king and was struck down by the king's men.
Furthermore, in his third birth as well, he became a tiger; with his fierce and sharp claws, he slaughtered wild boars.
By him as well, a certain Vaiśya was brought to his end within the forest; slain by Niṣādas with arrows, he too met his death.
In the fourth [birth] he was born as an elephant and met his death at the hands of a lion; in the fifth he was born as a crocodile in the salt waters of the great ocean.
Then that evildoer struck Rāmā as she desired to bathe; he was assailed by the fishermen with cries of "shame! and with fish-hooks.
Furthermore, in his sixth birth, he was born as a flesh-eating *piśāca*; then, by means of powerful mantras originating from the *Atharvaveda*, he was thoroughly subdued.

The minister, a Brāhmaṇa who was the best among those skilled in mantras, killed him; having been born again in his seventh [life], he possessed an exceedingly hideous body that was difficult to behold.
With sharp fangs and a terrifying mouth, feeding on flesh and blood, with emaciated limbs in desert lands, he was a most wicked Brahmarākṣasa.
Having been assailed by King Nimi, the enemy of the Rākṣasas, he was struck down in battle with the Brahmā weapon after the king had strung his bow. || 15 ||
In his eighth birth, he became a fierce and extremely black dog; he met his death from wounds inflicted by the strikes of a boar's hooves. || 16 ||
In his ninth birth he was born as a jackal in a cremation ground, and he was a flesh-eater; out of greed, he met his death, afflicted by suffering, from a forest fire. (17)
In his tenth birth, however, he became a terrifying vulture with a sharp beak; feeding on putrid flesh and fat, he met his death through disease. || 18 ||
O fair-faced one, on the eleventh day as well, a Caṇḍāla went to Avantī; indeed, for the purpose of stealing wealth, he entered the house of a twice-born man.
He was immediately caught and bound by the staff-bearer himself; indeed, he was brought for the purpose of execution and suspended from the top of a tree.
Right there, O virtuous lady, a Liṅga was situated near the north of Śūleśvara; it came within the range of vision of her, whose mind was extremely distressed.
In an instant he met his end and went to the abode of the thirty gods; having enjoyed excellent pleasures there, he descended once more to the surface of the earth.
A king named Viśveśa was born in Vidarbha, renowned for having attained the recollection of his past lives through the merit of beholding a linga.

He enjoyed rare pleasures and ruled the kingdom he had obtained; then, having consecrated his son—who was humble and deeply knowledgeable in dharma—in the kingdom, and remembering his former history, he departed for the city of Avantikā.
There, having seen the great Liṅga which was difficult to behold due to its extreme brilliance, he beheld with his divine eye all things mobile and immobile within the center of the Liṅga.
Within the center of the Liṅga abide all the oceans and rivers, as well as the islands, mountains, and other divine manifestations. || 26 ||
The Moon together with the constellations, the Sun along with Agni, as well as Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, and Śakra, the lord of the Maruts; || 27 ||
The Maruts, the divine Gandharvas, and the sages whose wealth is austerity; the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess. || 28 ||
O Goddess, Brahmā and the other deities, as well as Skanda and Lambodara—the entire three worlds—were seen within the center of the Liṅga.
Having fully understood the power of that Liṅga, the lord of the earth, self-restrained, worshipped Maheśvara, the source of the universe.
He became pleased and spoke these words to him: "Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—what desired thing shall I grant to you? (31)
The king spoke these words: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, then those men who behold you—whether with faith or even without faith—" (32)
"May there not be a falling of these [beings] into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra; indeed, may you become renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Viśveśvara. (33)
When these words had been spoken, Viśveśa, adorned by his attendants, departed for my world in a brilliantly shining celestial chariot.
O fair-faced one, being praised by various hosts, he—wearing a crown and earrings, and adorned with pearl necklaces—circled that divine celestial chariot on all sides. (35)
Sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and hosts of Apsarases, who dwell in various celestial abodes such as Samaha, Indra’s realm, and the world of wealth; || 36 ||
Entertaining himself by watching the dances of the celestial women, he remained in my presence for thousands of millions of yugas.
Therefore, O Goddess, the Lord renowned on earth as Viśveśvareśvara is such that, upon seeing the Liṅga of Viśveśa, one is liberated from all sins. || 38 ||
Having beheld the Liṅga of Viśveśvara, an embodied being attains the state of having fulfilled all duties through the mental, vocal, and physical actions performed during seven lifetimes. (39)
His misfortune perishes and his ill-fortune goes to destruction; the embodied soul attains his desires and constant mental prosperity.
Bad dreams, diseases, cruel planets, and terrible spirits perish, O lady of excellent limbs, whenever Viśveśa is constantly worshipped.
Whoever, endowed with faith, indeed worships the Liṅga, they are born in every age fully possessed of all their desires.
In the end, by my grace, that divine goal is attained; in whatever land the Liṅga is worshipped, in that place all actions become auspicious. (43)
Therein, there is no fear of famine, nor anywhere the fear of untimely death; and among the hungry ghosts (pretas), there are neither vetālas, nor nāgas, nor fanged beasts.
And these—Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, Varuṇa, and others of great majesty—attained supreme perfection through the worship of the Liṅga. (45)
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Viśveśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Kaṇṭeśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Viśveśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 53 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know, O beloved, that Kaṇṭheśvara is the fifty-fourth deity; by the mere sight of whom a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
O Goddess, in a former age, at the beginning of the kalpa, there was a king named Satyavikrama. He was defeated by his enemies in battle, his treasury plundered, and he became exceedingly distressed.
Exhausted by fatigue, he went alone into the dense forest; there he then beheld the hermitage of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
As soon as that king was seen by the sage Vasiṣṭha, he was respectfully honored with a seat and other offerings worthy of a king.
Having learned by the power of his asceticism that he was a king born of the solar dynasty, O Goddess, he asked him repeatedly about his arrival and his welfare.
Deeply distressed, that king said to Vasiṣṭha: "O Brahmin, my entire kingdom has been seized by my enemies."
"I have come to you for refuge, O Lord, since I am the sole abode of suffering. How shall the kingdom become free of thorns once again? You ought to show me favor by granting me instruction. (7)
Having heard those words of his, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha meditated and, filled with great curiosity, spoke.
O King, go to Mahākālavana for the accomplishment of your purpose; there is a divine river in that forest, renowned throughout the three worlds.

On its bank, O tiger among kings, to the south of Pṛthukeśvara, you will see an auspicious Liṅga and an ascetic performing penance, who has nothing but bones and skin remaining and who wears rags and bark garments.
At the word of that high-souled brahmin Vasiṣṭha, the king went immediately to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
There he beheld an ascetic who was long-lived and imperishable, emaciated by fasting, and possessing the splendor of twelve suns.
The ascetic saw the king and, recognizing him as his dear friend who had arrived after being deprived of his kingdom, spoke these words: (13)
"Come, come, O tiger among kings! By good fortune you have arrived in my presence. Having spoken thus, the ascetic then uttered the syllable "Hum. (14)
Then, by that sound of "Huṃ," having pierced through the netherworld (pātāla), five maidens emerged; one of them indeed grasped a golden pedestal.
Another emerged carrying a water-filled golden pitcher, and a third arrived, intent on washing their feet. (16)
Taking up two other fans and standing on either side, that one of great asceticism then once again uttered the syllable "Huṃ. (17)
At that sound of the syllable "huṃ," he beheld a host of Apsarases who had arrived from the world of the gods, captivating the mind with their dance and song.
Immediately thereafter, he then beheld the supreme, light-emitting Liṅga, in which the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, was born and into which it dissolves.
Seeing that, the best of kings was filled with wonder; bowing his head to the brahmin, he said, "O best of the twice-born, what is this? (20)
Thus questioned by the king, that brahmin then spoke these words: "O Indra among kings, for seven births I have been gratified by you."
Therefore, this illusion was shown to you by means of difficult penance; behold the power of my asceticism through the majesty of this Linga.
By the sound "huṃ," the earth was instantly filled with water; by the "huṃ" sound, that water was swallowed up, and fire was produced from his mouth.
From the sound "Huṃ," the entire earth was then born consisting of fire; having withdrawn that fire in an instant, the wind issued forth from his mouth.

O Pārvatī, by the sound of "huṃ," everything was accomplished at that very moment; neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate directions existed, nor were there stars or planets at that time.
Then he wandered about; that king was filled with wonder, for that [liṅga] was not there. He suddenly reflected: "Where is the liṅga, and where is the ascetic? (26)
As he was thinking thus, a great sound arose; and from that sound, a city enclosed by a rampart was produced.
The king suddenly beheld that vast city, adorned with pure gold, its courtyards fashioned with beautiful balconies, and inhabited by divine beings who were knowers of the Self.
A great sound arose once more, and from it a pair of women appeared; one was clad in white garments and was dark-complexioned, while the other was dressed in black garments and was fair.
Then, from that sound, there arose a most excellent being, having two heads, six faces, and endowed with twelve feet.

Furthermore, from that sound, a person was born who had become sevenfold; and after the twice-born one had shown how that [being] was withdrawn once again, he spoke thus, O large-eyed lady, to the king whose hair stood on end with joy: || 31 ||
Behold this world of mine, O King, created through ascetic power; for the sake of your pleasure, O best of kings, this world has been shown to you.
Thus addressed by that ascetic, the wise lord of men, his heart filled with wonder, questioned him with great composure.
O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, who are these two women, one white and one black? And who is this, O Brahmin, with twelve feet, two heads, and six faces? (34)
"And who is that man, O Brahmin, who became sevenfold from being one? Having heard those words of his, the ascetic spoke: || 38 ||
"O best of kings, these two women seen by you—the white and the black—are declared to be Night and Day, created of old by Brahmā. (36)

The two heads that were seen are proclaimed as the two solstices (ayana); the six mouths that were seen are remembered as the six seasons (ṛtu); and the twelve feet that were seen are remembered as the twelve months. || 37 ||
O Lord of Men, that person who was born sevenfold and has become one should be known as the ocean, which exists as both sevenfold and single. || 388 ||
This wheel of the year has been shown for your sake; having understood this, O lord of kings, you ought not to grieve. (39)
The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is perishable; indeed, I have witnessed this many times through the power of this Linga.
O King, by beholding this Liṅga for the destruction of your enemies, your kingdom will become free of thorns; of this there is no doubt. (41)
Thus addressed, the king then beheld that supreme Liṅga; by the sight of that Liṅga, even those thorns who were his enemies—the kings—were heard by that lord of the earth to have died.
Having gone to that region, the king indeed became a universal monarch (cakravartin); by the power of this Liṅga, he ruled his kingdom with great wealth.
Having performed various sacrifices, he attained supreme liberation; all of this was indeed heard and seen by that ascetic through his meditation.
"By the sight of this Liṅga, my friend—who had suddenly been deprived of his kingdom—indeed regained a kingdom free from all thorns."
Therefore, it shall become renowned on earth by the name Kaṇṭeśvara; of this there is no doubt, for its mere sight bestows a kingdom.
From this day forward, those who behold the god Śiva Kaṇṭeśvara will have their thorns destroyed instantly; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever merit shall arise from bathing or even from visiting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, and Puṣkara—that same merit will be fully attained simply by beholding the illustrious Lord Gaṇeśvara.
Whether they be householders or ascetics, those who observe their vows and behold the god Kaṇṭeśvara with devotion shall attain perfection.
Whatever sin has been accumulated previously over a thousand lifetimes, all of that will quickly perish by the sight of Śrīkaṇṭheśvara. (50)
Whatever has been given, recited, offered in sacrifice, performed as ritual action, or practiced as austerity, as well as meditation and study—all that becomes inexhaustible. || 51 ||
O large-eyed one, as that brahmin ascetic of rigid vows was speaking thus, the Liṅga, being pleased, spoke to him preceded by a boon.

Freed from old age and disease, devoid of all sorrow, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, a bestower of boons, honored by all, invincible to everyone, and endowed with the sovereign power of yoga. || 53 ||
Thus addressed by the Liṅga, O Goddess, the ascetic attained the status of a Gaṇa; surrounded by the Gaṇas, he came to my side.
O Goddess, when Andhaka formerly let out a lion’s roar in battle, my body became bristling with thrill. (55)

Then that Liṅga arose, which destroys all enemies; because those who were thorns to the gods were burnt by the fire of the Liṅga, the deity became renowned throughout the three worlds as Kaṇṭeśvara. (56)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Kaṇṭeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear of the supreme Siṃheśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kaṇṭeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 54 ||
The illustrious Lord said: O lady of beautiful hips, know that the fifty-first Lord is Siṃheśvara, the destroyer of great fear. || 1 ||

O Goddess with eyes like blue lotuses, for my sake you have indeed performed great, formidable, and rigorous penance according to the Sadya-kalpa; by your fierce austerity, the three worlds were scorched.
Having recognized that penance was indeed difficult, the four-faced Lord of Devas came and spoke to you, O Goddess, with auspicious words.
"What do you desire to obtain, my daughter? What unattainable thing shall I give to you? Desist from this excessive hardship of asceticism at my command. (4)
And having heard your words—pregnant with reverence for the Guru, agreeable, true, beneficial, definitive in their description, and desired—you [acted accordingly]. || 5 ||
Then Brahmā was answered by you with words humble in salutation: "Śaṅkara has been obtained by me as my husband through difficult penance."

Bhava has repeatedly called me "the dark-complexioned one" (Śyāmalavarṇā). I am dark, yet my form is like gold, and I am united with my beloved. My penance is for the purpose of how my husband, the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati), might become submissive to my will.
Having heard your words, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the bestower of boons who is worthy of choice, said, "So shall it be."
After how much time will the fulfillment of your desire come to pass? Your form shall indeed become radiant with splendor under the name Gaurī.
Having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, you became exceedingly angry, O Girijā; yet in due time, your desire shall be fulfilled.
From your mouth, out of anger, there emerged a terrifying lion—wide-mouthed, extremely fierce, with a neck matted with locks of hair. || 11 ||
O Goddess, with his tail lashing and his face made fierce by prominent fangs, you made the resolve to fall into his mouth.
That lion, overcome by hunger, was intent on devouring you; yet he was not even able to look upon her who was preeminent in asceticism.
Being suddenly scorched by your fiery ascetic power, he turned his face away, intent solely on saving his life. || 14 ||
Then, O lady of firm vows, compassion arose within you toward the lion; for you gave him, who was hungry, milk that was like nectar. (15)
Although it was produced from her two breasts for the sake of that lion, it nevertheless burns excessively, because she has fallen into a wicked state of mind.
He said: "O Mother, as I am being consumed, I am burnt by your splendor; I am a man of evil conduct, wicked, and a personification of sin. (17)
Desiring to devour you, this evil-minded one has now been begotten by me; therefore, as a slayer of my mother and a murderer of my teacher, I shall go to hell.
O large-eyed lady, having heard those words of her distressed son, you spoke thus to Siṃha out of maternal affection. (19)
"O son, there exists the most excellent field, Mahākālavana; go there quickly at my command, for it was fashioned by the gods. (20)
Near the god Kaṇṭeśvara is an excellent Liṅga, which arose from the lion’s roar of the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Formerly, during the battle with the demon Andhaka when Indra was being tormented, the lion of swift prowess heard your words.
Having gone to Mahākālavana, the god was seen by him at that very moment; through the sight of the Liṅga, he became a divine-bodied lion.
O Pārvatī, because of your attachment to that linga, you went there; O beloved, having assumed the form of Siṃhikā, a lion was quickly [summoned] by you.
Indeed, by the power of this Liṅga, a divine body was seen; and upon seeing the lion of great splendor, supreme satisfaction arose within you.
"O Goddess of beautiful countenance, you have indeed performed a great deed for this linga; by the sight of this linga, this lion has become possessed of a divine body. (26)
Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, the god Siṃheśvara shall become renowned on earth. In the meantime, Brahmā, surrounded by the gods, arrived there and spoke to you, O beautiful one. (27)
"O Goddess, since this lion has been born from your wrath as your son, he shall therefore become your vehicle; of this there is no doubt. (28)
He who, with concentration and devotion, beholds the Siṃheśvara Liṅga, shall have an imperishable and divine residence in heaven.
By chanting its name one is liberated from sin; by seeing it, one beholds auspicious things; and by touching this Liṅga, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
He obtains those abundant desires conceived by his mind; at that very moment, the person is liberated from birth, suffering, old age, and the like.
When he beholds the Lord of Lions, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, then serpents, tigers, and the like, as well as thieves and those who are violent, [flee].

There is no fear from those [demons] for one who beholds the illustrious Siṃheśvara. Whatever fruit arises from sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and so forth—that fruit is produced by properly beholding Śiva as Siṃheśvara. (33)
He who beholds with diligent effort the god Siṃheśvara at that time attains my own world, which is saluted by gods and asuras.

Having spoken thus, O beloved, Brahmā then departed for his own world. That body of yours which was previously stained by the luster of time has attained a wonderful whiteness through the power of that asceticism.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Siṃheśvara has been recounted to you; now hear that of Revanteśa.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Siṃheśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 55 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know that the fifty-sixth is named Revanteśvara, by the mere sight of which supreme perfection (siddhi) is produced. || 1 ||
O Goddess, in former times Saṃjñā, unable to endure the exceedingly unbearable brilliance of the Sun, went away to perform penance; that woman of noble vows was discovered by Sūrya.
Then, having assumed the form of a horse, he went to the Northern Kurus; there he beheld Saṃjñā, who had taken the form of a mare.
She went before him, intent on protecting his rear; then, as they met there, the union of their noses occurred.
From the end of the semen, the two Nāsatyas and Dasras emerged with the faces of horses; and Revanta appeared, bearing a sword, a shield, and wearing armor.

Then, mounted upon a horse and bearing arrows and a bow, he appeared; by that very one, as soon as he was born and while playfully mounted on his steed, this entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—was utterly conquered.
Then the gods, having been defeated, went to Brahmā for refuge; bowing down with their bodies trembling from fear, they spoke. (8)
"O Grandfather of the World, listen: our prosperity and splendor have been destroyed by Revanta, the son of the Sun, who acts like a lord of the gods."
The fire arising from his body rushed forth, overcoming Time; by it the trees blazed and mountain peaks fell down.
Everything became utterly agitated, filled with cries of "Alas!", and devoid of consciousness; everything was tormented by that very [fire] and overwhelmed by garlands of flames. || 11 ||
This prosperous bearer of oblations has spread throughout the ten directions; everything appears as if ablaze, resembling the kiṃśuka flower.
O fair-faced one, having heard these words of theirs spoken by Brahmā, I have understood, O best of gods, such to be your purpose.
"O best of gods, whatever you desire shall come to pass; therefore, O deities, go quickly for refuge to Śaṅkara."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the thirty gods, terrified with fear, approached me, bowed down, and spoke this to me: || 15 ||
O Maheśvara, by Revanta alone, the son of Āditya, the entire triple world was consumed by the fire residing within his body, through his great splendor, prowess, and strength.
"O best of gods, he is indeed incurable for all of us; O Śaṅkara, you alone have the power over him, and no one else. (17)
We all, afflicted by fear and seeking refuge, take refuge in you—the god who grants boons, the Great Lord of the thirty deities. (18)
O beloved, as soon as I remembered Revanta, the son of the Sun, he arrived with a soul gladdened by affection and spoke these words: ||| 19 ||
"O Lord, tell me everything without omission: what must be done by me? Then, at that time, the son of the Sun was placed upon my lap.
Out of affection, I have kissed you on the head and embraced you again and again; O illustrious one of noble vows, I grant you a boon—choose one!
I am well-pleased with you; O Kāma, obtain your desire according to your wish. I command you this, and thus you shall attain prosperity.

"O son, there exists on the surface of the earth a supreme, auspicious, and imperishable place called Mahākālavana, which remains even at the time of universal dissolution; there I shall grant you a station, and there your fame shall endure."
To the east is the station of Kaṇṭeśvara, which is exceedingly difficult to attain; dwell there, O Revanta, and you shall behold the eternal Liṅga.
"You shall always be worshiped by the gods, of this there is no doubt; you shall become the lord of the Guhyakas in the heavenly world. (25)
You shall be worthy of worship in all horse-stables, and you shall dwell in the houses of kings, highly honored. (26)
That eternal abode of mine is in the form of a Liṅga; it is worshipped by the thirty gods and should be diligently served by you there.
O Goddess, having been addressed thus by me, Revanta, the son of the Sun, then entered the sky and reached Mahākālavana in an instant. || 28 ||
There he beheld that eternal Liṅga in the form of light; O Pārvatī, Revanta, the son of the Sun, was seen by the Liṅga.
He was addressed with affection: "By good fortune you have been seen, O son of the Sun! From this day forward, I shall attain fame on earth by your name. (30)
O son of the Sun, you must always remain near me; your fame shall become imperishable throughout the three worlds. (31)
"I shall become known as Revanteśvara; of this there is no doubt. Those who behold me, O Revanta, endowed with supreme devotion, for them there shall be horses, victory, and exalted fame. (32)
Possessing sovereignty, the power of giving, and endless sons and grandsons, he shall become the lord of the Guhyakas and dwell in the heavenly world.
O large-eyed lady, having heard the speech of the Liṅga, it was indeed spoken by Revanta, the son of the Sun, with a satisfied inner soul.
Grant me indeed unwavering devotion; grant me the supreme abode; grant me the highest knowledge and grant me eternal fame.

O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, dispeller of the fear of the bonds of worldly existence! By the sight of you, the Divine, I have become one who has realized the meaning of the conditioned. (36)
Those embodied beings who behold you, having been thoroughly purified through ten million births, shall have no further return to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, Revanta, the son of the Sun and beloved of Ravi, stationed himself near the deity Revanteśvara.
Thus, O Goddess, has this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Revanteśvara been told to you; now hear about Ghaṇṭeśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Revanteśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Know that Ghaṇṭeśvara is the fifty-seventh; now listen further. By the mere sight of him, the attainment of one's desires occurs. || 1 ||

There was an excellent leader of the Gaṇas named Ghaṇṭa, who was dear to me; during the era of Cākṣuṣa Manu, he set out by chance for some purpose of curiosity to see the imperishable Brahmā in the abode of Brahman. || 2 ||
Then, beholding the Gandharva Citrasena, who was skilled in song, approaching, the foremost of the Gaṇas joyfully inquired after his welfare.
I must go right there to the abode of Parameṣṭhin; with songs, I shall propitiate Brahmā, the lord of the worlds.
Then, O Goddess, being thus addressed, Citrasena spoke to Ghaṇṭa: "The Lotus-born One, together with the gods, has deliberated upon a secret mantra. (5)
Having heard this, the attendant Gaṇa stood with a bewildered mind; barred by the doorkeeper, he reflected for a moment.
Having abandoned his own master, Īśāna, he has come to see Brahmā; yet even entry cannot be obtained, let alone the favor itself, which remains far away.
O Goddess, as he was thinking thus, more than a full year passed; yet Ghaṇṭa did not gain entrance at the door of Brahmā.
Then, seeing Nārada emerging from the interior of the house with a lute in his hand and full of eagerness, that best of attendants [addressed] the lotus-born Brahmā.
He was suddenly addressed by Ghaṇṭa: "O Nārada, announce me; I am a Gaṇa, a knower of the essence of song, and the beloved of Mahādeva."

Having arrived for the purpose of seeing the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, and having heard the words of Ghaṇṭa, the sage Nārada became filled with joy; then, consoling him with feigned affection, he replied as follows.

"O Lord of the Gaṇas, I have been sent to the side of Bṛhaspati by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, to inquire about a certain other matter. I shall return in just a moment; please wait for that time."
Having spoken thus, O Goddess, Nārada, the best of sages, approached my side and related the account of Ghaṇṭa.

"O Lord, such a servant as Ghaṇṭa is difficult to find; for, O God, having abandoned you, this Gaṇa has remained for more than a year in service to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), yet he has not obtained entry [into his presence]. (14)
Having heard those words of the sage Nārada at that time, I cursed him in anger: "Fall, Ghaṇṭa, onto the surface of the earth! (15)
"Indeed, having abandoned me, he has gone elsewhere for the sake of service in another's house. When these words were spoken by me, Brahmā, although standing right at the door, [remained there]. (16)
The bell fell upon the ground near the edge of the Devadāru forest. O Pārvatī, seeing himself fallen on the earth, Ghaṇṭa—
With words faltering with emotion, he spoke these words in the *Śokottara*: "He who abandons his own master and goes elsewhere for the sake of service [is a fool]. (18)
He goes to a terrible hell and incurs infamy; today, having been deceived by Nārada, both have departed from me, since neither Brahmā nor the god Maheśvara is my master. (19)
While he was thus lamenting, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived at that place where Ghaṇṭa was situated.
O Goddess, in the Devadāru forest, while [the sages] were intent on seeing the ascetics, Nārada was seen by Ghaṇṭa, who was terrified and agitated in mind.
"Having reduced me to such a state, what else will he do to me? While he was thinking thus, Nārada spoke these words to him.
"O Gaṇādhyakṣa, you should not harbor anger, which destroys merit; Ghaṇṭa has fallen for the sake of fame and indeed for the sake of expiation. (23)
With your soul purified by penance, you shall attain Lord Śaṅkara; therefore, go at my command to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
To the east of Revanteśvara, there exists an excellent, divine Liṅga that bestows all prosperity; it shall become famous by your name.
Thus addressed by Nārada, Jaigīṣavya arrived; he too related everything, for what was spoken by him was indeed the truth. (26)
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, by Nārada, Kaśyapa, Mṛkaṇḍu, Kaṇva, and Jamadagni, your fame shall become imperishable. (27)
O Goddess, having been addressed by Atri, Bhṛgu, and the celestial sage Lomaśa, Ghaṇṭa quickly went to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
O Goddess, while I was fighting in battle with the sound of my bell, an excellent linga that destroys sin appeared there; that auspicious, radiant linga was seen by my attendant alone.
Upon seeing that linga, Ghaṇṭa became a Gaṇa once more, endowed with splendor and beauty, possessing the form of the thousand-rayed sun.
Greatly praised by the sound of bells, he arrived at my side in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and became exceedingly dear to me. (31)
O large-eyed lady, those who behold the god Ghaṇṭeśvara Śiva shall be resounded by the ringing of bells and shall travel in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
They shall go for a very long time to my eternal world; this supreme Liṅga, Ghaṇṭeśvara, must not be told to just anyone.

O beloved, if a man—whether afflicted by disease, dejected, or suffering in distress—should behold Lord Ghaṇṭeśvara even incidentally, he shall depart by means of celestial chariots possessing the luster of blazing gold and fulfilling all desires.
Amidst the Gandharvas and Apsarases, that man rejoices in heaven; entertained by lutes and flutes, he obtains his desired objects of pleasure. (35)

Then, having descended from heaven, endowed with all sovereign powers, he is born into a prosperous family filled with gold and grain; he becomes either a king or one equal to a king, or even the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
He who worships the Lord of Gods, endowed with supreme faith, goes to the highest abode, which is the cause of no further rebirth.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Ghaṇṭeśvara has been recounted to you, O Goddess; now hear about Prayāgeśa.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Ghaṇṭeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 57 ||
Īśvara said: Know that the fifty-eighth Lord is the supreme one named Prayāgeśvara, who fulfills all desires. || 1 ||
In the first kalpa of old, there was Manu Svāyambhuva; his son was Priyavrata, a performer of sacrifices and supremely righteous.
Having performed many sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees, O beloved, he obtained Bharata and his other sons throughout the seven continents.
Having gone to Viśālā Badarī himself, he performed great penance; after a long time, Nārada arrived there.
Honored with a seat and the guest-offering by King Priyavrata, he was asked after being thus worshipped: "Tell me, what wonder is there? (5)
Thus addressed, Nārada, the best of sages, said: "O King, in Śvetadvīpa, I beheld a maiden at a lake."
And being questioned, that large-eyed woman said: "Why do you dwell in this desolate place? Who are you, noble lady, how are you here, and what business do you have here? (7)
"O lady of beautiful limbs, tell me what must be done, O auspicious one. Thus addressed by me, she indeed looked at me with her eyes closed.
While I remained silent after remembering this, my supreme knowledge was lost, and indeed all the Vedas and all the Śāstras were forgotten by me.
Then, O King, overcome with wonder and filled with anxiety and delusion, I took refuge in her alone and looked upon her.
At that moment, a divine man was seen within her body; in that man's heart was a second, and on his chest yet another; and in his heart also, a third was situated.
Then, having somehow questioned that maiden, the goddess, I said: "O blessed lady, all my Vedas have been lost; tell me, what is the cause? (12)
The maiden said: "I am the mother of all the Vedas, known by the name Sāvitrī. Since you did not recognize me, the Vedas have been taken away from you. (13)
When I had spoken thus, O lord of the earth, she was questioned by me with wonder: "O sinless one, you are indeed the mother of the Vedas; tell this to me. (14)
O Goddess, who are these three men in your heart? (15)
The maiden said: "This one who resides within my body, whose limbs are auspicious and who is so beautiful and radiant—this is indeed named the Ṛgveda, and the second is the Yajurveda. (16)
The Sāmaveda is the third; thus the three Vedas abide in me. O twice-born one, the three fires and the three gods abide within my body.
Having spoken thus, O King, that maiden suddenly vanished while I was looking on; at that, I was filled with wonder. || 18 ||
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? To which Lord shall I go for refuge? How will the Vedas and the scriptures manifest themselves now? (19)
"Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, is heard of in the Vedas as being most desirable; I shall go there, and perfect knowledge will arise. (20)
By Raibhya, who had lost his Veda, supreme perfection was attained; there, in the vicinity of the Akṣayyavaṭa tree, the Sāvitrī is heard.
Having thus reflected in my mind, O best of kings, I went to Prayāga, the desired sacred ford (tīrtha) saluted by all the gods.
There, O Indra among kings, I performed intense and most difficult penance; then Prayāga himself arrived there in personified form.
I was addressed by him with affection: "O Nārada, son of Brahmā, do not cause me distress; I am Prayāga, who has been made fearful by your ascetic power. (24)
O ascetic, you have come to my side out of affection; you are blessed in every way, O Brahmin, especially by virtue of your penance. (25)
"O Brahman, you must go with me without hesitation; in the delightful Mahākālavana, supreme knowledge shall arise for you—of this there is no doubt—and my fame shall remain firmly established. (26)
O best of kings, as Prayāga was speaking thus, Janārdana, clad in yellow garments, suddenly appeared before him.
Holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, seated upon Garuḍa and traversing the sky, that Supreme Person spoke these words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"Come, Nārada, let us go to Prayāga where he will go. Having heard Kṛṣṇa's words, I spoke to Janārdana: || 29 ||
"O Lord of Gods, grant me knowledge; O Lord of the World, how shall I go to that forest of Mahākāla, being destitute of both learning and wisdom? (30)
Thus addressed by Śrīdhara, O King, I was then quickly brought at that very moment to Mahākālavana along with Prayāga.
To the east of Ghaṇṭeśvara and to the south of Navanadī, there is a beginningless, eternal Liṅga in the form of light.
O King, while I was looking on, Prayāga performed worship; the Linga, being pleased, said: "For what purpose have you come here? (33)
O Prayāga, having become disciplined, I am forever pleased with you; my very sight shall never be in vain.
Thus addressed by that Linga, he was then entreated for my sake: "Grant knowledge to this brahmin, the high-souled Nārada. (35)
O Lord, the Vedas and the Shastras were lost through the sight of Savitri.
Then, from that *liṅga*, Brahmā emerged, surrounded by the Vedas, together with their six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), and the Purāṇas.
O best of kings, having been addressed thus by the goddess Sāvitrī at that time, [I spoke] indeed by the power of this Liṅga which had been requested for Prayāga.
"O Nārada, those Vedas and Dharmaśāstras will appear to you,"—when these words were spoken, O King, the Vedas were obtained by me once again. (39)
O Indra among kings, having attained knowledge—both the wisdom accompanied by its six limbs and the various scriptures—I then spoke those words.
"Worshipped at Prayāga for the sake of my knowledge, the Lord shall attain renown in the worlds by the name Prayāgeśvara. (41)
From that time forward, that Liṅga has been surrounded by hundreds of millions of sacred fords; it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, and you ought to go there.
O best of kings, what is the use of performing this horse sacrifice? By merely seeing it, the fruit of a hundred horse sacrifices is produced. (43)
What is the use of well-performed austerity that merely causes bodily suffering? One obtains one's desired object immediately from the sight of Prayāgeśvara.
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, having heard the words of Nārada, King Priyavrata, the son of Svāyambhuva, went to Mahākālavana.
There he beheld that Liṅga on the southern bank of the Navanadī river; by the sight of that Liṅga, he came into my presence.
O Goddess, I have honored him and appointed him as the lord of the Gaṇas. Those men who behold the Lord Prayāgeśvara with devotion are blessed in the world of mortals; others suffer in vain.
Whatever destination belongs to the wise man who is established in purity and disciplined in yoga, that same destination is fully attained by beholding Prayāgeśvara. 48.
For those humans who, having arrived in the month of Māgha, shall behold Prayāgeśvara, an Aśvamedha sacrifice is theirs at every step.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Prayāgeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear of the supreme Siddheśvara.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Prayāgeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 58 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know, O beloved, that the fifty-ninth deity is Siddheśvara, by the mere sight of whom perfection arises for men.
There was a king named Aśvaśiras, who was supremely righteous; he performed the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having bathed in the purificatory rite (avabhṛtha), joyful and surrounded by Brāhmaṇas, while that royal sage remained there, a highly effulgent Siddha appeared.
The illustrious Kapila, who knew the power of various medicinal herbs and was proficient in mantras and tantras, arrived, as did Jaigīṣavya, the king of the Siddhas.
Rising quickly from his seat, that king, the lord of the earth, filled with supreme joy, performed the rites of hospitality for the two guests.

Those two bulls among sages were honored and seated upon their seats; they were patient, observant of pure vows, possessed of great luster and great fortune, and seekers of liberation. They were endowed with learning and humility, devoted to the practice of celibacy, and dedicated to the tasks of creation, dissolution, and sustenance of the many worlds.
Resembling the rising sun and possessing a splendor equal to fire, they were endowed with a mass of brilliance and were difficult for ordinary people to behold.
Having approached with humility, prostrated, and offered his salutations, the king, with palms joined in reverence, questioned him as follows.
Aśvaśiras said: "O best of sages, I have heard that there is no god other than Janārdana who, when meditated upon and worshipped, grants men liberation from the bondage of worldly existence."
When Hṛṣīkeśa is remembered, the inauspiciousness born of ten million births of men goes to destruction; how then could one not bow down to Hari? (11)
Having propitiated the Lord of the World, Śakra and the other inhabitants of the celestial realms dwell joyfully in heaven, endowed with divine splendor.
Birth, death, old age, diseases, and various sufferings all immediately go to their dissolution when Garuḍadhvaja is pleased.
Thus questioned at that time by that illustrious one who had made his request, the two perfected ones, experts in the knowledge of supernatural powers, spoke to the king.
"O King, who is this Nārāyaṇa whom you have now mentioned? O monarch, we two are both Nārāyaṇas, and we have come before your very eyes. (15)
Aśvaśiras said: "You two are perfected Brahmins whose sins have been burnt away by asceticism; why do you say that you two are Nārāyaṇas? Thus he spoke these words. (16)
Holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments, Janārdana, Hṛṣīkeśa, seated upon Garuḍa—who on earth is his equal? (17)
Having heard the words of that king, those two, experts in yoga, manifested themselves by assuming the form of Nārāyaṇa. 18.
By the greatness of the mantra, Kapila himself became Viṣṇu at that very moment, holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and clad in yellow garments.
And at that very moment, Jaigīṣavya became Garuḍa; then a great wonder occurred there in the royal palace.

Having seen the eternal god Nārāyaṇa seated upon Garuḍa, and having witnessed such a marvel, the king was filled with wonder and said: "Forgive me, O Siddhas; this is not Viṣṇu, for he is not like this."
From the midst of his navel-lotus, Brahmā was born; from that Brahmā, Rudra arose, and he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
Having heard these words of the king, those two most excellent Siddhas, masters of yoga and skilled in mantras, then performed a supreme illusion.
Then Kapila, the lotus-navelled Prajāpati, suddenly became manifest there himself through yoga in the midst of the lotus.
Then Jaigīṣavya and Rudra were stationed upon his very lap; that king, bewildered by yoga, beheld a great marvel.

Out of curiosity, yet trembling with fear, he replied as follows: "The Lord of the Universe does not exist in this manner; for at that time, Māyā [was present] for the yogins. The glorious Hari is remembered as the one who possesses all forms, who is omnipresent, and the giver of everything. (26)
Then, at the conclusion of those words in the assembly of that king, mosquitoes, bedbugs, lice, bees, birds, and wild animals [appeared].
Horses, cows, steeds, lions, tigers, as well as oxen and buffaloes; and all other animals, both domestic and wild, including insects—[all these were born]. (28)
O Daughter of the Mountain, millions [of beings] were seen in the royal palace; having seen that multitude of spirits, the king was struck with wonder in his mind. || 29 ||
While he was still pondering what it might be, the king indeed came to know the greatness of Jaigīṣavya and the high-souled Kapila.
Then King Aśvaśiras, with his palms joined in reverence, asked those two best of perfected ones with devotion: "O most excellent Siddhas, what is this? (31)
"From the power of what austerity has such capability been obtained? Today my birth has become fruitful; today my learning has become fruitful. (32)
"Indeed, my mental state has become fruitful through the sight of you both. Having heard those words of his, Kapila spoke these words: [33]
O King, in Mahākālavana there exists an excellent liṅga known by the name Siddheśvara, which is always worshipped by the perfected ones (siddhas).
To the east of Saubhāgyeśvara is the bestower of good fortune and health; by the power of that Liṅga, unsurpassed perfection was attained.
"O best of kings, I myself have indeed attained perfection there along with Jaigīṣavya; therefore, O mighty-armed one, go to the auspicious Mahākālavana."
There you shall behold Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, stationed within the form of the Liṅga; he will grant you spiritual perfection.
O lord of men, many such as Sanaka and others attained perfection there upon hearing those words of the high-souled Kapila. (38)
Then that King Aśvaśiras went there suddenly and beheld those two Siddhas near Siddheśvara. || 39 ||

And many other perfected ones (siddhas), as well as other lords of the perfected (siddhanāthas), having recognized the god Siddheśvara, who is worshipped by hosts of perfected beings, [attained success]. (40)
Having realized that Viṣṇu was stationed within the liṅga, that best of kings worshipped him with supreme devotion and meditative concentration.
Then the gratified God said: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon; O King, I shall grant you everything that you desire. (42)
Having heard the speech of the Liṅga, listen to what was said by the king: "O Lord, if you have compassion for me, and if you are indeed pleased, O Master. (43)
O Protector, O Acyuta, show me that supreme form of yours; for this alone, O Lord, has been my constant desire in my heart. (44)

"O Lord of the World, from my very birth, when shall I behold Janārdana? O God, I desire this as the most excellent of all boons—the boon being granted by you, which is celebrated on earth as Siddheśvara. (45)
O fair-faced one, having heard the king's words, the Liṅga said: "Neither the hosts of gods, nor the asuras, nor the great sages know me. (46)
O best of kings, I am Kṛṣṇa, who has attained the state of the supreme form as the Liṅga; indeed, those sages adorned with mantras who have reached my world [attain this]. (47)
And they do not know me in the ultimate sense, O King, regarding this splendor of mine which is seen in the form of a linga. (48)
For indeed, these gods beginning with Brahmā meditate upon this very form; therefore, no one would be capable of beholding my supreme form.
Yogis purified through many births, by my grace, enter into my body, liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra. (50)
While he was speaking thus, the king indeed attained perfection; assuming the form of Viṣṇu, he entered into dissolution within that liṅga.
Therefore, O Goddess, those men who behold the supreme and highly renowned Liṅga Siddheśvara with devotion shall attain eternal perfection.
Eye-salve, foot-ointment, the perfection of sandals, the pill, and the sword-perfection—these are the great perfections, exceedingly difficult to attain. (53)
That perfection which arises from divine herbs and that which is born from the touch of mantras—these are declared to be the perfections; the others are "lightness" (laghimā) and so forth.
The accomplishment of dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as the unsurpassed accomplishment of liberation, arises from the sight of Śrī Siddheśvara; of this there is no doubt. (55)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the god Siddheśvara has been recounted to you; now listen to that of Mataṅgeśa.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Siddheśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 59 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: Know, O Goddess, that the Lord known as Mataṅgeśvara is the sixty-first [deity], who removes sins and always fulfills one's desires.
In the Dvāpara age, there was a lord of brahmins named Sugati; he was truthful, ever self-controlled, and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Mataṅga was his son, who from childhood had become cruel; O Goddess, out of mischief he suddenly struck with a wooden staff a young donkey that was standing near its mother. || 3 ||
Seeing him struck so violently, the she-ass, longing for her son, said: "Do not grieve, my son; this is a Caṇḍāla, certainly not a twice-born man."
"There is no cruelty in a brahmin; a brahmin is said to be friendly. Yet this man, evil-natured, inflicts pain and shows no compassion toward a child."
"Furthermore, a human being always resorts to his own innate nature. Having heard these harsh words of the she-donkey, Mataṅga—
Casting aside the wooden staff, he addressed the she-ass: "Speak, O auspicious she-ass, by whom my mother was defiled? (7)
"How do you know me to be a Caṇḍāla born of the Yāyāvara lineage? By what means was I born a Caṇḍāla, whereby my status as a Brāhmaṇa was lost? (8)
The she-ass said: "Indeed, you were begotten by a negligent barber, a *vṛṣala*, upon a Brāhmaṇī; therefore, you are a *caṇḍāla*, and your status as a Brāhmaṇī has departed."
Thus addressed, Mataṅga spoke these words to his father: "Father, today I have heard a marvel: I was indeed begotten by a barber."
"It was told correctly by the she-ass; therefore, I shall perform great penance. Having spoken thus to his father, he set forth with firm resolve. (11)
Having gone there to the forest, he performed great austerities; then, endowed with ascetic power, he caused the gods to burn with heat.

To him who was thus engaged in asceticism, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, said: "O Mataṅga, why do you perform penance, having renounced human enjoyments? I grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire. (13)
Mataṅga said: "Desiring the status of a Brāhmaṇa, I have undertaken this austerity. O Śakra, grant it to me forever; this is the boon chosen by me. (14)
Having heard these words, Purandara said to him: "Indeed, you are asking for Brahminhood, which is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined their souls."
"You shall meet your destruction, O evil-minded one; therefore, desist from this without delay! That cannot be attained in any way by one born in the womb of a Caṇḍāla. (16)
Thus addressed, Mataṅga, whose soul was disciplined and who was firm in his vows, stood on one foot for a number of years amounting to a hundred.
Then Śakra, of great renown, spoke to him once again: "O hero, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain; do not commit such a rash act in vain."
For it is not possible to attain this; otherwise, you will soon meet your destruction. Or choose some other desire, for the status of a Brāhmaṇa is very difficult to obtain.
Thus addressed, Mataṅga, whose self was disciplined and who was firm in his vows, then remained standing on one foot for a thousand years.
And the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra spoke that very same sentence again: "By one born from the womb of a Caṇḍāla, nothing whatsoever can be attained by you in any way."
"Choose another boon; do not undergo such toil yourself. Thus addressed, Mataṅga became deeply overcome with grief.
Having gone to Gayā, he remained there for a hundred years on his big toe, performing extremely difficult yogic practices and devoted to the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Reduced to skin and bone, that righteous-souled one performed supreme austerity; as he was performing penance, Vāsava rushed toward him and seized him.
He is the lord of boons, the giver, and one who delights in the welfare of all beings. || 25 ||
Śakra said: "O Mataṅga, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed seen here to be contradictory; for Brāhmaṇahood, my dear, is difficult to attain for the wicked who are of sinful character. (26)

In a Brāhmaṇa, the security and well-being of all beings are established; yet, having abandoned that state which is difficult to attain even for those of unrefined souls, they have disregarded this Brāhmaṇahood in this world. (27)
Choose another boon; for this boon is indeed difficult for you to obtain.

Mataṅga said: Why do you pierce me, who am already afflicted by grief? You are killing one who is as good as dead. But I grieve for that man who, having attained the status of a Brahmin, does not preserve it.
O Śatakratu, if the status of a Brāhmaṇa is so difficult for the other three varṇas to attain, how was it obtained by King Viśvāmitra through his ascetic penance?
And the royal sage Vītahavya attained the status of a Brahmin through austerity; therefore, I shall practice austerity, free from dualities and without possessions.
Established in non-violence, self-restraint, and truth, how am I not worthy of being a Brahmin? For even if this [condition] was brought about by fate due to my mother's fault, it remains so. (32)
"O Purandara, having reached this state through the turn of fate, it is certain that destiny cannot be turned back by human effort. (33)
"O Lord, since I do not attain liberation despite such effort, you ought, O Lord of Gods, knowing this, to grant me the supreme [state]. (34)
If I am worthy of your favor, or if I have performed some meritorious deed, then tell me the means by which I may indeed become a Brahmin. (35)
O Purandara, O Lord, you ought to act so that my fame may become inexhaustible; I propitiate you with my head bowed low. (36)
Thus addressed by Mataṅga, Vāsava, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, being well-pleased, recounted the supreme majesty of the Liṅga.
Indra said: "In the Mahākālavana forest, a divine Liṅga was formerly established by Brahmā; it possesses a divine form and is situated to the east of Śrīsiddheśvara. (38)
"By the mere sight of him, you shall attain the status of a Brahmin. At these words of Vāsava, Mataṅga then departed.
Then he beheld the delightful Mahākālavana, another field of spiritual perfection (siddhakṣetra), and there he saw that Liṅga which bestows all fruits without exception.
Having seen him, he honored him with various kinds of flowers; being thus honored, the best of gods replied this to Mataṅga: || 41 ||
"Oh! You are truly highly fortunate, since I have been gratified by you; from me has arisen the entire universe, including the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and the rest."
"I am the bestower of boons upon those worthy of boons, and the giver of curses to the evil-minded. By my grace, your status as a Brahmin shall become imperishable. (43)
Then, O twice-born one, that Mataṅga attained the state of a Brahmin by the sight of the Liṅga; furthermore, through the power of worship, he went to the world of Brahmā.
"O lady of beautiful hips, having obtained this Brahminhood which is difficult to attain through the power of this Linga, the God is praised by Mataṅga; therefore, he is celebrated. (45)
Mataṅgeśvara is renowned in the world as the bestower of the realm of Brahmā; [yet there are those] who are hostile toward the castes and stages of life, and who delight in the words of heretics.
In the Kali age, men are devoid of boundaries, lacking in good conduct, fearless, excessively greedy, merciless, cruel-minded, and audacious; yet even they go to heaven upon seeing that Liṅga.
O Goddess, those who are pure, highly fortunate, meditative, and partakers of liberation—they behold the Lord Mataṅgeśvara in the Kali age.
O Goddess, those who are devoted to the meditation on Brahman and those engaged in the acts of sacrifice and charity—they behold the Lord Mataṅgeśvara in the Kali age. 49.
O Great Goddess, those men who worship the Lord Mataṅgeśvara in this mortal world have performed meritorious deeds; their residence shall be eternal in heaven.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Mataṅgeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear of the lord Saubhāgya.
Īśvara said: Know that the sixty-first Lord is Saubhāgyeśvara; by the mere sight of whom one obtains incomparable good fortune.
In the first Prākṛta Kalpa, there was a king named Aśvavāhana in the beautiful city of Prāgjyotiṣa; he was righteous-souled and a promoter of fame.
The wise performer of many sacrifices was never defeated in battles; his wife, O large-eyed one, was named Madanamañjarī. (3)
The daughter of the King of Kāśī, possessed of beautiful eyebrows and exceedingly radiant in form, was skillful, virtuous, most righteous, and well-versed in domestic affairs.
Endowed with the sixty-four arts, she was always devoted to her husband's welfare; with a face like the full moon, she was gentle and always spoke sweetly. (5)
O Goddess, by the power of past karma she was born with deformed limbs; she was not desired by that king and was always a cause of distress to his eyes.
She spoke words that caused distress to the ears of that king; O King, the sight of her always burned his eyes.

The king fell into an unbearable swoon from her touch. O lady of beautiful countenance, when the king was gazed upon by her with love, he, as if burning with an extremely intense fire, spoke these words: ||| 8 ||
"O gatekeeper, take this unfortunate wife and abandon her quickly in the forest; you must not disregard these words of mine. (9)
Then, observing that the king’s word was not to be questioned, the doorkeeper placed that fair-browed woman upon a chariot and abandoned her in the forest.
Abandoned in the desolate forest, weeping again and again, she remembered that protector of the earth and regarded him as a deity.
Then she, whose every limb was beautiful, with her mind and heart attached to him there, spent the remainder of the day and likewise the night, devoted primarily to sighing.
Sighing, the faultless-limbed one with intoxicating eyes wept repeatedly, crying "Alas! Alas!", and reproached herself, saying, "I am unfortunate."

Neither in the monastery, nor in pleasant food, nor in that forest, nor in the mountain caves did she find delight at that time; abandoned by him, O lady of beautiful hips, she lamented her own youth. (14)
"Where was I born so unfortunate here, brought under the sway of evil fate? How did I obtain such a husband, that most excellent of kings? (15)
"Blessed is this man, most meritorious is he, who has come within the range of our youth; he will undoubtedly take his pleasure with other unchaste women as well. (16)
A beloved wife is desired by someone, and a beloved husband is sought after by another; a marital union rich with mutual affection is exceedingly rare. (17)
"This king is my beloved, yet I am not the king's beloved; for mutual affection arises only among those who are truly fortunate. (18)
If that protector of the earth does not unite with me today, then the unbearable fire of passion will surely consume me. (19)
That forest, which was once so delightful and resounded with the cries of male cuckoos, now burns me as if it were bereft of its beloved.
Thus, overcome by passion and lamenting again and again, she beheld there an ascetic of firm vows who knew the three periods of time.
He subsisted on a girdle, a deerskin, a loincloth, and a wooden staff; he was of great luster, highly fortunate, seeking liberation, and the foremost among sages.
Seeing him, who resembled the rising sun and possessed a splendor like that of fire, that wicked queen suddenly rose up.
Having restrained herself with decorum, and having prostrated and offered her salutations, she, bowing low, asked the king the reason for their separation.
"O Blessed One, I am the daughter of the King of Kāśī, most beloved to him; I am the sister of Śatrusena and exceedingly dear to my mother. (25)
O great sage, she was married by King Aśvavāhana according to the dharma, for he was like Dharma himself and equal to Prajāpati.
Why was I not desired by that king? And why, O Lord, was that monarch always so exceedingly dear to me? (27)
"O ascetic, by what karma have I become so unfortunate? How may my husband, the best of kings, come under my control? And how may I possess good fortune? Please tell me this truthfully. (28)
Having heard those words of hers, that sage of rigid vows explained the cause of her misfortune through his supernatural knowledge.
"At the time of your marriage, you were gazed upon by malefic planets; your husband, O daughter, was gazed upon by benefic planets. (30)

"Because of that, the king is dear to him, but you are not dear to the monarch. Hearing these words of his, the queen, with a dejected mind, questioned him with humility, her neck bowed low in devotion. (31)
O Blessed One, by what gift, by what bath, and by what observance, and by what action indeed, does supreme good fortune come to be? (32)
Having heard these words of hers, that sage of rigid vows related the greatness by which good fortune is obtained.
O daughter, in Mahākālavana there exists a Linga that bestows good fortune, located beside Mataṅgeśvara; it grants all desired objects. Merely by beholding it, you shall attain good fortune.

In ancient times, this Liṅga was propitiated by Indrāṇī for the sake of good fortune; she obtained supreme good fortune, and even Śakra, who had been lost, regained it. Therefore, at my command, go to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
There, good fortune shall arise from the sight of her beloved; O auspicious one, a son will be born to her from the sight of that linga.
Having been addressed thus by that ascetic at that time, O lady of beautiful countenance, she went to Mahākālavana, where that liṅga is located.
He beheld a linga endowed with grace that bestows good fortune; from the sight of that linga, the king remembered his beloved wife.
He asked Jamadagni: "O Lord, where has my beloved gone? O Brahmin, has she been devoured in the forest by lions, tigers, or night-stalkers? (39)
"I have been abandoned by that cruel man, yet I am his beloved. As the king was speaking thus, he was answered by Jamadagni: The king, speaking in this manner, was rebuked by Jamadagni. (40)
O protector of the earth, she was not devoured by lions, tigers, or night-stalkers; for she is one whose conduct is unimpaired, devoted to you, and faithful to her husband. (41)
O King, she went to Mahākālavana out of a desire for good fortune; "A wife must be protected, O protector of the earth"—this is the supreme sacred tradition. (42)
When the wife is protected, the offspring is protected; for one's own self is born from her, therefore she must be protected, O Lord of Men. (43)
O King, for one who has no wife, there occurs a daily loss of dharma; there is also a failure in the performance of daily rites, and that indeed leads to a fall.
A wife must remain well-disposed toward her husband, even if he is ill-behaved; O Lord of Men, a wife who is ill-behaved yet unfortunate must still be supported. (45)
Having heard these words of his, the lord of men arrived and then beheld his beloved in the delightful Mahākālavana.
Seeing his beloved, adorned with the ornaments of good fortune, the fair-browed one who was worshipping Maheśvara, he embraced her with affection and replied to her.
O lady of beautiful countenance, tormented by separation from you, today my eyes have borne fruit and my life is truly well-lived. (48)

"O fortunate one, since I behold you, I have been made successful by you. Seeing her husband thus with great joy, she then looked at him and, filled with delight, said again and again, "Be gracious! (49)
Then that king, having embraced the beautiful woman with impetuosity, said: "O beloved, I am indeed pleased; why do you say it again and again? (50)
Then a union occurred, and a son was born who was exceedingly righteous; due to the majesty of that linga, he is celebrated by the name Datta. (51)
Incomparable good fortune was obtained by that goddess, O daughter of the Himavat; from that time forward, it has been known on earth as Saubhāgyeśvara.
O large-eyed daughter of the mountain, misfortune never arises in the lineage of those who behold the Lord Saubhāgyeśvara.
Through the worship of the Liṅga, there shall be no poverty, nor separation from kinsmen, sons, friends, or wife. (54)
O fair-faced one, those who behold the deity known as Saubhāgyeśvara shall have no fear of calamities, nor shall they experience any fear of malevolent planets and the like.

O Goddess, by beholding Saubhāgyeśvara, a person is born completely freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth and grain; honored in all the worlds, he becomes the sole treasury of good fortune. (56)

O lady of beautiful countenance, by beholding the Lord of Saubhāgya, a woman is born in this world as a sovereign ruler over the entire earth; she is never born sonless, nor destitute, nor wretched, nor afflicted by sorrow, nor indeed unfortunate. (57)
Neither widowhood, nor disease, nor untimely death shall befall one for the sake of prosperity; nor does suffering born of children or a husband arise from the sight of the Liṅga. (58)

Just as Lakṣmī is eternally the consort of Hari, Sāvitrī is remembered as the consort of Brahmā, Rohiṇī as the beloved of the Moon, and Śacī as the beloved of Śakra, even so does that woman become [the beloved] through the sight of the Lord of Good Fortune.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Saubhāgyeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear, O beloved, about Rūpeśvara.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Saubhāgyeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O beloved, know that the sixty-second deity is Rūpeśvara; by the mere sight of whom a man becomes endowed with beauty.

O Great Goddess, in the Pādma Kalpa there was a lord of the earth named Padma; born from the womb of a lotus, he was exceedingly valorous, powerful, and devoted to righteousness, ruling over the earth bounded by its four oceans. || 2 ||
Once that mighty-armed one, possessing abundant forces and vehicles, went into a dense forest surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants.
It was thick with *bilva*, *arka*, and *khadira* trees, crowded with *kapittha* and *dhava* trees, and filled with lions and other fierce beasts of the forest.
Having slain thousands of wild animals there along with his army and vehicles, the king entered another forest in pursuit of deer.
Alone and possessed of supreme strength, yet afflicted by hunger and thirst, he reached the edge of the forest and entered a vast wilderness.
Having passed even that, the king beheld an excellent hermitage, which produced great joy in the mind and was exceedingly beautiful to behold.
Covered with flowering trees and possessing exceedingly pleasant grassy meadows, the mighty-armed one then proceeded there alone, having dismissed those ministers.
He did not see that rishi of rigid vows in that hermitage; he cried out loudly, "Who is here?", as if making the forest resound.
Then, hearing that sound, the maiden—who was like the goddess Śrī incarnate—issued forth from that hermitage, assuming the appearance of an ascetic.
As soon as she saw that king, who was born from the interior of a lotus, she honored him with a seat and then asked his name.
