Then, smiling, she said, "What task shall be performed? Thereupon, the king spoke to that sweet-spoken maiden.
Having seen her of faultless limbs and having honored her duly, O illustrious lady, I have come here to attend upon the best of sages.
"O blessed one, O beautiful lady, tell me where the Blessed One has gone. Thus addressed by the king in that hermitage, the maiden, smiling, replied with these words of sweet syllables: (14)
"I am the daughter, O protector of the earth, of one who has observed celibacy since his youth, an ascetic, steadfast, knower of dharma, and high-minded. (15)
"Know me thus, O lord of men, as the daughter of Kaṇva; for, not knowing my own father, I considered Kaṇva to be my father. (16)
Having heard those words of hers, the king said, "O fair-faced one, it is very clear that you are a princess, O auspicious lady, for such as you speak. (17)
"O lady of beautiful hips, become my wife; tell me, what can I do for you? [I shall give you] gold, jewels, garments, earrings, and bracelets."

"O beautiful one, I take you today; become my wife, O lovely lady. O timid one, O beautiful one, take me through the Gāndharva rite alone; for among all forms of marriage, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, the Gāndharva is said to be the best. (19)
Having heard the king's words, the maiden spoke these words: "Wait for a moment; he will give me to you."
The king said: "O blameless one of beautiful limbs, I desire you who are devoted to me; know that for this purpose I stand here, for my mind has been stolen away by you. (21)
The self alone is one's kinsman, the self alone is one's refuge, and the self alone belongs to the self; therefore, you ought to bestow yourself upon yourself in accordance with Dharma.
The maiden said: "If this is indeed the path of dharma, and if I am my own mistress, then give me your solemn word of truth: you have given yourself to me today. (23)
O Pārvatī, having heard these words of hers, the king, overcome by desire, married her indeed by the Gāndharva rite.
Desired by the king as if she were his own wish, he then prepared to depart; in that interval, O Goddess, Kaṇva arrived at the hermitage.
Seeing her father, that maiden did not approach him out of modesty; but then the brahmin, possessed of divine knowledge and great ascetic power, recognized her.
Greatly enraged, he spoke to that maiden who was deluded by passion: "O wicked woman, since you have acted thus toward me in secret, having shown me contempt... (27)
Out of delusion, you shall choose your own husband yourself; therefore, O Kṛṣṇā, you will become despised, pitiless, wretched, shameless, and devoid of beauty. (28)
"This king, your husband, will be of wicked appearance. (29)
Having been addressed thus, that maiden instantly became bereft of beauty; and by the curse of that great-souled one, the king became deformed.
Then that maiden propitiated her father: "I am a young girl, ignorant and deluded, tormented by the god of love. (31)
O dear one, you ought to forgive the sin committed out of ignorance; O dear one, this lord of the earth is deeply devoted to his great vows.
I was not solicited by him, but rather I was the one who solicited that king; therefore, O father, you ought to show favor toward us both.
Having heard her words, that brahmin, filled with great compassion, spoke thus to his daughter, consoling her again and again.
"O daughter, I do not recall ever having spoken a falsehood even today; I consider fate alone to be supreme here—fie on my intellect, fie on my prowess! (35)
"O blameless one, since you have caused me to perform an improper act by force, I shall give you instruction; it behoves you to carry out its true meaning here. (36)
In the meritorious Mahākālavana, there exists a Liṅga that bestows beauty; situated to the east of Paśupatīśvara, it grants all desired objects.
Go quickly with your husband, the king, to that Tattva; for you shall obtain a form difficult to attain merely by the sight of the Liṅga.
Having been addressed thus, O beloved, that maiden then went with her husband to the delightful Mahākālavana, where there is an unsurpassed Liṅga.

And that king, the best of men, beheld her with supreme devotion; at that very moment, she possessed a divine body, exceedingly beautiful in form, clad in celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
And that king was born thus, with a form resembling Kandarpa, peerless in beauty in the world, as a result of seeing that linga. || 41 ||
Therefore, O beloved, the god Rūpeśvara is renowned throughout the worlds; he is the bestower of beauty, the giver of wealth in abundance, as well as the giver of sons and the giver of heaven.
And that king, having regained his own kingdom which was endowed with abundant crops and other riches, ruled without any thorns in his side together with his beloved queen.
Having ruled the kingdom, O Pārvatī, he went to heaven together with his wife, resplendent in body like a second sun.
Being honored in the abode of the gods by means of a brilliantly shining celestial chariot, he attained the state free from suffering upon seeing that Liṅga.
O large-eyed one, those who behold the god Śiva, the Lord of Form, are never deprived of beauty, nor of fame, nor of noble lineage.
O lady of excellent hips, those who behold this linga, which always bestows form and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, their worlds shall be eternally imperishable.
Those men who constantly worship the supreme deity Rūpeśvara go, honored by him, to my eternal world by means of a celestial vehicle.
He alone is truly virtuous in this world, and by him his lineage is adorned, who worships the Lord of Form, the bestower of beauty and good fortune. (49)
O Pārvatī, he who worships the Lord of Gods even incidentally becomes wealthy, handsome, and a king upon this earth.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Rūpeśvara, extending for a thousand bows, has been recounted to you.
Śrī Hara said: O Pārvatī, listen to the divine *Dhanuḥsāhasranāman*, the Lord consisting of sixty-three [verses], which destroys sin through its mere sight. 1.
There was a king on earth named Vidūratha, renowned for his fame; to him were born two sons, Sunīti and Sumati.
Once, while out in the forest on a hunt, that Vidūratha beheld a very large chasm, which appeared like the gaping mouth of the earth.
Seeing that, the king reflected, "What is this? I think it is a fissure to the netherworld, resembling the submarine fire."
As if lost in thought, he beheld there in the lonely forest an ascetic named Suvrata, a Brahmin free from all blemish.
The king asked him, "O twice-born one, what is this?"
The Brāhmaṇa said: "A Dānava of great heroism and fierce nature dwells in the netherworld (rasātala); known by the name Kujambha, he pierces this earth."
"O lord of the earth, how will you enjoy the kingdom without having conquered him? O king, it was by him that the brahmins were destroyed after they had gone out at night."
Likewise, the countries have been harassed and the hermitages destroyed; this powerful Daitya, armed with a mace, is causing devastation.
If you cause him, who dwells within the depths of Pātāla, to be slain, then you shall indeed become the sovereign lord of the entire earth.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having heard these words of the Brahmin and having heard that the mace was infallible, the king consulted with his ministers.
Then Mudāvatī, the daughter who was standing by his side, heard that mantra being recited by him together with his two sons and his ministers.
Then, after a few days, the Daitya Kujambha carried off that lotus-eyed maiden from the grove as she was surrounded by her female companions.
Having heard this, the protector of the earth, his eyes agitated with anger, said: "O sons, I know that great asura Kujaṃbha."
"O dear sons, when I previously saw a hole in the ground and was filled with doubt regarding it, I was questioned by that foremost of the twice-born, and he explained [the matter] to me. (15)
"Let that evil-minded abductor of Mudāvati be slain! Then, out of devotion to the king, they set forth, surrounded by their own armies.
Those two sons, having arrived there in Pātāla by their father’s command, fought with Kujaṃbha according to their own power, surrounded by their armies.
Then, with iron clubs, swords, spears, tridents, axes, and arrows, their battle became exceedingly long and truly fierce.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, by that Daitya who possessed the power of illusion, with his peerless and infallible mace, at that very moment—
The two princes of great strength, their armies destroyed in battle, were captured.
Then, having heard this, the protector of the earth became pale-faced; with his son bound, O Daughter of the Mountain, he fell into the utmost agony.

The king wept excessively and in many ways out of affection for his son. Then, while he was thus lamenting, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya appeared—he who had witnessed the higher and lower workings of numerous creations and dissolutions.

Resplendent like the rising sun, self-controlled, and a follower through seven kalpas, the great sage arrived in the presence of the king; he beheld the monarch lamenting and, knowing the three periods of time, spoke to him.
"Do not grieve, O protector of the earth; you are a Kṣatriya of firm vows. Where is grief, and where is a king who is invincible like a guardian of the world? (24)
"O best of kings, abandon this grief practiced by base men; exert yourself, O lord of kings, and you shall slay Kujaṃbha. (25)
Neither is Mount Meru’s peak too high, nor is the subterranean realm Rasātala too low; for one whose companion is resolve, even the great ocean is not far away.
Worship the Liṅga with a concentrated mind in Mahākālavana, situated to the south, beside the god Rūpeśvara. || 27 ||
The warding off of the club is equal to a thousand bows; you shall obtain that bow, O Indra among kings, and strike down Kujambha.

That Liṅga was protected by the best of warriors with bows measuring a thousand cubits; it was worshipped by the thousand-eyed Indra during the battle between the gods and the asuras, and it was by him that the bow was obtained, by which Jambha was indeed struck down. || 29 ||
Having heard those words of his, O Goddess, King Vidūratha then went swiftly to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
There he beheld that liṅga and worshipped it with devotion; the god, being pleased with him, then granted him a divine bow.

The warding off of the club was equal to a thousand bows. Then, having obtained that bow and having fastened his leather arm-guard and finger-protectors, the resolute king quickly went down into Pātāla through that opening.
Then that king produced an exceedingly fierce sound from his bowstring, by which the entire Pātāla was filled to its depths.
Then, hearing the sound of the bowstring, Kujaṃbha, the lord of the Dānavas, arrived in great fury, surrounded by his own army.
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, a battle took place between him and the king; when that Dānava had fought with him for three days, [he was overcome].
Then, his soul overcome with anger, he rushed toward Musala; meanwhile, he remained there being honored with perfumes, garlands, and incense.
As soon as he took up the pestle, Mudāvatī touched him repeatedly under various pretexts of applying sandalwood paste.
Then, having gone there, the lord of the asuras fought with a mace; at that time, those falls of the mace were rendered powerless by his bow.
Then, at the sound of the bowstring striking, the Dānava named Kujambha fell to the earth and went to the world of Vaivasvata.
Then a rain of flowers fell upon that lord of the earth; the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the celestial instruments resounded.
And that king, having slain him and then obtained his two sons and his daughter Mudāvatī, was filled with joy, his voice choked with emotion by the intensity of his delight. || 41 ||
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, accompanied by his two sons and with all his desires fully realized, he returned once more along with his harem and retinue.
In the delightful Mahākālavana, where that supreme liṅga is located, he worshipped it with jewels, garments, and ornaments.
Then, having been worshipped repeatedly by the gods and by Śakra, the king obtained a bow through the majesty of this Liṅga. || 44 ||
The Daitya Kujaṃbha, who was a hater of the gods, has also been slain; therefore, this bow shall attain fame by the name "Dhanuḥsāhasra" (the Thousand-armed).
Those who worship the Lord with devotion at Dhanuḥsāhasra, their enemies shall go to destruction; there is no doubt about this.
When Śiva, the lord of the gods of gods, who is ten thousand bows tall, is worshipped, all the gods are worshipped and become bestowers of boons; of this there is no doubt. (47)
Those men who daily bow to the auspicious Dhanuḥsāhasraka in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon, do not experience the sufferings of hell.
And just as the Gaṅgā among sacred fords is protected by the best of warriors, so too is this protecting deity named Dhanuḥsahasraka.
Therein are found various sacred fords (tīrthas), such as the Gaṅgā and others, which are highly secret, exceedingly meritorious, and instantly remove all sins. (50)
The fruit for those who behold it with devotion is declared to be that which is named Dhanuḥsāhasraka, which always brings about the destruction of enemies. (51)
O Goddess, this power of the god Dhanuḥsāhasra, which destroys sins, has been told to you; now hear about the god Paśupati.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Dhanuḥsāhasra," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 63 ||
Īśvara said: Listen to [the description of] the Lord named Paśupati, the sixty-fourth Īśvara, by the mere sight of whom the state of birth as an animal is no longer obtained. (1)
O Great Goddess, there was a king on earth renowned as Paśupāla; he was supremely righteous and devoted to the protection of cattle. || 2 ||
Once, desiring to see [the deity], he went toward the ocean; there he beheld five men standing prominently, and a woman with disheveled hair who was wandering about again and again.
Then the king, overcome by fear, fell unconscious; he was surrounded by those bandits, and especially by that woman.
Then others, arriving all at once, surrounded that best of kings; thus, with them all standing encircling him, the lord of the earth was besieged.
When the king was obstructed, all those bandits became united; they were struck down by Paśupāla, yet they did not die and rose up again.
Perceiving that audacity and the steadfastness of the king in battle, those ten robbers merged into the very body of that king.
They all became as if formless and merged into one; seeing them thus, King Paśupāla instantly became distressed.
Then the king saw Nārada, the bull among sages, the son of Brahmā, who was endowed with ascetic power, arriving; he questioned him at that time.
The cowherd said: "O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, today I have witnessed a marvel: suddenly five terrifying men arrived. (10)
Then, surrounded by those wicked ones, I was made distressed; though being struck with their fists, O twice-born one, I became composed in an instant.
Then five other men arrived and, having fought with me, said: "Let this lowest of kings, who desires liberation, be slain! Let him be slain! (12)
Thus, being excessively tormented by them, I again fell into a state of delusion; in the meantime, that woman spoke to me again and again.
"Be firm, O Great King; do not despair, O Lord! For these thieves are of little prowess, while you are capable; remain steadfast. (14)
O best of brahmins, by her word and through my fortitude in battle, those ten principal persons were conquered by me, O Lord, yet they did not die.
"Having heard the words of the cowherd, Nārada spoke these words: 'That certain woman must have merged into my body; who else could it be? (16)

Those men whom you saw merged within you and conquered in battle are your five sense organs (buddhīndriyas) and your five organs of action (karmendriyas). And that woman who was seen wandering by you, O best of kings, [is your mind]. (17)
Indeed, that intellect wanders in the form of the mind and is not stable; those [senses] were conquered long ago by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
He too was brought under the sway of anger by his senses and beloved objects, for no portion had been assigned to Śambhu by the Grandfather in his own sacrifice.
O King, Mahādeva, the Lord of the World and the agent of creation and destruction, being deluded by the senses, directed his wrath toward the gods.
For him, for whom the three worlds and all their sovereign powers exist merely for sport, he then strung his bow for the sake of receiving his share.
The teeth of Pūṣan were shattered and the Sun was deluded; the eyes of Bhaga were broken and the Sacrifice, in the form of a deer, was pierced.
The gods were turned into beasts, and the sages were deprived of the Vedas; likewise, the dharma-śāstras of the ṛṣis were seized by the All-pervading Lord.
Sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas say that the senses are difficult to conquer; but that intellect which takes the form of the mind is exceedingly difficult to conquer. (24)
"Therefore, O King, O mighty-armed one, do not indulge in vain despair. Having heard those words of the high-souled Nārada, O Great Goddess, Paśupāla began to speak.
Paśupāla said: "O Blessed One, how were the gods, led by Śakra, liberated? And how was even Brahmā released from the state of a beast? I wish to hear this; let it be told. (26)
Having heard those words of his, Nārada spoke again: "Even while they had attained the state of animals, the gods were accompanied by the ṛṣis and munis. (27)
Placing Brahmā at their head, they went for refuge to the Lord; the God, who bestows grace upon his devotees, was gratified by their hymns of praise.
He spoke these words to the king: "Tell me what must be done."
The gods said: "O Lord Maheśvara, if you are pleased with us as before, O God, grant us knowledge of the Vedas and the Śāstras; do not delay."
Īśvara said: "All of you are indeed bound souls (paśus); come with me to the sacred field of Mahākālavana, which grants liberation from the state of being a bound soul."

"I shall become your husband, and from that you will attain liberation. Out of compassion for you and for the sake of favoring the worlds, I shall exist in the form of a *liṅga* by the name Paśupatīśvara. (32)

Then all those thirty gods, having beheld that Lord, were liberated from their state as sacrificial animals; filled with joy, they departed for heaven. Brahmā, with a serene inner soul, spoke to Paśupati: ||| 33 ||

O Lord of Gods, those who behold you endowed with supreme devotion—for them, O Lord, as well as for their ancestors who have fallen into the state of beasts due to the ripening of their own past actions—there shall be liberation. (34)
Whatever sin is committed by men, whether through ignorance or even knowingly, may that sin go to dissolution by the worship of that deity. (35)
Those men are beasts in this world; what is the fruit of their life, by whom Paśupati—the liberator from the womb of animals—has not been seen? (36)
Whatever sin has been accumulated in childhood, youth, infancy, or old age, that evil is dissolved upon seeing Śiva, the Lord of Creatures.
O God, when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, those men who behold you—you shall be the granter of boons to them and the constant fulfiller of their desires. || 38 ||
Just as a gift of gold given to a worthy recipient at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse is said to be inexhaustible and imperishable, so too [is this]. (39)
O Lord of Gods, by beholding him for even a single day in the month of Pauṣa, men will likewise attain that [merit]; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Having spoken thus, O King, the blessed Brahmā, having accomplished his purpose and with a joyful heart, departed for the world of Brahmā along with the sages and poets.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, if you desire the supreme goal, go to Mahākālavana to the south of Indreśvara and propitiate that Liṅga which grants liberation from animal birth. || 42 ||
Having heard those words of the high-souled Nārada, O beloved, Paśupāla also went to Mahākālavana; by the sight of that Liṅga, he attained the supreme goal.
This sin-destroying majesty of the deity named Paśupati has been recounted to you, O Goddess; now hear about the auspicious Brahmeśvara.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Paśupatīśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Hara said: O beloved, know that Brahmeśvara is numbered as sixty-fifth; by the mere sight of whom the world of Brahmā is indeed attained.
The lord of the Daityas named Puloman, possessed of great strength and prowess, dwells there while being honored by thousands of Paulomas.
They too honored that Daitya, just as the gods honor the Lord of the Suras; and on one occasion, he spoke these words in the presence of the Daityas.
Even today, [the power] of the world-protectors—the Sun, the Moon, Fire, and Water; of Śatakratu (Indra), Dhaneśa (Kubera), Yama, and Varuṇa—[remains].
If that indeed be the case, what use have I for asceticism or for life? Such as I am, I shall put all the inhabitants of heaven to flight.
"Surrounded by all these exceedingly powerful Pauloma [demons]," having spoken thus, O Goddess, he went to the ocean accompanied by the Daityas; there, he suddenly beheld Madhusūdana lying down.
Having beheld him, who possessed a luster like an autumnal cloud—a dense mass appearing at midday—he then spoke to his followers and the Daityas.
This Madhusūdana is indeed the thunderbolt for the mountain of the Dānavas; he is the one who pronounces the decree of widowhood upon the wives of his enemies, who are the beloveds of Fame.
He is the destroyer of the leafy creepers that were the beloved wives of the Daityas; he is the supreme one who has proclaimed the widowhood of our bride, Victory.
Free from fear, he alone always sleeps with a crooked intent; this wicked man, who was desired and has come into my sight, must be slain with haste.

Having spoken thus, that lord of the Daityas, Puloman, filled with extreme rage, rushed with speed toward the Grandfather who was right before him; he beheld him meditating again and again within the navel-lotus.
Then, seeing that wonder—the army of the lions among the Daityas, difficult to conquer in battle—approaching, Brahmā fell into a state of agitation.
Then the mighty enemy of Kaiṭabha, having quickly regained consciousness, saw Puloman before him, surrounded by his own army.
Invincible in battle and steadfast, he spoke this to Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said: "Let an effort be made for the destruction of Puloman; having obtained a boon, that Daitya will suddenly overcome me."
Therefore, go with haste to the auspicious Mahākālavana; there you shall behold the supreme Liṅga that has existed since seven kalpas.
To the north of Cyavaneśa is the place endowed with Śiva-śakti; by the majesty of that Liṅga, one shall obtain eternal strength.
"Bring water from the pool that constantly touches the hand of Kuṇḍeśvara; having taken it, let him be killed with it. || 18 ||
Having heard these words of his, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived in an instant at the place where that supreme liṅga was located.
Having seen him, the Grandfather (Brahmā) suddenly offered praise with devotion.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you of divine form; salutations to you of manifold forms; salutations to you of irresistible valor; salutations to you whose self is the activity of the universe.
Salutations to the one with tawny matted hair; salutations to the wearer of the crescent moon; salutations to the golden-hued one; salutations to the dweller in the forest.
I bow to you, the sustainer of all beings, the eternal destroyer of enemies, whose golden armlets jingle, and who bears the full orb of the moon.

I bow to you, the sovereign of the thirty gods, the sovereign of the universe, the Great Lord, whose flood of worldly suffering has been exhausted, and whose state is eternally meditated upon by sages.
I ever revere you, O God, the destroyer of the hosts of Daityas, who bear the axe, the sharp-edged spear, the trident-tip, the bow, the sword, and the mace.
Thus praised, the Blessed One, Maheśvara in the form of a liṅga, spoke with a slightly smiling face to Brahmā, the cause of the world.
"O Grandfather, what is desired by you that I may do today? What shall I give? O best of sages, why do you praise me? Why are you seen to be distressed? (27)
O beloved, having heard these words of the Liṅga spoken by Brahmā at that time, the Liṅga then related the entire account in detail.
"O Lord of Speech, take this water born from the weapon that wards off enemies; you shall slay Puloman along with his army in a mere instant. (29)
Thus addressed, Brahmā went in haste to where Janārdana was; with that water, he caused those Daityas to fall upon the earth.
That Pulomā was Mahān in the Svārociṣa Manvantara; Kṛṣṇa also came to Kuśasthalī together with Brahmā.

There Janārdana beheld that Liṅga and gave it a name: "Since the Lord has been praised by Brahmā for the sake of showing me favor, therefore it shall attain fame in the worlds by the name Brahmeśvara. (32)
Those men who behold the god Śiva as Brahmeśvara with devotion shall ascend to the world of Brahmā and come into my presence.
But that man who, even by chance, beholds the auspicious Lord Brahmeśvara, has accomplished all his duties and shall never grieve over death.
The merit of a person who, having gone to Puṣkara, performs austerities for a hundred years, is even greater than that of another who beholds Brahmeśvara. || 35 ||
Even that mortal of wicked mind who is burdened with the five great sins shall go to the abode of Śiva upon beholding the auspicious Brahmeśvara.
Whatever fruit is obtained from ten Cāndrāyaṇa penances performed according to the rules, that same fruit one attains by the sight of Brahmeśvara.
Having spoken thus, O beloved, Viṣṇu went to the eternal Vaikuṇṭha; then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, went to the world of Brahmā.
This sin-destroying majesty of the god Brahmeśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Jalpeśvara.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 65 ||
Īśvara said: O beloved, know that the sixty-sixth deity is Jalpeśvara, by the mere sight of whom even great sin goes to its pacification.
O Great Goddess, there was a king on earth renowned as Jalpana; he was constantly engaged in speech, always initiating debates and discussions. || 2 ||
Constantly full of conceptual constructions and contemplating the course of saṃsāra, five sons of great strength were born, headed by Subāhu. (3)

O lady of beautiful hips, that king had five sons who were like the five fires personified: Subāhu, Śatrumardī, Jaya, Vijaya, and Vikrānta as the fifth; all of them were masters of weapons and missiles.
By the father, King Jalpa, they were all established in separate kingdoms; indeed, all those sons were made lords of separate regions.
In the east was King Subāhu; in the south, Śatrumardana; in the west, King Jaya; and in the north, King Vijaya.
The one known as Vikrānta was appointed to his own position in the center; having established such an arrangement, he himself departed for the forest.
They had ministers who were well-wishers and hereditary by lineage; at that time, they enjoyed their respective kingdoms together with those ministers.
And there was a minister of Vikrānta who was solely devoted to conceptual thought; he spoke to King Vikrānta in a secluded place.
He who possesses this entire earth is proclaimed to be truly capable; by such exertion, the high-souled Vāsava attained his station.
And the nectar was obtained by the thirty gods through their exertion, O lord of the earth.
Those men who are deficient in effort, and especially those Kṣatriyas, become objects of ridicule day by day due to their lack of valor.

"A brother, greedy for the kingdom, shows affection for the sake of wealth; by that very power of wealth, the king finds contentment. O King, why then is counsel not accepted? Your entire kingdom is being enjoyed by me, the minister, through force. (14)
Even a stranger who is beneficial is a kinsman, while even a kinsman who is harmful is a stranger; a disease born of one's own body is harmful, whereas medicine from the forest is beneficial. 15.
These swallow up the earth, just as serpents dwelling in holes swallow their prey: namely, a king who offers no resistance and a Brahmin who does not travel abroad.
Everything is deluded by illusion; who indeed is the kinsman of whom? Therefore, let an effort be made immediately to restrain the brothers.
All brothers have been slain by their own brothers for the sake of the kingdom; and knowing the eternal Dharma, the Asuras were slain by the gods. (18)
Having heard these words of the minister, the king was filled with wonder; laughing, he replied, "This enemy of mine has arrived. (19)
Vikrānta said: "We five brothers desire the earth; being dissatisfied with separate sovereignties, how shall it become ours in its entirety? (20)
The eldest brother was Subāhu, and the second was Śatrumardana; Jaya and Vijaya were also among them, since I am the youngest of them all. (21)
The minister said: "They honor the eldest, established in the kingdom, with the finest marks of worship. But what is this 'eldest' or 'youngest' among men who strive for the kingdom? (22)
When the king Vikrānta had thus promised, the minister then caused the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra) to be performed.
The priest performed the rite with an Atharvaṇa mantra; once it was known by their priests, they too performed it with concentrated minds.
Then, once the Kṛtyā had arisen, four other Kṛtyās subsequently emerged and simultaneously devoured those [demons], along with their priests and servants.
Then, great wonder arose among all the people, since those inhabitants of separate cities perished at one and the same time.
Then, having heard of the death of his sons, King Jalpaka questioned Vasiṣṭha in the forest: "O Blessed One, O Lord, what is this? (27)
The high-souled Vasiṣṭha related everything to him as well; by means of his divine knowledge, he told the account, and the king resolved his doubt.
The king said: "I am the cause of this destruction; fie, fie upon my birth! Five Brahmins have died along with you and the sons of the ministers. (29)
Who else on this great earth could be more devoted to sin than I? If I were never to be born again upon the surface of the world... (30)
Then my sons and priests would not perish; shame on this kingdom, shame on my birth, and shame on the great lineage of kings! (31)

I, who have become the cause of the destruction of the twice-born—those priests of my sons who, while performing their duty for you, O Lord, met their end—am not wicked; rather, it is I who am wicked as the cause of that destruction. (32)
With his heart thus agitated, King Jalpa again humbly questioned Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among the wise.
The king said: "O Blessed One, tell me of a holy place (tīrtha) that always prevents separation; O Brahmin, or else, O Lord, tell me of a Liṅga that instantly removes sin. (34)
O Pārvatī, having heard those words of King Jalpa, Vasiṣṭha spoke by means of his divine knowledge.
"Go and, by my command, speak to the supreme Mahākālavana where Rāma performs penance after having rid the earth of Kṣatriyas; there, to the west of Kukkuṭeśvara, is the beginningless Liṅga. (36)
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, propitiate him while staying in the hermitage of Jamadagni. Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, that king Jalpa [departed].
Leaving the Devadāru forest, he went to Mahākālavana; there he beheld that primordial Liṅga praised by the gods, and he worshipped it according to the rules with supreme meditative concentration.

Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, a voice arose from the midst of the Liṅga: "You are not a perpetrator of sinful deeds, nor are you the cause of death; the unseen [karmic] cause lies there for these sons, the kings, and the brahmins. (39)
Having gone to the city of Vaivasvata by virtue of their own karmic fruition, do not grieve, O Indra among kings; the course of karma is profound.
"O best of kings, I am pleased by this pure disposition. Name whatever boon you desire; I shall grant it to you, and not otherwise. (41)
The king said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, let there be no further birth for me in this terrible ocean of worldly existence."
"Grant me imperishable fame; may I be renowned on earth by my name. This Lord Jalpeśvara, the omnipresent one, has been propitiated through my eloquence. (43)

"Let all the thirty gods speak: this is the boon I find difficult to obtain. May those men who behold you, having attained fame through my name, never suffer separation from their sons or even from their wealth. (44)
May they have no fear of saṃsāra, nor from robbers, nor even from kings; may they never have fear of spirits, seizing demons, or diseases. (45)
May there always be auspiciousness for those whom you have come to behold; blessed are they in the world of mortals who have come to you for refuge.
O Lord, whatever merit is obtained by men through ablutions at all sacred fords, all of that—and even more—is gained from the sight of you. (47)
They fall into this terrible saṃsāra, crowded with hundreds of miseries, as long as that God, the savior from the ocean of worldly existence, is not beheld. 48.
O Lord, when the evil of men is exhausted, then they may have a vision of You; this occurs only through great merit, not by means of slight austerity.
Having said, "It shall be so," O Pārvatī, he entered his own body by means of that *liṅga* while all the gods were looking on.

O lady of beautiful countenance, when that king Jalpa attained dissolution into that liṅga, the god became renowned on the surface of the earth as Jalpeśvara; he is declared by the gods to be the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is remembered as the eternal granter of desired boons. || 51 ||
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the god Jalpeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear that which is known as Kedāra.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Jalpeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 66 ||
Īśvara said: O lady of excellent hips, hear now of the deity named Kedāreśvara, numbered as the sixty-seventh, who destroys sins through his mere sight. (1)
O Goddess, in ancient times at the time of creation, the gods were indeed pervaded by cold; afflicted by the chill and overwhelmed, they all went to Brahmā for refuge. || 2 ||
"O God, Lord of the World, we are all afflicted by Himādri; O Four-faced One, Grandfather, protect us who are terrified! Salutations be unto you. (3)
O beloved, having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā indeed spoke: "She is being oppressed by the Himālaya mountain, the father-in-law of Śaṅkara."
"I am not capable of going; this which I have spoken is the truth. O Mahādeva, when the gods have perished, no other refuge exists. (5)
That very god shall be the refuge for all of us; by his command, all these mountains were fashioned by me in the past.
I have formed a manifold plan, and I have created the Himālaya mountain—a peak that is unapproachable, invincible, and inaccessible to all living beings.
The Lord Maheśvara is the ruler of that very Himācala; therefore, O gods, we shall go to Kailāsa, the best of mountains.

"Where the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods and the Soul of the Universe, resides. Having spoken thus, Brahmā went with the gods into my presence; he was seen by me, honored by them, and I was praised by them with various hymns.
The gods were honored by me, and the four-faced one was worshipped; having worshipped him, I questioned Brahmā regarding the cause of his departure.
"O Grandfather, what business do you have with the thirty gods that you have come? O beloved, everything told by Brahmā has been heard by me."
Having summoned Himācala, I established the boundaries [of his domain], and Himādri was installed in the sovereignty over all mountains.
The domains of the gods, and likewise those of the gandharvas, as well as those of the yakṣas, the nāgas, and the kinnaras. || 13 ||
Established separately for the pleasure of the Vidyādharas, this lord of mountains shines in form like pure crystal.
He whose crown is the cascade of the Jāhnavī, and likewise the progenitor of Śarvāṇī.
It was made divine, consisting of all the gods and containing all sacred fords; it was the abode of all stages of life and frequented by all the immortals.
Having thus established the Lord of Mountains, I remain in the form of a Liṅga, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Kedāreśvara. || 17 ||
O beloved, I have created water there filled with mantras; I have proclaimed the various greatness of both the Liṅga and the water.

O fair-faced one, whatever man comes here and worships me properly with devotion, or whoever takes water right here according to the prescribed rite, I shall undoubtedly abide within his belly in the form of a Liṅga.
When these words were spoken, O Goddess, the gods, asuras, and pannagas, along with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, vaitālas, and kiṃnaras, [were present].
And the hosts of Vidyādharas, longing for a sight of me, arrived there, O lady of beautiful hips, after drinking that auspicious water.

O beloved, I was seen by them in the form of a Liṅga according to the prescribed rite; established on that excellent mountain, they became equal to me, being worshipped by the Siddhas residing in Janaloka, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Then, after a long time, having heard of the supreme majesty of the god Kedāreśvara and especially of his water, || 23 ||
"O large-eyed one, since those humans who have arrived here are full of passion (rajas) and dominated by darkness (tamas), I then assumed the body of a buffalo."
He did this for the sake of instilling fear in them, yet they did not become afraid; here was a god, there was a god, and they wandered about, desiring to see him.

"O Great Goddess, because I was in the form of Mahiṣa, I was not seen by them; I remained there with an unperceivable form. Consequently, they became dejected in mind, agitated, sighing heavily, and fell into a state of supreme world-weariness."
"Here there is no god, no sacred fords, and no Ganges that bestows merit; there is neither dharma nor the next world—all of this is mere mockery. (27)
Thus, indeed, it is heard in the Purāṇas and always in the Śruti that at Kedāra on the Himālaya there is a Liṅga that bestows liberation.
O illustrious lady, while those humans were speaking thus, a voice arose from the sky, uttered by me out of compassion.
Do not speak here of what is not the path; the imperishable Śrutis are not to be censured. The Purāṇa was not proclaimed otherwise by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Those atheists who revile the Purāṇas and the treatises on Dharma go to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
The god Kedāra, who bestows heaven and liberation, is always present here; though he is constantly worshipped by the thirty deities, he is never seen.

Himavat performed worship for eight eternal months; by that merit, Himādri was made the king of mountains among all mountains, worthy of service, delightful, and saluted by all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 33 ||
It is a treasury of all jewels and likewise beloved by the gods; during both the summer and the spring, the God of Gods is seen here. (34)
If at all times, for human beings, through the very power of fixed time, the supreme wisdom has always arisen regarding the vision of me; 35.
I shall declare the means for that; listen with full attention. No doubt should be entertained here; you shall attain all your desires.

O men, Mahākālavana is declared to be the most excellent of all sacred fields, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and remaining imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution. (37)
There I shall manifest out of compassion for the worlds, in the form of a *liṅga*, on the meritorious and most beautiful bank of the Śiprā.
To the west of the god Someśvara is an excellent place; I shall go to that well-known site under the name Kedāreśvara. (39)
There, my vision shall be with them at all times; and I shall grant all desires to everyone, of this there is no doubt. (40)

"In this world, I shall give you even more than the fruit [of your merit] obtained from that. Having heard these divine, heart-gladdening words, which arose from the sky and were pleasing to the mind, all those men— (41)
They went to the Mahākāla forest, recollecting Maheśvara with various mental constructs, thinking, "This is indeed the truth, and not otherwise. (42)
Having bathed in the holy waters of the Śiprā, as long as they behold the sun, for that long the sin-destroying Liṅga remains within the range of their vision.
Then, filled with joy, they said: "This is Kedāra, there is no doubt; it has been seen by us, without a shadow of doubt, and the Gaṅgā stands within the waters of the Śiprā. (44)
Then they worshipped me with various kinds of flowers; O large-eyed one, O lovely-faced one, being thus worshipped by them, I was pleased.
An exceedingly rare and supreme boon has been granted; on Kailāsa, an excellent station has been bestowed—an imperishable state from which there is no return.
Therefore, I was addressed by the thirty gods as Kedāreśvara; I was entreated with supreme devotion out of compassion for the worlds. (47)
O Lord, you must grant a greater reward to those men who, having come here, behold you with true devotion. (48)
On the Himālaya mountain, men daily obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage to the Lord of Snow; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (49)
Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—any man who associates with such people becomes a doer of sin upon seeing you.
He too goes to the supreme abode, from which there is no return. One obtains that same fruit by beholding Kedāreśvara which is gained by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penances for a hundred years. 51.
Those men are like beasts in this world, and their birth is useless, by whom the Lord of Kedāra, known as Mahākāleśvara, has not been seen. || 52 ||
Whatever sin has been accumulated during childhood, youth, infancy, or old age, that sin goes to complete destruction by the sight of Kedāreśvara. (53)
Whatever merit is declared to result from a pilgrimage to the Himalayas, one obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kedāreśvara.
O Goddess, having been addressed thus by the gods with prostrations, I replied, "So be it," and those gods also departed for heaven.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of the deity Kedāreśvara has been told to you; now hear about the one named Piśāca.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kedāreśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: O Goddess, listen with diligence to the Lord named Piśāca, who is numbered as the sixty-eighth; by the mere sight of him, sins are destroyed.
In the beginning of the Kali age, O Goddess, there was a Śūdra who possessed great wealth; he was well-known by the name Soma, an atheist and a reviler of the Vedas.
He was hostile to Brahmins, cruel, miserly, and shameless; he was a betrayer of trust and devoted to seizing the property of others. || 3 ||
A destroyer of the three aims of life for others and one who follows only his own desires—he, O Goddess, once died with the greatest suffering.
In the Maru country there was a Piśāca who was naked, wretched, and terrifying; he was the destroyer of other Piśācas and the exterminator of his own kind. || 5 ||
Many exceedingly powerful piśācas were crushed by him.
Then, at one time, Śākaṭāyana—the learned scholar, eloquent, devoted to tranquility, and intent upon the private recitation of the Vedas—returned by that very same path.
Resembling the rising sun and possessing a splendor equal to fire, he always travels by means of a chariot while gazing [at you], O Daughter of the Mountain.
Having gone there, he beheld that fierce and terrifying Piśāca; overcome by hunger and desiring to devour him, the Piśāca rushed toward him.
Having seen that Brahmin Śākaṭāyana mounted upon the cart, having heard the sound of the cart, and having beheld the form of the twice-born one; || 10 ||
A Piśāca of such a kind, rendered deaf in both ears and intent on saving himself, fled with great difficulty, O Pārvatī. Seeing that Piśāca running away, the Brāhmaṇa said to him: ||| 11 ||
"O Piśāca, you appear terrified and seem to be in great haste; where are you running? Tell me, from what has this fear come upon you? (12)
The Piśāca said: Having heard the terrifying roar of this great cart, he has become deaf in both ears; he has lost consciousness from the mere sight of you.
The Brāhmaṇa said: It is heard that among the Piśācas, the Brahmarākṣasas are the most powerful; you are such a renowned Brahmarākṣasa who desires to devour me. (14)

The Piśāca said: "I am capable among the Piśācas, yet I have been ruined by the sight of you. For death is indeed a source of misery for all, and life is very difficult to obtain; therefore, out of fear, I flee for the sake of my life and for the sake of happiness. (15)
The Brāhmaṇa said: O Piśāca, whence can there be happiness for you? Death is indeed better for you; the wretched Piśāca birth is produced only for sinners. (16)
The Piśāca said: "Indeed, wherever a living being goes, it surely becomes a locus of happiness. Therefore, I wish to live; be gracious, O Brahmarākṣasa! (17)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "I do not desire to eat you; I am a Brāhmaṇa, not a Rākṣasa. I wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of the welfare of all living beings. (18)
A Brāhmaṇa is said to be one who possesses friendliness toward all living beings; do not fear me, for I have attained a state of friendship.
Having heard those words of his, the Piśāca, with a composed mind, bowed down and replied thus to the Brahmin Śākaṭāyana: || 20 ||
If you have indeed granted the gift of fearlessness to all beings, and if you have attained a state of friendship through action, mind, and speech; 21.
I ask you, O illustrious one, for a doubt resides in my heart; having heard it, you ought to explain it to me correctly out of compassion. (22)
By what ripening of karma does a human being go to the state of a Piśāca? And how is liberation from the state of a Piśāca attained despite those sinful deeds? (23)
Having heard these words of the Piśāca, O lady of beautiful countenance, Śākaṭāyana, overcome by the sense of "mine," spoke to him.
And having stolen the property of Brahmins and especially the property of the gods, those most wicked ones, by that sin, go to the state of being Piśācas.
A man who deceives his father, mother, wife, child, or a twice-born brahmin and steals their wealth shall become a piśāca.
He who, having taken royal property, neither performs sacrifice nor gives it away, nourishes only himself and goes to the state of a piśāca. || 27 ||
Those who are betrayers of trust, those who are devoted to the wives of others, and likewise those who revile the Vedas, attain the state of Piśācas. (28)
Those men who always revile the ancient scriptures of Dharma and are constantly backbiters become Piśācas. || 29 ||
Thus I have now told you everything according to the authority of the Vedas; now I shall tell you who you are born as—listen to that.
"You are a Śūdra named Somaka, a revealer of the secrets of others, born as a betrayer of trust and a defiler of gods and Brāhmaṇas. (31)
An atheist who has broken the bounds of conduct causes his entire family to fall into a most terrible hell even in this seventh birth.
Having reached the womb of a piśāca, you will again attain Raurava, as well as the hells known as Mahāraurava, Krakaca, Kālasūtraka, the fierce Yaṃtrapīḍanaka, Mathana, and Kumbhavāluka.
O illustrious lady, as that Brahmin was speaking thus, he remembered his own former birth, which had been base despite his association with the virtuous.
Overwhelmed by suffering and motionless, repeatedly crying out "Fie! Fie!", O Goddess, he fell upon the ground and then spoke these words: || 35 ||
"Aha! By some merit of mine—though I am one of little merit, wretched and miserable—this meeting with you has come to pass. (36)
There is no friend equal to the Dharma; there is no destination equal to the Dharma; there is no protection equal to the Dharma; and yet that [Dharma], O Lord, does not exist for me. (37)
"I am submerged in a vast ocean of suffering; I am mired in the mud of sin; I have wandered in blinding darkness; therefore, I have come to you for refuge. (38)
Salutations to you, O highly fortunate one! Command me, what shall I do? This which was ordained by the power of your asceticism has now been attained by me. (39)
O fair-faced one, as that piśāca was speaking thus, the brahmin Śākaṭāyana recounted his own greatness.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth reaching to the ocean, and whatever holy fields are here, this field is the most merit-bestowing among them.
The sacred field of Mahākālavana remains imperishable even at the time of universal dissolution; therein, within that great field, is the Liṅga that destroys the state of being a Piśāca.

To the south of the god Ḍhuṇḍheśvara, there exists another Piśāca shrine, worshipped by the thirty gods, which destroys the state of being born as a Piśāca; merely by seeing it, you will be liberated from the condition of a Piśāca. || 43 ||
O fair-faced one, having heard those words of his, that piśāca then arrived with haste and paid homage to the twice-born man.
In the meritorious Mahākālavana, which bestows desired fruits, he beheld that liṅga there after bathing in the auspicious waters of the Śiprā.
O lady of beautiful countenance, by the sight of that linga, that piśāca at that very moment became possessed of a divine body and adorned with celestial ornaments.
Having uplifted his entire lineage, both maternal and paternal, he ascended a divine celestial chariot and departed for the eternal world.

Having beheld that great marvel and the excellence of his majesty for the sake of prosperity, it was proclaimed by the gods stationed in their celestial chariots, as well as by the Siddhas traveling through the sky.
"Even a Piśāca has gone to heaven by the sight of this Liṅga; therefore, that deity shall become famous on the surface of the earth by the name Piśāceśvara, the destroyer of all sins. (49)

O Goddess, those men who behold the one known as Piśāceśvara—their ancestors, even those situated in hell, are immediately liberated from the state of being a piśāca and go to heaven; of this there is no doubt. || 50 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained from the Aśvamedha sacrifice when it is properly performed, that same fruit he also obtains simply by the sight of the Lord of the Piśācas.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to arise from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā, that merit is known to be even greater from the sight of Piśāceśvara. || 52 ||
Those who behold the one known as Piśāceśvara on the fourteenth day—for them, neither the state of a preta nor the state of a piśāca shall arise within their lineage. || 53 ||
That man who, even by chance, beholds the one known as Piśāceśvara, does not go to a womb of lower birth nor does he behold hell. (54)
Endowed with all sovereign powers and accompanied by all his kinsmen, he rejoices in the world of the ancestors upon beholding the Lord of the Piśācas. (55)
By chanting its name one is liberated from sin, and by seeing it one goes to heaven; by touching this linga, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
At that very moment, that man is liberated from the shackles of saṃsāra and other bonds, as soon as he beholds the Liṅga known as Piśāceśvara.
Whatever fruit belongs to sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—that fruit arises multiplied ten millionfold from the sight of him.
If one should behold [the deity] on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha as well as Kārttika, his merit becomes incalculable; there is no doubt in this matter. || 59 ||
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Piśāceśvara has been recounted to you; now let the [majesty] of Saṅgameśvara be heard.
The Lord said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen with diligence to the sixty-ninth [chapter], by the mere sight of which union is always attained. (1)
O Goddess, in the kingdom of Kaliṅga there was a king named Subāhu, renowned on earth, a performer of sacrifices, and supremely righteous.
His wife was Viśālākṣī, the daughter of Dṛḍhadhanvan, who resided in Kāñcīpura and was devoted to the vows of the kṣatriya.
Due to their mutual affection, the two of them experienced supreme joy; however, that king’s headache always arose at midday.
O beloved, the medicinal formulations prescribed by those foremost among the knowers of Āyurveda and physicians of the body result in an increase in suffering day by day.
When a great deal of time had passed in this manner, O Goddess, the large-eyed lady, afflicted by grief for her husband, replied to the lord of the earth: (6)

"O Lord of the Earth, how is it that this old age has afflicted you with a disease of the head? O King, many physicians, experts in various sciences, are striving to cure it, yet even so, it does not subside. || 7 ||
Thus addressed by his beloved, Subāhu, the lord of the earth, replied with affection to his dear wife who was full of love for him.
O Goddess, the body of all embodied beings is the locus of pleasure and pain; pleasure and pain arise in accordance with their past karma.
Thus addressed by that king, O lady of beautiful countenance, the queen, being deeply distressed, spoke once more to him with heartfelt affection regarding that very same matter.
When she, though strictly forbidden, continued to question him again and again, the king laughed and spoke to that queen.
If you desire to hear the origin of this disease, O Goddess, I shall certainly not fail to explain its cause to you here in accordance with reality.
"Having gone to Mahākālavana, which is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, I shall tell you about it there, if you have curiosity. (13)
"O lady of pure smiles, I shall go with you tomorrow at dawn. Having heard these words of his, the queen stood there amazed, eager to depart for the auspicious Mahākālavana.
Then, when that night had passed, at dawn, that best of kings set out together with his wife, surrounded by a great army.
In due course, the wise king arrived at the auspicious Mahākālavana and then established his residence on the bank of the Śiprā.
There flows the Gaṅgā, which travels through the three paths and descends into the netherworld; and there is a second river, the Nīlagangā, which has joined with the Śiprā.
And at their confluence is that Liṅga, Saṃgameśvara, which was worshipped together with Gaṅgā, Śiprā, and Nīlagangā.
Then, when Subāhu had arrived, that queen, filled with wonder and full of affection, asked: "O Lord, let the reason for this be told; indeed, I shall relate that which you previously mentioned. (19)
Thus addressed by his beloved, Subāhu, the lord of the earth, replied to his beloved with affection, laughing again and again.
"Sleep peacefully, O lady of auspicious limbs; we are weary, O blameless one. At dawn, I shall explain the cause of my headache. (21)
Then, when that night had passed, at dawn, the best of kings recounted the majesty of the divine Parameṣṭhin.
I was always a base Śūdra, a reviler of the Vedas, and a constant betrayer of trust; you, too, were exactly like that.
A son was born who was ill-behaved, a deceiver of gods and Brahmins; he was ugly, harsh, wicked, and by nature a sinful man.
Then, after a long time, a terrifying twelve-year drought occurred, causing fear to all living beings.
But separation from you, as well as from my son, has been obtained by me; therefore, consumed by grief, I have attained supreme detachment.
Desiring my immediate destruction, I have spoken these words; for I am devoid of merit and devoted to sinful thoughts. (27)
Reunion with one's wife is difficult to obtain again; how can that most wicked man sleep after having committed such a terrible sin? (28)

Thus, for the sake of his family, he acts alone and crosses over [suffering]; dharma alone is the supreme kinsman, dharma alone is the supreme refuge; everything is accomplished through dharma, therefore one should take recourse in dharma. (29)
O beloved, as I was reflecting thus intensely, my life-breaths departed; I underwent various torments in millions of hells.
Even at the time of my end, I offered praise to the Dharma; by that merit, I have been born as a fish in the auspicious waters of the Śiprā.
And you, Śyenī, were born from him in that very same excellent forest when the rainy season had arrived and the sun had entered the constellation Āśleṣā.
Having emerged from those waters with the speed of the three rivers, I was encountered by you at my head and pierced by your nails, O beautiful one. (33)
O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, I have been brought by fishermen into the presence of Saṅgameśvara; I have met my death along with you.
As I was dying, I beheld that god Saṃgameśvara, who was being bathed profusely by the Śiprā, the Gaṅgā, and the Nīlagaṅgā.
O Goddess, by the mere sight of him, I became the lord of the earth in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, honored by all kings.
You have been born as a beloved daughter to the dweller of Kāñcīpura, who is devoted to the vows of a kṣatriya, fortunate, and possessed of a firm bow. (37)
We two attained kingship through the sight of that liṅga; you, however, were pierced by its claws and struck down by those very clubs. (38)
Remembering that slaughter at midday, my head then ached; yet, upon seeing this deity, I remember my own previous birth.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, which I was previously asked by you; go, O beautiful one, may it be well with you, wherever your mind desires.
I must remain right here; this Lord Saṅgameśvara is to be served by me.
Then she, whose limbs were faultless and whose eyes were like blue lotuses, spoke these words to her husband in a piteous yet melodious voice: || 42 ||
"O Lord, I too have recollected my conduct in a previous birth; even while dwelling in an animal womb, it was all due to the majesty of this linga. (43)
We have attained human birth and been born into stainless families; we have obtained incomparable fortune in this world and acquired a kingdom free from thorns.
I have become your beloved wife, and you have been obtained by me, O King; this place shall be famous throughout the three worlds by the name Saṅgameśvara. || 45 ||
By the majesty of this god, there shall be no separation, just as there has been none between Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī, or between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Bowing down again, she who was prostrate and suddenly agitated by passion said: "May Subāhu become my husband in another birth here. (47)

"O God, by your grace, if you are truly the Lord of the Confluence (Saṅgameśvara), then, having gazed with a widening eye at my beloved who is rippling like a flower-arrowed wave, drink her in as it were with your glance and speak to that girl of tremulous eyes. (48)
O large-eyed one, adorned with innate nobility, virtues, and beauty, you have been obtained by me; the fruit of my birth has been attained.
Then, taking his beloved by the hand—she who was terrified with fear and whose sprout-like lower lip was trembling—he went to his own inner apartments.
Now, by fate, I have been bitten by the serpent Kandarpa; thus, with my intellect, I perceive this essence-less cycle of worldly existence as it unfolds.
O lady of excellent hips, the king took delight with her for a long time; thus, having regained his beloved and having related his own story, he remained there. (52)
Having celebrated a grand festival, he bestowed the kingdom upon her; realizing that this world is impermanent, he gave his wealth even to those who asked for it.
By that best of kings, who renounced what had never been acquired before, the three worlds were filled with wonder; having ruled for a long time together with his wife, he [departed]. (54)
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he attained dissolution into that liṅga; therefore, O Goddess, this deity is well-known as Saṃgameśvara.
Whoever beholds that Liṅga Saṃgameśvara with supreme devotion shall never suffer separation from sons, brothers, beloved ones, and the like.
But he who, by rule, beholds that Liṅga Saṃgameśvara, shall obtain a fruit even greater than that of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. || 57 ||
By beholding Saṃgameśvara, the merit of the Gaṅgā becomes fruitful, as does that of the Yamunā, the Narmadā, and the Candrabhāgā. || 58 ||
Whoever should behold that Liṅga, Saṃgameśvara, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, by him the pilgrimage to Kārtikasvāmin has been performed; of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, he who beholds the god Saṅgameśvara in the month of Āśvayuja has effectively performed a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices.
Whoever beholds that Liṅga Saṃgameśvara in the month of Kārttika has, without a doubt, performed a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
O beloved, he who beholds Saṅgameśvara during the four months of the rainy season goes to the supreme abode, which is most dear to me.
This sin-destroying power of the god Saṅgameśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear of the invincible Lord Durddharṣeśvara.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to the account of the seventieth deity, the Lord Durdhareśvara, by the sight of whom a man is liberated from sins. || 1 ||
In ancient times, there was a king named Durddharṣa in the realm of Nepal; he was Puṇyaketu, illustrious, true to his word, and firm in his vows.
He had three wives who were his equals and very beautiful; the lord of the earth sported with them in a forest garden during the spring.
When, impelled by fate upon a horse swift as the wind and possessed of the speed of a deer, did he reach the forest of beautiful trees? (4)
It was crowded with lordly elephants, deer, tigers, lions, and sambara deer, and it shone with throngs of bears, monkeys, boars, gaṇḍakas, and other animals.
In that forest was a very extensive lake, adorned with groves of plantain trees, crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and graced by ruddy geese.
He beheld a lake as clear as a mirror, radiant with lotuses, and tawny with the saffron from the breasts of throngs of bathing Siddha women.
There he beheld a maiden who was like the very goddess of the forest; seeing her, with her limbs so exquisitely beautiful, he was tormented by the god of love.
He became instantly motionless with wonder, as if fixed in a painting; she, like a female serpent drawn by a mantra, approached his side.
To the king, who resembled ten million gods of love and was resting, he said: "O Indra among kings, know me to be his daughter, as dear to him as life itself. (10)
"O Brahmin, let him who is devoted to austerity, who is peaceful, and who is always a celibate student, pray for me; I shall grant myself to you."
Having heard these words of hers, the king, agitated by the god of love, cast aside his shame and entreated her in that secluded place. (12)
O fair-browed one, the loss of my life has arrived because of you; for who, indeed, considers what ought and ought not to be done for the sake of preserving their own life? (13)
This lightness of intellect is that by which one abandons the nectar already attained; who knows what will happen to whom in the next world? (14)
"O lady of faultless limbs, resort to me; let this nectar of your mouth not fail to nourish me, for know me to be dead, my dear. (15)
"If I drink myself, know that I have indeed gone to the next world. Hearing this, the slender woman was startled and spoke with humility: (16)
"If I am fallen and the fruit of my maidenhood is destroyed, our entire lineage will perish; therefore, let this be considered. (17)
"O Lord of the Earth, if you have supreme love for me, let this Brahmin request [your kingdom] for my sake; he will surely grant it to me. (18)
Having heard those words of hers, [he thought], "It shall not be otherwise for me; I have learned that she is indeed the daughter of the twice-born Kalpa, who is a lifelong celibate. (19)
Having gone to his own penance grove, he stood bowing and made his request; and that lord of sages, seeing her who had a moon-like face standing there, joyfully gave her to him.
United with her right there, the king, brought under the sway of the god of love, took delight in amorous unions and did not remember his own city.

In groves of plantain trees, in delightful forest ranges, and amidst thickets of many mango trees, the king enjoyed his new bride; that clever man indulged in charming amorous play with her who was exceedingly lovely.
While that invincible one was thus dwelling in the excellent forest, an exceedingly difficult-to-restrain and most terrifying Rākṣasa arrived.

Blazing with a formidable form, his face terrifying with prominent fangs, he—possessed by the god of love—infatuated the king and swiftly carried off that woman of flickering eyes, who was endowed with beauty and youth.
And the king, seeing her abducted and fainting from the poison of separation, remembered that lady of beautiful limbs again and again and lamented with his senses overwhelmed. || 25 ||
Alas, my beloved, nectar of love, long pond of the ambrosia of affection! Alas, beautiful one with large eyes, where have you gone, truly abandoning me? (26)
"When shall I again behold your face, which brings joy like the moon? Thus he uttered lamentations, remembering her sweet smile; afflicted by love, he wandered here and there like a madman.
While that king, difficult to behold, was thus lamenting, Kalpa, the best of brahmins, arrived at that place; there he saw the monarch wandering about like a bee.

Having learned of this and properly consoled her son-in-law, she spoke these words: "Come, O Durddharṣa, O Indra among kings; the course of karma is profound. For where has your realm of Nepal gone, O protector of the earth? (29)
Where indeed have my three wives gone—noble and beautiful? O King, where has your kingdom gone, and where has my daughter gone? (30)
Everything in this world is perishable, like a city of Gandharvas; life is impermanent, O King, and sovereignty is indeed like a bubble. (31)
Thus consoled repeatedly by Kalpa, the king, tormented by the god of love, remembered her of the beautiful limbs.
"Tell me truly, O Blessed One, if you have compassion for me: how shall my own kingdom be restored, and how shall I have the arrival of my friends? (33)

"O Brahmin, how shall I behold your three wives upon the surface of the earth, O best of the twice-born, who are enriched with the nectar of loveliness? And how will my reunion with your daughter come about once again? (34)
Having heard these words spoken by the Brahmin, O lady of beautiful countenance, he said: "Go to Nepāla, O King, and from there proceed to Mahākāla. (35)
In that field, that most excellent of sacred sites, there exists a Liṅga that accomplishes all goals, where the Sun performed a most difficult penance.
On the delightful and holy bank of the Śiprā, to the west of Brahmeśa, merely by the sight of it, your desire shall be fulfilled. (37)
Having heard Kalpa’s words, that best of kings quickly departed for Nepal and there comforted his friends and kinsmen.
Accompanied by his harem and retinue, he went to the Mahākāla forest, the abode of all supernatural powers and the domain of prosperity.
Having bathed there in the holy waters of the Śiprā, which bestows swift success, that best of kings beheld the Liṅga worshipped by the Sun.
He worshipped with jewels, divine garments, and fine ornaments; at that time, the worship of the Liṅga was performed with fragrant camphor. || 41 ||
With pearls, clear water drops, and streams of water, he danced before him with devotion, praising him with various hymns.

In that auspicious celestial abode, he heard a song that was nectar to the ears; having heard that enchanting sound, he was filled with curiosity and beheld his beloved standing there, the very pinnacle of loveliness.
Upon seeing her, his eyes blossomed with wonder and he became absorbed in her; instantly, by that very sight, he was made restless by the god of love.
Having recognized her through the grace of the gods as that very wife of mine whom I had seen, she too—like a royal swan beholding a lotus pond of loveliness—gazed upon him.
Immediately, her breast-region shone with horripilation; in that interval, O Goddess, a voice arose from the Liṅga.
O best of kings, this daughter of Viśvāvasu, the lord of the Siddhas, who is as dear to him as his own life, has been properly nurtured by him for your sake throughout an entire kalpa.
"I have brought back your wife for you after slaying that lord of the Rākṣasas; accept her as given by me and enjoy the kingdom free from all thorns. (48)
Having been addressed thus, O Goddess, he then departed after obtaining his beloved wife, accompanied by his harem and retinue, through the power of this Liṅga.

He was propitiated by the high-souled King Durdharṣa; from that time forward, this deity has been known as Durdharṣeśvara, famous throughout the three worlds as the bestower of the fruits of one's desired objects. (50)
O large-eyed one, those who behold the deity known as Durddharṣeśvara shall always be invincible to their enemies in battle. (51)

O Goddess, those who go and worship the invincible Lord Īśvara on the occasion of a solar transit, on a Sunday, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, they depart by celestial chariot to my supreme abode.
And those living beings who follow evil conduct, men devoted to wicked deeds, are instantly liberated from their sin by the sight of the invincible Lord.
By seeing it, by touching it, or even by chanting its name, a thousand acts of killing a Brahmin perish at that very instant.

An ungrateful person, a slanderer, the wicked, one of evil deeds, one of corrupt soul, one devoted to another’s wife, a thief, a slayer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—such a person is liberated from all sins by the sight of the invincible Lord.

When the solstices, the equinoxes, and the lunar festivals have arrived, those who bathe in the auspicious waters of the Śiprā and behold the invincible one [the deity] obtain threefold the merit of the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
In that regard, there is no limit to the number of gifts that are given; by that, the ancestors are satisfied, and thereby one's own self is indeed satisfied. (57)
He shall dwell in my city, honored for thousands of millions of eons; and when he returns to the world of mortals, he shall become a sovereign of the earth.
Unassailable by the host of enemies, he attains imperishable fruit—that state which is worshipped by the gods and from which there is no return. (59)
This power of the god Durddharṣeśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Prayāgeśa. || 60 ||

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Durdharṣeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" section of the Umā-Maheśvara dialogue, in the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 70 ||
Īśvara said: Know that the seventy-first [liṅga] is named Prayāgeśvara; understand it to be peerless and the destroyer of great sins. || 1 ||
In the city of Hastināpura, during the Vaivasvata Manvantara, in the Kalpa and the age known as Dvāpara, there was the illustrious Śantanu, the best of kings.
He was a youth of marvelous and great heroism, with a body as firm as a diamond; he was proficient in all the scriptures and highly skilled in the multitude of arts.
Equal to Viṣṇu in strength and like the sun in splendor, he alone wandered along the Gaṅgā, which is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Once that mighty-armed one, possessing abundant forces and vehicles, went to a dense forest surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants.
Having gone there, that best of kings effortlessly slew deer and tigers, while striking down buffaloes, horses, and boars.
Once, in that forest, he beheld a most excellent woman, blazing with her physical form like another goddess Padmā manifest before his eyes.
Upon seeing her, his hair stood on end and he was struck with wonder by the perfection of her form; drinking her in as it were with his two eyes, the lord of men could not be satiated.
As soon as she saw the king of great splendor wandering about, that playful woman, her affection and friendship awakened, could not look enough at him.
Then the king spoke to her, consoling her with gentle words: "Whether you are a goddess, a daughter of the Dānavas, a Gandharva woman, or even an Apsaras," (10)
Whether you are a yakṣī, a pannagī, or a human woman, O lady of beautiful waist; I entreat you, O one with the luster of a lotus bud, become my wife, O beautiful one. (11)
Having heard these words of the king—well-spoken, gentle, and charming—the queen accepted them; thus the king was granted his request regarding the agreement.
Even if forbidden or if something unpleasant occurs, I would undoubtedly abandon you; O King, you must by no means ask me, "Who are you? or "To whom do you belong? (13).
"So be it," he said, by virtue of his truthfulness and his well-performed deeds; for he was captivated by her virtuous conduct and her qualities of beauty and nobility.
And the lord of the earth was pleased by her service and her secret praise; for that goddess Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths, possesses a divine form. (15)
Having assumed a human form, O lady of excellent complexion, she delighted the illustrious king, and he likewise took his pleasure with her.
That king, being attached to pleasure and captivated by the qualities of excellent women, did not perceive that many years, seasons, and months had passed.
Delighting with her as he desired, the lord of men begot upon her eight sons who possessed the splendor of the immortals.
And as each son was born, she cast him into the water for the sake of liberation, saying, "I gratify you in the purifying stream of the Gaṅgā."
That was not at all pleasing to King Śantanu then; yet, fearing her abandonment, the lord of the earth said nothing to the queen.
Then, when the eighth son was born, the king, afflicted with grief and desiring to save his own son, spoke to her as she seemed to be smiling.
"Do not kill! Whose [son] are you? Who are you? Why do you destroy my sons? The slaughter of one's own son is a great sin; do not incur it, stop, you despicable woman! || 22 ||
Gaṅgā said: "O best among those who possess sons, desiring a son myself, I shall not kill your son; however, this stay of mine has come to an end, according to the agreement I made. (23)
"I am Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, served by hosts of great sages; for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, I have dwelt together with you. (24)
These eight Vasu deities, who were most formidable and possessed of great majesty, attained the state of humanity due to the fault of Vasiṣṭha’s curse.
There is no one else on earth besides you who can bring them back; nor has there ever existed a human nurse like me. (26)
Therefore, for the sake of giving birth to him, I have come to this human state. May it be well with you; I shall depart. O observer of great vows, protect my son!
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, wept, having assumed a human state, she whose waist was slender.
"Alas! What great misery it is that these sons have been killed; for out of delusion, I, cruel as I am, have cast these children into the water. (29)

Alas, my dear ones! Alas, my daughters! Alas, my sons! Alas, my fathers! Alas, my children! Where indeed have you gone? Having abandoned me, where have you departed? Why does my heart not shatter? (30)
When shall I, out of affection, embrace my sons who have come of their own accord, crying piteously, "Mother! Mother!", like mother cows toward their calves? (31)
Whose excellent, reddish-brown dust from the earth will ever now stain my upper garment and my lap? (32)
"Alas! These children, born from my very limbs and members, who brought delight to my heart—by me, their mother, they have been killed and brought to their end! (33)
"To what worlds shall I go after having committed such a most dreadful deed? How shall I become virtuous, being a pitiless wife and mother of sons? (34)
Having thus lamented piteously and wept again and again, she, distressed and unconscious, fell motionless upon the surface of the earth.
In the meantime, O Goddess, Nārada, the best of sages, suddenly heard that sound of her lamentation at that time.
With eyes wide open in wonder, he thought, "What is this?"—this is that very Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, the purifier worshipped by the gods.
Why does the divine and holy river, the queen of the ocean who flows through the three paths, weep so distraught, having assumed a human form? (38)
Having reflected thus, the sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā, approached the weeping Gaṅgā; standing in the sky, he spoke aloud: "O Goddess Gaṅgā, salutations be unto you! (39)
"I am Nārada; O highly meritorious Pāvanī, why do you weep? You are the renowned daughter of the Himālaya mountain, served by gods and Gandharvas. (40)
It was borne upon his head by the divine Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
Having heard the words of Nārada, the divine river of the gods likewise looked upon the great sage seated in his celestial chariot and replied.
"O Nārada, out of delusion, I have committed a loathsome unrighteousness; knowing it to be a very great sin, I have killed my seven sons. (43)
"By fate, my separation from the ocean has occurred; a wife was born to me as a mortal, and sons were born who have now been slain. (44)
Therefore, having been submerged in an ocean of grief, I have lamented; O divine sage, tell me that by which I may indeed become meritorious. (45)
Having heard these words of hers, Nārada, the best of sages, pure-souled and knower of the three periods of time, spoke these words to Gaṅgā. || 46 ||
Nārada said: "O Goddess, who are worshipped by the world, have you forgotten the auspicious agreement of the gods? O Devi, you made a solemn promise for the sake of the liberation of the Vasus."
O lady of virtuous vows, by your grace those Vasus have attained the worlds; O Goddess, you caused the ocean to descend, and he is remembered as Śantanu.
