Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, the holy Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, replied to the great sage.
"O Brahmin, you have spoken the truth; everything has now been understood by me. However, because I obtained a human birth, I am deluded by that. (50)
Terrified by the fear of censure, we have come to you for refuge; grant us instruction and tell us of the supreme abode. (51)

Nārada said: O Goddess, honored by the world, have you forgotten the agreement made with the gods? O giver of merit, O lady of holy vows, if you ask me out of fear of censure, listen as I tell you of the supreme abode.
Avantī is indeed celebrated as eternal throughout seven kalpas; in that city, your friend Śiprā is always beloved by the brahmins. (53)
On its bank, to the south of Durddharṣeśvara, there exists an auspicious Liṅga, worshipped by the gods and frequented by all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 54 ||
"By the mere sight of him, you will have accomplished all that is to be done. Therefore, go, O highly meritorious Gaṅgā, who are served by gods and sages. (55)
Thus addressed by the high-souled Nārada, that most meritorious river of the three paths went there and beheld her friend Śiprā.
Then, having formed a union and beheld that most purifying Liṅga, she worshipped it with devotion and remained right there for a long time.
Then the goddess Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun and destroyer of sins, arrived there with great affection at the place where Gaṅgā was situated.
The Goddess beheld Gaṅgā meditating upon Śaṅkara, the Auspicious One; she too remained right there, worshipping the Supreme Śiva.
Then, at that very time, the goddess Prācī Sarasvatī arrived, well-concealed within the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
In the meantime, O Goddess, Nārada said to Śakra: "Prayāga is not to be seen; it has gone to Mahākālavana. (61)
Where the Sarasvatī is hidden between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, that should be known as Prayāga, the destroyer of all sins. || 62 ||
He has now gone to Prayāga in the excellent Mahākālavana; for some reason, he has departed, though it is not known by me why.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, they all, accompanied by Śakra, went together to Avantī.
Praising with various hymns the auspicious Gaṅgā who flows through the three paths: "O Goddess Gaṅgā, salutations to you, the destroyer of all sins! (65)
O Goddess, mother of the Vasus, bestower of liberation upon the Vasus, eternal purifier of the three worlds, who is borne upon the head by Hara. (66)
O Yamunā, you who are served by the Vālakhilyas and are the supreme portion of Kṛṣṇa, we bow to you, O Kālindī, the bearer of excellent waters.
O Goddess, you are the daughter of Pāvinī, the lord of heaven, Mārtaṇḍa; O auspicious Śiprā, born from the body of Brahmā, salutations to you!

You alone are renowned as Prācī Sarasvatī, the embodiment of merit; you who exist as Prācī in the Kaurava field, at Puṣkara, and in Mahālaya—you are that Śiprā, famous as the destroyer of all sins. (69)
You are compassion for all living beings, you are heaven and the refuge of men; you are the mother of all creatures, and you are celebrated on earth as the East.
O Goddess, you who, upon seeing the mark of the stain of many births among embodied beings on earth, perform their cleansing—you are she who dwells throughout the three worlds. 71.
The confluence of these rivers is known by the wise as Prayāga; having come here, you have now established and bathed it.
From this day forward, this deity shall be known by the name Prayāgeśvara; he is renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of sins through mere remembrance. (73)
Those who come here and behold Prayāgeśvara from that place shall become successful in their purpose, freed from all sins.

Their paternal and maternal lineages are likewise delivered; by beholding Prayāgeśvara, the merit of three circumambulations of the Gaṅgā is attained, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life—of this there is no doubt. (75)
At the Gaṅgā and at Prayāga, in the auspicious Devadāru forest, at Naimiṣa and Puṣkara, as well as at Śrīśaila and Tripuṣkara; || 76 ||
At Tryambaka, Dhautapāpa, Mahendra, and Bhairava, as well as at Gokarṇa, Suvarṇākhya, and the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā. || 77 ||
The accomplishment that is attained through the sight of these [deities] over twelve years is obtained in merely one month by the sight of Prayāgeśvara. (78)
Those who, having observed the prescribed restraints with devotion, behold the deity known as Prayāgeśvara specifically on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days; || 79 ||
For them, there shall be no return even after hundreds of millions of eons; their linga on the surface of the earth shall be the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation.
In this auspicious, liberation-granting Liṅga, there shall be three streams: the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Prācī, which destroys all sins.
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī, being praised by the gods with prostrations, then departed for their own respective abodes.
The gods, headed by Śakra, being greatly delighted, praised the one known as Prayāgeśvara with various hymns, and having worshipped him, they departed for heaven.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Prayāgeśvara has been recounted to you; now hear of Candrādityeśvara. || 84 ||

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Prayāgeśvara," in the Dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, within the Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas, in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 71.
Īśvara said: O beloved, know that Candrādityeśvara is the seventy-second Lord; by the mere sight of whom a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
O Goddess, in ancient times the gods were defeated in battle by Śambara; abandoning the field of combat, they fled, intent solely on saving their lives.
Seeing the moon seized by Rāhu and overwhelmed with fear, the elder son of Vinatā, who was the charioteer, was addressed by the Sun: ||| 3 ||
"O Vahāruṇa, quickly take the chariot to where no battle is found; it is heard that those two, the Moon and the Sun, are the most powerful among the Daityas. (4)
That third [Rāhu], terrifying with his formidable fangs, was fearsome; in the battle, it could not be discerned whether the Moon was dead or perhaps lost.
It was not known where Śakra had gone in the battle, nor Varuṇa; Yama was not known to be anywhere, so what need is there to mention the Giver of Wealth?
Thus addressed by Ravi in the midst of the battle, Aruṇa, being distressed, drove the chariot to where no fighting was taking place.
In the meantime, at that very moment, Candra arrived where the Lord, the Sun, was being seized by the planet Rāhu.
Terrified, with trembling eyes and rendered unconscious for a mere moment, Candra suddenly became so upon seeing the divine Divākara.
Held captive in battle by Śambara, the Rudras fled in terror; terrified by the lord of the asuras, they scattered in the ten directions out of fear.
All the Sādhyas, terrified with fear, fled to where the Dānavas were not; for those gods had been broken and only a remnant remained in the battle.
In that destruction of men, the powerful asura shattered all the limbs and armor of the fleeing gods with his arrows.
Then he struck them from behind, and they were cut down by the thousands; at that time, when the Asura was thus preoccupied, I became free from the deception.
Assuming the form of an asura and intent on saving his life, he departed quickly, thinking, "I must go before Śambara arrives."
Thus spoke the Lord of Night, terrified with fear, O Pārvatī; for in an instant, the Moon and the Sun were carried away by Varuṇa in his chariot.
There, the Lord of the World, Janārdana, the God who rides upon Garuḍa, resides in a cave crowded with hosts of gods, Kinnaras, and Saṃketas.

O illustrious lady, having beheld the Lord of the World there on Mount Mandara, in the Nandana grove, amidst excellent sandalwood trees—He who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace—the two deities, the Moon and the Sun, offered their praise.
Homage to you, the presiding lord of the three worlds, who has surpassed the sun with your own radiance! Homage to Viṣṇu, homage to Jiṣṇu; homage to you, the slayer of Kaiṭabha! 18.
Salutations to you, the performer of all actions and the protector of the world; salutations to you, the invincible one whose weapon is the discus, and salutations to the slayer of the Dānavas.

Salutations to you, who have caused the emergence of the three worlds by treading upon them through the three stages; salutations to you, the great power who is the death-knell for the lineage of the fierce lords of the Daityas.
Homage to the one of great splendor, whose lotus-womb arose from the lake of the navel; to the one of great radiance who generated Virañci, the Lord of all worlds. 21.
Salutations to you, who are resplendent in the great battle for the destruction of the enemies of the immortals; O Lord of the gods, be our refuge, O Master.
Having heard the hymn composed by Candra and Sūrya, the Lord Janārdana, the god Adhokṣaja, comforted them with words of praise and spoke.
Viṣṇu said: Welcome, O Moon and Sun, you who are worthy of praise! For what reason have you come here? Tell me that, free from all anxiety.
Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, the Moon and the Sun said: "In battle, the gods have been utterly defeated by the evil-minded Śambara."
They were not found; where have they gone? We two were lost despite our efforts, but we have been brought here by Aruṇa, and by divine providence, O Lord, you have been seen.
The gods were conquered by Śambara, and he was seen everywhere—both on land and in water—for Śambara possessed cruel prowess.
Following behind the lords of the gods as they fled, he cut down their armor, umbrellas, and bows with showers of arrows.
And various armors, great crowns, broad bows, and diverse shields.
And elephants by the millions, their temples streaming with rut, as well as horses adorned with chowrie-crests and ornaments of jeweled saddles, [were presented] by the gods.
With their armor shattered, their elephants destroyed, and their foot soldiers fallen, the army of the gods became like a mine of calamities.
Then the proud lord of the Daityas, having emerged from the great battle as a conqueror of his enemies, possessed of great splendor like a blazing fire, turned back.
Being saluted by hosts of sages, being praised by the great seers, and gladdened by the foremost of the best daityas with blessings of victory; || 33 ||

There, in that auspicious chamber, the lord of the Daityas occupied a throne adorned with gold and complete with every supernatural power. Seated there, the highly illustrious king of the Daityas shone resplendently.

His limbs were nourished by divine sandalwood paste, radiant with celestial flowers, his body adorned with the form of a crown, and he was fanned with white chowries; likewise, he was attended by Daityas and lords of Daityas who had risen from the dead.
The one of great power was being served by personified sacrifices, accompanied by heaps of all kinds of flowers and the songs of various birds.
Therein lies incomparable glory in the world, therein resides unimpeded fortune; therein is splendor, radiance, and beauty, where the Dānava Śambara dwells.
Thus that Daitya king, together with his servants, rejoices there; he himself has become Indra, and he has made the moon and sun his own.
Having heard those words of theirs, that god, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), meditated for a long time within his mind and then spoke this, O beloved: (39)
O Moon and Sun, I have understood the scheme of Śambara; by virtue of Brahmā’s boon, the fruit of my asceticism must be enjoyed [by him]. (40)
In ancient times, the thunderbolt was hurled at Śambara by the wielder of the vajra; though he was struck in the heart, that asura did not die nevertheless. (41)
"Go, you two who have been commanded by me, O best of Mahākālavanas; by my command, you shall attain success there. (42)
There, the infinite Maheśvara exists in the form of Mahākāla as a liṅga; and to the north of that is the auspicious liṅga that grants all desires.

By the mere sight of him, you two shall have accomplished your purpose; and by the mass of his flames, the death of Śambara will come to pass—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, you must go to that very place.
O illustrious lady, having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the Moon and the Sun quickly went to Mahākālavana with their hair standing on end in joy.
There he beheld Mahādeva, an immeasurable mass of splendor, who was being praised with various hymns and worshipped with auspicious flowers.
In the meantime, O daughter of Himavat, a voice arose from the midst of the Liṅga, swiftly consoling both the Moon and the Sun.
That Daitya Śambara was slain; those two, the Moon and the Sun, having gone there, were made into wicked [images] of the Daityas, stationed within the netherworld (pātāla).
Rāhu and Ketu were established at the end of the planets according to the prescribed rites; Śakra was established in his own station along with the gods, without a doubt. (49)
All the world-protectors, filled with joy, returned each to their own abode; you two shall remain endowed with splendor and majesty throughout the three worlds.
Together with the planets and constellations, you shall move through the sky; as before, you shall become witnesses to merits and sins. || 51 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, having been addressed with these words by her voice, the Moon and the Sun became satisfied and felt their purpose fulfilled upon beholding the Liṅga.
In the meantime, the gods, seated in their celestial chariots, assembled where the auspicious Moon and Sun were in the Mahākālavana.
Having understood the majesty of the Liṅga, they, with concentrated minds, gave it a name; it was a supreme, radiant Liṅga served by both the Moon and the Sun.
It shall become famous on earth by the name Candrādityeśvara; for by the mass of flames arising from this Liṅga, Śambara was burnt along with his servants through the service of the Moon and the Sun.
Having spoken thus, all the thirty gods stood on every side nearby, praising Śiva, the Lord of the Moon and Sun, with various hymns of praise.
The moon and the sun, stationed there in the vicinity of the Liṅga, worshipped the Lord of Gods and attained their former state.
Those men who behold Śiva, who moves within the moon and sun, with devotion, go indeed to the world of the Sun and likewise to the world of the Moon.
In auspicious celestial chariots resembling the sun and possessing the luster of the moon, their happiness shall endure as long as the moon and the sun exist.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, those men who, having bathed in the purifying Śiprā, behold Śiva as Candrādityeśvara with devotion; || 60 ||
For as many as a hundred generations on both the father’s and the mother’s side, they rejoice in the world of the Moon and the Sun for eternal years.
Those who, by chance, behold the Lord Candrādityeśvara at the conjunction of the new moon and Monday, do not go to the abode of Yama.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying power of Candrādityeśvareśa has been recounted to you; now let the [power] of Karabheśvara be heard.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Cadrādityeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section (Āvantya-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Śrī Hara said: O fair-faced one, know Karabheśa as Trisaptatīśvara; by the mere sight of whom a birth in a base womb is never obtained.
The wise Vīraketu was the lord of Ayodhyā, filled with the nectar of learning, humility, good fortune, and beauty. || 2 ||
With his mind perfected through the knowledge of the past and the future, he protected his subjects properly, like his own biological sons.
Then one day, the king went to a dense forest, teeming with deer, lions, and elephants, and crowded with tigers and sambara deer.
There, that slayer of enemy heroes pierced various wild animals—deer, buffaloes, and boars—by the thousands.
That entire forest, teeming with beasts, birds, and deer, was cleared of all predatory animals by that king.
When no wild beasts were seen in that dense forest, a young camel was then struck by an arrow with smooth joints.
And that young camel, O Queen, seizing an arrow, fled far away even though pierced, while that very king looked on; and the powerful king quickly pursued the camel.
Then that camel, moving with great speed, ran across both low ground and high ground; in a mere moment, O Goddess, it covered many yojanas.
Then that king, impelled by the passion of youth and his own strength, set out with bow in hand and sword at his side, accompanied by his horse.
Then, having bypassed and not bypassed rivers, streams, ponds, and forests, he pursued the forest-dweller.
And that swift young elephant, O Queen, having repeatedly reached the king, would then return again with great speed.
Rendered frantic by his many arrows, that young elephant returned again to his proximity from behind and from the flanks; and regaining speed once more, it was seen at his side and in front.
Then, having entered that most formidable forest, Karabha quickly vanished; and the king entered the forest.
Having entered the great forest, the king then reached the hermitage of the ascetics; there, his horses being exhausted, he dismounted and rested once more.
Seeing him then with a bow in his hand, afflicted by fatigue and hungry, the sages approached him and performed worship according to the prescribed rites.
Having accepted the worship offered by the sages according to the prescribed rites, he inquired of all the ascetics about their supreme progress in austerity.
Having received the words of that king, those sages whose wealth is asceticism questioned that tiger among kings regarding his purpose.
"For what purpose, O noble one, have you come to this grove of asceticism on foot, armed with a sword, a bow, and arrows, O lord of men? (19)
We wish to hear this: from where have you come, O giver of honor? In what family were you born, and what is your name? Tell us, O King. (20)
Then that king, a bull among men, duly declared to all the twice-born his lineage and family name according to the truth.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, O bulls among the twice-born, I am Vīraketu; I roam about slaying herds of deer with thousands of arrows.
When, despite being equipped with a great force along with his ministers and retinue, he could not find either a deer or even a boar in the thicket, (23)
Whether it was a buffalo, a wild boar, a hare, or a śambara deer in the forest, at that time my young camel was struck by a straight-knotted arrow.
While I was looking on, that arrow vanished in an instant; it reached this forest by chance as it was fleeing.

"Having lost my fortune and having my hopes destroyed, I have come into your presence, emaciated by fatigue. Everything is known to you, for ascetics rich in austerity are indeed omniscient. You are highly fortunate; therefore, I ask you about my doubt. (26)
"Where has the young camel gone, whom I have just now pierced with an arrow? And where shall I find it suddenly? Tell me that, being well-composed. (27)

Then, O Goddess, Ṛṣabha, the best of sages among all those ṛṣis, spoke these words while remembering Karabha: tatasteṣāṃ samastānāmṛṣīṇāmṛṣisattamaḥ | ṛṣabho devi karabhaṃ smarannidamathābravīt || 28 ||
O King, that camel has gone to the auspicious Mahākālavana; you too, O Great King, go to the auspicious Mahākālavana. (29)
Wherein the god Mahādeva, having assumed the form of a young elephant for the amusement of the gods, formerly became a linga-form.
O Lord of the Earth, to the west, near Kailāsa, the protector of the field, is Vighneśa, known as Modakapriya.
O King, honored by Brahmā for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, that King Dharmadhvaja was the upholder of the lineage of the Haihayas.
Once, however, he was led by a horse to Badarikāśrama, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.

There he saw a lean Brahmin wearing a hero’s skin; O Indra among kings, at that time his body was peerless to anyone else. And upon seeing him, the Brahmin was laughed at by that king out of negligence.
"Because you laughed upon seeing me, therefore you shall become a camel—long-lipped, long-toothed, with a discordant voice and a deformed appearance. (35)
Thus addressed by that brahmin, even though he had been cursed, the best of kings entreated him; and the brahmin, being pleased, spoke as follows.
"O King, my word has never been false at any time; you shall certainly become a camel and afterwards attain liberation. (37)
When you are born as a young camel and pierced by Vīraketu, the king who rules over Ayodhyā, you shall go forth struck by arrows.
There you shall go to the divine Mahākālavana; by beholding the Liṅga there, you will reach the supreme abode where Lord Maheśvara dwells.
O King, that immensely powerful Vīraketu, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) by beholding the Liṅga.

O King, having been addressed thus, that protector of the earth attained the state of a young camel. O King, he was struck by you with a straight-knotted arrow; you shall see him released from that state and seated in a celestial chariot upon beholding the Liṅga.
Thus addressed by that brahmin Ṛṣabha, the king departed in haste for the auspicious Mahākālavana.
There he beheld that Liṅga, which was constantly worshipped by the gods; in the meantime, a voice was heard by that lord of the earth.
Seated in his celestial chariot, he spoke in a sweet voice: "O Indra among kings, behold me, now that this auspicious chariot has been raised up! (44)

"By the sight of this linga, the supreme goal has been attained by me. I was struck by you with an arrow; therefore, I have come to you in the forest near this linga, since you are my highest kinsman. (45)
Having spoken these words of sweet syllables to the king, O Goddess, he departed for the supreme abode—eternal, immutable, and imperishable.
Then, in the sky, the hosts of gods, along with the kinnaras and mahoragas, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas, together with the piśācas and the throngs of apsarases, [gathered].
O Goddess, Brahmā, Indra, Hari, and the other chief deities, stationed in their celestial chariots, arrived there joyfully, their minds filled with curiosity to behold the sight.
Having beheld the elephant released, shining as it stood upon the celestial chariot, and having been praised with various hymns merely by the sight of the Liṅga; || 49 ||
Shining with a crown of radiant luster composed of a multitude of celestial gems, he illumines ten million suns and brings joy to the world.
Then the gods, having witnessed his supreme majesty, gave it a name because this camel was liberated through the sight of this liṅga.
Therefore, Karabheśvara shall become renowned throughout all three worlds as the liberator from animal births; of this there is no doubt. || 52 ||
Having spoken thus, all the gods departed for their own supreme abodes; and the heroic Vīraketu, lord of Ayodhyā, then ruled his prosperous and unrivaled kingdom from his own palace.
O Goddess, the man who beholds the one known as Karabheśvara goes to the imperishable worlds, honored as a lord of the Gaṇas.
When that great lord of the lords of kings arrives here in due time, having become the sole sovereign of the earth, he shall gradually attain liberation.
No suffering arises for those who, even by chance, behold that Liṅga Karabheśvara, nor do they experience disease, grief, or fear. (56)
O Goddess, whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all gifts—that fruit, and even more, is obtained from the sight of Karabheśvara. (57)
Diseases do not arise, nor does poverty ever occur; incomparable sovereignty always arises for them from the mere sight [of this]. (58)
Those ancestors who have entered the womb of animals, those who are suffering, and those who remain in the sky—all these are thinking of their own kinsmen.
"Will our son or grandson come here into this lineage? When will he behold the Lord of Gods, the Lord Karabheśvara? By the mere sight of him, our liberation will surely be attained. (60)
Whatever desire one may have in view when they behold [the deity], all that is fulfilled for them; and for one who has died, it becomes the supreme goal.
This sin-destroying power of the god Karabheśa has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear [the account] of Rājasthaleśvara.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Karabheśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the Umā-Maheśvara dialogue, in the fifth section (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 73 ||
Śrī Hara said: Know that the seventy-fourth [manifestation] is Śiva Rājasthaleśvara, by the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins. || 1 ||
Long ago, in the past Viṣṇu-kalpa, which is dear at the beginning of the Manvantara, when the surface of the earth was without a king, Brahmā became absorbed in anxious thought.
Without humans, the gods are not capable of sustaining the world; through giving, sacrifice, and recitation, the gods attain supreme nourishment.
"Who would be a fit king, a protector of subjects, and one who is affectionate toward the people? Then he saw the royal sage Ripuñjaya performing austerities.
Then Brahmā, the lord of gods and grandfather of the worlds, spoke to him, who was established in dharma, observing great vows, and endowed with all virtues upon the earth.
Brahmā said: O Ripuñjaya, my dear son, listen to these words of mine; protect the kingdom, my child, with a mind that is single-pointed.
Enough now of this painful austerity, my dear; all the worlds have been won by you through dharma, O best of men.
Now, let the protection of the world be carried out according to my command; for the benefit of others is indeed the fruit of the body for one who possesses a body.
There is no other dharma such as that, nor is there anything else that accomplishes the true purpose; indeed, even the attainment of hell is a blessing when it results from benefiting another.

One cannot attain the status of Lord of the World even by doing harm to living beings; rather, for the constant sake of the world’s welfare and out of respect for my command, protect the earth girt by the oceans and its inhabitants. (10)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, O daughter of the mountain, that royal sage Ripuñjaya spoke to Brahmā with his palms joined in reverence.
The earth was previously created by you as immovable by its very nature; indeed, without a protector, where will this world go? (12)
"O Grandfather, if the earth must necessarily be protected by me, then grant me the beautiful city of Avanti, which has endured for seven kalpas. (13)
Renowned throughout the entire world of men, including the realm of the gods, it was established as a dwelling place for those deities who have descended from heaven.
"If the inhabitants of my celestial abode were to follow my established law, no one would dwell in a place not granted by me. O Lord, I shall protect the earth according to this rule. (15)

Brahmā said: "O best of men, this desire which you have expressed shall come to pass for you. Whatever gods there may be, by virtue of my authority, they shall carry out your command and remain forever subject to your will."
"O observer of noble vows, your name shall indeed be Devanātha. Having spoken thus, Brahmā, mounted upon his swan-vehicle, vanished from sight.
Then the king, having pledged the protection of the earth to Brahmā, proclaimed it throughout the world and spoke to the inhabitants of heaven.
Heaven has been ordained for you, and the earth for human beings; as for those who are devoted to roots and tubers here, whether on dry land or upon the mountains.

"O gods who reside here, depart; this earth belongs to human beings. Hearing that proclamation of the king, the thirty deities, oppressed by fear, went to the third heaven out of respect for Brahmā’s word.
Then that king caused his subjects to prosper through righteousness; they were exceedingly contented, with hearts filled with affection like that for a son.
The subjects, nurtured by that happiness, were free from old age and death; they possessed sons, were rich in wealth and grain, and were endowed with all their desires. (22)
Those who were in the prime of youth remained free from dualities and constantly took refuge in the Dharma; on this earth, there was no mountain, no dry land, nor even an island that was not so.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed and was endowed with sweet fruits; the land was as radiant as the world of the gods, blazing with all desirable qualities.
As time passed in this manner while the king was ruling his kingdom, the gods, overcome by great indignation, prepared themselves for the sake of causing him harm. (25)
Repeatedly and many times they caused manifold sufferings for the subjects; then Indra, the subduer of Pāka, brought about a very long drought.
While the worlds were thus being withdrawn, that best of kings, having become a cloud and reached the heavens, caused a bountiful rain, O King.

By that very [act], O illustrious lady, the world was nourished and became happy. Then, at a certain time, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, becoming the rain-cloud Saṃvarta, caused the clouds indeed to fall.
Then the king, having become the wind, held her up; thereupon Anala vanished from the entire surface of the earth.
Neither sacrifice, nor recitation, nor oblation, nor the cooking of food took place; and the world, agitated by disease, then remained in a state of distress. || 30 ||
Then that king, having seen him, became the bearer of oblations; he sustained all creatures as well as the sacrifices and the inhabitants of heaven.
In the meantime, O Goddess, surrounded by hosts of spirits, I arrived together with you to behold my own city.
Then all the hosts of gods, together with the kinnaras and mahoragas, along with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas, as well as the siddhas, vidyādharas, and uragas [gathered]. || 33 ||
The spirits, the departed, the piśācas, and others who roam the sky; as well as the four oceans and the seas of salt water, milk, and the rest. || 34 ||
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, Carmaṇvatī, Bhīmarathī, and the holy river Godāvarī. (35)
The Vipāśā, the holy Devikā, the Śarayū, as well as the Kauśikī, the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, the Bāhudā, and the Dṛṣadvatī. || 36 ||
The Pārā, the Vedasmṛti, the Vetraghnī, the auspicious Narmadā, the Tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, and the Nirvindhyā—all these rivers gathered there. || 37 ||
Puṣkara, Prayāga, Prabhāsa, and likewise Naimiṣa; Pṛthutīrthodaka and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka. || 38 ||
Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, Nīlaparvata, Vārāhaparvata, and likewise the sacred site Kanakhala. || 39 ||
Bhṛgutuṅga, Sukukṣa, and Ajagandha, O Pārvatī; Kāliñjara, Keśarī, Rudrakoṭi, and Mahālaya. || 40 ||
And all the sacred places and holy shrines, as well as Meru, Mahendra, Malaya, Mandara, and Gandhamādana. || 41 ||
The sages, the Vālakhilyas, and the four Vedas themselves—these and many others have arrived along with me.

Immediately thereafter, O Goddess, I transformed Meru into the form of dry land; standing upon that land, surrounded by the gods, I sat down. The four oceans, beginning with the salt ocean, were stationed at its sides.
Then King Ripuñjaya, having fallen into a state of agitation, saw me standing in my own place and approached toward me.
O lady of beautiful countenance, although he was being consumed by my splendor and was terrified, he propitiated me, saying, "Who are you, O God? Salutations be unto you! (45)
"O King, in this place I am the king; and it was said by me in jest: 'The fourfold aims of life, the fourfold forms, and the king are established in a fourfold manner. (46)
Therefore, O beloved, I was seen by him everywhere within the realm of speech, including all that is moving and unmoving; immediately thereafter, I was praised by him with supreme devotion.

O Goddess, having seen my incomparable, pervasive, and supreme power, he took refuge in me with the highest devotion. Though I was praised by him further, I was indeed pleased with that king. He said: "O Lord, O Supreme Ishvara, if you are pleased with me..."
"O Lord of All, may my devotion toward you be firm and eternal. O King, I was pleased by those words and spoke to him again.
"Having said, 'It shall be so,' speak again to me, O King: the desire that dwells in your heart shall be fulfilled at all times. (51)
"You shall always be invincible to all the gods; therefore, O Goddess, I have requested this further, unsurpassed boon. (52)
O Lord, this place shines exceedingly in your presence; it is undoubtedly Meru, which is always dear to you. 53.
"You are the Lord of Rājasthala, renowned throughout the three worlds; O God, you ought to act in such a way that this shall come to pass. (54)
And whoever, O Lord, having come here endowed with supreme devotion, performs the pilgrimage with a sincere spirit according to the procedure declared in the Purāṇas; || 55 ||

To him, you must grant everything that has been contemplated in his mind: all the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, the perfection of the magic pill (*guṭikā-siddhi*), and the magical collyrium (*añjana*).
The man who beholds with devotion Khaḍga, Pādukā, Jalavāsa, Rasāyana, and Rājasthaleśvara—|| 57 ||
But on the tenth day, having performed [the rite] specifically according to the prescribed rules, one attains the divinity even of the gods; such is Maheśvara.
He who shall behold the Lord here at Rājasthala and perform a pilgrimage there will be worthy of worship by the gods of the three heavens, just like the god Purandara. || 59 ||
For him, prosperity and victory shall indeed be my boon; let his enemies go to destruction, and let his heart's desires be fulfilled. (60)
O Śaṅkara, may there be prosperity for our lineage through the sight of you; may all the gods remain here, and may Mount Meru remain right here. O Lord, may all the oceans remain in your presence.
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, O fair-faced one, I replied: "When the king named Sudyumna comes here," (62)
"Then, for the sake of a son, I shall grant your desire together with your wife; at that time, the four oceans will themselves become fruitful."

O King, by propitiating him, I shall grant you an excellent son. Furthermore, those men who perform the pilgrimage here with devotion will attain the fulfillment of their desires; of this there is no doubt. (64)
Out of devotion, King Ripuñjaya was made the Lord of the Gaṇas by me.
This sin-destroying majesty of Rājasthaleśvareśa has been told to you, O Goddess; now let the [majesty] of Vaḍaleśvara be heard.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Rājasthaleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said: Know, O Goddess, that the seventy-fifth deity is named Vaḍaleśvara; he removes sins and grants the desires of men through his mere sight. || 1 ||
O Goddess, Maṇibhadra was indeed the friend of Dhanada; his son was named Vaḍala, who was irascible and possessed the power of envy.
Possessed of beauty, always lustful, ever intoxicated, and superior in strength, he once went to the beautiful lotus-pond of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
For the sake of pleasure and for the purpose of indulging desire, he beheld a secluded chamber constructed in private, covered with flowers, and adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
It was indeed covered with coral, adorned with strings of pearls, most delightful, providing vast shade, and beautified by golden lotuses.
In the vicinity of Kubera’s abode was the beloved pleasure-garden of the high-souled Kubera, the king of kings and giver of wealth.
Seeing that city, which was constantly guarded by Rākṣasas and Kiṃnaras bearing swords, Vaḍala then became exceedingly joyful.
Accompanied by his beloved, he took delight in a secret and enchanting place; subdued by the god of love, he enjoyed himself through various amorous unions.
There, protected in battle, heroic Rākṣasas skilled in warfare—equipped with all kinds of weapons and accoutrements—guard a hundred thousand [soldiers].
But as soon as they saw Vaḍala, the son of Maṇibhadra, O beloved, with his mouth filled with food offerings and adorned with divine sandalwood paste, they [were struck with wonder].
With teeth resembling the inner petals of a *ketakī* flower, his divine face was most excellent; that subduer of enemies had girded his sword for the sake of battle and was equipped with a spear.
Knowing that he was always accompanied by his wife, seated upon a couch, and intoxicated, and perceiving that he had come for the sake of pleasure, they cried out to one another.
O hero, you ought not to proceed along this path with your wife; this is the pleasure garden of the high-souled Kubera, the giver of wealth. (13)
The gods, celestial sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, having addressed the preeminent yakṣa, sport and take their pleasure there.
It is not possible here to roam or play for long without one's teacher, brother, minister, friend, or even a son. (15)
Whoever, out of arrogance, treats the Lord of Wealth with contempt through some unjust means and constructs a monastery, shall undoubtedly perish. (16)
Thus was Vaḍala restrained by the terrible Rākṣasas from all sides, who were angrily threatening him, saying, "Do not do this! Do not do this! (17)
But disregarding those rākṣasas, he of terrible prowess and great splendor plunged forward; they all sought to restrain him.

"Seize him! Bind him! Cut him down! Let us drink his blood and devour this man devoid of virtue! Thus they cried out in their rage, rushing forward swiftly with eyes rolling as they brandished their weapons. (19)
Then, seizing that heavy great mace, bound with golden bands and resembling the staff of Yama, he rushed forward with speed and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (20)

Having seen his heroism and strength, as well as the power of his knowledge and the might of his arms, those assembled foremost warriors were unable to withstand him; they were struck down and suddenly retreated. (21)
Being torn apart right there, they quickly took to the sky; with their senses bewildered and shattered by the Yakṣas, those guardians fled toward the peaks of Kailāsa.

Having displayed his prowess and conquered the hosts of Dānavas and Daityas like Śakra, that capable son of a Yakṣa, though tormented by passion, entered that lotus pond and sported according to his desire.
Then those guardians, driven by Vātāpi, approached the Lord of Wealth and, being exceedingly terrified, reported exactly as it had occurred the Yakṣa’s fortitude and great strength in battle.
Having heard their words, the highly illustrious Maṇibhadra cursed his beloved son Vaḍala for the sake of his master.
Since that delightful lotus pond was frequented by Vaḍala, it became as dear to him as even the beloved of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), and indeed like a mother to him.
Therefore, my son shall be deprived of all fortune; he will be lame, blind, deaf, wretched, and will suffer from consumption.
Thus cursed, he was then born as a *vaḍala* snake, devoid of enjoyment; even though he had gone to that place, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Afflicted by the disease of consumption, he was unable to move; then, struck by his preceptor’s curse, he became blind and deaf.
He suddenly reflected upon that most wonderful and great curse: "By whom have I been suddenly cursed, having entered the interior of another while still alive? (30)
"How was I, your beloved son—youthful, heroic, and the destroyer of the enemy host—cursed by my father Maṇibhadra? (31)
Blessed indeed is that Maṇibhadra, my father, by whom, out of devotion to his Lord, his own son was cursed and abandoned on the earth at that very moment.
Vaḍala spoke again: "I am blessed because of my lord; for those who subsist on their master's provisions, death itself is called a festival. (33)
"Because I began and accumulated [this] for a long time through unrighteous means according to my own whims, I have incurred a curse and shall certainly go to hell. (34)
O fair-faced one, while Vaḍala was thus lamenting, the exceedingly powerful Maṇibhadra arrived at that place; he saw his son crippled, blind, and afflicted by consumption.

To his son, who was sighing, afflicted by great sorrow, and lamenting again and again, the Yakṣa Maṇibhadra, himself deeply distressed, replied: "Alas, my child! You have been cursed by me, your father, out of anger for the sake of my master."
This beautiful lotus pond, so dear to the giver of wealth, was enjoyed by you while scorched by passion; and the foremost Rākṣasas were slain by you. (37)
Therefore, my son, the curse pronounced by me shall not be in vain; for the god is the lord, the master is the lord, the mother is the lord, and the father is the lord.
He who, for the sake of his master, abandons his dear life in battle, goes to the supreme station, the eternal world of Brahmā. || 39 ||
This curse cannot be remedied by mantras, nor by medicine, nor by vows, nor by religious observances, nor by gifts; therefore, do as I say. (40)
I heard this ancient account, proclaimed by Skanda, as Nārada himself was speaking in the presence of the gods long ago in the world of Śakra.
The power of Mahākālavana has been described by him; for in this sacred field, there is a great Liṅga to the south of Svargadvāra.
There exists a remedy that pacifies disease and bestows beauty and good fortune; there I shall lead you and myself by means of a swiftly moving celestial chariot.
Having spoken thus, Maṇibhadra then brought his son to the place where that God of gods resides, to the south of Svargadvāra.
By the touch of that linga, he immediately became endowed with sight, possessed of beauty, strong, with excellent feet, and gifted with the power of hearing at that very moment.

O Pārvatī, having witnessed this great marvel, Maṇibhadra, being exceedingly delighted, bestowed upon his own son a name according to the name of this Liṅga; by the power of this Liṅga, he became possessed of sight, though previously blind.
"From this day forward, this deity shall be known as Vaḍaleśvara; he will become famous throughout the three worlds as the bestower of eyes. (47)
Those who shall worship the deity known as Vaḍaleśvara, the Liṅga renowned throughout the worlds, they shall attain their heart's desire. (48)
When seen, he removes sins; when touched, he bestows sovereignty; when worshipped with a spirit of devotion, he grants liberation—of this there is no doubt. (49)
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, those who shall worship the deity known as Vaḍaleśvara— || 50 ||
They have constantly given gifts; they go to the supreme state at Prayāga, at Prabhāsa, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. || 51 ||
By them, penance has been truly performed; they are liberated, of this there is no doubt. They are not born again in a womb, being endowed with all happiness.
By beholding Vaḍaleśvara, men are born in this world as followers of Gaṇapati, ever beloved by Śaṅkara, endowed with good fortune and beauty, and possessed of sons and grandsons. (53)
He who finds no pleasure in dwelling within the womb, a place of great suffering, let him worship with devotion the Lord Vaḍaleśvara.
Without the *liṅga*, success is not achieved; the supreme state is difficult to attain. No progress toward heaven occurs as long as one does not worship the *liṅga*.
For those who are devoid of the worship of the Liṅga, even spiritual perfection (siddhi) is very difficult to attain; yet my son has obtained his desired goal from the Liṅga.
Having spoken thus, Maṇibhadra also departed together with his son to where the god Dhanādhyakṣa had gone to his own supreme abode.
Thus, O Goddess, has this sin-destroying majesty of the god Vaḍaleśvara been told to you; now let the [majesty of] Aruṇeśvara be heard.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vaḍaleśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" section of the Umā-Maheśvara dialogue, in the fifth book (Āvantyakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 75 ||
Īśvara said: O Goddess, know that the sixty-seventh deity is named Aruṇeśvara; he removes sins and grants the desires of men upon being seen. || 1 ||
Formerly, O Goddess, in the age of the gods, there were two auspicious sisters, the daughters of Prajāpati, who were endowed with wonderful beauty and were faultless.
Kaśyapa had two wives, Kadrū and Vinatā; their husband, who was equal to Prajāpati, being pleased, granted a boon to them both.
Kaśyapa, filled with supreme joy upon hearing from Kaśyapa that those two excellent boons had indeed been granted, [was accompanied] by his two lawful wives.
The two excellent women experienced a joy exceeding even their delight; Kadrū chose as her sons a thousand nāgas of equal splendor.
Vinatā chose two sons who would be superior in strength to the sons of Kadrū, and likewise superior in vigor, splendor, and prowess.
Her husband granted her a boon, saying, "You shall obtain two most excellent sons. Then Kaśyapa said to Vinatā, "So be it."
And having obtained the boon as requested, Vinatā was then satisfied; she felt her purpose fulfilled upon obtaining two sons superior in prowess.
And Kadrū, having obtained a thousand sons of equal splendor, was told by that great ascetic: "The two embryos must be carried with great care. (9)
After those two wives had been greatly delighted, Kaśyapa entered the forest. After a long time, Kadrū, whose limbs were beautiful, gave birth to one thousand nāgas, and Vinatā then laid two eggs.
The delighted attendants placed their eggs in vessels with steam for five hundred years.
Then, after five hundred years had passed, the sons of Kadrū emerged from their eggs; however, no pair was seen from the eggs of Vinatā.
Then the ascetic Queen Vinatā, desiring a son and feeling ashamed, split the egg and beheld a son therein.
It is heard that her son, enraged with anger, cursed her as she revealed his excellence of the upper half of his body by means of the other [lower] half. || 14 ||
"O mother, since I have been made thus incomplete in body by you, overcome by greed, therefore you shall become a slave. (15)
"O mother, for five hundred years you have always vied with her; this son of yours shall indeed deliver you from that slave-woman."
O Mother, if you do not likewise make this son of mine bodiless through the breaking of his eggshell, or if you do not make him exceedingly swift like me; (17)
Therefore, you must wait with patience for his time of birth for another five hundred years, desiring that he attain preeminent strength.
Having thus cursed his own mother Vinatā, O Goddess, Aruṇa then lamented, overwhelmed by tears and grief.

Alas, alas! By me, a cruel man, my own mother, my very own progenitor, has been cursed despite being without fault; how shall I attain a happy state? A mother is the fire-drill for the bodies of men, and a mother is the supreme endurer of one's suffering.
The mother alone knows the supreme suffering that exists within the affliction of pregnancy; moreover, a mother's affection is seen to be greater than that of a father.
Among all gurus, the mother is remembered as the most venerable; for even a single son, no atonement has been seen in the Vedas.

If a son performs the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā after his father has passed away, that brings peace to the mother; for a father feels no sense of possessiveness toward one who is bereft of a mother.

Indeed, a son is then said to be "deficient" when he is deprived of his mother; when he grows old, he becomes sorrowful. When one is separated from one's mother, then the entire world becomes empty. (24)
Thus, having become one of sinful conduct and a violator of my mother, I shall die without a doubt after kindling the sacrificial fire.
"I was born with impaired limbs solely due to my past actions; for my mother is not the cause, since one must experience the fruits of one's own karma. (26)
O large-eyed one, while Kaśyapa’s son Aruṇa was thus lamenting, Nārada arrived.
Seeing Aruṇa afflicted by great sorrow and lamenting again and again, Nārada, with a tranquil soul, replied as if smiling: || 28 ||
"Ah, this Aruṇa, the son of Kaśyapa, the eldest son of Vinatā and a treasure-trove of ascetic powers, is crying out. (29)

"This one of great strength has been born from the half-body of the short-lived [Viprachitti]; I shall console him, who was born from the womb of Vinatā and is lamenting out of delusion; surely my own welfare will be secured. (30)
Having thus reflected in his mind, Nārada, the best of the twice-born, replied there to Aruṇa with words resembling honey and nectar.
O dear one, heir of Kaśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā, mass of splendor, invincible one, do not cause distress in vain.
In this world, the destined events of both suffering and happiness come to pass; for that which you, Vinatā, have cursed is a secret ordained by the gods.
If there is compassion in your heart for the mother who cursed you, then go at my command to the auspicious Mahākālavana.
To the north lies the merit-bestowing [shrine] of the God of gods, Yātreśa; it is auspicious, worshipped by the thirty deities, and always grants everything. (35)
Thus addressed by the high-souled Nārada, Aruṇa arrived at the auspicious Mahākālavana in half a moment.
There he beheld that auspicious liṅga, resembling a mass of radiant light; filled with devotion, he worshipped it according to the prescribed rites with flowers.
O Goddess, the Liṅga said to Aruṇa: "Always perform the office of charioteer for the Sun as he revolves; there is no charioteer equal to you. (38)
I have always granted this power to the Sun: O Aruṇa, your rising shall indeed be first, and only afterwards will the Sun rise. (39)
By your name, I shall become renowned in the three worlds as Aruṇeśvara; there is no doubt that I will be the bestower of wealth upon men. (40)
Those who constantly behold me as Cāruṇeśvara by your name shall go to the supreme abode, which is free from burning and dissolution.
Those who, with concentrated minds, behold [the deity] shall rejoice for a thousand crores of kalpas together with their families, born of both father and mother.
No suffering arising from the ocean of saṃsāra shall befall those who behold the Sun during the day, for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
He who beholds Aruṇeśvara on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [attains the highest state].

He will lead his ancestors to heaven who reside in hell; of this there is no doubt. He who beholds Aruṇeśvara on a Saṃkrānti day or on a Sunday has undoubtedly performed the pilgrimage to Śuṇḍīrasvāmin. (45)
Having been addressed thus by that Linga, the son of Vinatā then arrived, his purpose accomplished, at the place where the god Divaspati was.
By the power of this Liṅga, Kaśyapa’s own son, Aruṇa, is always seen in the sky in front of the Sun.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the deity Aruṇeśvara has been told to you; now hear about Puṣpavaṃteśvara. || 48 ||

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Aruṇeśvara," within the "Majesty of the Eighty-four Liṅgas" in the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Goddess, listen to the account of Puṣpadaṃteśvara, the seventy-seventh [Tīrtha], by the mere sight of which one is not born again in a womb. || 1 ||
O Goddess, there was formerly a twice-born man named Śini who was childless; for the sake of a son, he performed many austerities.
He subsisted on air, he subsisted on water, he remained without food with his arms raised, he ate vegetables, roots, and fruits, he ate only leaves, or he consumed one or two leaves at a time.
These and other such austerities lead to the highest good; among all these austerities, I shall resort to one particular austerity. (4)

"For the sake of pacifying obstacles, I shall propitiate the Lord. Having reflected thus in his mind, with arms raised and feet upturned, [he thought]: "He cannot be difficult to reach by these two means, nor will there be any offense."
In that manner, the sage indeed practiced it for twelve years; and seeing him performing penance, established in the highest discipline, [the gods were amazed].
"O Goddess, I have been informed by you that on Mount Mandara, in its beautiful caves, this great sage is performing severe penance for the sake of a son. (7)
Illuminating the mountain with his splendor and drying up the reservoirs of water, the inhabitants of heaven were agitated by his exceedingly difficult asceticism.
The lords of serpents became agitated, the sovereigns of mountains were shaken, the sages fell into forgetfulness, and even heaven and earth trembled.
The wise Śini, who is not born from a womb, desires a son not born from a womb; you are the source of the collection of qualities, and you are also the source of austerities.
You are austerity, you are the supreme abode, O you whose eyes are the peacock, the moon, and the sun; O Lord of All, you are the beloved son—what is not to be given to the Brahmin? (11)
O teacher of gods and asuras, why do you not grant a son to this one, whose defects have been worn away by austerity and whose self is purified for the state of Brahman?
O Śiva, at my word, grant a son to Śini; that great sage has been deeply afflicted by his extremely difficult penance.
Established in his own ordinance, he took away the splendors of even the great luminaries with his own brilliance, just as the sun consumes the darkness.
O Lord of Gods, why should the exertion of one devoted to you be in vain? When the sun has risen, darkness never remains here. (15)
“O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, I have been entreated by you thus: ‘O Divine One, for one who is devoted to you, the intimidation of suffering is not fitting. (16)
O Goddess, out of compassion for the Brahmins and especially for the sake of my son, I have summoned the Gaṇas through your honor.
The Rudras, the devotees of Hara, the Kūṣmāṇḍas who roam the sky, the Romaraudras, the Mahānīlas, the Śikhāvants, and the Kokilas. || 18 ||
And others of various forms, with black faces and tawny-brown hair, wearing matted locks, were variegated and moved along the paths of the constellations.
Blue-necked, black-faced, with tawny and matted hair and manes; Jvara, Diṇḍi, Mahākāla, Lāṅguli, and Maheśvara. || 20 ||
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Viśākha, and those who are the remaining Gaṇas, are mounted upon bulls; they are equal to Kāma in beauty and likewise possess the power to assume any form at will.
All of them bore tridents and crescent moons; all were equal in prowess. Having arrived at my command, they stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Praising him with various hymns, they spoke thus with concentrated minds: "O Lord, let an instruction be given; what should be done by us here? (23)
Having heard the words of the assembly and recognized such devotion, this power of the great asceticism of the Brahmin Śini has been proclaimed. (24)
The Śini, that best of Brahmins, is performing austerities for the sake of a son; at my word, who indeed will grant the status of a son to this sage? (25)
To him I shall grant all his desires exactly as he wishes; for at present, the sage desires a son who is immortal and free from old age.
Let my word be carried out immediately; let the Brahmin be released from his suffering. The resolve of one devoted to me ought not to be rendered false.
Having heard my words, all of them had their necks trembling; they all became downcast and were entirely absorbed in meditation. || 28 ||
At that time, no one spoke anything, nor did anyone look on; then Puṣpadanta, filled with pride, spoke impetuously.
O Lord, out of compassion for the hosts and without understanding my mind, these hosts will not depart from the surface of the earth, leaving you behind.
They shall dwell here constantly by your side, without a doubt; having attained supreme joy, how could they ever enter a womb again? (31)
Base, full of passion, wretched, and bearing an abundance of darkness—how can we abandon heaven and go to the supreme hell? (32)
O large-eyed lady, as he was speaking thus, impelled by his destiny which was yet to be, Puṣpadanta, the leader of the Gaṇas, was addressed by me with words born of delusion alone.
"Fall down into the world of men, for you have done me a displeasure. Having thus cursed Puṣpadanta, Vīraka was dispatched by me.
"O son, by my command, quickly attain the status of a Brahmin's son; then I shall grant you all your desires exactly as you wish. (35)
Thus addressed, O Goddess, Vīraka attained the state of being the Brahmin’s son; Puṣpadanta, however, being deeply distressed, lamented piteously.
Filled with remorse and sighing again and again, he said: "Aha! That birth is truly fruitful when one's commands are carried out by men. (37)
Such servants who serve their masters with single-minded devotion are considered rare; by them, wealth, dharma, and even their own lineage are delivered to salvation. (38)
The thirty gods are pleased with those men who are devoted to their Lord; for the duty of service is profound and difficult to perform even for yogins. (39)
By what means can the Lord, who is difficult to propitiate, be known in his true nature? For the Lord may fall into a rage over even a single offense. (40)
Benefits perish; therefore, service is extremely difficult to perform. For a master, a serpent, and fire all indeed tend toward a state of heat.
Therefore, those intent on self-protection should serve him with great effort; yet here I am, fallen upon the earth, a violator of my master’s command.
"To what worlds shall I go, defiled as I am like a slayer of an embryo? Having lamented thus many times, he sought refuge in me alone; bowing down again and again, he spoke with a piteous voice. (43)
"I am wretched, I am devoid of knowledge, and I am bowed before you, O Śaṅkara! Grant me grace, O Lord of Gods, and forgive my transgression. (44)
For the anger of lords does not subside toward those who have sought their protection; be gracious, O Lord of the gods, toward one who is wretched and miserable. 45.
"Even if I must become a worm or a moth by your command, O Lord, I shall remain forever devoted, firmly established in the state of being your son. (46)
O Pārvatī, having heard these words of Puṣpadanta, O Goddess, you then spoke these words out of a sense of possessiveness: ||| 47 ||
"Go, my son, at my command to the auspicious Mahākālavana; worship the Liṅga there quickly, and it shall become known by your name. (48)
"O son, your fame shall endure as long as the dissolution of all beings," thus was it said by you, O Goddess; and when this was spoken by you, O fair-faced one, I too replied.
"O son, my word shall never prove false in any way; by the mere sight of the Liṅga, you shall become dear to me. (50)
You shall ascend the flower-footed celestial chariot; being honored with flowers, you will attain the eternal state.
"You shall wander joyfully together with the hosts and with me; yet, my child, even for me there will be no pleasure without you."
"I shall come there to the auspicious Mahākālavana; I am always pleased, my child, having been made the leader of the Gaṇas. (53)
By means of this pure devotion, you will undoubtedly become a benefactor of the worlds once you have certainly gone to that sacred field.
O Goddess, having been addressed thus by me, the leader of the Gaṇas, Puṣpadanta—who was proud and observing silence at my command—performed auspicious rites in the Mahākālavana forest.
He then worshipped the Liṅga to the north of Durvāseśa. Addressed by the Liṅga, he was told: "O best of Gaṇas, I am pleased; I shall become famous by your name. Your favor has now been granted. (56)
In the meantime, O Goddess, I went together with you, along with Śakra and the other gods, as well as various kinds of Gaṇas.
Delighted, Puṣpadanta also, being strewn with flowers, arrived once more in my presence upon an auspicious flower-clothed seat.
"Out of affection, he was embraced by me and even placed upon my lap; O large-eyed one, I gave him this place and spoke these words at that time. (59)
Those men who behold the Liṅga worshipped by you on earth shall go to heaven, sporting in the Puṣpaka chariot.
They shall become leaders of the Gaṇas, adorned with all their desires; they shall remain as leaders of my Gaṇas in my world for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
By the mere sight [of me], sin—both of this life and that of the past—is destroyed; thereafter, through my grace, all knowledge shall become perfectly manifest.
Whoever worships on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, or on a Monday, rejoices forever in heaven, delighted along with the immortals.
That man who, having risen in the morning, does not speak with anyone, [is joined] together with seven generations of his paternal and maternal lineages.
Having seen Puṣpadanteśvara, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; even he who beholds it with deceit is liberated from sins and the like.

Upon death, he goes to the world of the Gandharvas, surrounded by Vidyādharas; there is no interruption of his lineage for him who beholds [the deity] day after day with regularity. O Lord of the Gaṇas, he is born as a leader of the Gaṇas for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Having enjoyed sovereignty and pleasures in the seven worlds in due order, and having become the sole ruler of the earth, he shall be born from my own body.
This sin-destroying majesty of the Lord Puṣpadanteśvara has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about Avimukteśvara.
Īśvara said: Know, O beloved, that the seventy-eighth is Avimukteśvara; by the mere sight of whom one obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage.
O Goddess, in the city of Śākala there was a lord of the earth named Citrasena, who was renowned on earth, handsome, and superior even to the God of Love. || 2 ||
His wife was Candraprabhā, dearer to him than his own life; she was devoted to her husband, virtuous in character, and endowed with beauty and youth. (3)
To the king, though he was childless, a daughter named Manoramā was born; then her father, that best of monarchs, bestowed a name upon her.
The goddess, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of great beauty, was also a rememberer of her former births; she recollected her past life.
Out of dispassion, the slender-waisted woman practiced celibacy; and when she had reached youth, she was indeed questioned by the king.
Placing her on his own lap and smelling her head with joy, he said: "O daughter, the time for your giving has arrived; to which excellent groom should you be given?"
To the king, to the prince, to the esteemed brahmin, to the elder with many wives, and to the villager who had sons—the king, filled with joy, questioned his daughter once again.
When the queen, having been questioned, did not speak to the king, she became downcast; yet she was addressed by the king once more.
"If my words do not seem appropriate to you now, daughter, then choose for yourself a husband according to your own desire through a svayaṃvara."
Thus addressed by the king, and spoken to again and again by her father, she wept piteously upon hearing of that contemptible fate.
He laughed with a loud laugh and again released sighs; and having quickly attained great joy, he again shed tears. || 12 ||
Seeing his daughter in that state, having fallen into madness, the king wondered, "What is this? Has she indeed been seized by a planetary spirit?"
"Or has my daughter, who is endowed with auspicious marks, been seized by a bhūta or a piśāca?"—when the king became thus absorbed in anxious thought, O illustrious lady. (14)
Then she was told by her daughter: "O father, do not be despondent; I have not been seized here by a planet, nor by a spirit, nor by a demon. (15)
"O lord of the earth, your daughter has not been seized by a piśāca or a yakṣa; I have been born with the memory of my former lives. Listen now to my birth story. (16)
O King, in the city of Prāgjyotiṣa there was a brahmin named Harasvāmī; I became his wife, O monarch, though born unfortunate. (17)
"O Lord, though I am endowed with beauty and youth, I am not dear to him; he is always filled with hatred toward me and speaks harshly. (18)
O Lord of the Earth, she has no hatred for anyone else except me; however, at the time of her marriage, she was gazed upon by malefic planets.
I was approached by a noble and highly virtuous Brahmin; and that Brahmin, O lord of men, was beheld by the auspicious planets.
Therefore, O King, he is dear to me, yet I am not dear to him; for he is endowed with virtuous conduct and is devoted to the study of the Vedas.

Established in the vow of celibacy, he did not direct his affection toward anyone else. Thereupon, filled with anger and eager for subjugation, O dear one, I questioned those women who were said to have been abandoned by their husbands.
"O King, they said to me, 'Your husband will become submissive'; we have gained confidence from this, therefore you ought to do it. (23)
Even if he is smeared with various medicines, powders, and other supreme deluding mantras, the husband will become like a servant.
Then, O King, having gone quickly at their word and having taken the powder and the mantra, I returned once more to my husband's house. || 25 ||
At twilight, this powder mixed with milk was administered to my husband, and I placed a mantra upon his neck and in all the joints of his limbs.
When the powder, thoroughly consecrated with the mantra, was drunk, he became subject to control at that very moment through the power of the mantra and the powder. || 27 ||
Standing at the doorway, he cried out: "I am your slave, O beautiful one! Protect me, who have come to you for refuge; I am under your power, O beautiful one! (28)
O King, having understood his weeping through the power of the mantra, the husband was then restored to health by means of the yoga of restoration.
From that time forward, my beloved remained in our home under my control; however, in due course, he met his death and likewise underwent the torments of hell.
I was burned in a copper frying pan for fifteen yugas; having been cut into many minute pieces the size of sesame seeds by the Kālasūtra hell, I was crushed in the nose-pressing machine.
She was boiled in hot oils in a pot and stirred with a ladle; then she was ground upon a stone slab and pounded with iron mallets.
I was crushed by the gnashing of teeth and severely scorched in the Raurava hell; with my face cast downward, I was thrown into excrement, pus, and blood.
Furthermore, O dear one, whatever young woman acts contrary to the will of her husband, that woman of wicked conduct, having practiced dharma in vain, is cooked intensely in hell.
The husband is the lord, the husband is the guru, the husband is indeed the supreme deity; the husband is the master, the husband is the friend, and the husband is the highest state. (35)

When the husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women; when he turns his face away, they all turn away. Therefore, the husband should always be served. That woman by whom the husband is not satisfied is reduced to ashes.
And how can she who brings him under her control—by whose grace various enjoyments are always obtained—ever attain happiness? (37)
One goes to a hundred animal births and becomes hundreds of worms and birds; therefore, women must always carry out whatever their husbands command. 38.
In this way, moreover, I experienced hells that were exceedingly terrible, as well as thousands of births among the animal realm due to my contemptible karma. (39)
For the sake of purifying a certain sin, I was born in the house of a Caṇḍāla with a beautiful form, yet afflicted by various wounds.

Surrounded by dogs and being devoured again and again, I was miserable; though I am wicked, even as I was being eaten, I was blocked on the path by wolves. Even while being tormented by them, I reached the Mahākāla forest.
While searching for my husband, I beheld Mahādeva near the deity Pippalādeśvara, the God of gods.

Merely by the sight of him, she departed toward the city of Śakra, traveling in a brilliantly shining celestial chariot garlanded with clusters of tinkling bells; she was divine, wearing celestial garments and adorned with celestial garlands.
There I was honored by the gods and likewise praised by the celestial bards; through the sight of that linga, I have been born in your household. (44)
My beloved, endowed with beauty, was in the auspicious city of Śākala; remembering that despicable birth, I uttered this lamentation. (45)
Upon remembering the majesty of the Liṅga, joy arose within me at that very moment; this is not madness on my part, nor have I been seized by a planetary spirit.

"O Father, having been born with the memory of my former lives, I am established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). Therefore, O Lord, I shall go once more to that God for the sake of seeing him, so that there may be no further birth for me in the ocean of saṃsāra. (47)
Having heard these words of his daughter, King Citrasena, accompanied by his servants and ministers, went to the Mahākāla forest.
There he beheld that Linga and worshipped it with devotion; she too, upon merely seeing that Linga, attained absorption into that very Linga.
And by the sight of that sign, O beloved, the king became a possessor of a son; he became a universal monarch (cakravartin), just like Svāyambhuva Manu.
In the meantime, O Great Goddess, having seen the princess absorbed into the God, the gods, filled with joy, bestowed a name upon her. (51)
"By the mere sight of this unliberated linga, may it become known at that very moment as the god Avimukteśvara. (52)
That very god Śiva, who is renowned as Viśveśvara in Kāśī, is here likewise well-known by the name Avimukteśvara.
Just as Vārāṇasī is meritorious, so too is Avantī the bestower of liberation; it is heard that the merit here is specifically ten times greater than that.
Therefore, the Lord Viśveśvara arrived at Kuśasthalī, where, having come, men became highly learned and possessed of praised vows.
Those who behold Śiva, the Lord of Avimukta, with supreme devotion, will undoubtedly attain unwavering liberation; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Those who are unliberated do not see it at all, while those who are liberated see it always; this may be attained through the vows of celibacy and by properly performing all sacrifices.
That fruit is fully attained through the vision of the Unfailing One; the meritorious state of ultimate liberation arises from that very vision alone. (58)

Whatever goal is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya, or whatever goal may be reached by those of Yoga—that goal is not properly attained without the vision of the Lord who is free from bondage. (59)
Having abandoned the fear of birth and death, he attains the supreme goal—he who worships Śiva, the Lord of Avimukta, with true devotion.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin who goes to Avimukteśvara and worships there, is freed from all sins through the majesty of that Liṅga. || 61 ||
And whoever, even through deceit, beholds the Lord Śiva in Avimukta, he abandons old age, death, and this impermanent birth.
When remembered, worshipped with devotion, or praised with various hymns, Śiva, the Lord of Gods and the Sovereign of Avimukta, indeed bestows liberation.
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of the Lord of Avimukteśvara has been told to you; now hear about Hanumatkeśvara.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O beloved, know that Hanumatkeśvara is the seventy-ninth [liṅga]; by the mere sight of whom one obtains the fruit of one's desires.
O Queen, when Rāma had obtained the kingdom and the slaughter of the rākṣasas was accomplished, the sages arrived to congratulate the descendant of Raghu.
Having been honored by Rāma, all those twice-born ones, headed by Agastya, with delighted minds, addressed these words to Rāma. || 3 ||
By good fortune, O Rāma, Rāvaṇa has been slain along with his sons and grandsons; by good fortune, we behold you today victorious together with your wife.
And together with the high-souled monkey Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god and the destroyer of the Rākṣasas—by good fortune!—(5)
May the monkey Hanumān, born from the womb of Añjanī and indeed a portion of Rudra upon the earth, live long and enjoy a full lifespan forever.
May Ākhaṇḍala, the lord Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Śiva, together with Brahmā—may these guardians of the directions protect [you] at all times.
Having heard the words of those sages of purified souls, Rāma was filled with supreme wonder and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
For what reason has this monkey been praised while abandoning Lakṣmaṇa? Of what sort is he, what is his power, what is his strength, and what is his valor? (9)
Then they said: "O best of monkeys, this is indeed true; however, there exists no one equal to him in valor within the three worlds. (10)
O Lord, this one of great wisdom leaped across a hundred yojanas; having overpowered the city of Laṅkā, he entered the inner apartments of Rāvaṇa.
Indeed, he fashioned a form the size of a span; Sītā was seen by him, spoken to, questioned, and likewise reassured.
The army leaders, the sons of ministers, and the servants—the sons of Rāvaṇa—were slain by Hanumān there, having been struck down at the abode of Rāvaṇa.
Furthermore, after conversing with the Ten-faced one who was liberated from his bonds, Laṅkā was reduced to ashes by him, as the earth is by sin.
Such deeds as those of Hanūmat are not heard of even in the case of Kāla, nor of Śakra, nor of Viṣṇu, nor even of Brahmā. || 15 ||
Rāma said: "By the strength of his arms, Laṅkā, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa were recovered; likewise, my victory, my kingdom, my friends, and my kinsmen were regained. (16)
Having released this bull among monkeys, his friend, who else would be capable of even knowing the news regarding Jānakī? (17)
For what reason was Vālin not burnt like straw at that time when enmity had arisen, by him [Rāma] who desired to do what was pleasing to Sugrīva? (18)
I believe that Hanumān did not recognize his own strength; why was he indifferent while the lord of the monkeys was suffering? (19)
To Rāma, who was speaking thus, the sages addressed these words: "O best of the Raghus, what you say concerning Hanumān is true. (20)
There is no one equal to him in strength, nor in speed, nor even in intellect; yet in the past, the sages pronounced a curse upon him with words that were unfailing.
Indeed, the strength by which that powerful one crushed Vālin was not known; for even in his childhood, great deeds were performed by this high-souled one.
That great power of his cannot be described; however, if you desire to hear it, listen as we speak. (23)
For even as soon as he was born, like the embodied young sun, desiring to seize the young sun, he leaped into the midst of the sky.
O Rāma, as he was running swiftly, his jaw was suddenly struck by Śakra—who knows his own self—as if by a thunderbolt.

Then, struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt, he fell upon the mountain; as he was falling with great force, his left jaw was broken. When that boy had fallen, nearly dead from the wound of the lightning bolt—
Then Vāyu, taking [the linga] with him, went to Mahākālavana; there, Pavana then propitiated the Linga for the sake of a son.
As soon as he was touched by the Liṅga, the monkey rose up; like a crop sprinkled with water, he regained his life.
Seeing him possessed of breath, the Wind-god was then delighted; with a gracious soul, he quickly took his son and replied.
"By the touch of this linga, my son has arisen; he shall become the renowned deity Hanumatkeśvara. (30)
In the meantime, Śakra arrived, surrounded by the gods; taking up a garland made of blue lotuses, he spoke as follows: || 31 ||
"Since his jaw has been struck by the thunderbolt released from my hand, therefore this tiger among monkeys shall be known as Hanumān."
Varuṇa granted him a boon, saying, "Death shall not befall him"; Yama granted him immunity from punishment; and Dhanada bestowed upon him health.
Then, in the presence of the gods, the Sun granted him radiance, the Wind granted swift movement, and the Liṅga granted him a boon.
Indeed, he shall be invulnerable to all weapons; he shall be free from old age and immortal—of this there is no doubt. (35)
For he is indeed the giver of fear to enemies and the bestower of fearlessness to friends; it has been stated again and again by the Liṅga that he shall be invincible in battle.
For the destruction of the enemy's strength and for the constant pleasure of Rāghava, how long will he not remember his own army due to the curse? (37)
But once Rāvaṇa is slain, remaining further under the authority of Rāma, he will request Vibhīṣaṇa and establish me here. (38)
Then all the gods, being purified, will worship me; by that very name, I shall again attain renown upon the earth. (39)
Then Gandhavaha, taking his son with him, brought him home; he then related to Añjanā the attainment of the boon as it appeared from the sign.
Thus, by the power of his mark (liṅga), that son of the Wind-god was born powerful; therefore, O Rāma, he is praised throughout the three worlds. (41)

In this world, who is there superior to Hanumān in valor, zeal, intelligence, and majesty; or in virtuous conduct, sweetness, and statesmanship; or in profundity, cleverness, great heroism, and fortitude? (42)
Who could stand before Hanumān—himself like an agitated ocean, like a fire wishing to consume the worlds, or like a cataka bird desiring to seize the creatures? (43)
I have indeed related to you all that you asked me concerning this youth Hanumān, whose deeds possess marvelous prowess.

"O Rāma, we have been seen and honored; now we shall depart. Having spoken thus, all the sages went to the region of Avantī and worshipped the Lord Śiva as Hanumatkeśvara. Those who devoutly worship the Liṅga Hanumatkeśvara, which is adored by the gods, have achieved their life's purpose in the Kali age. (46)
They indeed go toward the imperishable union with Brahman, which is so difficult to attain; having reached it, they do not undergo rebirth again, but obtain eternal liberation.
O beloved, the man who beholds the Liṅga at Hanumatkeśvara obtains abundant fruit, being liberated from all suffering. || 48 ||
In all worlds, his movement is never obstructed; he is endowed with divine sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (49)
Surrounded by thousands of women, he traveled with a radiant celestial chariot that resembled the rising sun, moving with unimpeded ease both to and fro.
He now wanders through all the worlds of the celestial dwellers without hesitation; most desirable to men, he is currently the highest among all castes.
