Falling from heaven, he shall be born handsome in a great family, a knower of dharma, a devotee of Rudra, and one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.
Upon seeing this, one becomes like a king or equal to a king; from touching it, supreme merit arises; and from worshipping it, the highest state is attained. (53)
O Goddess, this sin-destroying majesty of Hanumatkeśvareśa has been recounted to you; now hear about Svapneśvara.
Īśvara said: O beloved, know that the god Svapneśvara is eighty years old; by the mere sight of him, an evil dream is certainly destroyed.
O Goddess, there was once a king renowned in the world as Kalmāṣapāda, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, who was like the sun on earth in his splendor.

Once, in the forest, the king beheld Śakti, the legitimate son of Vasiṣṭha, who was supremely conversant with dharma and had conquered his senses; as he stood on the path, devoted to asceticism, the king said to him, "Move aside."
But when that sage did not yield the path, the best of kings, out of delusion, then struck the muni with a whip as if he were a Rākṣasa.
Then, struck by the lash, that bull among sages, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha, overcome with rage and faint with anger, cursed him.
"O lowest of kings, because you have slain an ascetic like a Rākṣasa, therefore from this day forward you shall become a man-eater. (6)
"You shall wander this earth constantly addicted to flesh. Thus was that best of kings cursed by him at that very moment.

He went for refuge to Śakti, honoring him in order to propitiate him; yet when the brahmin-sage Śakti was not pleased and remained exceedingly wrathful, even though he was being propitiated by the king, he was then devoured by him as well.
Having devoured Śakti, he then suddenly devoured those other sons of Vasiṣṭha, just as a lion devours small deer.
From that time forward, that best of kings became a man-eater; deluded by a multitude of sins, he saw evil dreams at night.
Having seen those terrifying dreams, the king was tormented; filled with remorse, he lamented in great distress.
Furthermore, it was said by the ministers: "O Lord of the Earth, what are you doing? Why is your radiance lusterless, and why are you pale, wan, and emaciated? (12)
That king related his bad dreams in succession: "In a dream, I saw the ocean dried up and the moon fallen upon the earth. (13)
And I beheld the world obstructed and enveloped in thick darkness, while I myself appeared soiled, with my hair disheveled.
Falling from a mountain peak into a foul pool of cow dung, he drank oil with his cupped hands, laughing as it were again and again.
With all my limbs anointed with oil and immersing myself in oil itself, I sat upon an iron seat with my face turned downwards.
Passionate women, adorned with red garlands and unguents, sing; others, wearing black garments and black garlands and unguents, do the same.
Although I was being drawn by them, I was led toward the southern direction, having been bound with ropes of gold, iron, and silver.
Sunk in the midst of dust and mud, I am bound by iron chains; I am being tormented by pigeons, vultures, and fierce crows. (19)
While being devoured by jackals, I remained upon the head of a madgura fish; then, seated upon the vehicle of a bear and a monkey, I departed toward the southern direction.
Immersed in a river that was devoid of water and level with the ground, I lay motionless; at night, I was bitten by a donkey and mangled by its teeth.
He is struck excessively in the heart with feet resembling vajras, and his vision is violently destroyed by vetālas with iron spears.
In a dream, I was struck excessively by terrifying, dark men with raised weapons, and by immeasurable, sharp arrows.
Thus was this terrifying night seen by me; it would be impossible to count the many other evil dreams [I have seen].

Having indeed beheld this course of a bad dream, so manifold in form and never before imagined, a great fear has seized my heart and it is not at peace; clasping my arms, I lament like one who is helpless. (25)
Having heard the king's words, the ministers were deeply distressed, as they then beheld ill omens such as the falling of meteors and other portents.
O son of the Sun, a city occupied by the Sun and Mars is now seen; likewise, the nāga, catuṣpada, viṣṭi, kiṃstughna, and śakuni [karanas] are present.
The astrological instruments were not auspicious, and the moments became dreadful; for they perceived the king’s defeat, as well as the ruin of the country and the destruction of his lineage. (28)
Consoling the king, they spoke these words: "Enough with grief, O descendant of Kakutstha; for delusions may be either true or false. (29)
For indeed, things are seen manifested in a person within a dream by the power of the bodily constituents; likewise, worship the gods such as the ancestors and the Brahmins as well.
By these means you shall then be liberated from mental agitation; for indeed, against the afflictions caused by fate, fate alone is the protection.
Thus consoled by his ministers, who were experts in the Dharma, the king confessed that sin, beginning with the murder of his preceptor’s son.
Śakti, the eldest son of Vasiṣṭha, was indeed devoured by me; likewise, one hundred ministers minus one were devoured by that cruel man. (33)
Tormented by that sin, how indeed can I become well? Even a single act of killing a Brahmin is very difficult to overcome, even by fate.

But I, cruel as I am, did not avoid her in that manner. Having committed such a most dreadful deed, what worlds shall I go to? As a Rākṣasa, I shall bring an end to my own lineage with this very body. (35)
"Born indeed in the lineage of the Raghus, yet evil-minded and born of sin, I shall die here after having entered the fire. (36)
Having heard these words of Saudāsa, his ministers—those who knew the essence of the Vedas and were experts in all the scriptures—were greatly amazed. (37)
"Alas! This vast evil has been committed by us in every way; we do not know the expiation now, without Vasiṣṭha. (38)
Therefore, you must go this very day for the sake of this king, to where the venerable sage Vaśiṣṭha, the brahmin-seer, resides.
Having spoken thus, those ministers, accompanied by him and deeply distressed, went to the hermitage where the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, the brahmin, was staying.
There, the Lord consoled his distressed bride Adṛśyantī; but Adṛśyantī, seeing that man of cruel deeds before her, spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha with a voice trembling with fear: ||| 41 ||
Like Death himself with his fierce staff, this terrifying Rākṣasa approaches, brandishing a raised wooden club and filled with great pride.
O highly fortunate one, best among the knowers of all the Vedas, no one else on earth today is capable of warding that off except for you. (43)
"Save me, O Blessed One, from this terrible-looking evil! This Rākṣasa has surely come here with the intent to seize us both. (44)

Vasiṣṭha said: "Do not fear, daughter; you must not be afraid of the Rākṣasa in any way. This is not a Rākṣasa whose presence you perceive before you; this is the powerful King Kalmāṣapāda together with his ministers. (45)
He has arrived here in this forest region and come into my presence. Then, perceiving that best of kings approaching, the venerable and radiant seer Vasiṣṭha restrained him with the sound "Hum."
Then, having sprinkled him with water purified by mantras, he indeed liberated that best of kings from his state of being a rākṣasa.
Then, having regained consciousness and saluted with palms joined in reverence, the king spoke at that time to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
"O illustrious one, I am Saudāsa; O observer of noble vows, I am your slave. At this time, tell me what is desired by you; what may I do for you? (49)

Having heard those words of the king and having understood Viśvāmitra’s intention through the power of his asceticism, that best of the twice-born spoke thus to the king, who was likewise bowed down in humility.
"It is already known; go at the proper time, O King Kuśa, to Kuśasthalī, where near Mahākāla is the Liṅga that destroys bad dreams. (51)

It bestows royal prosperity, is divine, and increases one's sons and grandsons; it shatters thousands of sins of killing a Brahmin and destroys all evil. Merely by the sight of it, you shall become free from sin.
The terrible fear born of bad dreams will perish, there is no doubt; and the planets shall become favorable to you, O best of kings. (53)
Thus addressed once more by his high-souled preceptor Vasiṣṭha, O Goddess, he went quickly to the auspicious Mahākālavana. There he beheld that Liṅga, which destroys evil and bad dreams.
Then all bad dreams vanished and auspicious dreams appeared; the king, having become free from taint, regained his own station and went to Ayodhyā, where he then ruled the kingdom with joy.
From that time forward, this deity became renowned in the world by the name Susvapneśvara, the destroyer of all evil dreams. || 56 ||
Those who, having bathed in the auspicious waters of the Śiprā, behold the god Śiva as Svapneśvara on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days—their evil dreams originating from birth shall perish. (57)
That man who beholds with devotion the Lord Śiva as Svapneśvara is indeed worthy of worship at all times, both in this world and in the next. (58)
Whatever desire a person contemplates in his mind as being dear to him, he attains that very thing, even if it is difficult to obtain, by beholding the Lord in a good dream. (59)
Those who always behold the Lord Svapneśvara with constancy, O beloved, go to my abode after casting off their bodies.
O illustrious lady, even one who is devoid of devotion and devoid of ritual action, if he beholds [it] by chance, attains a most meritorious state that is accessible only to yogis.

And those embodied beings who worship with various flowers on the sacred festival days (parvan) are endowed with all their desires; possessed of prosperity, strength, and health, they become long-lived, virtuous in conduct, and pure.
And these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Kubera, Agni, and the others—attained a supreme and auspicious dream through the vision of the illustrious Svapneśvara.
This power of the god Svapneśvara, which destroys sins, has been told to you, O Goddess; now hear about the four Liṅgas.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Svapneśvara," in the Umā-Maheśvara dialogue within the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
